case_text:
A 15‐year‐old girl presented to the outpatient department with a primary complaint of umbilical discharge for 2 weeks. The discharge was whitish in color, continuous, and not foul‐smelling. She also reported localized umbilical pain for 3 weeks, which subsided following the onset of discharge. There was no associated fever, vomiting, altered bowel habits, gastrointestinal bleeding, or weight loss. She had no prior history of similar complaints, abdominal surgery, or significant medical treatment. Menstrual history was normal, and there was no history of tuberculosis contact.

On examination, the patient was clinically stable with normal vital signs. Local examination revealed a papillomatous growth at the umbilicus, consistent with an umbilical polyp (see Figure 1). There was also an active whitish umbilical discharge. The surrounding skin showed no erythema, induration, or signs of cellulitis. The abdomen was soft and non‐tender, with no palpable masses or organomegaly. Systemic examination was unremarkable.

case_text:
A 65-year-old man was referred for evaluation of suspected anorectal malignant melanoma after undergoing colonoscopy for hematochezia at a local clinic, revealing an elevated lesion immediately above the anal verge. Histopathological examination of biopsy specimens revealed malignant melanoma.

Repeat colonoscopy demonstrated a pigmented, elevated lesion measuring approximately 15 mm in diameter on the anterior wall of the lower rectum (Rb), proximal to the dentate line (Figure 1). Endoscopic ultrasonography showed no definite invasion of the muscularis propria, although focal thinning of the submucosal layer was suspected (Figure 2). Contrast-enhanced CT revealed no regional lymph node enlargement or distant metastases. Accordingly, the clinical diagnosis was anorectal malignant melanoma, stage cT1bN0M0.

Given the aggressive nature of AMM, abdominoperineal resection was initially considered. However, the patient wished to preserve anorectal function and avoid permanent stoma formation. After multidisciplinary discussion, a hybrid endoscopic-surgical approach combining ESD and transanal local excision was selected.

The procedure was performed under general anesthesia. Circumferential markings were placed around the lesion. On the oral side, markings were placed approximately 1 cm from the visible tumor margin to ensure adequate surgical margins. Following submucosal injection, a circumferential mucosal incision was created using an endoscopic electrosurgical knife (DualKnife; Olympus Medical Systems, Tokyo, Japan) (Figure 3). Trimming was performed on the oral and anal sides to establish a complete circumferential incision line (Figure 4). Subsequently, partial submucosal dissection was performed on the oral side to facilitate precise surgical resection.

After completion of the endoscopic phase, transanal full-thickness excision was performed from the anal side, including a portion of the internal anal sphincter. The specimen was removed en bloc, and the bowel wall defect was closed with interrupted 4-0 polydioxanone sutures (Figure 5). The postoperative course was uneventful, and the patient was discharged on postoperative day 24.

Histopathological examination confirmed anorectal malignant melanoma measuring 18 × 20 mm. The tumor had invaded beyond the submucosal layer and was classified as pT2. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for HMB-45 and S-100 proteins and negative for cytokeratin (AE1/AE3), chromogranin A, and synaptophysin. The Ki-67 labeling index was approximately 70%. Lymphatic invasion was absent (ly0), while venous invasion was observed (V1). Both the horizontal and vertical resection margins were negative (pHM0 and pVM0, respectively), indicating R0 resection (Figure 6).

Although additional radical surgery was recommended owing to venous invasion, the patient declined further treatment. The patient underwent regular surveillance, remaining free of local recurrence and distant metastasis 4 years postoperatively (Figure 7).

case_text:
A 32‐year‐old male, a laborer by profession, sustained a penetrating injury after a fall from a height of approximately 5 ft, following which an iron rod penetrated his left gluteal region. The injury occurred at approximately 10:00 AM. The patient was subsequently presented to the Emergency Department at 5:30 PM on the same day. At the time of presentation, the iron rod remained intact and in situ (Figure 1).

On initial clinical assessment, the patient was conscious, oriented, and vitally stable. His Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score was 15/15. Neurological examination revealed intact motor power and intact sensory power in both lower limbs. The anal sphincter tone was normal. Tetanus toxoid was administered in the triage.

case_text:
An 18‐year‐old male from a remote rural area of the Lower Shabelle region of Somalia, where access to healthcare was limited, was brought to the Emergency Department following multiple episodes of generalized tonic–clonic seizures. Following these episodes, he developed persistent postictal confusion and impaired consciousness without returning to his baseline mental status. His altered consciousness persisted for approximately 4 days before presentation. The available history did not establish continuous convulsive seizure activity throughout this period. He had experienced multiple seizure episodes during the preceding months but had not received regular antiseizure medication. There was no known history of chronic medical illness, head trauma, toxin exposure, or familial neurological disorders. A formal toxicology screen was not performed.

On examination, the patient was comatose, with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of ≤ 8. His pupils were equal and reactive to light, his vital signs were stable, and there were no signs of meningeal irritation or focal neurological deficits. Given the history of recurrent generalized tonic–clonic seizures and persistent impaired consciousness without recovery to baseline, suspected status epilepticus was considered, and emergency antiseizure treatment was initiated. Intravenous diazepam was administered, followed by a 1‐g loading dose of intravenous phenytoin. Despite treatment, the patient remained unconscious. He was intubated for airway protection and underwent general anesthesia because of concern for ongoing seizure activity and persistent failure to recover consciousness. Electroencephalography (EEG) was not performed; therefore, ongoing electrographic seizure activity could not be confirmed.

Initial laboratory investigations revealed severe hypocalcemia, with a total serum calcium concentration of 3.8 mg/dL, hypoalbuminemia (albumin, 1.8 g/dL), hyperphosphatemia (10.4 mg/dL), and hypomagnesemia (1.35 mg/dL). Arterial blood gas analysis performed during emergency management showed a pH of 7.33, a partial pressure of carbon dioxide (pCO2) of 33.1 mmHg, bicarbonate of 17.6 mmol/L, and oxygen saturation of 98.7%. Blood lactate was 1.7 mmol/L. Other reported electrolyte values included sodium, 144 mEq/L; potassium, 3.7 mEq/L; chloride, 104 mmol/L; and bicarbonate, 21 mmol/L. Using the conventional albumin‐correction formula, the estimated albumin‐corrected serum calcium concentration was approximately 5.56 mg/dL, indicating severe hypocalcemia despite adjustment for hypoalbuminemia. This estimate was calculated using the measured total calcium and albumin concentrations.

The blood glucose concentration at admission was 94 mg/dL. Renal function was preserved, with a serum creatinine concentration of 0.9 mg/dL and a blood urea concentration of 24 mg/dL. Inflammatory markers were elevated, with a C‐reactive protein (CRP) concentration of 140 mg/L and a white blood cell (WBC) count of 11.67 × 109/L.

Further biochemical investigations revealed a PTH concentration of 12 pg/mL (reference range, 15–65 pg/mL), together with severe hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia. This biochemical profile supported a diagnosis of hypoparathyroidism. The serum 25‐hydroxyvitamin D concentration was 57 ng/mL, renal function was preserved, and there was no history of neck surgery or radiation exposure. These findings supported hypoparathyroidism without an identified postsurgical cause. However, autoimmune investigations and genetic testing were not performed; therefore, the underlying etiology could not be definitively established. Blood cultures and serum procalcitonin testing were also not performed. Follow‐up laboratory investigations demonstrated improvement in the reported biochemical parameters and inflammatory markers following treatment. Admission and 1‐month follow‐up laboratory findings are summarized in Table 1.

Noncontrast computed tomography (CT) of the brain revealed bilateral, symmetrical calcifications involving the basal ganglia, thalami, dentate nuclei, and gray–white matter junction, consistent with secondary Fahr syndrome (Figure 1A–D). A chest radiograph demonstrated right‐sided pulmonary infiltrates consistent with aspiration pneumonia (Figure 2). The diagnosis of aspiration pneumonia was based on the clinical context of recurrent seizures and prolonged impaired consciousness, together with the radiological findings. Microbiological confirmation was unavailable because blood cultures and respiratory specimen cultures were not performed.

The patient received intravenous moxifloxacin (400 mg once daily) and metronidazole (500 mg three times daily) for suspected aspiration pneumonia. Intravenous calcium replacement was initiated, followed by oral calcium and magnesium supplementation. Following treatment, calcium levels improved, seizure activity ceased, and the patient demonstrated progressive neurological recovery, including restoration of consciousness. As his condition stabilized, levetiracetam was reduced to 500 mg twice daily and continued at discharge. He was discharged in stable condition on levetiracetam, oral calcium, and magnesium supplementation, with planned neurology and endocrinology follow‐up.

At follow‐up visits conducted 1, 6, and 12 months after discharge, the patient remained neurologically stable, with no reported recurrent seizures or other neurological symptoms. Serum calcium and PTH levels showed sustained improvement according to the follow‐up laboratory results. Levetiracetam was continued throughout the follow‐up period under neurological supervision. No additional hospitalizations or complications were reported.

case_text:
A 2‐year‐old male (weight: 11.8 kg, height: 87 cm both between the 15th and 50th percentiles; mid‐upper arm circumference (MUAC): 16.5 cm) presented to Pentecost Hospital Madina, with a one‐day history of frank hematuria after 2 weeks of intermittent cola‐colored urine, with lethargy, anorexia, and cough. The mother reported intermittent fever over the preceding month, during which she administered over‐the‐counter medications, including oral artemisinin‐based combination therapy (ACT; artemether–lumefantrine), paracetamol, and vitamin C. The antimalarial was given empirically at home, as an over‐the‐counter purchase, without laboratory confirmation of malaria; this preceded, and may plausibly have influenced, the negative peripheral blood film for malaria subsequently obtained on admission. The vitamin C was an oral over‐the‐counter preparation (ascorbic acid syrup), reportedly given several times daily during febrile episodes; however, the exact dose and frequency could not be independently verified. A neonatal G6PD screening had previously indicated no defect.

There was no known family history of G6PD deficiency, recurrent jaundice, hemolysis, prior transfusions, or episodic dark urine in first‐degree relatives. On direct questioning there was no exposure to primaquine, sulfonamides, nitrofurantoin, naphthalene, or fava beans. On examination, the child was acutely ill, severely pale, jaundiced, and in severe respiratory distress. Skin turgor was normal, there was no bipedal oedema, and capillary refill time was < 3seconds. Vital signs were: temperature 37.4 C, pulse 164 beats per minute, respiratory rate 47 cycles per minute, oxygen saturation (SpO2) 66% on room air. Chest auscultation revealed reduced air entry bilaterally with vesicular breath sounds. Cardiovascular and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Examination of the throat revealed mild tonsillar inflammation.

case_text:
A 32‐year‐old Hispanic woman, G5P4014, presented on postpartum Day 15 following a reported term repeat low‐transverse cesarean delivery with bilateral salpingectomy performed at an outside institution. According to the available records, the index cesarean delivery was scheduled and performed at 37 weeks and 2 days. The procedure was complicated by uterine atony resulting in postpartum hemorrhage requiring blood transfusion and the estimated blood loss was 2808 mL. The uterine closure technique was with #1 chromic in 1 layer and Surgicel powder application at the level of the lower uterine segment to ensure hemostasis. Intraoperative findings showed no abnormalities with normal uterus, normal ovaries and fallopian tubes bilaterally.

The patient had a body mass index of 33.2 kg/m2 and no known chronic medical comorbidities, including diabetes mellitus or chronic hypertension. Her antenatal course was reportedly uncomplicated aside from the postpartum hemorrhage occurring during cesarean delivery. She denied tobacco use, vaping, or nicotine exposure. The bilateral salpingectomy performed at the time of cesarean delivery was reported to be uncomplicated. Her initial postpartum recovery was reassuring, with expected lochia and no reported fever or excessive vaginal bleeding immediately following hospital discharge. She was both breastfeeding and formula feeding.

On postpartum Day 3, she presented to an outside emergency department because of persistent tenderness near her cesarean incision. She was discharged after symptomatic treatment with analgesics without additional imaging or intervention. In retrospect, this early postoperative pain may have represented the initial manifestation of evolving uterine incision dehiscence.

On postpartum Day 14, the patient developed fevers and chills with a reported maximum temperature of 101°F. Approximately 1 day later (postpartum Day 15), she experienced sudden heavy vaginal bleeding with passage of large clots accompanied by dizziness and worsening lower abdominal pain. Emergency medical services estimated approximately 500 mL of blood loss at home and documented profound hypotension (76/50 mmHg), consistent with hemorrhagic shock. Prehospital resuscitation included whole blood transfusion, intravenous crystalloid, tranexamic acid, calcium supplementation, antiemetics, and analgesia before transport to our institution.

On arrival, the patient appeared pale, lethargic, and ill appearing but remained oriented. Physical examination demonstrated active vaginal bleeding with large clots, uterine fundal tenderness, abdominal tenderness, and delayed capillary refill. Laboratory evaluation demonstrated hemoglobin of 7.9 g/dL and lactate of 3.0 mmol/L. Transabdominal ultrasound demonstrated a heterogeneous 4‐cm endometrial stripe without free intraperitoneal fluid, raising concern for retained intrauterine clot burden or retained products of conception. Given the patient's preceding fever, progressive abdominal pain, and hemodynamic instability, endometritis with secondary postpartum hemorrhage was initially considered the leading diagnosis.

case_text:
A 65-year-old woman with a history of frontal meningioma resection in 2007 presented with diffuse abdominal pain. Colonoscopy revealed a mid-rectal tubulovillous adenoma with low-grade dysplasia, measuring 45 × 30 × 20 mm on pelvic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), located 7 cm from the anal verge, with no mesorectal fat infiltration or lymphadenopathy (Fig. 1a and b). Thoracoabdominal computed tomography (CT) confirmed a 4 cm polypoid rectal tumor without peripheral infiltration. She had no risk factors for ischemic or thrombotic complications. After two failed endoscopic resection attempts, she was referred for TEM.

The lesion, located 7 cm from the anal verge on the posterior rectal wall, was resected en bloc via full-thickness excision using ultrasonic dissection. Dissection extended into the mesorectum, complicated by fibrosis from prior endoscopic attempts. The resulting 3 cm defect exposed mesorectal fat and was closed with clips. Operative time was 79 min with no blood loss. The 52 × 46 × 12 mm specimen was villous on gross examination (Fig. 1c). Histopathology revealed a traditional serrated adenoma with high-grade dysplasia and focal positive margins. Prophylactic metronidazole and perioperative intravenous antibiotic prophylaxis were administered. No mesorectal breach was visible post-procedure.

On postoperative day 2, the patient developed fever (38.2°C), tachycardia, and hypotension. Lab tests revealed elevated CRP (300 mg/L), leukopenia (0.90 G/L), and lactate (3.7 mmol/L). CT showed a rectal wound with retroperitoneal and peritoneal gas, pneumoperitoneum, and pneumomediastinum (Fig. 2). Emergency laparoscopy found generalized peritonitis without visible perforation. Peritoneal lavage and a diverting colostomy were performed. Antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam and amikacin) were started, with Escherichia (E.Coli) isolated. Between days 2–6, her condition worsened: multiorgan failure (respiratory distress, renal failure), persistent fever (38.8°C), and subcutaneous inflammation. On day 6, leukocytosis (26 G/L) and procalcitonin (14.10 μg/L) were noted. A day 5 CT showed no contrast extravasation or vascular defect (Fig. 3).

Due to ongoing deterioration, a second laparotomy on day 6 revealed extensive mesorectal ischemia and necrosis. A low Hartmann procedure with total mesorectal excision was performed. Histopathology confirmed ischemic and suppurative necrosis of the mesorectum, recent arterial thrombosis, and no residual tumor (Fig. 4a). The distal margin showed ulcerated mucosa with necrotic perirectal fat, while the epithelium was sub-atrophic but well-differentiated (Fig. 4b and c).

Post-surgery, the patient improved with empirical meropenem (2 weeks) and fluconazole (3 weeks). Inflammatory symptoms resolved that vasopressors were weaned, and bowel function returned. She was discharged but experienced prolonged fatigue. A year later, a CT scan showed a normal abdomen. Colonic continuity was restored via coloanal anastomosis with a protective ileostomy, which was closed five months later without complications. Follow-up details are summarized in Table 1.

Post-surgery, the patient improved with empirical meropenem (2 weeks) and fluconazole (3 weeks).

A year later, a CT scan showed a normal abdomen.
Colonic continuity was restored via coloanal anastomosis with a protective ileostomy, which was closed five months later without complications.

title: Mesorectal ischemic necrosis after transanal endoscopic microsurgery: a diagnostic challenge

case_text:
A 39‐year‐old male farmer, living in Pagouda (a village 53 km from Kara) with no history of disease presented for consultation regarding a perineal tumor that had been progressing for 5 years. At first, there were small, isolated condylomatous lesions that gradually merged and grew larger. Over the past 2 years, they began to develop new growths and bleed in places. In addition to these perineal lesions, the patient reported that a mass had appeared in the right inguinal region about a year ago. Over the course of the 5‐year progression, the patient reported having used traditional treatments for several months, administered locally as poultices or injected directly into the lesions through incisions. He had also visited several local health clinics in his area, where he underwent examinations and was treated with antibiotics, but without success.

He finally sought care at the dermatology department of Kara University Hospital due to foul‐smelling discharge, discomfort, and pain caused by the tumor during walking and bowel movements.

On clinical examination, the body mass index was 17.2 kg/m2. The patient’s general condition was impaired, with a reported weight loss of approximately 7 kg over the past 12 months, significant asthenia, and pallor of the conjunctiva. The perineal region was the site of multiple cauliflower‐like tumors, with areas of necrosis in some places and ulcerated fungating lesions that bled upon contact. At the margins of these lesions, numerous smaller condylomatous lesions were noted (Figure 1). These lesions covered an area of approximately 15 cm × 12 cm on either side of the anus. In the right inguinal region, a tumor mass was noted with ulcerated and fungating lesions on its surface (Figure 2). These lesions were very painful, malodorous, and interfered with walking and daily activities. Based on these clinical signs, we considered a clinical diagnosis of BLT for the large perineal tumor and cutaneous carcinoma for the ulcerated areas. Regarding the inguinal lesions, we suspected cutaneous metastases from the carcinoma that had developed from the large perineal tumor.

The complete blood count revealed hypochromic microcytic anemia (Hb: 7 g/dL), and the HIV serology test was negative. Prior to this negative test result, the patient had taken several HIV tests, all of which were negative; the most recent one had been 6 months ago. HPV testing and genotyping were not performed because they are not available in our city and the patient could not afford it.

Liver and kidney function tests were normal. Histological examination of a biopsy sample from one of the ulcerations on the large tumor that we clinically diagnosed as a BLT showed a well‐differentiated squamous proliferation, characterized by acanthotic squamous epithelium with exophytic papillary projections topped by hyperkeratosis and parakeratosis. The squamous cells had an eosinophilic cytoplasm enclosing an enlarged, hyperchromatic nucleus with a prominent nucleolus. Distinguishing this from a conventional, well‐differentiated squamous cell carcinoma can be difficult; however, the latter is generally less exophytic, with an infiltrating growth pattern, at least focally. In our case, the proliferation was clearly exophytic, with no apparent infiltration; this is more consistent with a diagnosis of verrucous carcinoma (Figure 3). The histology of the lesion excised from the inguinal mass revealed cellular atypia identical to that found in the perineal tumor, namely, a verrucous carcinoma (Figure 4). We therefore concluded that this was a verrucous carcinoma arising from a perineal tumor clinically diagnosed as BLT, with regional cutaneous metastases in the groin.

We requested a staging workup, specifically a thoraco‐abdominal‐pelvic CT scan, which the patient did not undergo due to lack of financial resources. We requested a surgical evaluation, which determined that the tumor was inoperable. We then arranged for an oncology consultation for this patient. Because the patient lacked the financial means, he was unable to see the nearest oncologist, who is 443 km from his home. The patient was prescribed pain medication and a topical antiseptic while awaiting the CT scan and the oncology consultation, which will take place as soon as his financial situation allows. To date, we have lost track of the patient. He did not attend his appointment with the oncologist and has not returned to our department either.

case_text:
The pregnant woman had been diagnosed with MMIHS during the first pregnancy trimester following genetic counselling, prompted by a family history of gastrointestinal and urinary tract motility disorders. Genetic testing identified a heterozygous mutation in the ATCG2 gene (MMIHS type 5) with an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern, considered pathogenic and disease-causing.

The patient’s medical history was notable for chronic (sub)ileus, intestinal malrotation, recurrent urinary tract infections and chronic constipation since early childhood, necessitating between 2009 and 2013 five laparotomies with procedures such as colopexy, colectomy and ileo-sigmoidostomy.

As mentioned at the outset, there was a positive family history of gastrointestinal and urinary motility disorders, with variable severity among affected relatives. It was also noted that the patient’s mother, also affected by the condition, had delivered three children, both spontaneously and by caesarean section, and had experienced “manageable atonic bleedings”.

Prenatal ultrasound exams performed during patient’s current pregnancy also identified a moderately enlarged fetal stomach and bladder, with normal amniotic fluid volume, raising suspicion of fetal MMIHS (Figure 1). Invasive diagnostics to confirm the diagnosis were offered but declined.

At prenatal counselling for delivery, the woman expressed a strong preference for vaginal delivery, and in absence of clear contraindications, it was agreed to attempt a trial of labor (vaginal delivery), and as spontaneous onset of labor didn’t occur, medical induction of labor was performed at 41+4 weeks of gestation. Pharmacological induction with oral misoprostol and mechanical induction using a double-balloon catheter were unsuccessful, necessitating a secondary caesarean section (Robson Group 2). A uterine myopathy potentially related to MMIHS was therefore suspected, and given the risk of uterine atony in this condition, interdisciplinary preparations were made for potential significant hemorrhage. Despite prophylactic administration of carbetocin, pronounced uterine atony occurred intraoperatively and was initially managed with additional uterotonics (sulprostone), a B-Lynch suture and a Celox™ PPH tamponade. The blood loss amounted to 1,900 mL.

Two hours postoperatively recurrent vaginal bleeding was observed necessitating surgical re-exploration. Intraoperative findings revealed recurrent massive postpartum hemorrhage due to uterine atony. Despite escalating measures, (suction curettage with replacement of Celox™ PPH tamponade, re-laparatomy with uterine exploration and renewed B-Lynch suture, insertion of a Bakri balloon, insertion of additional tamponades, aortic compression), the persistent bleeding due to severe uterine atony could only be controlled finally by hysterectomy.

The postoperative course was marked by significant blood loss totaling 9,900 mL. The patient required extensive transfusion support including 14 units of erythrocyte concentrates (EC), 12 units of fresh frozen plasma, 3 units of thrombocyte concentrates, 9 g of fibrinogen, 3,500 IU of prothrombin complex concentrate. The patient was transferred to the intensive care unit intubated, mechanically ventilated and receiving norepinephrine support. The patient recovered rapidly and was transferred back to the maternity ward on the first day after surgery. As anemia persisted, a further blood transfusion of two EC was necessary. The remainder of her postoperative and postpartum course was uneventful, and the patient was discharged to outpatient care on the 5th postoperative day.

A 34‐year‐old male presented to our Level 1 trauma center following a motorcycle accident with severe injuries to the head, spine, abdomen, pelvis and extremities. He sustained a Young–Burgess APC III injury with right‐sided high superior and inferior pubic ramus fractures, complete disruption of the pubic symphysis, and complete disruption of the bilateral SI joints (AO/OTA 61C3.1). This was an open injury with a large perineal wound communicating directly with the ramus fractures and symphyseal disruption. An associated bowel rupture was present resulting in fecal contamination of the perineal wound. Initial computed tomography (CT) of the spine revealed atlantooccipital dislocation and flexion‐distraction injury at T4/5.

Upon arrival, the patient was intubated and taken emergently to the OR in a multidisciplinary approach. He was positioned supine, and a midline laparotomy was performed and ultimately resulted in a diverting colostomy, followed by closure. Ultimately, the pelvis was stabilized with an anterior external fixator utilizing supra‐acetabular pins linked with a curved carbon fiber rod. Posterior stabilization was attained with a transacroiliac 7.5‐mm screw at the S2 level. The injury was reduced with the help of an open anterior reduction. Given the perineal contamination, a spanning internal fixation plate posed too high an infection risk and was not placed.

The patient returned to the OR 2 days later with the neurosurgery team for PSF. He was successfully positioned from a supine to a prone position onto an open‐frame Jackson table with the addition of extra padding to thigh and hip pads, which were strategically positioned to straddle the EF pins. PSF was performed from the occiput to C4, and from T3 to T6 by the neurosurgical team. Radiographs taken immediately after PSF demonstrated 7.8 mm of interval symphyseal widening (Figure 3A), and the patient tolerated the procedure without loss of fixation or hemodynamic instability. At 6 weeks postoperatively, the EF was removed, and final radiographs demonstrated an additional 2.1 mm of symphyseal widening. No positioning‐related complications, pin‐site problems, pressure injuries, or neurovascular complications were observed throughout the course of this patient’s care.

A 58‐year‐old male presented after a motorcycle accident with multiple life‐threatening injuries to the head, spine, abdomen, pelvis, and multiple extremities that resulted in hemorrhagic shock and necessitated emergent stabilization. He was initially seen at an outside facility where he was intubated and transfused with blood products prior to transfer to our Level 1 trauma center for further resuscitation and definitive management.

He sustained a Young–Burgess APC III injury with anterior and posterior pelvic ring disruption along with left‐sided Denis zones 1–3 sacral fractures (AO/OTA 61C3.2). CT of the lumbar spine demonstrated an unstable L6 vertebral body fracture extending into the left pedicle facet and lamina. The abdomen contained bladder rupture with hemoperitoneum, retroperitoneal hematoma, and a traumatic abdominal wall hernia. The right upper extremity had been traumatically amputated at the level of the elbow joint, and the left upper extremity consisted of open metacarpal shaft fractures of the second and third digits.

Upon arrival to our trauma bay, the patient was taken emergently to the OR in a multidisciplinary approach. He was positioned supine, and a midline laparotomy was performed, resulting in evacuation of the hemoperitoneum and retroperitoneal hematoma. The ruptured bladder and traumatic abdominal wall hernia were also repaired. The pelvis was stabilized provisionally with anterior EF using supra‐acetabular pins.

The patient returned to the OR 2 days later with the neurosurgery team for PSF. The patient was successfully flipped from supine to prone position onto an open‐frame Jackson surgical table. Transverse chest rolls were used, a Mayfield head holder was utilized to hold the head in a neutral position, the arms were tucked at the patient′s sides, and the lower extremities elevated on padding. Additional padding was used to support the ex‐fix pins. As in the prior case, positioning was performed in a combined effort by the neurosurgery, orthopedic, and anesthesiology teams, as well as the OR staff. Spinopelvic fixation was performed from L4 to the ilium. The patient tolerated the procedure without complications. Postoperative radiographs did not show significant changes in apparent stability of the pelvis, with interval symphyseal widening of 8 mm (Figure 3B).

Given the provisional nature of the anterior EF placement, and given that this patient resided out of state and would need to establish follow‐up at an outside facility, the decision was made to return to the OR 2 days later for exam under anesthesia to confirm the overall stability of the pelvis. After less than 10 mm of symphyseal widening following removal of the EF rod, pelvic stability was confirmed. Manual manipulation of the anterior pelvis was performed to completely reduce the symphyseal disruption, the pins were secured to the rod with rod‐to‐pin combination clamps to hold this position, and the pelvis was found to be fully stable to stress. Anterior symphyseal plating was deemed to be high risk for infection given the patient′s bladder rupture, and therefore anterior EF was the definitive fixation modality. Radiographs confirmed decreased interpubic distance following the reduction (Figure 3B). The patient followed up at an outside facility for EF removal following discharge. No positioning‐related complications, pin‐site problems, pressure injuries, or neurovascular complications were observed during our care of this patient.

case_text:
A 30-year-old woman with a history of HT in infancy presented to the HT clinic and was found to have RV apical hypertrophy on annual surveillance transthoracic echocardiography (TTE). She was asymptomatic, with a blood pressure of 134/75 mmHg and otherwise normal vital signs. Continued TTE surveillance was recommended.

She underwent heart transplantation at 5 weeks old for hypoplastic left heart syndrome. Her course was complicated by post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (gastric at age two, pulmonary at age seven), hypertension treated with carvedilol, and progressive chronic kidney disease secondary to calcineurin inhibitor (CNI) toxicity. Allograft function remained stable through her 20s managed with tacrolimus monotherapy (goal trough 5–7 ng/mL). She was intolerant of mycophenolate derivatives and discontinued sirolimus in her late twenties due to renal dysfunction.

Sixteen months later, contrast-enhanced TTE revealed worsening RV apical hypertrophy with RV dilation, new asymmetric septal LV hypertrophy (LVH), stable LV function, and mildly decreased RV systolic function (Video 1 and Video 2). The interventricular septum measured 14.2 mm, the LV posterior wall measured 11.2 mm, the RV septal wall measured 10.1 mm, and the RV lateral wall measured 13.3 mm (Figure 1). There were no signs of outflow tract obstruction. The LV outflow tract peak gradient was 5 mmHg and the RV outflow tract peak gradient was 1.44 mmHg. The patient remained asymptomatic.

Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (cMRI) confirmed asymmetric distal septal hypertrophy (septum 15 mm, LV lateral wall 8 mm) extending into the RV apex (22 mm), LV ejection fraction 63%, RV ejection fraction 62%, and no systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve (Video 3). Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) demonstrated patchy fibrosis involving the basal to apical anteroseptum and inferoseptum, basal-to-mid lateral wall, and RV apex, comprising approximately 30% of myocardial mass (Figure 2). These findings supported a diagnosis of RV apical variant HCM with asymmetric LV septal involvement.

Holter monitoring showed rare PVCs without sustained tachyarrhythmias or heart block. As she remained asymptomatic without left or right ventricular outflow tract obstruction, her carvedilol dose was not increased, and calcium channel blocker was not initiated. She received an S-ICD for primary prevention of sudden cardiac death (SCD) given the extensive LGE burden.

She remains asymptomatic 16 months after ICD placement, and device interrogations have revealed no arrhythmias.

case_text: The decedent was found in his secured apartment which provided a presumptive identification. There were moderate decomposition changes with insect activity and no signs of trauma. Because of the decomposition changes affecting the face, the use of visual comparison to antemortem photographs was deemed a nonviable method for positive identification. Given the need for a timely identification to provide closure to the family, and the advanced state of decomposition, fingerprint and DNA analysis were deemed unlikely to yield results within an appropriate timeframe. With the presumptive identification and unreliable primary identifiers, identification was pursued through the following routes. The name of the decedent was inscribed within the upper denture (Figure 1), and this was deemed a positive match. Next, there was a unique tattoo depicting a tiger on the extensor surface of the left upper arm (Figure 2). The shape, color, and location were all verified via antemortem photography, yielding a positive match. Finally, medical record examination revealed documentation of the surgical procedure implanting a cerebral artery aneurysm coil. The presence of this coil was confirmed upon autopsy in the LODOX images (Figure 3) and compared with an antemortem imaging study. Although cerebral artery aneurysm coils may be nonspecific, it was used as a confirmatory finding in combination with the unique tattoo and upper denture. This yielded a positive scientific identification.

A 68‐year‐old man, a current smoker (40 pack‐years) with chronic alcohol use (CAGE 3/4, AUDIT 9), presented with acute‐on‐chronic dyspnea (mMRC Grade I progressing to IV over 2 years, with rapid worsening over 3 days), productive cough with whitish sputum, and fever with chills. There was no hemoptysis, weight loss, or prior tuberculosis. Examination showed poor oral hygiene, tachycardia (110/min), hypoxia (SpO2 75% on room air), and right infrascapular inspiratory crepitus with expiratory wheeze. He was admitted with acute infective exacerbation of COPD and Type 1 respiratory failure and was started on oxygen at 3 L/min via nasal prongs (later tapered), nebulized bronchodilators, corticosteroids, and empirical ceftriaxone and azithromycin.

Laboratory workup showed elevated inflammatory markers (CRP 173.2 mg/L, neutrophils 76.3%) and mild thrombocytopenia (platelets 81,000/μL); sputum AFB, culture, GeneXpert, and fungal stains were negative. HRCT and contrast‐enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen showed active infection superimposed on chronic lung damage, with right‐predominant cavitary lesions, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and features of pulmonary hypertension (Figure 1A,B).

Bronchoscopy revealed a right lower lobe endobronchial mass causing partial obstruction (Figure 2A). Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) GeneXpert showed very low MTB detection with indeterminate rifampicin resistance. Given the radiological and microbiological picture, empirical anti‐tubercular therapy (ATT) (HRZE) was initiated, and the patient was discharged against medical advice because of financial constraints, with bronchoscopic biopsy results pending.

Biopsy showed suppurative, necrotic inflammation with sulfur granules of filamentous organisms and no malignant cells (Figure 2B). PAS staining highlighted the filamentous organisms, confirming pulmonary actinomycosis (Figure 2C).

The patient was started on amoxicillin‐clavulanate (1 g twice daily) alongside anti‐tubercular therapy (2HRZE/4HR). He became asymptomatic, with resolution of cough by 4 weeks. Repeat CT chest at 3 months showed marked resolution of the extensive right middle and lower lobe consolidation, indicating a favourable treatment response (Figure 1C,D), although the severe cystic bronchiectasis and architectural distortion remained unchanged, reflecting irreversible parenchymal destruction. At the time of publication, he is in the fourth month of treatment (HRZE intensive phase completed, HR continuation phase ongoing), with both amoxicillin‐clavulanate and ATT planned for 6 months in total.

case_text:
A 39-year-old woman with a history of psychiatric illness was referred to our neurology clinic with a one-year history of persistent left upper limb tremor and newly developed gait disturbance that had started approximately one week prior to presentation. She had been receiving treatment with haloperidol and citalopram. Based on the clinical suspicion of drug-induced tremor, haloperidol was gradually tapered and eventually discontinued.

Due to the lack of clinical improvement after discontinuation of haloperidol and the recent onset of gait disturbance, the patient was referred to a neurologist.

Neurological examination revealed left-sided limb ataxia, gait ataxia, generalized hyperreflexia, and Holmes tremor. A tremor was noted in the left upper limb, characterized by a low-frequency, (<5 Hz) high-amplitude rest tremor involving both distal and proximal segments that worsened when the arms were outstretched and increased more in a wing-beating position (rest < postural < wing-beating). This tremor was accompanied by intention tremor. There was no rigidity or bradykinesia and no dystonic posturing, null point, or sensory trick was observed on examination.

MRI demonstrated demyelinating lesions consistent with MS. Brain MRI showed multiple typical MS lesion in periventricular lesions with Dawson’s fingers, posterior fossa (brainstem and cerebellum), cortical/juxtacortical, and cervical cord (Figure 1). The MS diagnosis was confirmed with 2024 McDonald criteria based on typical clinical and paraclinical findings. In patients with typical clinical presentations, like our patient (cerebellar symptoms and signs), the presence of typical lesions in four anatomical locations is sufficient to diagnose MS (Table 1).

The patient was treated with intravenous methylprednisolone (IVMP) (1 g/day for 5 days), followed by ocrelizumab (every six months) as disease-modifying therapy (DMT). Primidone was prescribed for tremor management. She was followed for six months after the initiation of treatment, during which she showed marked clinical improvement. Rest tremor markedly improved, and action tremor improved significantly (Video 1). Her ataxia also improved substantially. There was no evidence of clinical and MRI activity and improvement of tremor continued after 2 years follow up (Video 2). The timeline is shown in Table 2.

case_text:
A 76‐year‐old woman presented with a 1‐week history of gross hematuria, accompanied by dizziness but no lower urinary tract symptoms. Her medical history included hypertension, glaucoma, diabetes mellitus, left breast cancer, cerebral infarction, intracranial and aortic aneurysms, and schizophrenia. She had no history of radiotherapy.

On presentation, her vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination revealed conjunctival pallor. Ultrasonography demonstrated an intravesical hyperechoic mass, suggestive of blood clot (Figure 1A). Laboratory data were notable for severe anemia (hemoglobin, 4.7 g/dL), hyponatremia (sodium, 120 mEq/L), and class II urine cytology. Computed tomography without contrast showed several intravesical tumors (Figure 1B) and a 10.8‐cm aortic aneurysm without endo‐leak. No apparent source of bleeding other than the tumors was identified. Furthermore, CT revealed neither another potential primary tumor site nor evidence of direct invasion from an adjacent tumor. MRI was not performed in this case because the patient was unable to follow commands or remain still during the examination.

A urinary catheter was placed, and blood transfusion was initiated upon admission. On hospital days 2 and 3, the hemoglobin level increased to 6.1 and 6.0 g/dL, respectively, but subsequently decreased to 4.9 g/dL on day 6. On hospital day 7, transurethral electrocoagulation and transurethral resection of a bladder tumor (TURBT) were performed. Intraoperatively, visualization was markedly impaired due to a large volume of intravesical clots. Following evacuation of the clots using an Ellik evacuator, erythematous and edematous mucosal changes with continuous oozing were identified at the trigone (Figure 2). The affected area was resected and sent for histopathological examination.

case_text:
A 7‐year‐old boy was presented to our emergency department with a complaint of a sudden episode of loss of consciousness of about 2 min, which was not associated with abnormal body movements, upturning of eyes, frothing from mouth, or urinary or fecal incontinence. He regained consciousness spontaneously and had no post‐ictal confusion, tongue bite, or focal neurologic deficit. He also had an episode of vomiting. For the preceding 3–4 days, he had intermittent low‐grade fever without chills, rigors, or diurnal variation along with weakness and reduced appetite. His mother reported that he had been excessively fatigable with a progressive decline in appetite for the past 6 months and playing less than his peers. There was no history of bleeding from any site, jaundice, bone pain, or recent drug or toxin exposure.

Nine months earlier, the child had been evaluated for an upper respiratory tract infection at a different center where pancytopenia was discovered. Bone marrow examination and subsequent whole exome sequencing during that time had established a diagnosis of Fanconi Anemia. Following the diagnosis, the family didn't attend any follow up sessions and the child didn't receive any hematological monitoring. The present episode was his first contact with the medical services after the diagnosis. He was born at term by spontaneous vaginal delivery after an uneventful antenatal and postnatal period. He was second in birth‐order and was the offspring of a marriage reported by family as non‐consanguineous. Developmental milestones were age‐appropriate and immunization was complete for age. There was no family history of anemia, bleeding disorder, congenital malformation, malignancy or childhood death.

On arrival to our center, the child was ill‐looking but conscious, alert and oriented, with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15/15. He was thin built and visibly short for his age, extremely pale with marked conjunctival and palmar pallor and had signs of mild dehydration. There was no icterus, cyanosis, clubbing, pedal edema or generalized lymphadenopathy, and no petechiae, purpura or ecchymoses. The pulse rate was 142 beats/min, regular in rhythm but weak in volume; respiratory rate and peripheral oxygen saturation on room air were within normal limits. Axillary temperature was 99.4°F. His height of 99 cm and weight of 13.6 kg were both below −3 Standard Deviations for age and sex, with a body mass index (BMI) of 13.9 kg/m2 and a mid‐upper arm circumference of 13 cm indicating undernutrition and a head circumference of 47 cm indicating microcephaly.

Targeted examination for physical stigmata of inherited bone marrow failure revealed several characteristic findings. The face was triangular with small almond‐shaped palpebral fissures. Multiple hypopigmented macules were present over the anterior chest wall, both shoulders and the upper abdomen as shown in Figure 1. The right thumb was absent with an absent thenar eminence and four digits on the right hand, whereas both forearms appeared normally formed as shown in Figure 2. There was bilateral pes planus as shown in Figure 3. External ears, palate and genitalia were normal on inspection. Respiratory examination was normal. Cardiovascular examination demonstrated normal heart sounds with no murmur. The abdomen was soft, non‐tender and non‐distended, with normal bowel sounds and no hepatosplenomegaly. Neurologic examination was unremarkable with normal tone, power and reflexes in all four limbs and no meningeal signs. Perianal examination showed an acute fissure in ano.

case_text:
A 68-year-old man with severe CD involving the cecum, ascending colon, and transverse colon at diagnosis had been treated sequentially with sulfasalazine, mesalamine, and adalimumab before transitioning to infliximab plus methotrexate 25 mg weekly. He had prior cytomegalovirus (CMV) colitis treated with ganciclovir and traveled annually to Arizona, California, and Mexico.

He developed fatigue, drenching night sweats, low-grade fever, and a 15-pound weight loss. A computed tomography (CT) urogram for an elevated prostate-specific antigen had incidentally shown pulmonary nodules up to 1.1 cm. Positron emission tomography-CT (PET-CT) demonstrated markedly avid mediastinal, left hilar, and right supraclavicular lymphadenopathy (Figure 1). QuantiFERON-TB Gold and HIV testing were negative. Endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspiration revealed caseating calcified granulomas. Coccidioidal IgG and complement fixation (CF) antibodies were positive (CF titer 1:32), and fungal and acid-fast bacilli cultures were negative, establishing disseminated coccidioidomycosis.

Fluconazole was started at 400 mg daily. At Infectious Disease follow-up, he reported a new headache; brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was unremarkable, but he declined lumbar puncture (LP). Given the risk of progressive dissemination, infliximab was discontinued, and fluconazole was increased to 800 mg daily. His headache resolved, he again declined LP, and CF titers became undetectable (Figure 2). Colonoscopy showed moderate-to-severe active CD of the descending colon, sigmoid colon, and rectum (CMV negative), and vedolizumab was started for its gut-selective mechanism. Because of pruritus, dry skin, and rash, fluconazole was tapered to 200 mg daily over 14 months.

Two months after this reduction (16 months after initial presentation), he presented with worsening severe headaches. He was afebrile, and head CT was unremarkable. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) showed 181 cells/μL (65% neutrophils, 31% lymphocytes, <1% eosinophils), glucose 55 mg/dL, and protein 641 mg/dL. CSF coccidioidal serologies were negative. CSF West Nile virus (WNV) IgG was reactive (index 2.05), whereas CSF WNV IgM was 0.90 (equivocal). CSF Coccidioides antigen, CSF β-D-glucan, and WNV plaque reduction neutralization testing were not performed. Empiric antibiotics were discontinued once bacterial meningitis was considered unlikely, and probable coccidioidal meningitis was diagnosed. Fluconazole was increased to 800 mg daily, and vedolizumab was continued after multidisciplinary discussion. He improved clinically and serologically, and fluconazole was reduced to 400 mg daily as lifelong suppression, which he tolerates well (Figure 2).

case_text: A woman in her 70s residing in a nursing home presented with recurrent right upper quadrant pain and nausea. She had a history of left invasive ductal breast carcinoma treated 10 years earlier with breast-conserving surgery, radiotherapy, and 5 years of adjuvant anastrozole. Examination and laboratory tests, including inflammatory markers and liver function tests, were unremarkable. Ultrasound demonstrated multiple gallstones without acute cholecystitis (Fig. 1), while computed tomography (CT) abdomen/pelvis confirmed cholelithiasis without biliary obstruction, mass, or lymphadenopathy (Fig. 2). She underwent uncomplicated elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy for symptomatic cholelithiasis.

case_text:
The patient is a 51‐year‐old Chinese male, with multiple drug allergies, who has a past medical history of G6PD deficiency and iron deficiency anaemia and associated melena, for which esophagogastroduodenoscopy and colonoscopy performed was normal. He is also a chronic hepatitis B carrier for which he undergoes regular surveillance hepatobiliary US scans to monitor for liver cirrhosis.

During his most recent surveillance hepatobiliary US, an incidental non‐specific hypoechoic focus was noted in the spleen. As such, a CT scan of his abdomen and pelvis was performed, which showed a 1.8 cm large ill‐defined splenic soft tissue nodule. This splenic nodule was noted retrospectively on prior CT scan performed 12 months earlier (which was completed as part of his workup for iron deficiency anaemia and associated melena), where the lesion was smaller at 0.7 cm. Given the size increase over a year, the radiological report suggested exclusion of a malignant process.

He subsequently underwent a laparoscopic splenectomy. The intraoperative findings were that of a 1.8 cm splenic lesion, with no other gross lesions seen. The patient′s postoperative recovery was uneventful and he was discharged on postoperative Day 4.

The splenectomy specimen was sent to our laboratory for histological analysis. On macroscopic examination, the specimen consisted of a spleen weighing 83 g and measuring 10.8 cm × 6.5 cm × 5.2 cm. The visceral surface of the spleen, near the splenic notch, showed a firm exophytic nodular lesion. Cut sections revealed a firm, fairly well‐circumscribed, tan to reddish nodular lesion with a central greyish stellate fibrous area, which measured 2.7 cm × 2.6 cm × 2.3 cm (Figure 1). The rest of the splenic parenchyma appeared unremarkable. The entire splenic lesion was submitted for histological evaluation.

On microscopic examination, the lesion was well‐circumscribed and nonencapsulated. It was composed of numerous round to convoluted and coalescing angiomatoid nodules with intervening fibrosclerotic stroma (Figure 1). These angiomatoid nodules contained a mixture of branching, dilated and slit‐like vessels which were lined by small bland uniform endothelial cells with no evidence of cytologic atypia or multilayering. There were numerous erythrocytes within and around these vessels. The fibrosclerotic stroma contained a mixture of inflammatory cells including lymphocytes, plasma cells, eosinophils and hemosiderin‐laden macrophages.

Immunohistochemical staining highlighted three distinct vascular populations within these angiomatoid nodules: capillaries expressing CD34 and CD31 but lacking CD8, sinusoidal channels that are CD8 and CD31 positive but CD34 negative and small venous structures that demonstrate CD31 positivity alone, without expression of CD34 or CD8 (Figure 2). CD8 also highlighted scattered T cells within the angiomatoid nodules. SMA highlighted myofibroblasts within the angiomatoid nodules. CD68 highlighted scattered macrophages within the angiomatoid nodules and fibrosclerotic stroma. These findings support the diagnosis of SANT of the spleen.

The lesion was negative for CD21 (providing no support for a follicular dendritic cell sarcoma [FDCS]), MNF116 (providing no support for a metastatic carcinoma), HHV8 (providing no support for Kaposi sarcoma), ALK (providing no support for inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour [IMT]) and SOX10 (providing no support for metastatic melanoma). The lesion was negative for EBER by in‐situ hybridisation (providing no support for EBV‐positive inflammatory FDCS). The background spleen was normal.

title: Case of Sclerosing Angiomatoid Nodular Transformation (SANT) in a G6PD Patient: Discussion of Histological Differential Diagnosis

case_text:
A 23-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of worsening intermittent claudication in her right lower extremity. Her previous physician noted an absence of peripheral pulses distal to the right popliteal artery and a decreased ABI, prompting a referral to our institution.

Physical examination confirmed the absence of arterial pulses distal to the right popliteal artery. A treadmill test (12% incline, 3.2 km/hr) revealed a PFWD of 80 meters and a MWD of 138 meters. The initial ABI was 0.72 on the right and 1.02 on the left. SPP on the dorsal and plantar surfaces was 46/36 mmHg on the right and 52/69 mmHg on the left.

Contrast-enhanced CT showed a cystic lesion measuring approximately 1.0 × 5.0 cm along the right popliteal artery, causing arterial occlusion and the formation of collateral circulation (Fig. 1A). No anatomical abnormalities of the gastrocnemius muscle were observed. T2-weighted MRI revealed a multilocular cyst with high signal intensity in the right popliteal fossa (Fig. 1B). Based on these findings, we diagnosed the patient with ACD of the right popliteal artery.

Due to the exacerbation of her symptoms and the complete occlusion of the popliteal artery, the patient opted for surgical revascularization involving complete arterial resection rather than simple cystotomy to minimize the risk of recurrence. The patient was initially placed in the supine position to harvest the great saphenous vein from the left thigh. After repositioning her to the prone position, we approached the popliteal artery via a posterior incision. A 5-cm cystic dilation was identified, adhering to the surrounding tissues. During meticulous dissection, a portion of the cyst wall ruptured, releasing a clear, gelatinous fluid. The cyst was found to branch and extend toward the knee joint capsule, and the popliteal artery was entirely occluded by the lesion. A direct communication with the knee joint or an association with a specific articular branch, such as the middle genicular artery, could not be definitively identified intraoperatively.

We resected the affected artery with healthy margins (more than 1 cm from the cyst) and ligated and divided the branch extension at the edge of the joint capsule. Although a minimal amount of macroscopic cystic tissue extending deep into the joint space was left behind to avoid iatrogenic joint capsule injury, the cystic stalk was definitively ligated to completely interrupt the communication between the cyst and the knee joint. Arterial reconstruction was performed using an autogenous vein graft (Fig. 2). Histopathological examination revealed a multilocular cyst located within the adventitia external to the external elastic lamina, with no communication to the vascular lumen, consistent with ACD (Fig. 3).

The patient had an uneventful postoperative recovery. One month after surgery, her right ABI improved to 1.02, and the SPP increased to 66/56 mmHg (dorsum/sole). The treadmill test demonstrated significant improvement, with a PFWD of 800 m and an MWD of 1600 m. Postoperative CT confirmed graft patency, and no recurrence has been observed during the 1-year follow-up. The patient was treated with clopidogrel (75 mg/day) and rivaroxaban (2.5 mg/day); rivaroxaban was discontinued after 3 months, while clopidogrel was maintained.

case_text:
A 43-year-old woman with a 10-year history of mitral valve regurgitation was admitted to our Department for mitral valve repair. She also had moderate tricuspid regurgitation and persistent atrial fibrillation; preoperative echocardiography showed reduced left ventricular systolic function (LVEF 45%).

The procedure was performed endoscopically using 3D vision, with cardiopulmonary bypass established via femoral cannulation. Crystalloid cardioplegia with Bretschneider histidine–tryptophan–ketoglutarate (HTK) solution was administered. Mitral and tricuspid valve repairs were performed using annuloplasty rings, and the left atrial appendage was closed with the AtriClip system. Immediately after reperfusion, transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) revealed severe left ventricular dysfunction with near-global akinesis, while right ventricular function remained preserved.

Suspecting iatrogenic injury to the coronary arteries, both rings were removed. A mitral ring (Physio II, size 40) was then re-implanted, and the tricuspid valve was repaired by bicuspidization with a single suture.

Despite these measures, severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction persisted. Venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) was initiated, and urgent coronary angiography revealed no significant coronary pathology. An Impella CP pump was subsequently implanted to unload the left ventricle. Cardiac biomarkers remained only mildly elevated, arguing against inadequate myocardial protection as the underlying cause, and myocardial stunning was therefore suspected. On postoperative day 6, because cardiac contractility had not improved, an endomyocardial biopsy was performed. At the same time, the Impella pump was explanted in accordance with the manufacturer’s recommendation.

Histopathology showed interstitial edema and sparse inflammatory infiltrates containing eosinophils and neutrophils, without cardiomyocyte damage or definitive evidence of active myocarditis (Fig. 1). After the biopsy result became available, systemic glucocorticoid therapy was initiated. Clinical and echocardiographic improvement was observed shortly thereafter.

On postoperative day 7, a gradual recovery of myocardial contractility was observed; on day 9, ECMO was explanted at an LVEF of ~30%.

The patient was discharged home on postoperative day 12 with an LVEF of 45%, a satisfactory mitral valve repair, and only mild residual tricuspid regurgitation.

case_text: A 72‐year‐old man presented to our hospital with a 2‐month history of a rapidly growing asymptomatic hyperkeratotic nodule on the left nasolabial fold. His medical history included hypertension and gastroesophageal reflux disease, for which he was receiving telmisartan, amlodipine, and vonoprazan. There was no history of immunosuppression, significant sun exposure, or previous trauma to the affected region. No family history of KA or gastrointestinal, urinary tract, or endometrial neoplasms was documented. Clinical examination at his initial visit revealed a pink‐colored, dome‐shaped nodule with a central crater‐like keratotic plug, 15 × 10 mm in size, on the left nasolabial fold (Figure 1a). Dermoscopy showed a central keratin plug with peripheral vessels (Figure 1b). Consultation with his family dentist reported no evidence of an external dental fistula. Based on a presumptive diagnosis of KA, surgical excision was planned. Meanwhile, the patient noticed spontaneous regression of the nodule 1 week later. On the day of surgery, 2 weeks later, the lesion reduced to 13 × 8 mm in size (Figure 1c). For a definitive diagnosis, the patient underwent excision of the nodule. The lesion was excised by elliptical excision with a 1‐mm lateral margin, at the level above the muscle. Because of marked fibrosis, a small portion of the underlying muscle was included in the excised specimen. Histopathological examination showed a symmetrical, shallow cup‐shaped epidermal invagination with central hyperkeratosis and peripheral epithelial lips. The epidermis displayed no significant nuclear atypia or dermal invasion, and the dermis exhibited prominent inflammation with fibrosis. Additionally, foreign body‐type multinucleated giant cells engulfing keratinized materials without cellular components were observed in the lower dermis (Figure 2a–d). Although well‐differentiated cSCC was considered in the differential diagnosis, the absence of significant cytological atypia or invasive growth, together with the characteristic architecture and clinically documented spontaneous regression, supported the diagnosis of regressing KA. After the surgical excision, no recurrence was observed during 2 years of follow‐up.

case_text: A 56‐year‐old Chinese multiparous woman (gravida 2, para 2) with an unremarkable family medical history was admitted for evaluation. Her menarche occurred at 15 years old, and she experienced menopause at 48 years old. She presented with 3 months of vaginal bleeding, accompanied by 1 week of progressive exertional dyspnea, chest tightness, and a low‐grade fever (≤ 39°C). Chest computed tomography (CT) demonstrated bilateral multifocal nodular and patchy opacities. High‐flow nasal oxygen at 50 L/min (FiO2 80%) was used to maintain oxygen saturation at 80%–86%. Severe hypoxemia prevented tissue biopsy during bronchoscopy, leading to the collection of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid and brushings from multiple lobes, including the bilateral upper and lower lobes and the right middle lobe, with negative microbiological findings. Clinical deterioration took place on December 21, presenting with severe respiratory distress (SpO2 75%, PaO2/FiO2 66 mmHg), which necessitated transfer to the ICU. Vital signs indicated tachycardia (130 beats/min), tachypnea (30 breaths/min), and normal blood pressure (117/84 mmHg). Physical examination showed altered consciousness, moist rales in both lungs, and decreased breath sounds.

case_text:
A female aged 55 years came to the outpatient department with complaints of progressive dysphagia. She had been having dysphagia with solid food items for about 3 months. Over the last 15 days, she developed dysphagia involving semi‐solid and liquid food items.

She also had a 2‐year history of left‐sided nasal obstruction. This was associated with left facial pain, discharge around the left orbit, difficulty in breathing from the left nostril, and headache. Fever and weight loss were also mentioned. Cough and expectoration were not seen.

She had a history of Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease for 5 months. In the family history, there was a history of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus. Her Obstetric history revealed that she had four term spontaneous vaginal deliveries. She also had a history of blood transfusion in the past without any adverse effects. Drug allergies were not known.

On the basis of her presenting symptoms, the severity of dysphagia was rated at Grade 3 on the four‐grade ordinal rating scale for dysphagia which includes: Grade 1, normal swallowing; Grade 2, dysphagia for solid food only; Grade 3, dysphagia for solid, semisolid and liquid food; and Grade 4, dysphagia with inability to swallow. However, no validated dysphagia specific instrument like EAT‐10 was administered formally.

case_text:
A 30-year-old Chinese woman presented to a local hospital in October 2024 with crushing precordial pain accompanied by dizziness and palpitations. She had previously been healthy, with no history of hypertension, diabetes, coronary heart disease, or relevant family history, and no smoking history. Initial coronary angiography on October 30, 2024, showed 95% stenosis at the ostium of the left main (LM) coronary artery, and stent implantation was performed (Figures 1A–C).

She subsequently received dual antiplatelet therapy and lipid-lowering therapy. Detailed contemporaneous results of the initial physical examination, including bilateral upper-limb blood pressure, pulse examination, and vascular bruits, were unavailable in the transfer records. Approximately 3.5 months later, on February 16, 2025, dizziness recurred, accompanied by facial redness and swelling and left upper-limb numbness. Repeat coronary angiography showed 95% restenosis at the original LM stent, and balloon dilation was performed (Figures 1D–F). Because symptoms persisted, she was transferred to a higher-level hospital on February 25, 2025. Cardiopulmonary examination was unremarkable. Limb blood pressures were as follows: right upper limb 119/57 mmHg, left upper limb 112/64 mmHg, right lower limb 131/63 mmHg, and left lower limb 131/63 mmHg. Ancillary tests showed a white blood cell count of 13.16 × 10^9/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 22 mm/h, and C-reactive protein (CRP) 2.36 mg/L. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, antinuclear antibody spectrum, rheumatoid panel, supine renin-aldosterone, adrenocorticotropic hormone, and cortisol were unremarkable. PET/CT on February 26, 2025, showed wall thickening of the ascending aorta and aortic arch with increased FDG uptake (Figure 2). After rheumatology consultation and consideration of alternative causes, TA was clinically diagnosed. On February 28, 2025, intravenous methylprednisolone 40 mg daily and oral methotrexate 10 mg weekly were started. Symptoms improved, and she was discharged on March 4, 2025, with oral methylprednisolone 40 mg daily, planned to taper by 2.5 mg every 2 weeks, together with methotrexate, antiplatelet therapy, rosuvastatin plus ezetimibe, rate-control therapy, and nicorandil.

Four months later, in June 2025, she presented to the cardiac surgery department of our hospital because of persistent angina. Physical examination showed normal peripheral arterial pulses in all limbs and no pistol-shot femoral bruits. Angiography showed severe proximal stenosis of the left anterior descending and left circumflex arteries. Under general anesthesia with cardiopulmonary bypass standby, off-pump coronary artery bypass grafting was performed. Despite glucocorticoid and methotrexate therapy, clinically significant coronary artery disease persisted. Subsequently, during repeated hospitalizations from July 2025 to August 2026, intravenous tocilizumab 480 mg was administered every four weeks. During this period, CRP and ESR repeatedly remained within reference ranges, although IL-6 receptor blockade limited their interpretation as indicators of vascular inflammation. Mild leukocytosis and neutrophilia and mildly elevated B-type natriuretic peptide were occasionally observed.

In September 2025, echocardiography reported mild mitral regurgitation and an estimated mean pulmonary artery pressure of 21 mmHg, described as mild pulmonary hypertension; repeat echocardiography in October did not report pulmonary hypertension. Because of occasional chest tightness, right heart catheterization and pulmonary angiography were performed on October 15, 2025. Perioperative blood pressure was 112/70 mmHg, heart rate 69 beats/min, and oxygen saturation 100% while breathing 33% oxygen. Pulmonary artery pressure was 39/10 mmHg (mean 20 mmHg), and pulmonary artery wedge pressure was 9 mmHg. The mean pressure did not meet the current definition of pulmonary hypertension (>20 mmHg) (7). Pulmonary angiography showed nonvisualization of the right upper and middle lobar pulmonary artery branches (Figure 3). No pulmonary vascular intervention was performed, and medical therapy was continued. The last recorded follow-up was in August 2026, approximately 10 months after angiography, when she reported no dizziness or chest tightness. The clinical timeline is shown in Table 1.

case_text:
We present the case of a female patient in her 50s who received a knee prosthesis due to posttraumatic knee osteoarthritis. Seven years following the primary implantation, the patiet underwent a revision surgery with a linked knee prosthesis. Managing this structural joint damage required multiple surgical procedures over time. In total, the patient underwent more than 40 knee procedures. Medical history included hay fever, house dust allergy, and nicotine dependence with approximately 20 cigarettes per day. The extensive clinical progression is graphically illustrated in Figure 1, and the Co and Cr measurements with major treatments are summarized in Table 1. The need for IRB approval was waived because this was an individual case report that did not include any personally identifiable information that could be traced back to the patient, nor did it involve any intervention.

Thirteen years following the implantation of the linked knee prosthesis, the patient developed a variety of unclear symptoms listed in Figure 1. The following year (i.e., nearly 14 years after implantation of the coupled knee prosthesis), laboratory testing revealed markedly elevated whole blood Cr 13.3 μg/L (reference 0.14–0.52) and whole blood Co 9.9 μg/L (reference < 3.9). Under the suspicion of prosthetic wear, revision surgery in February 2022 showed grayish synovitis consistent with metal corrosion (Krenn Type I). Since there were no signs of prosthesis loosening and the coupling mechanism showed only minor abrasion, synovectomy and debridement were performed. Histology confirmed wear‐induced neosynovialitis. Months later, when whole blood Cr rose to 22.8 μg/L (ref 0.14–0.52), complete prosthesis removal with cement‐spacer implantation was undertaken. Intraoperatively, black bone discoloration was observed; histology revealed high‐grade particle‐induced neosynovialitis with abundant fine black granules, marked sclerosis, hypersensitivity‐related necroses, and fibrinous‐exudative reaction. Nephrological coassessment initiated a conservative approach with furosemide under strict fluid monitoring to enhance renal metal clearance. A couple of months later, Cr 7.01 μg/L (whole blood) and Co 3.9 μg/L (whole blood) had declined, with preserved renal function and enhanced urinary elimination (urine: Cr 10.6 μg/L, Co 3.1 μg/L).

After the two‐stage reimplantation with a titanium‐nitride–coated linked knee prosthesis, metal levels decreased further (serum Cr 5.3 μg/L, ref < 0.5; whole blood Co 1.7 μg/L, ref < 3.9; December 2022). Urine concentrations suggested enhanced elimination (urine Cr 20.0 μg/L and urine Co 6.6 μg/L). Despite declining metal concentrations, there was only a temporary subjective clinical improvement, with persistent severe headaches. A cranial MRI revealed no toxic or degenerative signal abnormalities were detected. Symptoms persisted, including tinnitus and cognitive decline. Serum Cr 5.47 μg/L (ref < 0.5) and whole blood Co 1.30 μg/L (ref < 3.9) remained detectable.

Because of continuing flushing and fatigue, oral N‐acetylcysteine (NAC) 1200 mg/day was initiated. The patient underwent several plasma exchange sessions (10 L cumulative), due to progressive symptoms with new gastrointestinal complaints, urticaria, and night sweats. This however provided transient relief. Despite ongoing chelation and enhanced urinary metal‐elimination (serum Cr 4.4 μg/L, ref < 0.5; serum Co 1.9 μg/L, ref < 1.2; urine Cr 11.8 μg/L, urine Co 9.9 μg/L), the patient developed word‐finding difficulties, optic neuritis, and skin discoloration. Neurological re‐evaluation showed axonal polyneuropathy with preserved blink reflexes, excluding trigeminal nerve injury. ENT examination found no objective correlate for persisting tinnitus. Finally, two Inuspheresis sessions (double‐filtration plasmapheresis) were performed to remove high‐molecular‐weight and protein‐bound metal complexes. Concurrent testing showed persistent but further reduced serum Cr 2.93 μg/L (ref < 0.5) and serum Co 0.77 μg/L (ref < 1.2). Clinically, headache and flushing improved transiently, but later recurred. [18F]FDG‐PET/CT (February 2025) revealed no metabolic correlate of Co/Cr neurotoxicity.

Throughout 2022–2025, renal function remained stable (creatinine and eGFR normal). Hematology showed transient iron‐deficiency anemia that normalized after substitution. Liver, thyroid, and glucose metabolism were unremarkable. Despite removal of all suspected sources and steadily declining systemic metal concentrations, symptoms continued, highlighting the complex and protracted course of Co and Cr toxicity.
