The extensive clinical progression is graphically illustrated in Figure 1, and the Co and Cr measurements with major treatments are summarized in Table 1.

The need for IRB approval was waived because this was an individual case report that did not include any personally identifiable information that could be traced back to the patient, nor did it involve any intervention.
Thirteen years following the implantation of the linked knee prosthesis, the patient developed a variety of unclear symptoms listed in Figure 1.

The following year (i.e., nearly 14 years after implantation of the coupled knee prosthesis), laboratory testing revealed markedly elevated whole blood Cr 13.3 μg/L (reference 0.14–0.52) and whole blood Co 9.9 μg/L (reference < 3.9).
Under the suspicion of prosthetic wear, revision surgery in February 2022 showed grayish synovitis consistent with metal corrosion (Krenn Type I).
Since there were no signs of prosthesis loosening and the coupling mechanism showed only minor abrasion, synovectomy and debridement were performed.
Histology confirmed wear‐induced neosynovialitis.
Months later, when whole blood Cr rose to 22.8 μg/L (ref 0.14–0.52), complete prosthesis removal with cement‐spacer implantation was undertaken.

Intraoperatively, black bone discoloration was observed; histology revealed high‐grade particle‐induced neosynovialitis with abundant fine black granules, marked sclerosis, hypersensitivity‐related necroses, and fibrinous‐exudative reaction.
Nephrological coassessment initiated a conservative approach with furosemide under strict fluid monitoring to enhance renal metal clearance.
A couple of months later, Cr 7.01 μg/L (whole blood) and Co 3.9 μg/L (whole blood) had declined, with preserved renal function and enhanced urinary elimination (urine: Cr 10.6 μg/L, Co 3.1 μg/L).

After the two‐stage reimplantation with a titanium‐nitride–coated linked knee prosthesis, metal levels decreased further (serum Cr 5.3 μg/L, ref < 0.5; whole blood Co 1.7 μg/L, ref < 3.9; December 2022).
Urine concentrations suggested enhanced elimination (urine Cr 20.0 μg/L and urine Co 6.6 μg/L).
Despite declining metal concentrations, there was only a temporary subjective clinical improvement, with persistent severe headaches.
A cranial MRI revealed no toxic or degenerative signal abnormalities were detected.
Symptoms persisted, including tinnitus and cognitive decline.
Serum Cr 5.47 μg/L (ref < 0.5) and whole blood Co 1.30 μg/L (ref < 3.9) remained detectable.
Because of continuing flushing and fatigue, oral N‐acetylcysteine (NAC) 1200 mg/day was initiated.
The patient underwent several plasma exchange sessions (10 L cumulative), due to progressive symptoms with new gastrointestinal complaints, urticaria, and night sweats.
This however provided transient relief.

Despite ongoing chelation and enhanced urinary metal‐elimination (serum Cr 4.4 μg/L, ref < 0.5; serum Co 1.9 μg/L, ref < 1.2; urine Cr 11.8 μg/L, urine Co 9.9 μg/L), the patient developed word‐finding difficulties, optic neuritis, and skin discoloration.
Neurological re‐evaluation showed axonal polyneuropathy with preserved blink reflexes, excluding trigeminal nerve injury.
ENT examination found no objective correlate for persisting tinnitus.
Finally, two Inuspheresis sessions (double‐filtration plasmapheresis) were performed to remove high‐molecular‐weight and protein‐bound metal complexes.
Concurrent testing showed persistent but further reduced serum Cr 2.93 μg/L (ref < 0.5) and serum Co 0.77 μg/L (ref < 1.2).
Clinically, headache and flushing improved transiently, but later recurred. [18F]FDG‐PET/CT (February 2025) revealed no metabolic correlate of Co/Cr neurotoxicity.
Throughout 2022–2025, renal function remained stable (creatinine and eGFR normal).
Hematology showed transient iron‐deficiency anemia that normalized after substitution.
Liver, thyroid, and glucose metabolism were unremarkable.
Despite removal of all suspected sources and steadily declining systemic metal concentrations, symptoms continued, highlighting the complex and protracted course of Co and Cr toxicity.
title: Heavy Metal Toxicity Following Metal‐on‐Metal Knee Arthroplasty Revision Surgery: A Case Report

case_text:
A 70-year-old female patient was diagnosed with sigmoid colon carcinoma in December 2022 and subsequently underwent laparoscopic left hemicolectomy (the patient’s clinical timeline is illustrated in Fig. 1. Histopathological evaluation revealed a moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma with areas of necrosis (Fig. 2A). Immunohistochemical analysis demonstrated a high proliferative index with Ki-67 approximately 90% (Fig. 2B) and alongside positive expression of p53 (Fig. 2C). Following surgery, the patient received adjuvant chemotherapy with oxaliplatin (130 mg/m²) and capecitabine (1000 mg/m²) for eight cycles.

Fig. 1Clinical timeline of the patient, illustrating diagnosis, treatment, and disease progressionColorectal cancer was diagnosed and surgically treated in December 2022. Eight cycles of chemotherapy began in January 2023 and ended in June 2023. A disease-free interval followed until parotid metastasis in January 2026. The patient died in February 2026.

Fig. 2Histopathological and immunohistochemical features of the primary colorectal adenocarcinoma. (A) Moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma showing prominent glandular formation, with marked nuclear atypia and elongated, stratified nuclei (H&E × 100). (B) High proliferative activity with a Ki-67 labelling index of approximately 90% (× 100). (C) Nuclear positivity for p53 (× 100)Colorectal tumor tissue forms irregular glands. Ki-67 and p53 staining is widespread in the nuclei of cells lining the glands.

In January 2026, the patient developed persistent right-sided facial pain that did not respond to oral analgesics or antibiotics. On presentation to the Department of Stomatology at Guangzhou First People’s Hospital, a palpable firm mass measuring approximately 2 × 2 cm was identified in the right parotid region (Fig. 3). There was no evidence of facial nerve dysfunction or sensory deficits. Her past medical history was notable for hypertension and coronary heart disease.

Fig. 3Clinical presentation of the right parotid mass. (A, B) Lateral views of the patient’s face showing a palpable mass in the right parotid region (red circle). The lesion measured approximately 2 × 2 cm and was associated with mild overlying facial swellingTwo views show mild swelling below and in front of the right ear, with the affected area circled.

Ultrasonography of the right parotid gland demonstrated abnormal morphology with heterogeneous echotexture. A solid intraglandular lesion measuring approximately 24 × 20 mm with irregular contours, indistinct margins, and heterogeneous internal echogenicity was observed (Fig. 4A). Computed tomography (CT) of the head and neck confirmed a lobulated mass in the right parotid region measuring approximately 27 × 22 mm, with ill-defined margins (Fig. 4B, C). The lesion was well separated from the right masseter muscle and the retromandibular vein, with no bony involvement of the right mandible. At the same time, baseline systemic imaging, including chest CT, was performed. No abnormalities were detected on these examinations.

Fig. 4Imaging findings of the right parotid lesion. (A) Ultrasonography revealed a solid intraglandular hypoechoic mass with irregular margins and heterogeneous internal echogenicity in the right parotid region. (B) Axial contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a lobulated, heterogeneous soft tissue lesion with pronounced enhancement and ill-defined borders. (C) Coronal CT image showed the craniocaudal extent of the lesion and its anatomical relationship with adjacent structures, including separation from the right masseter muscle and retromandibular vein, with no evidence of bony involvementUltrasound and CT views show an irregular, heterogeneous mass in the right parotid gland. The coronal CT shows the mass separate from the masseter muscle and retromandibular vein, without visible bone involvement.

Definitive diagnosis was established via ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration, providing representative tissue for histopathological and immunohistochemical analysis. The lesion was positive for CDX-2 and Villin, markers of gastrointestinal adenocarcinoma, and negative for p63, effectively excluding squamous cell differentiation (Fig. 5). Histopathological and immunohistochemical features were therefore consistent with metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma.

Fig. 5Histopathological and immunohistochemical features of the right parotid mass. (A) Adenocarcinoma arranged in glandular structures, showing enlarged, hyperchromatic and pleomorphic nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and frequent mitotic figures (H&E × 100). (B) Positive cytoplasmic staining for Villin (× 100). (C) Strong nuclear positivity for CDX-2, confirming intestinal differentiation (× 200). (D) Absence of p63 expression (× 400), excluding squamous differentiationParotid tumor tissue forms irregular glands. Immunostaining shows villin and CDX-2 positivity, consistent with intestinal differentiation, while the tumor cells lack p63 staining.

After multidisciplinary consultation and discussion with the patient and her family, systemic therapy with the FOLFIRI regimen (5-fluorouracil, leucovorin, and irinotecan) was planned. Unfortunately, before treatment initiation, the patient developed severe COVID-19 pneumonia and succumbed to respiratory failure two weeks after hospital admission.

case_text:
A 21-year-old previously healthy man presented with sudden severe generalized headache, slurred speech, progressive confusion, and deteriorating consciousness over several hours. He had no prior bleeding, anticoagulant or antiplatelet use, or family history of bleeding disorders.

Blood pressure was 166/81 mmHg, heart rate 98/min, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score was 12/15 (eye-opening 3, verbal 4, motor 5), with objective right-sided weakness. There were no petechiae, ecchymoses, active bleeding, or stigmata of chronic liver disease. Hemoglobin was 13.9 g/dL and platelets 446 × 103/μL. Prothrombin time (PT) was markedly prolonged at 24.5 s (INR 2.1) with a normal activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT, 31.2 s), fibrinogen, and hepatic biochemistry.

The acute lateralizing deficit raised immediate suspicion of intracerebral hemorrhage; brain imaging and coagulation studies were obtained concurrently in the routine emergency work-up. Non-contrast computed tomography (CT) showed a large acute left parietotemporal hemorrhage (6.3 × 4.0 cm) with surrounding edema, left lateral ventricular compression, and 7.6-mm midline shift (Fig. 1). CT angiography excluded aneurysm, arteriovenous malformation, and venous thrombosis. As a hemorrhagic stroke was confirmed early, other young-adult stroke etiologies were not separately pursued.

Given the isolated PT/INR prolongation, an extrinsic-pathway deficiency was suspected. A 1:1 mixing study with normal pooled plasma corrected the prolonged PT (and aPTT) both immediately and after two-hour incubation, supporting a factor deficiency rather than an inhibitor. Acquired causes were unlikely: hepatic biochemistry was normal, there was no anticoagulant use, and platelet count and fibrinogen were normal; vitamin K deficiency was clinically unlikely but not definitively excluded. FVII activity was markedly reduced at 8.9% (reference 70%–120%), with mild reductions in factors X (63.2%) and XI (45.5%) and normal factors II, V, and IX. By the ISTH-SSC classification (severe < 10%, moderate 10%–20%, mild 20%–50%), the patient met criteria for severe deficiency, although FVII activity correlates imperfectly with phenotype. Molecular testing was unavailable, so a congenital basis was presumed but not confirmed.

Recombinant activated FVII (rFVIIa) was initiated at 30 μg/kg every six hours under hematology guidance, with shortening of PT from 24.5 to 9.4 s and INR from 2.1 to 1.0; laboratory correction reflected replacement rather than hemostasis, judged clinically and by serial imaging. Despite initial stabilization, the patient deteriorated, with GCS falling to 5/15 (eye-opening 2, verbal 2, motor 1); repeat CT showed midline shift progression to 12 mm with uncal and tonsillar herniation and obstructive hydrocephalus.

Emergent left decompressive craniectomy with partial hematoma evacuation was performed. Preoperative FVII activity was 89% (six hours after the preceding dose), and intraoperative hemostasis was adequate; postoperative CT showed midline shift reduced to 6 mm without new hemorrhage. rFVIIa was continued at 30 μg/kg every six hours, reduced to every eight hours for a persistently high trough (>200%), with daily FVII monitoring targeted to 70%–100%. It was discontinued after cranioplasty, and thromboprophylaxis was introduced once surgical hemostasis was secured.

The patient underwent neurorehabilitation and later cranioplasty, recovering without recurrent hemorrhage or thrombotic complications. At discharge, muscle strength was 5/5 in all limbs with intact sensation; he was ambulating, self-caring, and continent; his anomic aphasia had largely resolved, with residual mild cognitive impairment. The hematology team initiated secondary prophylaxis with rFVIIa 30 μg/kg three times weekly. No family history of bleeding was reported, and no relatives were available for screening.

case_text:
A 61‐year‐old man presented to the emergency department with two weeks of scrotal pain, gradual in onset and progressively worsening, associated with scrotal swelling and subjective fever. There were no aggravating or relieving factors, and over‐the‐counter analgesia had not helped. The scrotal symptoms had been preceded by 2 days of coryza and mild upper respiratory symptoms. He reported no dysuria, frequency, hematuria, urethral discharge, trauma, or new sexual contact and no diarrhea, cough, dyspnea, or rash.

His past medical history comprised hypertension, hyperlipidemia, coronary artery disease, subtotal parathyroidectomy, and end‐stage kidney disease (ESKD) treated with DDKTxP 4 weeks earlier. The donor kidney had a kidney donor profile index (KDPI) of 94%, with four human leukocyte antigen (HLA) mismatches and a calculated panel‐reactive antibody (cPRA) of 0%. The early posttransplant course was complicated by delayed graft function requiring one session of hemodialysis, which resolved 2 weeks before this admission.

Induction immunosuppression comprised antithymocyte globulin with a methylprednisolone taper. Maintenance immunosuppression at the time of presentation was tacrolimus 6 mg orally every 12 h (admission trough 10 ng/mL; center target 8–10 ng/mL during the first three months), mycophenolate mofetil 500 mg orally every 12 h, and prednisone 5 mg daily. He received no mTOR inhibitor, no belatacept, and no azole antifungal at any stage. Anti‐infective prophylaxis consisted of valganciclovir 450 mg daily (Cytomegalovirus donor/recipient serostatus high risk [D+/R−]) and atovaquone 1500 mg daily. Other medications include aspirin, amlodipine, pravastatin, and calcitriol.

He was hemodynamically stable, with blood pressure 126/80 mmHg, heart rate 71 beats per minute, temperature 37.6°C, and normal oxygen saturation on room air. Examination of the scrotum revealed bilateral tenderness and swelling with overlying erythema; the cremasteric reflex was preserved, and there was no evidence of torsion. The allograft in the right iliac fossa was nontender. The rest of the examination was otherwise unremarkable.

Laboratory results are summarized in Table 1 and the complete diagnostic evaluation in Table 2. Scrotal ultrasound with color Doppler demonstrated bilateral enlargement of the epididymis with heterogeneous echotexture and marked hyperemia, together with symmetrically increased intratesticular flow and diffuse scrotal wall edema, consistent with bilateral epididymo‐orchitis (Figure 1). Chest radiography was unremarkable.

Urinalysis was bland, without pyuria, nitrites, or hematuria. Empiric intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g twice daily was started on admission. Urine culture, two sets of blood cultures, and nucleic acid amplification testing for C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae were negative, and ceftriaxone was discontinued after 48 h. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assays for Cytomegalovirus, BK polyomavirus, Epstein–Barr virus, SARS‐CoV‐2, and parvovirus B19 were negative. A respiratory multiplex PCR panel was positive for HAdV, and HAdV PCR from blood was subsequently also positive. HAdV species and serotype were not determined. Urine and seminal HAdV PCR was not performed, as the timeline of prior results was sufficient for probable diagnosis, and the patient was improving following reduction of immunosuppression.

Serum creatinine had been improving since transplantation, reaching a nadir of 1.35 mg/dL, although a definitive baseline had not yet been established. It was 1.43 mg/dL on admission, plateaued through Hospital Day 2, rose to 1.45 mg/dL on Day 3, and then declined to 1.32 mg/dL by Day 6. The tacrolimus trough was within the target range.

On the basis of viremia together with clinical involvement of two anatomically distinct organ systems, the upper respiratory tract and the genital tract and after exclusion of bacterial, sexually transmitted and alternative viral causes, the presentation was attributed to probable disseminated HAdV disease. The clinical course is summarized in Figure 2.

Management consisted of reduction of immunosuppression and supportive care. Mycophenolate mofetil was reduced from 500 mg to 360 mg every 12 h and tacrolimus from 6 mg to 5 mg every 12 h, targeting a trough of 6–8 rather than 8–10 ng/mL. Prednisone 5 mg daily was continued unchanged. Following consultation with infectious diseases, no antiviral therapy and no intravenous immunoglobulin were administered, on the grounds of mild, nonprogressive and already improving disease.

Scrotal pain and swelling improved progressively and had resolved by Day 7. Serum creatinine rose transiently to 1.45 mg/dL on Day 3 before falling to 1.32 mg/dL by Day 6, below the preadmission nadir. He was discharged on Day 7 with weekly clinic follow‐up. At 1 month of follow‐up, serum creatinine was 1.2 mg/dL; there had been no rejection episode and no recurrence of scrotal symptoms, and repeat blood HAdV PCR was negative on the first patient visit postdischarge.

case_text:
A woman in her 60 s had a fever of 37.9°C a few days before admission and went to her family doctor. She was followed up for cold-like symptoms. The night before admission, she developed chest pain and progressive dyspnoea on exertion, and was referred to our hospital for suspected pneumonia. She had no cardiac history and no regular medication.

Vital signs were normal, and auscultation revealed heart sound III and coarse crackles in the right lower lung region, without signs of low cardiac output. Blood tests indicated significant neutrophilic leucocytosis, high C-reactive protein (CRP) and brain natriuretic peptide levels. She had elevated high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I (hs-cTnI) levels (reference range: 0∼45.2 pg/ml), but not creatine phosphokinase (CPK) and creatine phosphokinase MB (CPK-MB) levels. Although she had no diabetes or liver disease, she also had elevated levels of liver enzymes and high haemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) (Table 1). Chest X-ray imaging showed bilateral congestion (Figure 1A), and electrocardiography (ECG) revealed low voltage in all leads (Figure 1B). Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) showed diffuse hypokinesis with a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 36%, left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH), an apical sparing pattern (Figure 1C–1E). TTE also showed an enlarged inferior vena cava of 15 mm without respiratory variability and grade II–III mitral regurgitation. She was admitted with congestive heart failure for further evaluation and treatment.

Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) was initially suspected from the ECG and TTE findings. On Day 4, she deteriorated with respiratory distress, cold extremities and non-sustained ventricular tachycardia (NSVT), worsening rapidly despite a dobutamine infusion. Evaluation for CA, including serum free light chains, was negative, whereas cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and scintigraphy were precluded by her haemodynamic instability. Emergent right heart catheterization (RHC) revealed postcapillary pulmonary hypertension with a low cardiac index (CI) (Table 2), and coronary angiography showed no obstructive coronary artery disease (Figure 2A–2B). case_text:
A woman in her 40s experienced prolapse of a perianal mass and occasional discharge for approximately 5 years. She did not seek medical attention until she tested positive for fecal occult blood during a routine health check. She visited the Inoue Gastroenterology and Endoscopy Clinic, where colonoscopy revealed 5-mm sessile polyps in the sigmoid colon and rectum, as well as a 30-mm pedunculated anal polyp near the anal verge. Polypectomy of the sigmoid and rectal polyps was performed at the clinic, and histopathological examination revealed tubular adenomas with low-grade atypia. She was subsequently referred to our clinic for further management of the pedunculated anal polyp.

A physical examination confirmed prolapsed internal hemorrhoids without ulceration, induration, or bleeding (Fig. 1). The laboratory results were unremarkable, and no evidence of systemic disease or immunosuppression was identified.

Hemorrhoidectomy was performed under spinal anesthesia. The prolapsing hemorrhoidal tissue had a polypoid appearance and was excised using a standard hemorrhoidectomy procedure. On gross inspection, the specimen appeared consistent with hemorrhoidal tissue, without obvious ulceration or induration. A histopathological examination unexpectedly revealed a small focus of SCC in situ within the polypoid lesion (Fig. 2A). The lesion showed proliferation of atypical squamous epithelial cells with nuclear enlargement, hyperchromasia, and disordered maturation involving the full thickness of the epithelium, without invasion beyond the basement membrane (Fig. 2A, 2B). No lymphovascular invasion was identified, and the resection margins were free of tumors. Immunohistochemical examination showed strong and diffuse p16 overexpression (Fig. 2C, 2D). Direct HPV testing, such as HPV DNA polymerase chain reaction or RNA in situ hybridization, was not performed. No additional treatment was performed because the lesion was confined to the epithelium, with negative resection margins and no lymphovascular invasion. The postoperative course was uneventful, and the patient was discharged in good health. The follow-up consisted of clinical and anoscopic examinations every 3 months, and CT performed 1 year after surgery showed no distant metastasis. At 15 months after surgery, she remained free of local recurrence, with no abnormal findings on an anoscopic examination.

case_text:
Failure to recognize and adequately treat maternal tuberculosis during pregnancy may result in congenital infection, a rare but potentially fatal condition in which delayed diagnosis remains one of the major determinants of mortality. The clinical presentation is often nonspecific and overlaps with more common neonatal conditions such as bacterial sepsis or pneumonia, making early recognition particularly challenging. Consequently, a high index of clinical suspicion, together with appropriate microbiological and imaging studies, is essential for timely diagnosis and treatment. Figure 5 summarizes the principal clinical manifestations and diagnostic approaches currently used in the evaluation of newborns with suspected congenital tuberculosis.

Initial manifestations are usually nonspecific and frequently mimic neonatal sepsis or pneumonia. Affected newborns may present with persistent fever, respiratory distress, lethargy, irritability, poor feeding, or signs of multiple organ dysfunction. Hepatomegaly and splenomegaly are common findings, often accompanied by abdominal distension and, less frequently, jaundice. Neurological manifestations, including seizures or altered mental status, may occur in cases with central nervous system involvement.

Laboratory tests provide complementary information but are not diagnostic on their own. Hematologic abnormalities include leukocytosis or leukopenia, anemia, and platelet disorders, along with significant elevations in inflammatory markers. Cultures of gastric aspiration generally offer a higher yield than other samples, although their success depends on the bacterial load. Molecular tests such as Xpert MTB/RIF allow for rapid detection, while more advanced techniques such as next-generation sequencing have been used with increasing success in challenging cases. Immunological tests such as the tuberculin skin test or IGRA are not sufficiently sensitive in newborns and should therefore not be used to rule out the disease.

Imaging is essential for identifying patterns consistent with congenital tuberculosis. Chest X-rays frequently show diffuse infiltrates or a miliary pattern. Additionally, CT scans provide more detailed visualization of pulmonary lesions, multiple nodules, or effusions. Meanwhile, abdominal ultrasound may reveal hepatic or splenic granulomas, as well as ascites. When neurological involvement is suspected, CT or MRI scans of the brain may demonstrate tuberculomas or other findings suggestive of central nervous involvement.

Despite advances in diagnostic techniques and antituberculous therapy, congenital tuberculosis continues to be associated with high morbidity and mortality, particularly when diagnosis is delayed. Early recognition based on maternal history, clinical suspicion, and rapid molecular confirmation substantially improves neonatal outcomes, emphasizing the importance of integrating maternal and neonatal evaluation whenever congenital tuberculosis is suspected.

case_text:
A 23‐month‐old male was born full term to healthy parents, with no known family history of thyroid disease, food allergies, or immune deficiencies. The patient had previously been evaluated by a nutritionist at 9 months of age after developing multiple immunoglobulin E–mediated food allergies, including cow’s milk, eggs, and peanuts.

During infancy, the patient experienced multiple viral illnesses, including one episode of dehydration associated with gastroenteritis, had recurrent ear infections, and had ongoing difficulty with weight gain. At his initial nutrition telehealth visit, dietary history revealed significant dietary restrictions related to food allergies and caregivers expressed difficulty identifying appropriate meal options. The nutritional assessment concluded that the patient had increased energy needs related to recent illness and dietary limitations, as evidenced by poor weight gain. The recommended intervention included provision of three meals and two to three snacks per day, along with nutritional education for the parents.

At the patient’s 2‐year well‐child visit, the primary care provider noted only a minimal increase in height between 18 and 24 months of age (Figure 1) and ordered broad laboratory evaluation in addition to the routine two‐year screening. Thyroid function testing performed at this time revealed severe hypothyroidism, with markedly elevated TSH levels (204.81 mIU/L) and suppressed free thyroxine (free T4) levels (0.37 ng/dL) (Table 1).

The patient was referred to pediatric endocrinology and evaluated one week after the 2‐year appointment. Physical examination revealed a diffusely enlarged thyroid gland, estimated to be greater than twice normal size and consistent with goiter; the gland was nontender on palpation. Additional laboratory testing demonstrated persistent elevation of TSH (18.2 mIU/mL), markedly elevated thyroglobulin (1591.2 ng/mL), and a low urinary iodine‐to‐creatinine ratio of 12.9, consistent with iodine deficiency (Table 1). Thyroid peroxidase and thyroglobulin antibodies were negative. The patient was also noted to have a low 25‐hydroxyvitamin D level (23.5 ng/mL) (Table 1).

Thyroid ultrasonography performed two days later demonstrated diffuse thyroid enlargement, with the right lobe measuring 3.1 × 1.3 × 1.2 cm and the left lobe measuring 3.2 × 1.2 × 1.7 cm. The isthmus was mildly thickened at 4 mm. No solid or cystic lesions were identified; however, pronounced hypervascularity was observed throughout the thyroid gland.

Treatment with levothyroxine at a dose of 25 mcg daily was initiated on the date of the thyroid ultrasonography appointment. Supplementation of 20 mcg/day vitamin D was also initiated, along with calcium (700 mg/day spread out over 2‐3 servings), and a multivitamin containing 75 mcg of iodine. Follow‐up laboratory testing one week later demonstrated normalization of free T4 (1.15 ng/dL) and TSH normalized to 4.57 mIU/mL after one month. Vitamin D levels normalized within days of supplementation. Subsequent endocrinology evaluation identified iodine deficiency as the underlying etiology of the patient’s hypothyroidism based on the low urinary iodine‐to‐creatinine ratio and elevated thyroglobulin levels. In addition to avoiding dairy and eggs, review of the patient’s diet suggested that commercially available allergy‐free foods consumed by the patient did not consistently contain iodized salt. This was further exacerbated by minimized iodized salt use in the home. The family was advised to incorporate iodized salt into the diet, and no other dietary modifications were implemented.

Six months posttreatment, laboratory studies demonstrated evidence of iodine repletion, with a urinary iodine‐to‐creatinine ratio of 112.1 (Table 1). Thyroid function tests remained within normal limits (free T4, 1.49 ng/dL; TSH, 4.41 mIU/mL). Repeat thyroid ultrasonography demonstrated interval reduction in the thyroid size, with the right lobe measuring 2.7 × 1.1 × 0.9 cm, the left lobe measuring 2.4 × 0.9 × 0.9 cm, and the isthmus measuring 1.9 mm in thickness (Table 1). Sonographic grayscale imaging was consistent with resolution of thyroid enlargement. Findings were considered markedly improved and consistent with iodine repletion and resolution of hypothyroidism. Levothyroxine was then discontinued.

At the patient’s 3‐year visit, after 1 year of iodine supplementation, the patient demonstrated sustained resolution of hypothyroidism and thyroid enlargement, with no ongoing clinical concerns. The patient continues to take the multivitamin containing 75 mcg of iodine.

case_text:
While the most common irAEs involve the skin, gastrointestinal tract, and endocrine systems, the kidney is an increasingly recognized site of injury. The incidence of ICI-AKI ranges from 2% to 5%, with the highest rates (approximately 5%) in patients receiving combination therapy, such as nivolumab plus ipilimumab. Unlike the immediate injury seen with contrast media or cisplatin, ICI-AKI usually develops gradually, with a median onset of 14–16 weeks in two multicenter cohorts, although cases occurring more than one year after ICI initiation have been reported. Most patients present with a slow rise in serum creatinine (sCr) without oliguria.

Several risk factors for ICI-AKI have been identified in large multicenter studies. In two case–control cohorts, lower baseline estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and proton pump inhibitor (PPI) use were each associated with a higher risk of ICI-AKI. Combination ICI therapy was an independent risk factor in one cohort and extrarenal irAEs in the other. The association with lower baseline eGFR may partly reflect reduced renal reserve rather than a true increase in immune-mediated kidney injury. These risk factors are easy to identify in clinical practice. Patients with reduced baseline eGFR, those receiving PPIs or combination therapy, and those with other irAEs may need closer monitoring of kidney function, and the indication for PPIs should be reviewed.

Pyuria is a common but non-specific urinary finding in ICI-associated acute tubulointerstitial nephritis (ATIN). In multicenter cohorts, pyuria was observed in approximately half of patients and in 57.8% (≥10 white blood cells per high-power field), whereas hematuria (≥1+ blood on dipstick) was less frequent (39.7%). Because these urinary abnormalities are absent in many patients, a bland urinalysis does not exclude ICI-AKI. Proteinuria is usually mild (<1.0 g/day) in ATIN. Sudden-onset nephrotic-range proteinuria (>3.5 g/day) with edema should raise suspicion of a glomerular lesion—most commonly a podocytopathy such as minimal change disease (MCD).

Based on the reported timing of onset, we propose a practical framework that divides ICI-AKI into three clinical phases. This framework is our own and has not been formally validated; it is intended to help clinicians plan kidney monitoring. The early phase (approximately weeks 4–8) is seen mainly with combination anti-CTLA-4 and anti-PD-1 therapy, when kidney injury may be overshadowed by other irAEs such as colitis or skin rash. The maintenance phase (approximately weeks 12–24) is the typical window for ICI-AKI, when sCr rises slowly and is often found on routine tests before scheduled infusions. The late phase includes cases that occur after more than one year of treatment or months after the drug is stopped. The reason for late onset is not known. Persistent memory T cells have been suggested as one explanation, but this has not been shown in the kidney. Because laboratory monitoring is often less frequent in long-term survivors, some cases may be diagnosed late, which may lead to incomplete renal recovery and chronic kidney disease.

case_text:
A 47‐year‐old man was referred to the Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery at Tehran University of Medical Sciences with a 2‐month history of a painful, progressively enlarging intraoral mass. His medical and dental histories were unremarkable, with no history of malignancy or significant infectious disease. No relevant family history was reported. Poor oral hygiene was noted on clinical examination.

Intraoral examination revealed a soft, exophytic, irregularly shaped mass involving the left posterior hard palate and maxillary tuberosity. The lesion measured approximately 3 × 3 cm and exhibited a papillary surface with areas of ulceration. The lesion was associated with underlying bony destruction. No tooth displacement was observed. Extraoral examination revealed no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy.

A panoramic radiograph demonstrated a destructive lesion involving the left maxillary region and extending into the maxillary and ethmoidal sinuses (Figure 1). The lesion appeared to expand toward the oral cavity without apparent invasion of the dental arch. Computed tomography (CT) was subsequently performed to further evaluate the extent of the lesion and its relationship with adjacent anatomical structures (Figure 2). CT revealed an osteolytic mass occupying the left maxillary sinus, with involvement of the left ethmoidal sinus and extension toward the left nasal and oral cavities. The lesion had eroded the posterior aspect of the hard palate.

An incisional biopsy was performed on the lesion on April 14, 2021 (Figure 3). Histopathological examination revealed a malignant small round cell neoplasm composed of relatively uniform round‐to‐oval cells with scant cytoplasm arranged within a fibromyxoid stroma. Significant cytological atypia was observed. Immunohistochemical evaluation demonstrated strong, diffuse membranous expression of CD99, patchy positivity for S100, and focal positivity for MyoD1. The tumor cells were negative for pancytokeratin (PanCK), CK7, CD45, p63, myogenin, synaptophysin, and chromogranin. The Ki‐67 labeling index was approximately 40%. Additional immunohistochemical staining was performed to further evaluate the differential diagnosis. The tumor cells showed negative immunoreactivity for HMB‐45, MART‐1, and SATB2.

The histopathological and immunohistochemical findings supported the diagnosis of ES. In particular, the strong and diffuse membranous CD99 expression, together with the characteristic small round cell morphology and the absence of epithelial, lymphoid, myogenic, and neuroendocrine marker expression, supported the initial biopsy diagnosis and helped exclude the main histopathological differential diagnoses. Molecular testing for EWSR1 rearrangement was recommended; however, it could not be performed because of the patient′s refusal and financial constraints. Thus, the final diagnosis was established based on the integrated clinical, radiographic, histopathological, and immunohistochemical findings, with the absence of molecular confirmation acknowledged as a limitation.

The initial clinical and radiographic differential diagnosis included a range of benign and malignant lesions arising from the maxilla and sinonasal region. Pleomorphic adenoma and adenoid cystic carcinoma were initially considered because of the palatal location and soft‐tissue component. However, the extensive osteolytic destruction and rapid progression raised concern for a malignant small round cell neoplasm or other aggressive malignancy.

The differential diagnosis was subsequently broadened to include sinonasal carcinoma, lymphoid malignancies such as lymphoblastic lymphoma and non‐Hodgkin lymphoma, neuroblastoma and rhabdomyosarcoma (Table 1). Histopathological examination demonstrated a malignant small round cell neoplasm, whereas the immunohistochemical profile showed strong, diffuse membranous CD99 expression with negativity for pancytokeratin, CK7, CD45, p63, myogenin, synaptophysin, and chromogranin (Figures 4 and 5). This immunophenotypic profile helped exclude epithelial, lymphoid, myogenic, and neuroendocrine neoplasms and, together with the characteristic morphology and clinical and radiographic findings, supported the diagnosis of ES.

No metastasis was observed in the metastatic workup. The patient subsequently underwent surgical excision of the lesion on June 12, 2021. During surgery, the surgeon aimed for a gross surgical safe margin in line with the recommended principles of surgical management for ES, achieving adequate oncological margins. Histopathological examination of the resected specimen was consistent with the initial biopsy diagnosis, with no discordant findings. Following the surgical procedure, the patient underwent adjuvant chemotherapy but did not receive radiotherapy, as it was considered unnecessary.

Until August 20, 2026, the patient was monitored clinically for a duration of 5 years. Throughout this follow‐up period, he maintained good clinical health, with no indications of local recurrence or other complications related to the disease.

case_text:
A woman in her 40s was evaluated due to recurrent haemoptysis. She had been aware of a right chest wall deformity since childhood and had no history of chest trauma. Eighteen months previously, she was examined at another hospital due to haemoptysis, which resolved spontaneously. At that time, chest CT revealed right middle lobe consolidation and nodular shadows with right rib deformity. Fourteen months later, she developed recurrent haemoptysis. Follow‐up CT suggested bleeding from the right middle lobe, and she was referred to our hospital.

At presentation, the haemoptysis had subsided and her vital signs were stable. Physical examination was unremarkable except for slight depression of the right chest wall. Chest radiography showed ground‐glass opacities in the right middle lung field and fusion of the right fourth and fifth ribs (Figure 1A). Chest CT revealed consolidation and bronchiectasis in the right middle lobe and fusion of the right fourth and fifth ribs (Figure 1B,C). Pulmonary function tests (PFTs) showed normal findings. Dynamic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed limited respiratory motion of the chest wall and adjacent lung region at the level of the fused ribs (Figure 1D and Video 1A). Exploratory quantitative motion analysis was subsequently performed using regions of interest placed in the anterior chest wall and adjacent lung region (Figure 1D). Laboratory findings were unremarkable except for positive serum anti‐ M. avium complex antibodies. Repeated sputum examinations, including acid‐fast bacilli smear, culture and polymerase chain reaction, failed to identify any pathogenic organisms. CT angiography revealed no vascular source of bleeding.

Despite the lack of microbiological confirmation, based on the imaging and serological findings, right middle lobe M. avium complex disease was suspected. The local mechanical effect of the fused ribs was considered a possible additional factor. Given the recurrent haemoptysis and localised lesion, video‐assisted thoracoscopic right middle lobectomy was planned (Figure 2A). Thoracoscopic inspection revealed that the fused segment of the right fourth and fifth ribs protruded into the pleural space (Figure 2B), compressing the adjacent right middle lobe. The compression was primarily attributable to the fused portion of the fourth rib; thus, the fused rib segment was divided (Figure 2C), and partial resection of the right fourth rib was performed (Figure 2D). Right middle lobectomy was performed during the same operation (Figure 2E).

Histopathological examination revealed bronchiectasis and granulomatous inflammation consistent with NTM infection, although no acid‐fast bacilli were identified using Ziehl–Neelsen staining. Microbiological analysis identified M. avium . Postoperative dynamic MRI showed increased regional respiratory motion in the affected area (Video 1B). As an exploratory analysis, frame‐to‐frame displacement was quantified within regions of interest (ROIs) placed in the anterior chest wall and the adjacent lung region using a custom MATLAB (MathWorks) program implementing the Farnebäck optical flow method. Mean and peak displacement per frame were derived from frame‐wise ROI‐averaged displacement measurements across respiratory motion phases. Identical imaging conditions and frame intervals were used before and after surgery. In the adjacent lung region, mean displacement per frame increased from 0.188 to 0.219 mm/frame, and peak displacement per frame increased from 0.236 to 0.281 mm/frame (Video 2A,B). In the anterior chest wall, mean displacement per frame increased from 0.175 mm/frame preoperatively to 0.205 mm/frame postoperatively, and peak displacement per frame increased from 0.253 to 0.336 mm/frame (Video 2C,D). The patient has remained free of haemoptysis, and M. avium complex disease did not recur during 6 months of follow‐up.

case_text:
A 33-year-old primigravida was diagnosed with velamentous cord insertion (VCI) by color Doppler ultrasound during the routine fetal anomaly scan at 21 weeks of gestation (Figure 1).

At 37 weeks of gestation, she was admitted to the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology for planned cesarean delivery. On admission, her recorded vital signs included a blood pressure of 125/68 mmHg, a temperature of 36oC, a pulse rate of 80 beats per minute, a respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute, and an oxygen saturation level of 98%. Her body mass index (BMI) was reported to be normal at 23.5 kg/m2. Her medical history was notable for serious cardiac arrhythmias and a previously implanted permanent pacemaker. No other relevant medical conditions or drug allergies were reported, and she did not report smoking or alcohol consumption. This was her first pregnancy, conceived naturally without the use of assisted reproductive technology. Gynecological history indicated that menarche started at age 12, with menstrual cycles occurring every 28 days and lasting four days. A prior Pap smear examination yielded a negative result for malignancy. On obstetrical vaginal examination, a 0 cm cervical dilatation was recorded. A non-stress test (NST) performed at admission was reported as reactive, with brief intermittent variable decelerations (Figure 2).

Preoperative laboratory investigations included the following findings: hemoglobin 13.3 g/dL, hematocrit 39.7%, platelet count 194 × 10³/μL, and white blood cell count 11.24 × 10³/μL with neutrophils at 70.5%. Coagulation parameters included an international normalized ratio (INR) of 0.98 and activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) of 25.4 seconds. Renal and liver functions were also normal, with creatinine at 0.78 mg/dL and urea at 22 mg/dL. Serial laboratory measurements, including a postoperative rise in white blood cell and neutrophil counts and a decline in hemoglobin by day four, are presented in Table 1.

The patient was prepared by the nursing staff for the scheduled cesarean section. At the theatre, the patient was positioned supine under general anesthesia. Α Pfannenstiel transverse skin incision was made; the abdominal wall tissues were opened, and we identified the pregnant uterus. A low transverse uterine incision was performed, and a male neonate weighing 2,160 g was delivered. This meets the definition of low birth weight (<2,500 g). The placenta was delivered following the administration of 4 IU of oxytocin diluted in 500 mL of normal saline, with gentle application of the Credé maneuver to the uterine fundus to promote uterine contraction and reduce the risk of postpartum hemorrhage. On physical examination, VCI of the placenta was identified (Figure 3).

The uterine incision was sutured in two layers, and hemostasis was confirmed throughout the surgical area. Examination of the ovaries and fallopian tubes revealed no abnormalities. The layers of the abdominal wall were carefully returned to their proper anatomical arrangement, and the skin was closed with continuous intradermal stitches. Her postoperative course was uneventful. Her daily medical regimen in postpartum care included administration of methylergometrine in 3 L normal saline for two days. Ferrous sulfate 800 mg/15 mL twice daily for one month. Calcium 500 mg was administered twice daily for one month. Tinzaparin sodium 4,500 IU was administered subcutaneously once daily for 15 days as postoperative thromboprophylaxis, and cefuroxime twice daily for three days. Both the mother and the neonate were discharged on the fourth day after admission. At the gynecology outpatient follow-up visit 40 days postpartum, the mother was reported to be in good overall health.

case_text: A female fetus was prenatally diagnosed with a giant SCT around 20 weeks of gestation and was referred to our tertiary referral center for further evaluation at approximately 22 weeks. Antenatal ultrasound at 30 0/7 weeks of gestation showed progressive tumor growth with a large external component measuring 13.5 × 9.6 × 10 cm and increasing polyhydramnios. Minimal pericardial effusion was observed, without evidence of cardiac failure or fetal hydrops. A planned cesarean section was performed at 32 0/7 weeks of gestation due to the tumor size and anticipated perinatal risks. The neonate was born with an estimated birth weight of 1,600 g (excluding the tumor) and Apgar scores of 5 and 6 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. The infant required endotracheal intubation shortly after birth due to respiratory insufficiency resulting from mechanical airway obstruction because of difficult head and body positioning due to the SCT. On physical examination, a large sacrococcygeal mass was present with superficial skin excoriations and oozing. The neonate was hemodynamically stable and was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) performed within the first hours after birth confirmed a giant SCT with a predominantly cystic external component measuring 15 × 15 × 9 cm and a smaller intra-abdominal extension of 5.5 × 5 × 3 cm ( Fig. 1 ). The intra-abdominal component extended cranially to just below the level of the superior mesenteric artery. The mass displaced adjacent abdominal organs without evidence of solid organ invasion. In the hours after birth, recurrent oozing from the tumor was observed, accompanied by a mild decline in hemoglobin from 6.6 to 5.5 mmol/L, requiring red blood cell transfusion. Given the high risk of intraoperative hemorrhage, preoperative angiographic assessment was performed within 12 hours after birth. Angiography demonstrated a relatively small middle sacral artery, while the dominant tumor supply originated from hypertrophic branches of the bilateral internal iliac arteries ( Fig. 2A ). Selective glue embolization of the major feeding vessels was performed via femoral and axillary arterial access ( Fig. 2B, C ). Approximately 6 hours after embolization, the infant developed transient hyperkalemia, with arterial potassium levels rising to 7.3 mmol/L, suggestive of tumor lysis. The hyperkalemia resolved after treatment with glucose and insulin infusion for 48 hours. On the second day of life, surgical resection of the 1,100 g tumor, including coccygectomy, was performed via an open posterior approach. The neonate weighed 2,100 g following resection. In addition, a laparotomy was performed to address the intra-abdominal component, which proved to be cystic without evidence of a solid residual tumor. Blood products were prepared in advance and administered throughout the procedure, including 280 mL packed red blood cells, 160 mL plasma, and 48 mL platelets. Hemodynamic stability was maintained throughout the procedure, and the estimated blood loss was approximately 500 mL. The defect was closed by a plastic surgeon using local flaps. Postoperatively, the infant was monitored in the NICU and remained hemodynamically stable, with vasopressor support discontinued on the first postoperative day. Eleven days after the surgery, the postoperative course was complicated by a bilateral chylothorax requiring thoracic drainage and a special diet. Although the exact etiology of the chylothorax remained uncertain, this may have been related to disruption of abdominal lymphatic channels during the extensive abdominal dissection. The surgical wound healed adequately, and the infant was discharged from the NICU 4 weeks after birth and was subsequently discharged home 2 months after birth at 40 2/7 weeks of gestational age. Histopathological examination confirmed an immature teratoma (grade 2) without evidence of malignancy. At follow-up, α-fetoprotein levels decreased from 14,000 µg/L in the first week of life to 48 µg/L at 3 months and 39 µg/L at 6 months, with no evidence of residual or recurrent SCT on ultrasound. At follow-up at 6 months of age, overall development appeared appropriate for age; however, long-term functional outcomes, including bowel and urinary function, cannot yet be assessed.

case_text:
A 90-year-old woman was admitted with a painful right hip and a progressively enlarging right gluteal mass associated with bleeding, drainage, and exposure of the prosthesis.

Nine years previously, she had sustained a right femoral neck fracture treated with bipolar hemiarthroplasty through an anterolateral approach. The postoperative course was complicated by infection, wound-healing problems, and intermittent fistula formation. She ambulated with a walker for approximately 2 years but subsequently became wheelchair-dependent because of progressive hip pain.

During the following years, a gradually enlarging gluteal mass developed. Eventually, the overlying skin broke down, with bleeding, drainage, and surrounding inflammation. On admission, the metallic bipolar component was visibly protruding through an ulcerated defect in the gluteal skin (Fig. 1A and B).

Laboratory investigations showed haemoglobin 98 g/l, erythrocytes 3.73 × 1012/l, haematocrit 0.31, and C-reactive protein 23.8 mg/l. Alkaline phosphatase was 157 U/l, uric acid 455 μmol/l, and albumin 33 g/l. Other laboratory findings were within normal limits. A microbiological wound swab was negative.

Pelvic radiography demonstrated marked superolateral migration of the right bipolar hemiarthroplasty, with the prosthetic head positioned outside the native acetabular region and extensive destruction and remodelling of the proximal femur (Fig. 2). Computed tomography (CT) angiography, including scout/localizer images and axial contrast-enhanced imaging, confirmed pronounced posterolateral displacement of the prosthesis into the right gluteal soft tissues (Fig. 3A–C). CT angiography was specifically obtained to evaluate the regional vascular anatomy and potential risk of vascular injury during extraction.

Surgery was performed under spinal anaesthesia. Despite transcutaneous extrusion, simple traction failed to remove the implant because it remained firmly entrapped within the surrounding soft tissues. Surgical dissection and release were required for controlled extraction. A cavity containing necrotic tissue was identified and extensive debridement performed. Cultures remained negative.

Considering the patient’s advanced age, preoperative wheelchair dependence, general condition, and extensive local tissue destruction, immediate reimplantation was not planned. The wound was closed over a drain, which was removed after 3 days (Fig. 4).

Ceftriaxone 2 g daily was administered during the 7-day hospitalization, followed by oral cefixime for 10 days. At 1-month follow-up, the wound had healed without recurrent fistula or drainage. The patient’s general condition and pain had improved, although she remained wheelchair-dependent.

case_text:
A 75-year-old man with opioid use disorder maintained on methadone 80 mg daily presented with nausea, vomiting, and chills after missing two to three consecutive doses. His history included hypertension, alcohol use disorder in remission, untreated hepatitis C, and major depressive disorder. Five months earlier he had presented with sudden chest pain and dyspnoea and a raised high-sensitivity troponin; the electrocardiogram (ECG) showed sinus rhythm without ischaemic ST-segment or T-wave change, coronary angiography demonstrated non-obstructive disease, and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed normal biventricular systolic function and no late gadolinium enhancement (see Supplementary material online, Figure S1). One month before the index admission he re-presented with the same syndrome and a further troponin rise; the ECG then showed a new incomplete left bundle branch block (LBBB), and regadenoson stress positron emission tomography (PET), performed to assess for inducible ischaemia and possible coronary microvascular dysfunction, demonstrated normal perfusion with reduced global myocardial flow reserve (Figure 1). Each episode was diagnosed as myocardial infarction with non-obstructive coronary arteries (MINOCA), and each occurred during opioid withdrawal. Home medications were amlodipine 10 mg, isosorbide mononitrate 90 mg, aspirin, atorvastatin, duloxetine, and trazodone.

On arrival, blood pressure was 153/90 mmHg, heart rate 81 b.p.m., and oxygen saturation 98% on room air; examination was notable for cachexia, diaphoresis, and mild diffuse abdominal tenderness. ECG showed sinus rhythm with incomplete LBBB unchanged from prior tracings (Figure 2A), troponin I was undetectable, and creatinine was 1.5 mg/dL (baseline 0.8 mg/dL). Urine toxicology was positive for methadone. He received intravenous fluids and ondansetron for prerenal acute kidney injury and nausea.

The following evening he developed dull left-sided chest pain radiating to the left arm and jaw, with blood pressure 121/72 mmHg and heart rate 52 b.p.m.; the cardiopulmonary examination was unchanged. The differential included plaque rupture, supply-demand mismatch, vasospasm, stress-induced cardiomyopathy, and myocarditis. Repeat ECG demonstrated first-degree atrioventricular block with dynamic ST-segment elevation in the precordial (V1–V6) and inferior (II, III, aVF) leads (Figure 2B); troponin I rose to 0.9 ng/mL (reference 0.00–0.30) and lactate to 3.3 mmol/L. After aspirin 325 mg, atorvastatin, morphine, sublingual nitroglycerine, and intravenous heparin, emergent angiography revealed a right-dominant system with severe narrowing of the mid right coronary (RCA) and mid left anterior descending (LAD) arteries (Figure 3A,B; Supplementary material online, Videos S1 and S2), both improving markedly after intracoronary nitroglycerine with approximately 40% residual stenosis (Figure 3C,D; Supplementary material online, Videos S3 and S4). Three hours later, ECG showed near-complete resolution of the inferior ST-segment elevation (Figure 2C).

In the cardiac care unit, duloxetine and trazodone were discontinued because serotonergic agents may promote coronary vasoconstriction. Amlodipine and isosorbide mononitrate were exchanged for nifedipine 90 mg daily and isosorbide dinitrate 40 mg three times daily; recurrent chest pain prompted a continuous nitroglycerine infusion, after which he became pain-free, and oral nitrates were resumed on day 5. Echocardiography on day 3 showed an ejection fraction of 35% with hypokinesis and akinesis of the anterior, anteroseptal, septal, and inferior walls; by day 6, the ejection fraction had normalized to 69% with a resolution of all wall motion abnormalities (see Supplementary material online, Videos S1 and S2). By day 16, the ECG had returned to its baseline pattern (Figure 2D). He was discharged on day 19 on nifedipine 90 mg daily, isosorbide mononitrate 60 mg daily, and sublingual nitroglycerine as required, with addiction medicine follow-up to ensure uninterrupted methadone. Two months after discharge, he remained well, with no further admissions or emergency department attendances for angina.

case_text:
A 39‐year‐old man with epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)‐positive metastatic lung adenocarcinoma was treated with osimertinib after baseline positron emission tomography‐computed tomography (PET–CT) demonstrated a hypermetabolic right lung mass with nodal, hepatic, and osseous metastases. After 6 months, follow‐up imaging showed a complete metabolic response, and treatment was discontinued. Six months later, surveillance PET–CT raised concern for metastatic recurrence, and osimertinib was resumed.

Three months after restarting osimertinib, he developed unilateral left lower‐limb pain and swelling. Compression duplex ultrasonography showed extensive subacute deep vein thrombosis (DVT) involving the left iliac, femoral, popliteal, and calf veins, and anticoagulation was initiated and continued thereafter. Despite ongoing anticoagulation, dyspnea progressively worsened over the following three months. Computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA) confirmed acute massive pulmonary embolism (PE) with right ventricular (RV) strain (Figure 1A1–A3).

Transthoracic echocardiography showed a left ventricular ejection fraction (EF) of 55%, severe RV enlargement, moderate RV systolic dysfunction, and an estimated pulmonary artery pressure (PAP) of 75 mmHg.

Because of progressive dyspnea, oxygen dependence, and severe pulmonary hypertension, the first bedside electrical impedance tomography (EIT) examination was performed while the patient was spontaneously breathing. EIT was performed using an Infivision ET1000 system with a 16‐electrode thoracic belt positioned at the 4th–5th intercostal space in the supine position, in accordance with current consensus recommendations for EIT examination. Data were acquired at a sampling rate of 20 frames per second for 60 s (approximately 1200 image frames). Regional ventilation was derived from respiration‐related impedance changes. The cardiac‐synchronous pulsatility signal was separated from the respiration‐related impedance signal using the device's built‐in frequency‐domain separation, with a cut‐off frequency distinguishing the cardiac‐rate and respiratory‐rate impedance bands, and was used for non‐contrast regional perfusion mapping. The device's Match View function co‐registered the regional ventilation and perfusion maps on a pixel‐by‐pixel basis to generate ventilation–perfusion matching images.

Preoperative non‐contrast, pulsatility‐based perfusion mapping (the device's heart‐pulsation‐based “HPB” dynamic and status displays; Figure 1B1) demonstrated marked regional perfusion asymmetry: the right and left hemithoraces accounted for 60% and 40% of the total perfusion signal, respectively. At the quadrant level, the right upper, right lower, left upper, and left lower regions accounted for 48%, 12%, 20%, and 20% of global perfusion, respectively, indicating that the perfusion deficit was most pronounced in the dependent lower regions, with overall perfusion relatively reduced on the left side. Simultaneously recorded regional ventilation was comparatively preserved and symmetric (51% vs. 49%, right/left), and the Match View image demonstrated regional ventilation–perfusion mismatch characterized by underperfusion despite preserved ventilation (Figure 1B2). The device‐derived Match, Shunt, and Dead‐space indices were 0.70, 0.10, and 0.20, respectively (Table 1). Lung perfusion scintigraphy showed heterogeneous radiotracer distribution with multiple segmental perfusion defects, most prominent in the lower lung zones (Figure 1C1,C2); the regional distribution of these defects was broadly concordant with the areas of reduced perfusion signal on EIT. Thereafter, the patient's clinical condition deteriorated, and he was admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) because of worsening dyspnea, increasing oxygen requirements, and hypoxemia. Repeat echocardiography showed a left ventricular EF of 40%–45%, severe RV enlargement, severe RV systolic dysfunction, abnormal septal motion with septal bowing toward the left ventricle, and an estimated pulmonary artery pressure of approximately 100 mmHg. Right‐heart catheterization subsequently confirmed severe precapillary pulmonary hypertension, with a pulmonary artery pressure of 100/30 mmHg, mean pulmonary artery pressure 53 mmHg, pulmonary capillary wedge pressure 12 mmHg, pulmonary vascular resistance 25 Wood units, right atrial pressure 9 mmHg, and cardiac index 0.8 L/min/m2. The findings supported acute‐on‐chronic thromboembolic pulmonary vascular disease culminating in chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH).

case_text:
A 71-year-old woman with arterial hypertension, grade II obesity [body mass index (BMI) of 36.4 kg/m2], symptomatic cholelithiasis and an 8-year history of VH, with no prior surgery. She reported progressive enlargement of the hernia and episodes of colicky abdominal pain. Physical examination revealed an irreducible VH measuring ~20 × 25 cm in the upper hemiabdomen, soft in consistency and non-tender (Fig. 1).

She was assessed by a multidisciplinary team comprising cardiology, respiratory medicine, dietetics, psychology, surgery, and anaesthesiology. Abdominal CT revealed a hernia sac containing the stomach, transverse colon, small bowel and greater omentum, together with cholelithiasis. The fascial defect measured 6.58 × 4.79 cm, HSV was 2657 cm3, and ACV was 4631 cm3 (Fig. 2A and B). The Sabbagh index was 36.5%, confirming VHLD.

After obtaining informed consent, preoperative optimization was carried out. The BMI was reduced to 29.3 kg/m2, and specialist assessments were normal. A total of 300 IU of BTX (Botox®) was administered by an interventional radiologist, in the presence of the surgeon, under ultrasound guidance and using aseptic technique. The toxin was diluted in 10 ml of 0.9% saline, with 1 ml (30 IU) injected at each infiltration site in the internal oblique muscle, following the Ibarra-Hurtado technique (Fig. 3A and B). Three weeks later, PPP was initiated using the Goñi Moreno technique, with a catheter placed at Palmer’s point. Daily volumes of 500 to 1000 ml of air were administered for 14 days, up to a cumulative total of 13 500 ml, with IAP monitoring (Fig. 4). PPP was discontinued at the patient’s request due to abdominal discomfort.

Follow-up CT showed partial reduction of the hernia contents and defect, expansion of abdominal capacity, and thinning of the lateral muscles. ACV reached 6285.5 cm3 (a 35.7% increase) (Fig. 2D and E). As the 36.5% threshold calculated using the Sabbagh index was not reached, omentectomy was proposed to the patient as an alternative to facilitate tension-free repair. Antibiotic prophylaxis was administered as recommended by the EHS/Americas Hernia Society (AHS), International Endohernia Society, and the Society of American Gastrointestinal and Endoscopic Surgeons (SAGES) for mesh procedures.

Follow-up CT demonstrated partial reduction in the hernia contents and defect, increased ACV, and thinning of the lateral abdominal muscles. The ACV reached 6285.5 cm3 (a 35.7% increase) (Fig. 2D and E).

An open approach was performed via a supraumbilical midline incision and opening of the hernia sac; the greater omentum was found adhered to it, and both structures were fully resected (Fig. 5B). Cholecystectomy was also performed. After posterior fascial closure, a medium-weight macroporous polypropylene mesh was placed in the retromuscular plane, extending 5 cm beyond the defect (Fig. 5C). The anterior sheath was closed with polypropylene 1 (Fig. 5D), excess skin was resected, a subcutaneous Jackson-Pratt drain was placed, and closure was completed in layers.

The postoperative course was favourable, with normal IAP. The patient was discharged on the third day, and the drain was removed on the 10th (Fig. 6A). At 15 months’ follow-up, she showed satisfactory healing (Fig. 6B and C), and CT demonstrated muscular recovery with no hernia recurrence (Fig. 7).

title: Ventral hernia with loss of domain: a multimodal strategy with botulinum toxin, progressive pneumoperitoneum, omentectomy, and retromuscular reconstruction. Case report and literature review

case_text:
A 17-year-old male presented with a 2-month history of diffuse abdominal pain that had recently worsened and radiated to the left hypochondrium and lumbar region, accompanied by constitutional symptoms. On admission, he was tachycardic. Abdominal examination revealed deep tenderness predominantly in the epigastrium and left hypochondrium.

Laboratory investigations demonstrated a white blood cell count of 15 560/μl with 80% neutrophils, hemoglobin of 11.4 g/dl, and a platelet count of 487 000/μl.

Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a rounded hypoechoic lesion measuring 5.0 × 5.9 × 4.8 cm, with an estimated volume of 76.4 ml, located at the inferior pole of the spleen. Peripheral vascularity was observed on color Doppler imaging, initially raising suspicion of a splenic neoplastic lesion (Fig. 1).

Subsequent contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a large splenic collection with an estimated volume of 96 ml and capsular rupture. Imaging also revealed complicated appendicitis involving a pelvic appendix with an extraluminal appendicolith and multiple intra-abdominal collections involving the parasplenic, supravesical, and parailiac regions (Figs 2–4).

Given the extent of intra-abdominal infection and the need for definitive source control, exploratory laparoscopy was undertaken. Severe adhesions and a dense inflammatory plastron involving the omentum and small bowel loops prevented safe laparoscopic dissection, requiring conversion to open laparotomy.

Intraoperative exploration revealed a pelvic appendix perforated at its middle third, with free appendicoliths adjacent to the mesenteric root. Multiple localized purulent collections were identified, including approximately 100 ml in the pelvis, 100 ml in the splenic region, and 50 ml between small bowel loops.

Appendectomy, drainage of all identified collections, and extensive peritoneal lavage were performed. Splenectomy was not required, allowing successful splenic preservation. Two Jackson–Pratt drains were placed.

Empirical intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy was initiated. Culture of the purulent material isolated Escherichia coli susceptible to the tested antimicrobial agents, and antimicrobial therapy was subsequently guided by the susceptibility results.

The postoperative course was uncomplicated, with progressive clinical improvement and no evidence of persistent intra-abdominal infection. The drains were removed, and the patient was discharged on postoperative day 5. At the 15-day outpatient follow-up, he remained asymptomatic with complete clinical resolution.

title: Splenic abscess with capsular rupture associated with perforated appendicitis in an adolescent: a rare case report

case_text:
A 76-year-old man with left main and triple-vessel coronary artery disease underwent emergency coronary artery bypass grafting under cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB). The LIMA was harvested using a takedown-pattern retractor. After an uneventful side-to-side anastomosis to the LAD was completed, transit-time flow measurement (TTFM) demonstrated severely reduced graft flow.

Suspecting a technical problem, we reopened the distal end of the LIMA, but almost no bleeding was observed. We then conducted a systematic evaluation. Antegrade cardioplegia was administered through the aortic root. Brisk efflux of cardioplegic solution from the reopened distal LIMA demonstrated unobstructed passage from the LAD through the side-to-side LIMA-LAD anastomosis, suggesting that the anastomosis was patent and technically satisfactory. Gentle probe passage excluded conduit stenosis. Neither direct stretching of the LIMA pedicle nor conduit kinking was evident on visual inspection. The graft remained appropriately oriented without obvious twisting or positional deformation. In addition, no mediastinal structure capable of causing focal compression of the graft was identified. After these evaluations failed to identify an anastomotic, conduit-related, or mechanical cause of the reduced flow, brisk free flow immediately returned once the sternal retractor was released.

Following reclosure of the distal LIMA, TTFM confirmed adequate graft flow only when the sternum was approximated, whereas excessive retraction consistently produced a characteristic to-and-fro pattern, strongly suggesting a dynamic, retraction-dependent inflow disturbance (Figure 1).

Sequential saphenous vein grafts to the left circumflex artery and posterior descending artery were completed, and the patient was weaned uneventfully from CPB. Postoperative CT angiography confirmed the patency of all grafts.

Intraoperatively, we observed a markedly asymmetric pattern of sternal opening during wide sternal retraction, which we termed ‘unilateral sternal retraction’. Specifically, the right sternal edge exhibited minimal displacement, whereas the left sternal edge showed excessive lateral displacement. As demonstrated in Supplementary material online, Video S1, the right sternal edge (blue line) remained nearly stationary despite progressive opening of the retractor, while the left sternal edge (red line) moved markedly laterally. During observation of the left thoracic cavity, a second-rib fracture and buckling of the lower ribs at the costal cartilage were identified. Postoperative computed tomography subsequently revealed an additional fracture of the left first rib. These findings suggested the presence of multiple left-sided rib injuries that may have contributed to asymmetric chest wall compliance and thereby predisposed the sternum to open unevenly during retraction.

case_text:
A 52‐year‐old woman was admitted to our hospital with a one‐year history of recurrent upper abdominal pain. One year prior to admission, she developed paroxysmal, colicky upper abdominal pain without an obvious precipitating factor. The pain was severe, radiated to the back, and was accompanied by nausea but no vomiting. There were no associated chills or fever; however, jaundice of the skin and sclera was noted. She was initially evaluated at an outside hospital, where abdominal computed tomography (CT) revealed cholelithiasis with cholecystitis and situs inversus totalis. Oral analgesic therapy provided temporary relief of symptoms, but the condition recurred intermittently.

For further evaluation and treatment, the patient presented to our hospital on February 26, 2025, and was admitted with the diagnoses of (1) cholecystitis with cholelithiasis, (2) choledocholithiasis, and (3) situs inversus totalis. She had no significant past medical history.

On admission, physical examination revealed the following vital signs: temperature 36.2°C, pulse 97 beats/min, respiratory rate 21 breaths/min, and blood pressure 125/88 mmHg. Jaundice of the skin and sclera was evident. Mild tenderness was noted in the epigastric region without rebound tenderness or muscular guarding. Murphy's sign was negative. Abdominal percussion revealed tympany throughout, with no shifting dullness. Bowel sounds were normal.

Laboratory investigations showed a white blood cell count of 5.63 × 109/L, red blood cell count of 5.32 × 1012/L, hemoglobin level of 153 g/L, and platelet count of 233 × 109/L. Liver function tests demonstrated marked hyperbilirubinemia, with a total bilirubin level of 155.1 μmol/L, direct bilirubin 82.0 μmol/L, and indirect bilirubin 78.1 μmol/L. Alanine aminotransferase was 126 U/L, and aspartate aminotransferase was 53 U/L.

case_text:
A previously healthy, fully vaccinated 5‐year‐old boy presented to the emergency department with two episodes of large‐volume hematemesis occurring 1 h apart. Each episode consisted of fresh blood and clots, without preceding retching, vomiting, or abdominal pain. There was no history of prior epistaxis, hemoptysis, trauma, or bleeding from other sites.

Two weeks earlier, he had developed progressive right‐sided neck swelling, initially presumed to be tonsillitis or mumps, for which no treatment was received. There was no history of fever, cough, weight loss, or recent dental procedures. His past medical history and family history were unremarkable.

On arrival, his vital signs were within normal limits for age, and he was alert and hemodynamically stable. Physical examination showed a non‐pulsatile swelling over the right side of the neck, without overlying erythema, along with tender cervical lymphadenopathy. There was no pallor, respiratory distress, or neurological deficits. The abdomen was soft and non‐tender with no hepatosplenomegaly.

case_text:
We present the case of a 65‐year‐old female with a past medical history of nephrolithiasis, hypertension, and past surgical history of total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingectomy who presented to the hospital with a chief complaint of abdominal pain lasting 3 days. On presentation to the emergency department, the patient was tachycardic and normotensive. Physical exam demonstrated a non‐distended abdomen and palpable groin bulge with tenderness and guarding in the right lower quadrant. Labs showed an elevated white blood cell count. Due to concerns for incarceration and leukocytosis, CT of the abdomen and pelvis was performed and showed AH with initial concern for acute appendicitis (Losanoff and Basson Type 2), with concern for fluid around the appendix in the hernia sac (Figures 1 and 2). Antibiotics using ceftriaxone and metronidazole were initiated in the emergency department. She had severe pain, and after discussion of the risks and benefits of surgery, the patient agreed to proceed with open right inguinal hernia repair with potential open appendectomy vs. laparoscopic appendectomy.

She was taken to the operating room and placed in a supine position. General anesthesia was induced, and the abdomen and pelvis were prepped. Initial plans were for open right inguinal hernia repair with tissue closure without mesh placement due to active infection, with potential open appendectomy vs. laparoscopic. An incision was made 2 cm above the inguinal ligament using the landmarks of the right anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic tubercle. The incision was carried through subcutaneous tissue down to the level of external oblique aponeurosis. Using a 15‐blade aponeurosis, it was dissected along its fibers. The aponeurosis was split medially and laterally to the level of the external ring using Metzenbaum scissors. The hernia sac was identified, the round ligament was encircled with a Penrose drain, and a small cord lipoma was identified; however, the appendix was not easily visualized within the hernia sac. Discussion was had that the appendix likely reduced back into the abdomen upon induction of anesthesia or during manipulation of the hernia.

The decision was made to proceed with laparoscopic appendectomy; an infraumbilical incision was made to accommodate a 15 mm port via an open Hassan cutdown. Two additional ports were placed under laparoscopic visualization in the suprapubic and left lower quadrant. Laparoscopy showed evidence of bilateral inguinal hernias, which appeared to be indirect in nature. The appendix was identified within the right inguinal hernia, it was necrotic, and it was carefully reduced into the abdominal cavity, and the mesoappendix was carefully dissected using a LigaSure Bipolar device. The base of the appendix was stapled using an Endo‐GIA stapler 45 mm gray load. After the removal of the appendix, attention was redirected back to the right inguinal hernia. A Bassini primary tissue repair was performed by suture‐ligating the hernia sac and the round ligament and then dividing it. The remainder of the hernia; sac was reduced into the abdominal cavity. The posterior wall was reconstructed using a 2‐0 Vicryl absorbable antibiotic‐coated suture to join the inguinal ligament to the conjoint tendon. The external oblique aponeurosis was approximated using a 3‐0 Vicryl absorbable antibiotic‐coated suture. This was used due to the concern for infection.

She was discharged the next day, tolerating a diet; her pain was well controlled and she had bowel function without antibiotics. She followed up in clinic 3 weeks later with no new symptoms. After a thorough discussion of the circumstances of her initial repair, she underwent definitive robotic bilateral inguinal hernia repairs with mesh 2 months later due to the presence of a contra‐lateral side.
