case_text:
A 60‐year‐old man with Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease Stage IV chronic obstructive pulmonary disease was referred for worsening exertional dyspnoea despite optimal inhaled therapy. He had a 52.5 pack‐year smoking history, modified Medical Research Council dyspnoea Grade III, and 6‐min walk distance (6MWD) of 324 m, with oxygen saturation decreasing to 86%. Post‐bronchodilator forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV1) was 0.78 L (24.7% predicted), residual volume 207.4% predicted and total lung capacity 128.0% predicted. Chest computed tomography (CT) demonstrated upper‐lobe predominant emphysema (Figure 1a,b) and StratX analysis confirmed > 95% completeness of both major fissures.

After absent collateral ventilation was confirmed using the Chartis system, 4.0‐mm Zephyr EBVs were placed in the left B1 + 2, B3a, B3b + c, B4 and B5 segmental bronchi (Figure 1c,d). Chest radiography 4 h after BLVR revealed a left pneumothorax (Figure 2a). An 18‐Fr chest tube was inserted and initially managed with water seal. Because the air leak persisted, −12 cmH2O suction was subsequently applied. Despite drainage, the air leak persisted with residual pneumothorax and subcutaneous emphysema (Figure 2b,c).

On Day 9, the air leak persisted with bubbling observed in the chest drainage system during expiration and was classified as Grade 2 (expiratory) according to the Cerfolio classification. ABP pleurodesis was performed before removal of any EBV. A total of 100 mL of autologous blood was instilled through the chest tube. The air leak resolved within 24 h. After a successful clamp test, the chest tube was removed on Day 16 (Figure 2d), without recurrence of pneumothorax. At 3 months, CT confirmed sustained left upper lobe atelectasis and resolution of the pneumothorax (Figure 2e). At 6 months, 6MWD had increased from 324 to 533 m and FEV1 from 24.7% to 34.2% predicted.

case_text:
A 17‐year‐old female with a 3‐year history of restricting‐type AN was admitted for nutritional rehabilitation. Her body weight was 31.3 kg and body mass index was 13.2 kg/m2. Laboratory evaluation on admission revealed severe iron‐deficiency anemia, with a hemoglobin concentration of 5.5 g/dL, serum iron concentration of 9 μg/dL, and ferritin concentration of 9.9 ng/mL. Fecal occult blood tests were negative, urinalysis was negative for occult blood, and the patient had amenorrhea. In the absence of an apparent source of blood loss, her markedly restricted dietary intake was considered a likely contributor to the iron‐deficiency anemia. Serum phosphate was 3.0 mg/dL. Serum intact FGF23, measured at admission as part of an observational study before intravenous iron administration, was within the reference range at 36.4 pg/mL. Serum 25‐hydroxyvitamin D was low at 15.2 ng/mL. Laboratory findings on admission and during hospitalization are summarized in Tables 1 and 2.

Nutritional rehabilitation was initiated at 1345 kcal/day according to our institutional refeeding protocol and progressively increased under close clinical and biochemical monitoring to 1942 kcal/day by hospital Day 7 and to a maximum of 3400 kcal/day by hospital Day 21. Prophylactic oral sodium phosphate supplementation was initiated on hospital Day 1 at 400 mg of elemental phosphorus/day (12.9 mmol phosphorus/day) because of the risk of refeeding‐related hypophosphatemia. Given the severity of the iron‐deficiency anemia and the need for prompt iron repletion, oral iron was considered unlikely to provide sufficiently rapid iron replacement. Intravenous saccharated ferric oxide was therefore initiated on hospital Day 3 at a dose equivalent to 80 mg/day of elemental iron. It was administered daily from hospital Days 3 to 15 and subsequently on alternate days (hospital Days 17, 19, 21, and 24), for a total elemental iron dose of 1360 mg.

Despite prophylactic phosphate supplementation, serum phosphate progressively decreased during nutritional rehabilitation. Serum phosphate first fell below the reference range on hospital Day 13, reaching 2.6 mg/dL. Refeeding‐related hypophosphatemia was initially suspected, and oral phosphate supplementation was gradually increased. Intravenous phosphate supplementation was subsequently added because serum phosphate continued to decline. However, hypophosphatemia persisted despite intensified oral and intravenous phosphate replacement. No concomitant hypokalemia or clinically meaningful hypomagnesemia was observed during the period of persistent hypophosphatemia.

Because hypophosphatemia persisted despite substantial phosphate supplementation, the underlying mechanism was reassessed. Renal phosphate handling was evaluated using paired serum and urine samples obtained in the morning under fasting conditions, before breakfast and before administration of the morning phosphate dose. The percentage of tubular reabsorption of phosphate (%TRP) was calculated as {1 − [(urine phosphate × serum creatinine)/(serum phosphate × urine creatinine)]} × 100. TmP/GFR was calculated as previously described. 16 With TRP expressed as a fraction, TmP/GFR was calculated as serum phosphate × TRP when TRP was ≤0.86 and as serum phosphate × [0.3 × TRP/(1 − 0.8 × TRP)] when TRP was >0.86.

Serum intact FGF23 was measured using a chemiluminescent enzyme immunoassay (Determiner CL FGF23 NX; Canon Medical Diagnostics Corporation, Tokyo, Japan) on a CL‐JACK NX analyzer. According to the manufacturer, the reference ranges (2.5th–97.5th percentiles) are 11.5–48.9 pg/mL in healthy adults and 12.9–51.2 pg/mL in healthy children.

On hospital Day 22, serum phosphate was 1.8 mg/dL (reference range, 2.7–4.6 mg/dL), while %TRP was 36.4% and TmP/GFR was 0.66 mg/dL. These findings were consistent with inappropriate renal phosphate wasting in the setting of hypophosphatemia. Serum intact FGF23, which had been 36.4 pg/mL before intravenous iron administration, increased markedly to 782 pg/mL on hospital Day 24 and subsequently peaked at 838 pg/mL on hospital Day 27. The combination of hypophosphatemia, impaired renal phosphate conservation, and marked elevation of intact FGF23 supported an FGF23‐mediated mechanism rather than an intracellular phosphate shift alone. Given the temporal relationship to saccharated ferric oxide exposure, intravenous iron‐associated FGF23‐mediated hypophosphatemia was regarded as the most likely explanation, and saccharated ferric oxide was discontinued on hospital Day 24.

Hypophosphatemia did not resolve immediately after discontinuation of intravenous iron. Intact FGF23 decreased to 482 pg/mL on hospital Day 29. Serum 1,25‐dihydroxyvitamin D decreased from 118 pg/mL on hospital Day 1 to 29 pg/mL on hospital Day 29, while intact parathyroid hormone remained within the reference range. On hospital Day 36, serum phosphate reached a nadir of 1.6 mg/dL, while %TRP decreased further to 7.1% and TmP/GFR to 0.11 mg/dL, indicating persistent and pronounced renal phosphate wasting. The clinical course, including phosphate supplementation, intravenous iron administration, alfacalcidol treatment, serum phosphate, intact FGF23, TmP/GFR, and %TRP, is shown in Figure 1a,b. Because hypophosphatemia persisted despite phosphate supplementation, alfacalcidol, an active vitamin D analog, was initiated on hospital Day 38, when intact FGF23 had decreased to 205 pg/mL. Serum phosphate gradually increased, reaching 3.2 mg/dL by hospital Day 58. Alfacalcidol was discontinued on hospital Day 55.

By hospital Day 57, intact FGF23 had decreased to 54.1 pg/mL. The patient was discharged with continued oral phosphate supplementation. Fifteen days after discharge, serum phosphate had increased to 3.8 mg/dL, allowing phosphate supplementation to be discontinued. No symptoms or organ dysfunction attributable to hypophosphatemia occurred during the clinical course.

case_text:
An ex‐term male born to consanguineous parents presented at 3 weeks‐of‐age in hypovolemic shock with significant metabolic acidosis. His parents reported up to 20 episodes of watery stool per day. Assessment with upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and flexible sigmoidoscopy was unremarkable and histopathology normal. Initial genetic screening with microarray was non‐diagnostic, however identified regions of homozygosity spanning 10.69% of the genome. Despite maximal enteral caloric provision, his diarrhoea continued with poor weight gain and PN was commenced. At 4 months‐of‐age, a trio whole‐exome sequence was performed, identifying a previously undescribed likely pathogenic homozygous missense mutation at codon 107 in NEUROG3 (c.320 G > A; p.Arg107His; gnomAD allele frequency 6.20e‐7), 5 found to be present in heterozygous form in both parents. He was discharged on home PN. He progressed onto oral diet with supplemental oral formula (Peptijunior®), achieving enteral autonomy at 2.5 years‐old.

At 3.5 years‐old, following a period of clinical stability, the patient presented with acute clinical deterioration. He had significantly increased stool output up to 2 L (164 mL/kg/day) and metabolic acidosis (pH 7.21, bicarbonate 14 mmol/L, base excess‐13), hypernatraemia (149 mEq/L), hypokalaemia (3.2 mEq/L), and dehydration requiring intravenous resuscitation (Supporting Information: Table 1). Multiple infectious screens were negative; blood glucose level and thyroid function were within normal limits; there were no consistent cytopaenias nor history of frequent infection to suggest immunodeficiency. Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth was considered given urine organic acids panel consistent with bacterial overgrowth, 6 however treatment with antibiotics yielded no clinical improvement. His stool output significantly decreased with gut rest, and PN was recommenced as an inpatient. After 2 weeks of unsuccessful attempts to re‐introduce oral or enteral feeding, coeliac serology returned strongly positive: tTg IgA > 128 U/mL (normal < 6), DGP IgG 133.9 U/mL (normal < 20). Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was performed showing flattened appearance of duodenal villi with scalloping; flexible sigmoidoscopy appearances were normal. Histology revealed moderate–marked villous blunting in duodenal biopsies, basal crypt hyperplasia and generalised intra‐epithelial lymphocytosis (IEL; 45 lymphocytes:100 enterocytes). Scattered enteroendocrine cells were noted (Figure 1). Rectal biopsies were normal. A diagnosis of coeliac disease was made and initiation of a gluten free (GF) diet led to rapid clinical improvement with cessation of PN 2‐weeks later.

Over the next 12 months, the patient reported ongoing clinical improvement on a strict GF diet with frequent dietician review to ensure adherence. However, weight gain became suboptimal in the context of progressive refusal of supplemmental oral formula. Further work‐up identified a very low faecal elastase (<15 mg/g) and he was commenced on pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy. Reassessment endoscopy opportunistically done at the time of a planned nasogastric tube insertion (after 8 months on strict GF diet) showed macroscopic improvement, confirmed on histology (milder villous blunting without basal crypt hyperplasia and IEL (35:100) (Figure 1) despite persistently high antibody titres (DGP IgG 198.7 U/mL, tTG IgA >128 U/mL). Weight gain improved significantly with enteral supplementation via nasogastric tube (Figure 2). Further reassessment 7 months later (5 years‐old) at the time of elective percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy insertion showed similar findings (DGP 81.1 U/mL, tTG 113 U/mL, histology with patchy areas of villous blunting, IEL 35:100).

Although this patient remains unaffected by diabetes mellitus at 5 years‐old, autoimmune screening post coeliac diagnosis identified autoimmune thyroid disease and he commenced thyroxine replacement therapy. He was also noted to have asthma and atopic dermatitis. Although there is a paternal history of hypothyroidism, these evolutions alongside concurrent coeliac disease, sparks the question of potential autoimmune associations in NEUROG3.

At 4 months‐of‐age, a trio whole‐exome sequence was performed, identifying a previously undescribed likely pathogenic homozygous missense mutation at codon 107 in NEUROG3 (c.320 G > A; p.Arg107His; gnomAD allele frequency 6.20e‐7), 5 found to be present in heterozygous form in both parents.
He was discharged on home PN.
He progressed onto oral diet with supplemental oral formula (Peptijunior®), achieving enteral autonomy at 2.5 years‐old.
At 3.5 years‐old, following a period of clinical stability, the patient presented with acute clinical deterioration.

He had significantly increased stool output up to 2 L (164 mL/kg/day) and metabolic acidosis (pH 7.21, bicarbonate 14 mmol/L, base excess‐13), hypernatraemia (149 mEq/L), hypokalaemia (3.2 mEq/L), and dehydration requiring intravenous resuscitation (Supporting Information: Table 1).

Multiple infectious screens were negative; blood glucose level and thyroid function were within normal limits; there were no consistent cytopaenias nor history of frequent infection to suggest immunodeficiency.
Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth was considered given urine organic acids panel consistent with bacterial overgrowth, 6 however treatment with antibiotics yielded no clinical improvement.
His stool output significantly decreased with gut rest, and PN was recommenced as an inpatient.
After 2 weeks of unsuccessful attempts to re‐introduce oral or enteral feeding, coeliac serology returned strongly positive: tTg IgA > 128 U/mL (normal < 6), DGP IgG 133.9 U/mL (normal < 20).
Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was performed showing flattened appearance of duodenal villi with scalloping; flexible sigmoidoscopy appearances were normal.
Histology revealed moderate–marked villous blunting in duodenal biopsies, basal crypt hyperplasia and generalised intra‐epithelial lymphocytosis (IEL; 45 lymphocytes:100 enterocytes).
Scattered enteroendocrine cells were noted (Figure 1).
Rectal biopsies were normal.
A diagnosis of coeliac disease was made and initiation of a gluten free (GF) diet led to rapid clinical improvement with cessation of PN 2‐weeks later.
Over the next 12 months, the patient reported ongoing clinical improvement on a strict GF diet with frequent dietician review to ensure adherence.
However, weight gain became suboptimal in the context of progressive refusal of supplemmental oral formula.
Further work‐up identified a very low faecal elastase (<15 mg/g) and he was commenced on pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy.

Reassessment endoscopy opportunistically done at the time of a planned nasogastric tube insertion (after 8 months on strict GF diet) showed macroscopic improvement, confirmed on histology (milder villous blunting without basal crypt hyperplasia and IEL (35:100) (Figure 1) despite persistently high antibody titres (DGP IgG 198.7 U/mL, tTG IgA >128 U/mL).
Weight gain improved significantly with enteral supplementation via nasogastric tube (Figure 2).

Further reassessment 7 months later (5 years‐old) at the time of elective percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy insertion showed similar findings (DGP 81.1 U/mL, tTG 113 U/mL, histology with patchy areas of villous blunting, IEL 35:100).

Although this patient remains unaffected by diabetes mellitus at 5 years‐old, autoimmune screening post coeliac diagnosis identified autoimmune thyroid disease and he commenced thyroxine replacement therapy.
He was also noted to have asthma and atopic dermatitis.
Although there is a paternal history of hypothyroidism, these evolutions alongside concurrent coeliac disease, sparks the question of potential autoimmune associations in NEUROG3.
title: A rare presentation of coeliac crisis in a patient with Neurogenin‐3 mutation congenital enteropathy

case_text:
A 12-year-old Asian male, born of a consanguineous marriage, presented to our emergency department with sudden-onset severe shortness of breath, chest pain, and cyanosis. On examination, he was tachypneic, hypoxic, and in severe respiratory distress with absent breath sounds on the left side. An urgent chest radiograph revealed a large left-sided tension pneumothorax with mediastinal shift (Fig. 1). A chest tube was promptly inserted, resulting in immediate clinical improvement and subsequent radiographic confirmation of chest tube placement at a proper place (Fig. 2). Although tension pneumothorax has not been described as a direct complication of Shabbir Syndrome, it occurred in our patient, likely in relation to his underlying airway disease, chronic tracheostomy, or secondary infections.

His past medical history was significant. At the age of six, patient developed acute airway obstruction with severe dyspnea and cyanosis, necessitating admission to hospital. At that time, a tracheostomy tube was inserted to secure the airway. A subsequent CT scan demonstrated marked laryngeal, tracheal, right mainstem bronchus stenosis and comparatively normal left mainstem brochus (Fig. 3). The patient had undergone endoscopic assessment of the larynx and trachea at another center; however, detailed records were unavailable at the time of presentation. From the last 6 years, he is on tracheostomy tube for adequate breathing. The patient has been followed up regularly since tracheostomy placement at 6 years of age, with routine tube changes, standardized stoma care, and ongoing monitoring for local or respiratory infections. No recurrent tracheostomy-related infections were documented prior to the current event.

Over the following years, the patient developed progressive fibrovascular epithelial growths over the conjunctiva, which intermittently caused functional blindness. Ophthalmic examination revealed dense fibrovascular membranes covering both eyes (Fig. 4). The family was counseled about the potential role of surgical excision with amniotic membrane transplantation; however, the parents declined surgical intervention. Instead, they opted for laser therapy, despite being informed that its efficacy in this condition is not well-documented. Interestingly, the patient did show meaningful improvement after each laser session, with restoration of visual function for approximately 5–6 months before relapse occurred, necessitating repeated treatments.

The patient also exhibited dystrophic nail changes with features of onychomycosis, documented clinically and supported by photographic evidence (Fig. 5). He was taking oral Terbinafine occasionally for infection of his nails.

Taken together, the triad of laryngeal stenosis, ocular fibrovascular epithelial membranes, and onychodystrophy, along with the consanguineous family background, supported the diagnosis of Shabbir Syndrome (also termed Laryngo-Oculo-Cutaneous Syndrome or Onycho-Laryngo-Ocular Syndrome). During the current presentation, the occurrence of left-sided tension pneumothorax highlighted an additional challenge in the management of this child. While it may not represent a direct manifestation of Shabbir Syndrome itself, it significantly complicated the patient’s clinical course and required urgent intervention.

The patient was managed through a multidisciplinary team approach involving pediatric surgery, pediatric pulmonology, otolaryngology, anesthesiology, pediatric intensive care, radiology, and specialized nursing staff with expertise in tracheostomy care. Coordination among these specialties was essential given the complexity of Shabbir syndrome and the presence of a tracheostomy.

Pediatric intensivists and pulmonologists were responsible for respiratory stabilization, ventilatory assessment, and monitoring for complications related to pneumothorax. Pediatric surgeons led the emergency management and definitive treatment of the tension pneumothorax. Otolaryngology specialists supervised airway evaluation and tracheostomy care, while anesthesiology ensured safe airway management during interventions. Radiology played a key role in timely diagnosis and follow-up imaging.

Parental support and education were integral components of care. The parents were counseled regarding the patient’s condition, treatment plan, potential complications, and long-term prognosis. They received structured training on tracheostomy care, recognition of respiratory distress, and emergency response measures prior to discharge.

Now after 2 months of discharge, the patient is clinically stable and maintaining adequate oxygenation without supplemental oxygen.

Although genetic testing is considered the gold standard for confirming Shabbir Syndrome, it was not performed in this patient due to limited funding and lack of availability at our center. Moreover, the patient exhibited the full phenotypic spectrum of the disease—including laryngeal stenosis, conjunctival fibrovascular growths, and onychodystrophy—which made the clinical diagnosis compelling even in the absence of molecular confirmation.

case_text:
A 77‐year‐old man with a history of androgen deprivation therapy for locally advanced prostate cancer since 2005 was referred to our institution in March 2023 after progression to CRPC. At this point, his PSA level was 28.5 ng/mL, and 18F fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)‐positron emission tomography (PET)/magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and contrast‐enhanced computed tomography (CT) showed seminal vesicle invasion and multiple lymph node metastases (Figure 1a,b). Subsequently, prostate needle biopsy showed adenocarcinoma with a Gleason score of 5 + 5 (Figure 2a).

After administration of enzalutamide (160 mg/day), PSA decreased to 15.3 ng/mL; however, CT showed progression of lymph node metastases in July 2023. Treatment was switched to abiraterone acetate (1000 mg/day) and prednisolone (5 mg/day). Following further PSA elevation and radiological progression, docetaxel (75 mg/m2) was started in October 2023. After 4 courses, CT showed progression of prostate lesions. At the end of the first course of docetaxel, a FoundationOne CDx test was submitted using the prostate biopsy specimen initially obtained at our institution. Because the tumor content was insufficient for analysis, prostate needle biopsy was repeated in January 2024 (Figure 2b), and the test was resubmitted. After 4 courses of docetaxel, 3 courses of cabazitaxel (25 mg/m2) were administered, but PSA increased to 68.6 ng/mL, and CT showed progression of the para‐aortic lymph nodes and prostate lesions (Figure 1c,d). Because FoundationOne CDx detected MSI‐H with an MSH2 (c.366+1G>C) variant and TMB‐H (29 Muts/Mb), pembrolizumab was initiated in May 2024. PET/MRI in July 2024 showed regression of the lesions without significant FDG uptake, which was interpreted as a radiological complete response. No residual viable tumor cells were identified in the follow‐up prostate needle biopsy specimen obtained in August 2024. By September 2024, the PSA decreased to 0.01 ng/mL (Figure 3). A total of 17 pembrolizumab doses were administered over approximately 2 years, and treatment was completed in April 2026. Complete response was maintained as of August 2026, approximately 25 months after the radiological complete response, and no immune‐related adverse events occurred.

Genetic counseling and single‐site testing were performed at our institution. The variant was not detected in peripheral blood DNA and was therefore interpreted as somatic rather than germline following consultation with the Department of Clinical Genetics.

MSH2 immunohistochemistry was performed on prostate specimens obtained at the initial visit and after docetaxel therapy, using an anti‐MSH2 antibody (clone FE11, 1:100 dilution; Biocare Medical, Pacheco, CA, USA). The initial specimen showed preserved nuclear MSH2 expression (Figure 2c), whereas the post‐docetaxel biopsy specimen showed loss of nuclear expression (Figure 2d). Non‐neoplastic stromal cells retained nuclear staining as an internal positive control. Thus, serial biopsies demonstrated a temporal loss of MSH2 expression.

title: Complete Response to Pembrolizumab in a Case of Microsatellite Instability‐High, Castration‐Resistant Prostate Cancer With Somatic MSH2 Mutation

case_text:
A 58-year-old male with a history of end-stage renal disease, status post deceased-donor kidney transplant eight months prior to presentation and maintained on immunosuppressive medications consisting of a calcineurin inhibitor (Envarsus XR 2 mg daily), mycophenolate mofetil 540 mg twice daily, and a corticosteroid (prednisone 5 mg daily), presented to the emergency room with initial complaints of a one-week history of right anterior chest wall pain that later migrated to the left chest wall associated with a palpable, tender mass on the left shoulder. On arrival, he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Vital signs were temperature: 36.9 degrees centigrade (98.4 degrees Fahrenheit); heart rate (HR) 81 beats per minute; blood pressure (BP) 135/85 millimeters of mercury (mmHg); respiratory rate (RR) 16. Admitting laboratory indices showed hemoglobin (Hb) 9.7 g/dL, elevated white blood cell count (WBC) 11.04 thou/mcL, platelets 259 thou/mcL, creatine kinase (CK) 34, creatinine 1.78 mg/dL, glomerular filtration rate (GFR) 44 ml/min, blood urea nitrogen (BUN) 32.4 mg/dL, potassium 5.0 mmol/L, and elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) of 71.1 mg/L (Table 1).

Computed tomography (CT) of the chest was performed and revealed multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules with spiculated margins and mass-like consolidation, a radiographic pattern highly suggestive of pulmonary nocardiosis (Figure 1).

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the left shoulder confirmed a 3.4 cm intramuscular collection within the pectoralis musculature suspicious for an abscess (Figure 2).

Orthopedic teams evaluated the patient, who underwent debridement and irrigation (D&I) and washout of the left shoulder; surgical cultures were sent. These later became positive for N. farcinica, and susceptibility was requested. While the conventional blood cultures remained negative, plasma metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS/Karius) also identified N. farcinica. Transplant infectious disease was consulted, and the patient was started on an antibiotic regimen consisting of IV ceftriaxone (2 grams daily) and oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) one tablet twice daily. Despite the absence of focal neurologic deficits, the known predilection of N. farcinica for the CNS prompted a brain MRI to be performed, and this revealed multiple peripherally enhancing intra-axial lesions in the left frontal lobe and both temporo-occipital regions consistent with abscesses, confirming "silent" intracranial abscesses (Figure 3).

With the presence of brain lesions, a third antibiotic, linezolid 600 mg twice daily, was added. The transplant nephrology team modified immunosuppression by holding Envarsus and reducing the dose of mycophenolate mofetil from 540 mg twice daily to 180 mg twice daily. His current antibiotic regimen was continued, and he was later discharged home on the three antibiotics with plans to follow up with infectious disease, as susceptibility results were still not available at the time of discharge.

Post-discharge, he was doing well initially, but his recovery course was complicated by two significant adverse drug reactions. Approximately 18 days after discharge, the patient was readmitted for a diffuse rash attributed to TMP-SMX hypersensitivity. The rash was refractory to diphenhydramine tablets and topical steroid cream. Simultaneously, the patient developed bicytopenia (Hgb 6.1 g/dl, platelets 103 x 10^9) presumed to be secondary to linezolid, given the known side effects of the medication. He received a blood transfusion of two units of packed red blood cells. Infectious Diseases were reconsulted, and by this time the susceptibility report was now available 22 days after collection (Table 2). Based on the susceptibility report, the antibiotic regimen was discontinued and changed to a new oral salvage regimen consisting of moxifloxacin 400 mg daily, Augmentin 875 mg twice daily, and tedizolid 200 mg daily (the latter an oxazolidinone chosen for its improved hematologic safety profile compared to linezolid). Tedizolid susceptibilities were extrapolated from the results for linezolid, as testing was not available for it. This regimen was selected based on previous adverse reactions and anticipated tolerability of the available susceptible agents (Table 2).

Due to the considerable risk of relapses associated with N. farcinica and the patient’s ongoing iatrogenic immunosuppression, a 12-month duration was planned for the oral antibiotics. The patient’s clinical status significantly improved, and he was discharged in a stable condition. At a post-admission clinic visit three months later, while still on this antibiotic regimen, pancytopenia resolved (Hgb 12.4 g/dl, platelets 210 x 10^9, and WBC 8.23 x 10^9). At both the six- and 12-month clinic visits, he remained free of symptoms and side effects of antimicrobials, and he successfully completed his treatment course. Long-term management will involve serial head and chest imaging to ensure sustained resolution of previously seen lesions and monitor for recurrence for the next one to two years or more.

case_text:
A previously healthy 14-year-old boy presented with acute low back pain, rapidly progressive neurological deterioration, intraventricular hemorrhage, and obstructive hydrocephalus. External ventricular drainage and subsequent ventriculoperitoneal shunting were performed. Neuroimaging showed persistent leptomeningeal abnormalities, while infectious, inflammatory, and vascular investigations were negative. The patient was then lost to follow-up.

Two years later, he returned with progressive bilateral lower-extremity weakness, gait impairment, paresthesia, and bladder dysfunction. Lumbar decompression and biopsy were nondiagnostic because of tissue-processing failure. One year later, worsening posterior fossa compression, brainstem compromise, and further neurological decline prompted median suboccipital craniotomy and tumor resection. Histopathological and immunohistochemical evaluation of this representative specimen established the diagnosis of diffuse leptomeningeal glioneuronal tumor.

Initial computed tomography (CT) demonstrated intraventricular hemorrhage and obstructive hydrocephalus; CT angiography excluded a vascular lesion (Fig. 1). Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed diffuse nodular leptomeningeal enhancement involving the suprasellar cisterns, posterior fossa, basal leptomeninges, and lumbosacral spine, with extensive thoracolumbar intramedullary cystic lesions (Fig. 2). Subsequent MRI documented posterior fossa enlargement, brainstem compression, and craniospinal progression. After systemic treatment, intracranial enhancement decreased, although stable residual sellar and spinal disease, cervical syringomyelia, and postoperative changes persisted (Figs 3 and 4).

Management included cerebrospinal fluid diversion, lumbar decompression and biopsy, median suboccipital craniotomy with tumor resection, and subsequent lumbosacral tumor resection with L2–L5 decompression, posterolateral fusion, and iliac fixation. Diagnostic tissue from the posterior fossa contained glial fibrillary acidic protein- and S100-positive, synaptophysin-negative tumor cells.

The patient received six cycles of carboplatin/vincristine followed by maintenance temozolomide. At 5 years, he remained neurologically stable and independently ambulatory despite mild lower-extremity weakness and stable residual spinal disease under multidisciplinary surveillance.

case_text:
Clinical Presentation and Definition: Catatonia is defined as an acute neuropsychiatric syndrome or movement disorder distinguished by significant alterations in motor behaviour, vigilance, thought, and mood. While more than 40 distinct signs have been identified in the literature, clinical assessment has been significantly refined by the development of the Bush–Francis Catatonia Rating Scale (BFCRS), which identifies 23 objective signs to facilitate standardised examination and diagnostic reliability. Clinical recognition generally requires the presence of two or more prominent features for a duration of at least 24 h. The syndrome primarily manifests in two clinical forms: retarded catatonia, characterised by immobility, mutism, staring, and withdrawal; and excited catatonia, which involves intense, non-purposeful psychomotor agitation. Notably, excited catatonia can progress to “malignant” or “lethal” catatonia, a life-threatening emergency marked by fever and autonomic instability. In these cases, intramuscular antipsychotics could be useful.

Epidemiological Distribution: Historically restricted to a subtype of schizophrenia, contemporary evidence identifies catatonia as a transdiagnostic syndrome prevalent in approximately 10% of acute psychiatric admissions. Longitudinal surveys in general psychiatric inpatient populations have confirmed a consistent frequency of presentation, with approximately 9% of consecutively admitted patients exhibiting the syndrome. More broadly, epidemiological studies estimate that catatonia occurs in 5–18% of psychiatric inpatients and approximately 3.3% of patients admitted to general medical units, with a pooled prevalence of around 9.2% across clinical populations. The successful delineation of catatonia as an independent entity has even served as a nosographic model for other conditions, such as melancholic depression, highlighting its shift from a psychotic specifier to a distinct psychomotor disturbance. Epidemiological data suggests a much higher prevalence in affective disorders, affecting up to 20–25% of patients with mania or major depression. Furthermore, catatonic features are increasingly recognised in neurodevelopmental conditions; a meta-analysis indicates that approximately 10.4% of individuals with autism spectrum disorders (ASD) meet the criteria for catatonia. Conversely, schizophrenia accounts for only a minority (approximately 10–15%) of catatonia cases in contemporary surveys.

Pathophysiological Hypotheses: The pathophysiology of catatonia is hypothesised to involve a complex failure of top-down modulation. Specifically, a deficit in GABAergic inhibitory activity within the orbitofrontal cortex is thought to dysregulate the connectivity between prefrontal/parietal regions and the basal ganglia. This neurochemical imbalance, characterised by reduced GABAA receptor density in the sensorimotor cortex and concomitant NMDA receptor overactivity, results in an inability to correctly monitor and terminate motor acts, leading to the characteristic “deadlock” of posturing. Additionally, an underlying hypodopaminergic state in the mesostriatal pathways has been suggested, which contrasts with the bottom-up dopaminergic deficits seen in Parkinson’s disease. Since catatonia is more frequent during manic episodes and may resolve with pantoclastic aggression as one exits the catatonic state, we may hypothesise that mania drives these changes.

The syndrome primarily manifests in two clinical forms: retarded catatonia, characterised by immobility, mutism, staring, and withdrawal; and excited catatonia, which involves intense, non-purposeful psychomotor agitation.
Notably, excited catatonia can progress to “malignant” or “lethal” catatonia, a life-threatening emergency marked by fever and autonomic instability.

case_text:
This case report was prepared in accordance with the CARE guidelines. A structured patient timeline summarizing presentation, imaging, tissue diagnosis, systemic therapy, surgery, and available follow‐up is provided in Table 1. A completed CARE checklist accompanies the revised submission as supporting information (available here).

A 45‐year‐old woman presented with acute right‐sided chest pain and dyspnea after initially experiencing a stretching sensation in the neck. There was no prior history of malignancy or known previously treated soft‐tissue tumor. The available clinical record did not identify a prior extrapulmonary synovial sarcoma. Detailed smoking history, ECOG performance status, complete physical examination findings, and baseline laboratory values were not available in the source material used for this retrospective case report and therefore are not inferred.

Frontal and lateral chest radiographs demonstrated a large right lower lobe opacity abutting the diaphragm (Figure 1), prompting contrast‐enhanced CT. CT revealed an 8.7 × 6.7 cm lobulated, irregular, heterogeneously enhancing mass centered in the right lower lobe with central necrosis (Figure 2). The mass abutted the diaphragm but was described as a right lower lobe pulmonary mass rather than a pleural, diaphragmatic, or chest wall primary. Additional retroperitoneal soft‐tissue nodules, mesenteric nodules, and enlarged bilateral pericardiophrenic lymph nodes were suspicious for metastatic disease; a trace pericardial effusion was also present. Exact imaging dates were not available in the source material used for this revision.

Whole‐body FDG PET/CT was performed for staging and demonstrated intense hypermetabolism of the dominant right lower lobe mass, bilateral pericardiophrenic lymph nodes, and retroperitoneal nodules (Figure 3). No alternative extrapulmonary primary soft‐tissue tumor was identified. The distribution therefore supported a presumed primary pulmonary origin with metastatic disease, although an occult extrapulmonary primary could not be completely excluded. Exact examination dates and SUVmax values were not available in the source material and are not estimated.

Core needle biopsy of the pulmonary mass revealed poorly differentiated synovial sarcoma, FNCLCC Grade 2; the reported grade was therefore based on the pulmonary core biopsy rather than the later resection specimen. Histopathologic examination demonstrated a spindle‐cell neoplasm with admixed epithelioid cells and prominent nucleoli. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated tumor cell positivity for SS18‐SSX fusion‐specific antibody, SSX C‐terminal antibody, and MAGE‐A4, rare positivity for calretinin, retained BRG1 expression, negative nuclear WT1 expression, and markedly reduced INI1/SMARCB1 expression with faint residual nuclear staining (Figure 4). The original diagnostic explanatory note called this “apparent loss of INI1”; subsequent clarification by the pathologist established that faint residual tumor nuclear staining was present. An internal positive control was not separately documented in the material available for this report. The available pathology summary did not provide mitotic count, percentage necrosis, Ki‐67 proliferation index, the individual FNCLCC score components, or a broader negative marker panel. Nuclear WT1 was the documented negative marker used in the submitted pathology summary, whereas retained BRG1 helped argue against a SMARCA4‐deficient thoracic neoplasm.

Biopsy of one of the retroperitoneal soft‐tissue nodules identified on staging imaging confirmed metastatic synovial sarcoma, establishing disseminated disease at presentation. Because synovial sarcoma commonly metastasizes to the lung, an extrapulmonary primary was specifically considered. Whole‐body staging FDG PET/CT and the available clinical history did not identify another primary soft‐tissue tumor, whereas the largest and dominant lesion was centered in the right lower lobe. Pathology cannot distinguish a primary pulmonary synovial sarcoma from a pulmonary metastasis of an occult primary. The absence of another identifiable primary site together with the dominant intrapulmonary mass therefore supported designation as presumed primary pulmonary synovial sarcoma, but did not definitively prove the primary site.

The diagnostic workup included SS18‐SSX fusion‐specific immunohistochemistry and SSX C‐terminal immunohistochemistry, both of which were performed and showed tumor cell positivity. This combination is highly sensitive and specific for synovial sarcoma and provided strong diagnostic support in conjunction with morphology. No molecular confirmation by FISH, RT‐PCR, or sequencing was available in the material reviewed for this report; accordingly, the immunostains are described as fusion‐specific immunohistochemical testing and must not be interpreted as direct molecular testing.

The patient received ifosfamide‐based systemic chemotherapy followed by right lower lobectomy. Detailed chemotherapy administration records, interval response assessment, operative intent, complete resection pathology (including margin status, lymph node findings, and treatment effect), subsequent therapy, and long‐term follow‐up were not available in the records reviewed for this retrospective case report. Accordingly, only the documented treatment sequence is reported here; these additional patient‐specific details are not inferred.

case_text:
A 90‐year‐old female patient, with no history of inflammatory bowel disease and known for hypertension, bilateral breast cancer treated by mastectomy, and hysterectomy for a benign lesion, was referred to our surgical department with significant weight loss, cachexia, and anemia. Clinical examination revealed a mass in the left upper abdominal quadrant. Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) was elevated at 475 ng/mL. Colonoscopy demonstrated a stenotic, necrotic, and fibrinous lesion of the transverse colon. Ten biopsies contained acellular necrotic material with scant leukocytic exudate and bacterial colonization, without a viable tumor, consistent with nonrepresentative sampling rather than exclusion of malignancy. Abdominal CT scan confirmed a mass of 8 cm arising from the transverse colon, infiltrating the abdominal wall (Figure 1). The thoracic CT scan did not show any metastatic lesion. Despite negative biopsies on colonoscopy, endoscopic visualization and CT imaging were highly suspicious of malignancy. Although 90 years old, the patient was considered sufficiently fit for curative‐intent surgery; hence, the multidisciplinary tumor board (MDT) proposed oncological resection. Laparotomy with extended right hemicolectomy and en bloc resection of a 7 cm × 6.5 cm adherent abdominal‐wall patch, composed predominantly of peritoneum, was performed, followed by ileocolic anastomosis. Bacteremia on day (D) 9, arising from a central venous catheter infection, was treated with intravenous antibiotics for 48 h followed by oral antibiotics for another 5 days, and the patient was discharged home on D14.

The histopathologic specimen revealed a 100 mm × 85 mm × 75 mm stenosing and ulcerated tumor, attached to an infiltrated patch of the abdominal wall (Figure 2), composed of a major component of poorly differentiated NEC (PDNEC) and a minor component (30%) of moderately to poorly differentiated mucinous adenocarcinoma (Figure 3). Regarding immunostaining, the neuroendocrine component expressed INSM1, chromogranin, and synaptophysin (Syn), whereas the mucinous adenocarcinoma component expressed CK7, CDX2, and CK20 and was negative for neuroendocrine markers. The mitotic rate was 102 per 10 high‐power fields in PDNEC, and the Ki‐67 proliferation index was 90%. Molecular analysis of the adenocarcinoma component revealed a BRAF p.V600E mutation, wild‐type KRAS and NRAS, and microsatellite instability with loss of MLH1 and PMS2 expression. The combination of BRAF p.V600E and MLH1/PMS2 loss favored sporadic MLH1 promoter hypermethylation rather than Lynch syndrome. Twenty‐eight lymph nodes were negative. The abdominal‐wall resection margin was microscopically negative, with tumor approaching within 2 mm. The final diagnosis was a high‐grade MiNEN, classified as pT4b pN0 (0/28) L1 V1 Pn0 R0 according to the TNM Classification (8th edition, 2017).

Following a discussion at the MDT expressing concerns regarding the potential adverse effects of adjuvant chemotherapy or immunotherapy in an elderly, frail, and sarcopenic patient, we opted for active surveillance. During the 3‐month follow‐up, a significant rise of the CEA was observed at 749 ng/mL. The CT scan demonstrated an isolated heterogeneous 6.4 cm × 3.8 cm × 6.5 cm intramuscular lesion in the left anterior paraumbilical abdominal wall, at the site of the previous direct tumor invasion, without bowel involvement or distant disease (Figure 4). A core needle biopsy confirmed local recurrence, identifying an adenocarcinoma with neuroendocrine differentiation. MDT recommended local control (LC) RT without systemic therapy. At 6 weeks postrecurrence, using intensity‐modulated RT with 6‐MV photons, the patient underwent 18 fractions of RT with five daily fractions of 2.5 Gy per week, over 26 days, with a total of 45 Gy. Treatment was completed without interruption or bowel toxicity and achieved complete radiologic remission. Trimestral CEA and semestral CT scan follow‐ups in our oncology department show no evidence of local recurrence 2 years after treatment (Figure 5).

case_text:
A 38-year-old female with a past medical history of intravenous drug use (heroin and benzodiazepines), untreated hepatitis C, and seizure disorder was admitted with a one-week history of diffuse chest pain worsened by coughing and deep inspiration. Her symptoms were associated with fevers relieved with acetaminophen.

On presentation, she was tachycardic and met criteria for sepsis. A chest CT revealed bilateral infiltrates with cavitary lesions concerning for septic emboli. She was started on broad-spectrum antibiotics. Shortly thereafter, she aspirated following emesis, developed respiratory failure, and required intubation and vasopressor support. Arterial blood gas showed severe mixed acidosis. Blood cultures grew MRSA, and transthoracic echocardiography revealed a large tricuspid vegetation with moderate tricuspid regurgitation and preserved ejection fraction.

Despite 33 days of antibiotics, she continued to have intermittent fevers and worsening pulmonary complications, including empyema requiring chest tube drainage. Cardiothoracic surgery deferred valve replacement due to her unstable condition and high operative risk. Interventional cardiology performed AngioVac-assisted debulking of the tricuspid valve vegetation through standard femoral venous access, removing approximately 80% of the mass.10,11 There were no procedural complications. Post-procedure imaging showed a reduction in vegetation burden but persistent regurgitation.

Her course was further complicated by massive hemoptysis leading to cardiac arrest, requiring resuscitation. She underwent bronchial artery embolization for pulmonary hemorrhage and video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) decortication for empyema. Ultimately, she required tracheostomy and PEG tube placement for long-term ventilatory and nutritional support. She stabilized and was discharged to a long-term acute care hospital (LTACH) for continued recovery.

Approximately 3 months after discharge to the LTACH, once her clinical condition permitted, the patient underwent tricuspid valve replacement, which she survived. Information on the type of prosthesis implanted and on her course after valve replacement was not available to the authors at the time of writing.

case_text:
A 61-year-old man with no known underlying disease underwent colonoscopy at another hospital after a positive immunochemical fecal occult blood test (iFOBT) in colorectal cancer screening. A 30-mm polypoid lesion was found at the hepatic flexure, and he was referred to our hospital for endoscopic removal. The lesion was large, lobulated, and irregular, with a central whitish necrotic coating, patchy erythema, and easy oozing (Figure 1A). He was admitted the day before the procedure, and EMR was performed 20 days after the initial colonoscopy. The procedure consisted of submucosal needle injection followed by hot snare polypectomy; the lesion was retrieved in one piece, and the mucosal defect was closed with hemoclips (Figure 2A–C). The clinical course is summarized in Table 1.

The specimen was a single brownish, elastic tissue fragment measuring 30 × 28 × 12 mm. A spindle-cell neoplasm was located in the submucosa beneath the colonic mucosa (Figure 1B). The tumor cells formed intersecting fascicles and showed marked cellular and nuclear atypia (Figure 1C), with approximately 30 mitoses per 10 high-power fields (HPFs). Immunohistochemistry showed strong desmin expression, and the tumor cells were negative for DOG1, CD34, and S-100. The Ki-67 labeling index was approximately 50% (Figure 1D–F). The diagnosis was LMS, and tumor reached the deep resection margin. Additional immunostains, including smooth muscle actin (SMA), h-caldesmon, and CD117 (KIT), were not performed, and tumor necrosis, lymphovascular invasion, and histological grade were not reported.

Abdominal CT on the day after EMR showed focal wall thickening at the hepatic flexure with stranding of the mesocolon. The radiology report suggested colon cancer and assigned a clinical stage of T3N0M0 (stage IIA) according to the colorectal cancer staging system. No enlarged lymph nodes or distant metastases within the imaged abdomen were reported, and colonic diverticulosis and fatty liver were noted incidentally. At the outpatient visit 9 days after EMR, the patient was referred to colorectal surgeons for resection because of the malignant diagnosis and the involved deep margin. Colonoscopy 14 days after EMR showed the post-EMR site, which was marked by endoscopic tattooing to guide surgery (Figure 2D,E). The patient was admitted 17 days after EMR and underwent laparoscopic-assisted right hemicolectomy with lymph node dissection the next day (Figure 2F).

The colon showed post-treatment changes at the EMR site without residual malignancy in the examined colectomy sections. An incidental tubular adenoma was present, and the ileum and appendix were free of tumor. One of 16 nodes submitted as regional lymph nodes contained metastatic LMS. The other 15 regional nodes, 23 mesenteric nodes, and five nodes from the high point of resection were negative, giving one positive node among 44 examined. No enlarged node had been reported on preoperative abdominal CT; nodal involvement was identified on pathological examination.

In the involved node, an atypical spindle-cell tumor occupied the peripheral part of the node, adjacent to lymphoid tissue (Figure 3A,B). The deposit showed strong desmin expression and was negative for DOG1 and HMB45 (Figure 3C–E). Ki-67 immunostaining of the deposit is shown in Figure 3F; a labeling index was not recorded for the node. The size of the deposit and the presence or absence of extranodal extension were not recorded. The morphology and immunophenotype of the nodal tumor matched those of the primary lesion (Table 2). Both specimens were reviewed at a departmental pathology conference by at least three attending pathologists, including the department head.

The patient declined chemotherapy after surgery. At his one-month postoperative visit, he was noted to be recovering well. He declined chest CT at that visit. Pulmonary metastatic status therefore remained unknown. He agreed to return six months after that visit, approximately seven months after surgery. This assessment was not yet due at the time of revision.

case_text: A healthy seven‐year‐old boy presented at the dermatology clinic with a 5‐month history of persistent, slowly progressive skin lesions. The lesions were largely asymptomatic, though the patient had reported transient mild burning pain when the affected skin came into contact with water, with no other identified triggering or relieving factors. Past medical history and review of systems were unremarkable. The parents are not consanguineous and have no history of similar conditions in the family. Skin examination revealed multiple grouped and scaly skin colored follicular papules scattered across the trunk and limbs (Figure 1). Examination of the hair, nails, and mucous membrane was unremarkable. Dermoscopic examination was not performed. The differential diagnosis includes lichen spinulosus, phrynoderma (vitamin A deficiency), pityriasis rubra pilaris (PRP), keratosis pilaris (KP), and keratosis pilaris atrophicans (KPA). A skin biopsy was obtained. Histopathological examination revealed perifollicular edema with the presence of mononuclear cellular infiltrates (Figure 2). Serum vitamin A level was within normal limits 46 mcg/dL, reference range: 20–60 mcg/dL. Based on the above clinicopathological findings, a diagnosis of DRIF was made. The patient was started on oral vitamin A, 5000 IU twice daily for 3 months, topical urea 20% cream twice daily, and topical lactic acid 12% cream twice daily and put under periodic follow up.

Past medical history and review of systems were unremarkable.

case_text: A 29‐year‐old Eritrean female presented to the emergency department at Teseney Hospital with a 5‐day history of generalized skin exfoliation. The patient reported onset of redness and pruritus 7 days after receiving a 12.5 mg intramuscular injection of Fluphenazine decanoate, prescribed for management of schizophrenia (Figure 1). The patient had been receiving Carbamazepine and Chlorpromazine for approximately 1 month prior to the Fluphenazine injection without any dermatologic adverse reactions. Three days after initial symptoms, she developed widespread skin scaling and exfoliation, beginning at the elbow flexures and rapidly progressing to involve the entire body within 2 days. The patient had no prior personal or family history of dermatologic disease. She was diagnosed with schizophrenia 7 years earlier following postpartum psychosis and had been stable on Olanzapine until recent unavailability led to a medication change to Carbamazepine and Chlorpromazine 1 month prior to the current event. On presentation, vital signs were within normal limits except for a low‐grade fever of 37.9°C. Physical examination revealed non‐icteric sclera and hyperemic conjunctiva. The skin was dry with widespread scaling and exfoliation involving more than 90% of the body surface area, most pronounced over flexural areas, which significantly limited joint mobility (Figure 2). Notably, the flexural scales exhibited deep fissures with an exudative base and foul odor. Perioral and nasal skin involvement impaired mouth opening. Mucous membranes were intact. No lymphadenopathy or organomegaly was noted. Hair and nails were unremarkable.

case_text:
Patient was a 15-year-old adolescent boy presenting in March 2025 with 3 months of intermittent nausea and vomiting, 10-pound weight loss (body mass index 16.9), and diarrhea alternating with constipation. His father had ileal stenotic CD.

He was referred to a pediatric gastroenterologist. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) in August 2025 demonstrated severe antral gastritis with erosions, friability, granularity, and the scope could not pass beyond the pylorus due to a stricture. Histology of the antrum demonstrated sparse giant cells. Colonoscopy with ileoscopy was normal, with unremarkable histology in the colon and ileum. Abdominal ultrasound and MR enterography were normal. Capsule endoscopy was not performed because the patient had a pyloric stricture.

The patient was referred to an adult inflammatory bowel disease expert. Based on review of the prior EGD, empiric prednisone (20 mg daily) was initiated. This dose had a minimal effect on his symptoms. Repeat EGD in October 2025 showed disease progression with distal esophageal aphthous ulcers, discontinuous severe antral inflammation, longitudinal incisural ulcers, and a pyloric stricture that could not be passed (Figure 1). Biopsy of all sites showed non-necrotizing granulomata and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes, consistent with CD (Figure 2). Laboratory test results included Hgb 10.4 g/dL (reference range, 12.0-16.9), mean corpuscular volume 82.9 fL (reference range, 79.4–99.7), platelets 681k (reference range, 140–400), ferritin 17 ng/mL (reference range, 11–172), albumin 3.9 g/dL (reference range, 3.6–5.1), C-reactive protein <3 mg/L (reference range, <8.0), and negative QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus and hepatitis B surface antigen.

Combination IFX and AZA was considered but ultimately rejected after discussing the lymphoma risk with the patient's parents.4 Instead, shared decision-making led us to select dual therapy with IFX and upadacitinib (UPA) (JAK1 inhibitor) in an effort to achieve rapid disease control and healing while avoiding the prolonged time to maximum effect associated with thiopurine use. Dietary therapy was not used. Due to difficulty swallowing pills, the patient was prescribed liquid UPA at an induction dose of 12 mg twice daily for 12 weeks given his age and weight. Prednisone was increased to 40 mg daily at this time while awaiting insurance approval.

While awaiting medication insurance approval and still on prednisone, the patient was briefly hospitalized in November 2025 for persistent vomiting and abdominal pain. Abdominal computed tomography showed gastric wall thickening with mucosal hyperenhancement and submucosal edema. Intravenous steroids were initiated and he received the first induction IFX infusion (5 mg/kg) in the hospital. He continued standard induction and maintenance infusions after discharge along with prednisone. UPA was approved by insurance in mid-December 2025 and prednisone was tapered off.

At office follow-up in February 2026, the patient had resolution of all gastrointestinal symptoms. EGD a week later showed normal esophageal mucosa, resolution of all ulcers, gastric scarring with small pseudopolyps, and a persistent pyloric stricture that was easily balloon-dilated to 10 mm, allowing passage of the scope into the duodenum (Figure 3). The duodenal bulb appeared scarred and foreshortened, while the second portion appeared normal. Biopsies revealed reactive gastropathy without granulomas and regenerative changes in the duodenum.

Based on these results, UPA was tapered by 5 mg every 2 weeks and discontinued by April 2026. At follow-up in May 2026, the patient felt well, was eating an unrestricted diet, had gained weight (BMI 19.3, from low of 14.7), and had regained his energy and quality of life. As of July 2026, laboratory test results included Hgb 11 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume 82.5 fL, platelets 314k, ferritin 7 ng/mL, albumin 4.2 g/dL, and C-reactive protein <3 mg/L. He continues maintenance IFX infusions.

case_text:
A 61‐year‐old man with a relevant medical history of Stage IIIB melanoma undergoing treatment with nivolumab (480 mg every 4 weeks) presented with an erythematous patch on the scalp 5 days after the first infusion. He initially sought evaluation from a private dermatologist, who diagnosed psoriasis and initiated topical corticosteroid therapy. However, the patient showed no clinical improvement. Two days after the third nivolumab infusion, he developed widespread involvement of the trunk and oral cavity, accompanied by a 2‐day history of constitutional symptoms, including fever (39°C), fatigue, and diaphoresis, prompting an urgent dermatology referral to our hospital.

On physical examination, two distinct dermatoses were identified; a disseminated dermatosis involving the scalp, groin, and legs, consisting of well‐demarcated erythematous plaques with fine scaling on the surface, ranging from 4 to 9 cm in diameter (Figure 1); and a generalized dermatosis affecting the face and the oral cavity, trunk and both upper and lower extremities, consisting of multiple erythematous macules with violaceous centers (raised atypical targets), some of which exhibited bullae, whereas others showed erosions involving more than 30% of the total body surface area; a positive Nikolsky sign was also observed (Figure 2A), along with conjunctival hyperemia (Sotozono Grade 1), whereas the oral mucosa displayed ulcerations covered by hemorrhagic crusts (Figure 2B).

A targeted interrogation revealed that the patient had taken acetaminophen and nivolumab within the preceding 3 months, questions about respiratory symptoms such as rhinorrhea, cough, and dyspnea, all of which were denied. Based on the clinical findings, toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) was suspected, in addition to a psoriasiform eruption secondary to nivolumab. A skin biopsy was taken as part of the initial management, demonstrating keratinocyte necrosis with a sparse inflammatory infiltrate (Figure 3), which supported the diagnosis of TEN.

During Day 1 of hospitalization the SCORTEN was 3, suggesting a 35.3% mortality risk, because of the severity of the condition, the patient received intravenous corticosteroids and immunoglobulin 2 g/kg, resulting in significant improvement of both dermatoses (Figure 2C,D), he was discharged after 8 days and continued outpatient management without recurrence of TEN. However, psoriasiform plaques persisted and required treatment with topical corticosteroids and oral methotrexate.

case_text:
A 52‐year‐old male from Southeast Asia with no significant past medical history presented with a 6‐month history of left‐sided otalgia and aural fullness. Three months prior to presentation at our institution, he had sought treatment from another physician and was diagnosed with left otitis media with effusion. He underwent a 2‐month course of conservative management, presumed to consist of standard oral and topical antibiotics for otitis media. Despite this treatment, his symptoms progressively worsened, with the onset of persistent, purulent left‐sided otorrhea. Otoscopic examination at that time reportedly revealed the emergence of granulation tissue and a lesion suspicious for cholesteatoma on the tympanic membrane.

Due to the failure of conservative management, he was referred to our otolaryngology department. On initial examination, the left external auditory canal contained a significant amount of purulent effusion. After careful suctioning, otoscopy revealed that the middle ear cavity was completely obliterated by extensive, pale‐appearing granulation tissue (Figure 1). The right ear examination was unremarkable.

Pure‐tone audiometry demonstrated a severe‐to‐profound mixed hearing loss on the left side (Figure 2A): the four‐frequency (500, 1,000, 2,000, and 4000 Hz) averages were 86.3 dB HL for air conduction and 38.8 dB HL for bone conduction, with an air‐bone gap of 47.5 dB. Hearing in the right ear was normal. This degree of hearing impairment, particularly the elevation of bone‐conduction thresholds, was considered disproportionately severe for chronic otitis media of a few months’ duration and raised suspicion of an alternative etiology. High‐resolution computed tomography (CT) of the temporal bones showed soft tissue density completely opacifying the left middle ear cavity and mastoid antrum, with no bony erosion of the ossicular chain, scutum, or labyrinthine structures (Figure 3); this preservation of bony architecture argued against an aggressive cholesteatoma.

Given the refractory course and the atypical findings, a comprehensive diagnostic workup was initiated. An incisional biopsy of the middle ear granulation tissue was performed through the external auditory canal as an office‐based procedure. Histopathological examination revealed necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with epithelioid histiocytes and Langhans‐type multinucleated giant cells, without evidence of malignancy. A blood Interferon‐Gamma Release Assay (IGRA) was positive, indicating sensitization to Mycobacterium tuberculosis. In the middle ear effusion, an acid‐fast bacilli (AFB) smear with fluorescent staining was positive, and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was positive for M. tuberculosis complex and negative for atypical mycobacteria.

The diagnosis of TOM prompted a systemic evaluation for other sites of involvement. Nasopharyngoscopy revealed an irregular, ulcerative lesion with a whitish coat on the posterior wall of the nasopharynx, near the pharyngeal orifice of the left Eustachian tube (Figure 4). An office‐based endoscopic biopsy and microbiological analysis of this lesion yielded results identical to those from the middle ear, confirming concurrent nasopharyngeal TB. A subsequent chest CT scan identified an infiltrate in the left lung, highly suspicious for active pulmonary TB.

A final diagnosis of left TOM, nasopharyngeal TB, and pulmonary TB was established. Tissue sampling was thus limited to the two office‐based incisional biopsies; no exploratory tympanotomy, mastoidectomy, or other surgical intervention was undertaken during the diagnostic workup. The patient was transferred to a specialized TB hospital for isolation and treatment and was started on four‐drug antitubercular therapy (ATT) consisting of rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide. One month after the start of treatment, a follow‐up sputum AFB test was negative, and a repeat chest CT showed no progression of the pulmonary infiltrate. Drug susceptibility testing of the initial isolate revealed no resistance to any first‐line agent. After the intensive phase, the patient was discharged to continue a two‐drug maintenance regimen of rifampicin and isoniazid. ATT was well tolerated, and no adverse events were observed.

Upon completion of the full course of ATT, the patient’s condition had resolved completely. Follow‐up otoscopy of the left ear, performed approximately 2 years after the initial presentation, showed a healed, dry middle ear space. Stable, multiple tympanic membrane perforations remained, but there was no evidence of otorrhea, inflammation, or residual granulation tissue (Figure 5). Pure‐tone audiometry at the same visit showed partial recovery of hearing in the left ear (Figure 2B): the air‐conduction average improved to 65.0 dB HL and the bone‐conduction average to 23.8 dB HL, whereas an air‐bone gap of 41.3 dB persisted. The residual hearing loss was, therefore, predominantly conductive. No otologic surgery was performed during or after ATT. The patient reported that he was relieved that the disease had been cured.

title: Refractory Chronic Otitis Media: A Case Report of Tuberculous Otitis Media With Nasopharyngeal and Pulmonary Manifestations

case_text:
A male in his 20s presented to the emergency department with a one‐day history of acute, severe epigastric pain. The pain was burning in character, radiated to the back and was exacerbated by oral intake. It was associated with nausea and multiple episodes of nonbilious vomiting. He had a background of recurrent alcohol‐associated AP since 2021. The patient was not forthcoming about the exact weekly alcohol intake or any binge drinking episodes.

A review of previous records available at our facility showed that he was admitted with mild AP in 2023. At that time, he reported four earlier episodes requiring hospitalization at a different facility. A CT report described mild interstitial pancreatitis involving the pancreatic head and uncinate process.

He was admitted again in 2024, approximately a year before the current presentation. Although that episode was initially described clinically as mild, CT subsequently demonstrated pancreatic changes suggestive of necrosis, with extensive peripancreatic and mesenteric fluid. The scan also described an equivocal finding in a branch of the right portal vein that could have represented a developing thrombus. The major arteries were described as normal in calibre and did not identify a thrombus.

His medical history included Helicobacter pylori–negative gastritis treated with proton pump inhibitor therapy during a previous admission for AP. There was no known personal or family history of thrombosis, autoimmune disease, malignancy or thrombophilia. He denied smoking and recreational drug use and reported a recent long‐haul flight approximately one and a half weeks prior to presentation. His only regular medication was omeprazole 40 mg twice daily, and he had no known drug allergies.

On examination, the patient appeared uncomfortable and in pain but was alert and fully oriented. His temperature was 36.0°C, pulse rate 79 beats per minute, respiratory rate 19 breaths per minute, blood pressure 144/95 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Abdominal examination revealed a soft abdomen with normal bowel sounds and localised epigastric tenderness, without guarding, rigidity, rebound tenderness or organomegaly. Cardiovascular, respiratory and neurological examinations were, otherwise, unremarkable. There was no pallor, jaundice, cyanosis, lymphadenopathy, peripheral oedema, dehydration or muscle wasting.

Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated a normal full blood count, elevated serum lipase, mild transaminitis and elevated gamma‐glutamyl transferase, with preserved hepatic synthetic and renal function. Serum calcium, glycated haemoglobin, immunoglobulin G4 levels and lactate were within normal limits (Table 1).

Contrast‐enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen performed on admission revealed features of AP involving the head and uncinate process, with a low CT severity index score of 2. There was peripancreatic fat stranding extending into the intraperitoneal mesentery, with subcentimetre reactive peripancreatic lymph nodes. There was a significant improvement in the extent of inflammation and peripancreatic fluid collection compared with the 2024 CT. A small peripancreatic fluid collection measuring approximately 5.5 mL anterior to the pancreatic tail was considered to be a sequela of a prior episode. An eccentric, nonocclusive filling defect was identified in the peripancreatic portion of the SMA, superior and anterior to the neck of the pancreas, spanning approximately 2.3 cm and resulting in approximately 58% luminal stenosis, consistent with thrombus (Figure 1). The remaining mid and distal portions of the SMA were patent, with no CT features of downstream mesenteric ischaemia. The small bowel loops enhanced normally, without bowel wall thickening, pneumatosis, portal venous gas or ascites.

In light of the incidental SMA thrombosis, cardiothoracic surgery and haematology consultations were obtained. Because the thrombus was nonocclusive and there was no clinical or radiological evidence of bowel compromise, conservative management was recommended. The clinical team also advised evaluation for alternative causes of arterial thrombosis, including embolic disease, inherited or acquired thrombophilia, inflammatory or autoimmune disease and occult malignancy. Initial haematological investigations were unremarkable (Table 2).

The patient was managed conservatively for RAP with intravenous fluid resuscitation, analgesia and early enteral feeding. For the SMA thrombosis, therapeutic anticoagulation with enoxaparin at 1 mg/kg 12‐hourly was initiated. His symptoms resolved promptly, and he remained hemodynamically stable throughout his admission, without clinical features suggestive of mesenteric ischaemia. He was discharged two days after admission on oral apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 10 days, followed by 5 mg twice daily for three months, with planned outpatient haematology follow‐up. He was counselled regarding signs of bleeding and advised to avoid sporting activities while receiving anticoagulation.

Haematology review was planned for two weeks after discharge. Haematological evaluation was initially directed toward testing for coagulation studies, lupus anticoagulant and JAK2 mutations. Owing to the prolonged turnaround time for these investigations, further thrombophilia testing was planned contingent on follow‐up and initial results. A stepwise and cost‐conscious diagnostic approach was adopted, prioritising clinically relevant and treatable aetiologies rather than extensive upfront testing. Unfortunately, the patient was subsequently lost to follow‐up; therefore, additional evaluation was not completed, and thrombus resolution, anticoagulation duration, recurrence risk and long‐term gastrointestinal outcomes could not be assessed.
