His medical history included Helicobacter pylori–negative gastritis treated with proton pump inhibitor therapy during a previous admission for AP.
There was no known personal or family history of thrombosis, autoimmune disease, malignancy or thrombophilia.
He denied smoking and recreational drug use and reported a recent long‐haul flight approximately one and a half weeks prior to presentation.
His only regular medication was omeprazole 40 mg twice daily, and he had no known drug allergies.
On examination, the patient appeared uncomfortable and in pain but was alert and fully oriented.
His temperature was 36.0°C, pulse rate 79 beats per minute, respiratory rate 19 breaths per minute, blood pressure 144/95 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% on room air.
Abdominal examination revealed a soft abdomen with normal bowel sounds and localised epigastric tenderness, without guarding, rigidity, rebound tenderness or organomegaly.
Cardiovascular, respiratory and neurological examinations were, otherwise, unremarkable.
There was no pallor, jaundice, cyanosis, lymphadenopathy, peripheral oedema, dehydration or muscle wasting.

Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated a normal full blood count, elevated serum lipase, mild transaminitis and elevated gamma‐glutamyl transferase, with preserved hepatic synthetic and renal function.
Serum calcium, glycated haemoglobin, immunoglobulin G4 levels and lactate were within normal limits (Table 1).
Contrast‐enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen performed on admission revealed features of AP involving the head and uncinate process, with a low CT severity index score of 2.
There was peripancreatic fat stranding extending into the intraperitoneal mesentery, with subcentimetre reactive peripancreatic lymph nodes.
There was a significant improvement in the extent of inflammation and peripancreatic fluid collection compared with the 2024 CT.
A small peripancreatic fluid collection measuring approximately 5.5 mL anterior to the pancreatic tail was considered to be a sequela of a prior episode.

An eccentric, nonocclusive filling defect was identified in the peripancreatic portion of the SMA, superior and anterior to the neck of the pancreas, spanning approximately 2.3 cm and resulting in approximately 58% luminal stenosis, consistent with thrombus (Figure 1).
The remaining mid and distal portions of the SMA were patent, with no CT features of downstream mesenteric ischaemia.
The small bowel loops enhanced normally, without bowel wall thickening, pneumatosis, portal venous gas or ascites.
In light of the incidental SMA thrombosis, cardiothoracic surgery and haematology consultations were obtained.
Because the thrombus was nonocclusive and there was no clinical or radiological evidence of bowel compromise, conservative management was recommended.

The clinical team also advised evaluation for alternative causes of arterial thrombosis, including embolic disease, inherited or acquired thrombophilia, inflammatory or autoimmune disease and occult malignancy.
Initial haematological investigations were unremarkable (Table 2).
The patient was managed conservatively for RAP with intravenous fluid resuscitation, analgesia and early enteral feeding.
For the SMA thrombosis, therapeutic anticoagulation with enoxaparin at 1 mg/kg 12‐hourly was initiated.
His symptoms resolved promptly, and he remained hemodynamically stable throughout his admission, without clinical features suggestive of mesenteric ischaemia.
He was discharged two days after admission on oral apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 10 days, followed by 5 mg twice daily for three months, with planned outpatient haematology follow‐up.
He was counselled regarding signs of bleeding and advised to avoid sporting activities while receiving anticoagulation.
Haematology review was planned for two weeks after discharge.
Haematological evaluation was initially directed toward testing for coagulation studies, lupus anticoagulant and JAK2 mutations.
Owing to the prolonged turnaround time for these investigations, further thrombophilia testing was planned contingent on follow‐up and initial results.
A stepwise and cost‐conscious diagnostic approach was adopted, prioritising clinically relevant and treatable aetiologies rather than extensive upfront testing.

Unfortunately, the patient was subsequently lost to follow‐up; therefore, additional evaluation was not completed, and thrombus resolution, anticoagulation duration, recurrence risk and long‐term gastrointestinal outcomes could not be assessed.
title: Incidental Nonocclusive Superior Mesenteric Artery Thrombosis in Recurrent Acute Pancreatitis: A Vascular Finding Without Bowel Ischaemia—A Case Report

case_text:
A 12-year-old Asian boy (body weight 62 kg) was referred to the pediatric rheumatology clinic for recurrent episodes of bilateral digital color change. He was diagnosed with ADHD at 9. Initial methylphenidate (18 mg/day) was discontinued after 1 month due to appetite loss and epigastric pain. He was then switched to atomoxetine, initiated at 30 mg/day (0.48 mg/kg/day), maintained at this dose for one full week, and then increased to 75 mg/day (1.21 mg/kg/day); 1 month later, the dose was further increased to 80 mg/day (1.29 mg/kg/day) and maintained at this dose for 2.5 years with good symptom control and no vascular complaints.

After 2.5 years, he developed progressive cold-induced pallor and cyanosis of both hands with livedo reticularis (Figures 1A,B), and similar changes on the nasal tip and earlobes (Figures 1C,D). Symptoms resolved upon rewarming but recurred with cold exposure. Episodes worsened after an upper respiratory tract infection. Physical examination showed cool extremities but normal peripheral pulses, no ulcers, atrophy, or sclerodactyly. Laboratory tests revealed mild leukopenia (3.59 × 109/L; reference 4.1-11) with normal inflammatory markers and normal hemoglobin(153 g/L; reference 129-172), bilirubin (10.52 μmol/L; reference 3.42-20.50) and lactate dehydrogenase (207U/L; reference 110-295) within their reference ranges; mildly decreased complement (C3 0.71 g/L, reference 0.89-1.87; C4 0.12 g/L, reference 0.14-0.44); while a comprehensive autoantibody panel (including antinuclear antibodies [ANA], extractable nuclear antigen [ENA] antibodies, anticardiolipin, anti-β2-glycoprotein I, and lupus anticoagulant), Coombs test, cryoglobulins, arterial Doppler ultrasonography of upper-extremity arteries, echocardiography and nailfold capillaroscopy were unremarkable. Given the normal hemoglobin, bilirubin and lactate dehydrogenase levels and the negative direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test, there was no evidence of a hemolytic process, and cold-agglutinin testing was therefore not pursued.

On the basis of the characteristic triphasic color changes, the patient was diagnosed with RP; other causes of cold-induced digital discoloration were considered and excluded: acrocyanosis was deemed unlikely because it is persistent and lacks the episodic triphasic color change observed in this patient, and pernio was likewise unlikely, as it typically presents with persistent erythematous-to-violaceous papules or nodules accompanied by itching or burning, without a color-change cycle. An exhaustive workup revealed no evidence of CTD, cryoglobulinemia, or vascular abnormalities. Given the temporal association with atomoxetine use and the absence of any prior history of RP, atomoxetine was considered the most likely trigger. The Naranjo Adverse Drug Reaction Probability Scale (Naranjo et al., 1981) yielded a total score of 7, corresponding to a “probable” adverse drug reaction (Supplementary Table 1). After consultation with the child psychiatry team, atomoxetine was discontinued and replaced with clonidine for ADHD management.

Within 2 weeks of withdrawal, the cold sensitivity had improved markedly, and a cold-water provocation test no longer induced digital color change (a non-standardized maneuver of limited diagnostic value, reported here only as supportive evidence rather than as a diagnostic criterion). At follow-up 3 weeks after discontinuation, repeat laboratory testing showed normalization of the white blood cell count (5.37 × 109/L) and complement levels. The patient remains on clonidine with stable ADHD symptoms and no recurrence of RP. The patient has now been followed for 18 months since withdrawal: complement levels and the autoantibody panel, re-checked every 6 months, have remained persistently normal, and no clinical features of connective tissue disease have emerged.

case_text:
A nineteen‐year‐old female presented to the emergency department (ED) by ambulance with a one‐day history of worsening shortness of breath and blue discoloration of the lips.

The patient had been taking 100 mg of dapsone orally each day for the treatment of subcorneal pustular dermatosis (SPD) for the past year. On the day prior to presentation, two tablets were ingested unintentionally, one at 6 p.m. and another at midnight after uncertainty about whether the first dose had been taken. Approximately 2 h after the second dose, she awoke with shortness of breath. Over the following hours, symptoms progressed and were associated with palpitations, prompting presentation to a health center. At that time, oxygen saturation was recorded at 80%–81% on room air, with a respiratory rate of 26 breaths/min. Oxygen was administered via a non‐rebreather mask (NRM) at 15 L/min, resulting in a partial improvement of saturation to 89%, and a transfer to the ED was arranged.

In the ED, the patient presented with a blood pressure of 101/69 mmHg, a heart rate of 117 beats/min (bpm), and a point‐of‐care (POC) blood glucose level of 5.4 mmol/L. A 12‐lead electrocardiogram (ECG) showed a sinus rhythm with sinus arrhythmia (Figure 1). Chest pain, dizziness, headache, nausea, and vomiting were denied.

The patient had been diagnosed with SPD 10 months earlier and had initially been treated with ixekizumab, dapsone, and topical tretinoin with a good response. Later, after stopping the medications, she started to have new lesions; accordingly, dapsone was restarted at a dose of 100 mg once daily. No other significant medical or surgical history was reported.

On physical examination, the patient was alert, conscious, and oriented to time and place. Her oxygen saturation was 90% while receiving oxygen via a NRM at 15 L/min. She was speaking comfortably in full sentences and did not appear to be in respiratory distress. Bluish discoloration of the lips, tip of the tongue, and nail beds was noted.

case_text:
A previously well, white, male in his sixties developed CRSwNP (Table 1) and flexible nasendoscopy, performed by ENT, revealed bilateral grade 3 nasal polyps. Initial management included standard medical therapy as per ENT guidelines. Imaging also identified a frontal sinus osteoma, and the patient was subsequently listed for functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS). Table 1Social and past medical history of the patientSocial and past medical history of patientLikely asthma Inhalers, including salamol and fostairNo seasonal allergic rhinitisNever smokedNo industrial exposureNo bird keeping

Although the initial surgical intervention was successful, the patient re-presented with vertical binocular diplopia, hyposmia, and hypogeusia. Imaging confirmed a left superior orbital abscess with frontal sinus dehiscence. He underwent urgent surgical drainage under joint ENT and ophthalmology teams.

Approximately 1 month later, the patient experienced recurrence of the same symptoms and Computerise Tomography (CT) imaging again confirmed a left orbital collection. He returned to theatre for revision drainage and was discharged with an extended course of antibiotics. Histopathological analysis revealed evidence consistent with inflammatory nasal polyps with the absence of fungal hyphae (Table 2). Table 2Microbiology, biochemistry and immunology investigationsMicrobiology, biochemistry and immunology investigationsMucin Neutrophils present No fungal hyphae Presence of eosinophils No bacterial growthSkin prick testing to aeroallergensNegativeTotal IgE 148 kU/L (mildly elevated)Blood cultures negativeCRP: <1–8 mg/L (over course of events)Aeroallergens tested included dog and cat dander, mixed trees, feathers, mixed grass and timothy grass, house dust mite and mould

Despite prior interventions, the patient presented a third time with similar symptoms and underwent another combined surgical procedure. Post-operatively, he was managed with a tapering course of oral corticosteroids, antibiotics and antihistamines.

Given the recurrent nature of his CRSwNP within months and severe complications posing threat to his eyesight, he was referred to clinical immunology for further management and consideration of biologics. At the time of presentation, Dupilumab was not NICE (National Institute for health and Care Excellence) funded for treating CRSwNP. Following an extensive but successful funding application, treatment with Dupilumab was started. Initial doses were observed in hospital and then education given to continue the treatment at home. SNOT-22 (Sino-Nasal Outcome Test) scores were completed at baseline, and throughout treatment, to assess symptom burden. Follow-up with ENT 2 weeks after initiating Dupilumab demonstrated symptomatic improvement, with complete resolution of nasal polyps observed on flexible nasoendoscopy at 6 weeks. He has since been discharged from ENT follow-up and remains stable under immunology care with ongoing Dupilumab therapy, with no further recurrences or adverse effects noted. An annual report is provided to the NHSE IFR (National Health Service England Individual Funding Request) panel detailing patient progress and response to treatment. Included within this are any ongoing healthcare cost savings, such as reduced out-patient visits compared to pre-treatment levels, and improvements in symptom and quality of life scores compared to baseline. If continued benefit can be adequately demonstrated via this report, funding for a further year of treatment is authorised. A trial of extended dose interval has thus far been unsuccessful; however, a further trial may be considered in the future.

Extreme rapidity of recurrence of polyps and collections

Absence of fungal hyphae

Threat to vision and disfigurement

Frontal sinus dehiscence

The severity of symptoms had a profound impact on the patient’s quality of life, with escalating concerns about potential unilateral vision loss and disfigurement. Encouragingly, the patient experienced rapid and sustained relief following initiation of therapy, contrastingly with previous surgical interventions, where symptoms would often recur within days. The current regimen involves self-administered subcutaneous injections every 2 weeks, which the patient is managing well. Interval dose duration extension has been attempted, however; there remains some anxiety around the potential return of symptoms. Notably, the patient reports a sensation of periocular tightness as they approach the end of the fortnightly cycle, which contributes to their hesitation in altering the dosing schedule.

CT of the paranasal sinuses in the coronal plane, with bone reconstructions (Fig. 1) and soft tissue window (Fig. 2) shows complete opacification of the maxillary, ethmoid and frontal sinuses as well as extensive nasal polyposis bilaterally. There is erosion of the floor of the left frontal sinus resulting in extension of inflammatory soft tissue into the left orbit.Fig. 1Coronal CT viewFig. 2 CT of a coronal soft tissue view

CT of the paranasal sinuses axial view in bone window (Fig. 3) shows complete opacification of the ethmoid and sphenoid sinuses together with a left posterior ethmoid osteoma.Fig. 3Axial view

title: A case of complicated chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps treated with dupilumab, in the UK: a case report

case_text: From age 35 years, the patient experienced episodes of chest discomfort when lying on her left side. At around age 38 years, she developed intermittent severe headache, palpitations, chest tightness, profuse sweating, hand tremors, facial pallor, and blanching of the fingertips. She also developed severe constipation and lost 7 to 8 kg over approximately 1 year. Physical exertion, such as carrying her child, exacerbated her palpitations and dizziness. No cushingoid features were observed. During the same period, hypertension (180/100 mmHg) was detected at a routine medical checkup. One year later, her blood pressure remained unstable despite treatment with candesartan and nifedipine. Abdominal ultrasonography subsequently revealed a 35-mm right adrenal mass, and she was referred to our hospital.

case_text:
A 16‐year‐old male was admitted to the Department of Neurology, Henan Provincial People’s Hospital, in January 2025 with a 1‐month history of fever and cough and a 7‐day history of left‐sided limb weakness.

One month before admission, he developed fever (maximum temperature, 38.5 °C), cough, yellow sputum, and blood‐streaked sputum. Blood culture and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) mNGS performed at an outside hospital both detected Klebsiella pneumoniae. His fever resolved after antibacterial therapy, but the pulmonary lesions showed limited radiographic improvement (Figure 1). Repeat BALF mNGS detected the Aspergillus flavus/oryzae complex (7243 reads) and herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV‐1; 4021 reads).

On January 1, 2025, the patient developed sudden left‐sided limb weakness and a dragging gait. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed multiple ring‐enhancing lesions in the bilateral frontal lobes, left temporal lobe, and right parieto‐occipital region (Figure 2). Since childhood, he had experienced recurrent upper respiratory tract infections (URTIs) several times per year, most of which improved after outpatient antimicrobial treatment, and he had a history of erysipelas. He had not previously undergone immunologic evaluation. There was no history of chronic diarrhea, arthritis, or autoimmune disease. Growth and development were normal, and there was no known family history of an inherited disease.

Physical examination revealed crackles over the right lower lung field. Neurologic examination showed Medical Research Council grade 4 strength in the left limbs, brisk tendon reflexes on the left, a positive Babinski sign, and a hemiparetic gait.

Immunologic testing showed an IgG level of 0.24 g/L, with both IgA and IgM < 0.10 g/L. Peripheral blood lymphocyte subsets were as follows: CD3+ T cells, 95.77% (1729/μL); CD3+CD4+ T cells, 33.12% (610/μL); CD3+CD8+ T cells, 60.97% (1126/μL); CD4/CD8 ratio, 0.54; CD19+ B cells, 0.00% (0.333/μL); and CD3−CD16+/CD56+ natural killer (NK) cells, 3.33% (59.9/μL). B‐cell subset analysis showed naïve B cells (CD19+CD27−IgD+), 0.00%, and memory B cells (CD19+CD27+CD38 dim/−), 0.01%. The serum galactomannan (GM) index was 1.627.

The opening pressure at the first lumbar puncture was normal, with a mild increase in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cell count. The CSF GM index was 1.54, and mNGS detected Staphylococcus hominis (758 reads). On repeat lumbar puncture, inflammatory indices in the CSF improved; GM remained positive in two independently collected CSF specimens.

Whole‐exome sequencing identified a hemizygous missense BTK variant, c.1039G > C (p.Ala347Pro), located in the Src homology 2 (SH2) domain. His mother and elder sister were heterozygous carriers, consistent with X‐linked recessive inheritance. The variant was classified as likely pathogenic according to American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) criteria (Figure 3).

The variant was classified as likely pathogenic according to American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) criteria (Figure 3).
title: X‐Linked Agammaglobulinemia Diagnosed in Adolescence Complicated by Invasive Aspergillosis: A Case Report

case_text: A 65-year-old female was evaluated for osteoporosis after sustaining multiple fragility fractures: a left hip fracture in 2017, a right tibial fracture in 2023, and a lumbar L2 compression fracture. Medical history included gastroesophageal reflux, chronic pancreatitis, chronic tobacco use disorder for 50 years, anxiety, and early surgical menopause at the age of 38 because of endometriosis. Her family history is also significant for osteoporosis in her mother, who sustained a hip fracture at the age of 84. The patient received vitamin D and calcium supplementation but no osteoporosis treatment. Her dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) revealed osteoporosis (T-scores: lumbar spine −3.3, right total hip −3.4, right femoral neck −3.9). She was deemed a high-risk patient because if her history of multiple fragility fractures and abaloparatide 80 mcg daily subcutaneous injection was initiated in September 2023.

case_text:
We report the case of a 3‐day‐old female neonate who was referred from a peripheral facility to the Tamale Teaching Hospital on account of congenital malformation of the eyelids (Figure 1). She was delivered as a late preterm neonate at 36+0 weeks via spontaneous vaginal delivery, with a birth weight of 2.8 kg. Her APGAR scores were 7 and 8, respectively. Her antenatal and perinatal periods were unremarkable, with no history suggestive of ichthyosis at birth, birth trauma, or prolonged labor.

On examination, she appeared stable and well‐hydrated. Vital signs were within normal limits for her age: oxygen saturation of 95% on room air, pulse rate of 121 bpm, temperature of 36.6°C, and respiration rate of 38 cycles/min. Anthropometric measurements showed a weight of 2.8 kg, a head circumference of 32 cm, and a length of 45 cm. Eye examination revealed bilateral upper eyelid eversion with severe chemosis of the palpebral conjunctiva. There was conjunctival prolapse. Slit‐lamp examination revealed clear corneas bilaterally, with no corneal epithelial defect, ulceration, or stromal thinning. There was no clinical evidence of exposure keratopathy at presentation. Complete eyelid closure was possible despite severe conjunctival chemosis and prolapse, which provided additional physical coverage of the cornea and may have reduced corneal exposure.

She was diagnosed with bilateral congenital ectropion based on the history and eye examination. Conservative management was initiated immediately and consisted of the following protocol:•Saline cleansing: The exposed conjunctiva was gently cleansed with gauze soaked in 0.9% isotonic sodium chloride solution every other day for 9 days.•Ocular lubrication: Approximately 1% tetracycline ointment was applied every other day for 9 days to prevent dryness and corneal exposure.•Manual reduction and pressure dressing: Following saline cleansing and ocular lubrication, manual repositioning of the ectropion was performed. Sterile gauze was then placed over the eyelid and secured with plaster to provide gentle pressure and maintain the eyelid in an anatomical position. This was performed on an alternate‐day basis.•Parental education: Parents were educated on care, monitoring, and the nature of the condition to dispel superstitious beliefs that accompany congenital anomalies in Northern Ghana.

Ocular lubrication: Approximately 1% tetracycline ointment was applied every other day for 9 days to prevent dryness and corneal exposure.

Manual reduction and pressure dressing: Following saline cleansing and ocular lubrication, manual repositioning of the ectropion was performed. Sterile gauze was then placed over the eyelid and secured with plaster to provide gentle pressure and maintain the eyelid in an anatomical position. This was performed on an alternate‐day basis.

Parental education: Parents were educated on care, monitoring, and the nature of the condition to dispel superstitious beliefs that accompany congenital anomalies in Northern Ghana.

A pediatric review was conducted prior to the neonate′s presentation to the ophthalmology department to exclude associated congenital conditions, including ichthyosis and Down syndrome, and to rule out systemic involvement. Progressive improvement was noted with the above conservative management. By Day 7, the left upper eyelid ectropion had fully resolved (Figure 2), and by Day 9 (Figure 3), the right upper eyelid ectropion also resolved completely.

case_text:
A 67-year-old woman presented to a local clinic after noticing a palpable mass, approximately 9 cm in diameter, in her right breast. She was subsequently referred to Fukushima Medical University Hospital for further evaluation. Her medical history was unremarkable, and she had no family history of breast malignancy. Clinical examination revealed a firm, elastic, and smooth-surfaced mass measuring 10 cm in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast. The overlying skin appeared erythematous without nipple discharge, and no axillary lymphadenopathy was noted.

Mammography revealed a well-circumscribed, high-density mass (Fig. 1). Ultrasonography demonstrated a smooth-marginated, hypoechoic mass, classified as BI-RADS Category 4C. Core needle biopsy raised the suspicion of a stromal sarcoma or a malignant phyllodes tumor. Immunohistochemical analysis revealed that the tumor was negative for ER, PgR, and HER2, but positive for SMA, CD34, and BCL2. The tumor cells were also negative for the broad-spectrum cytokeratin AE1/AE3, desmin, h-caldesmon, and S-100 protein, and the Ki-67 labeling index was 20%. Spindle cell metaplastic carcinoma was included in the preoperative differential diagnosis but was considered unlikely because no carcinomatous or in situ epithelial component was identified in any of the core biopsy specimens, and the spindle cells were negative for AE1/AE3 while diffusely expressing CD34. The absence of desmin and h-caldesmon argued against a smooth muscle tumor, and S-100 negativity against a peripheral nerve sheath tumor. STAT6 immunostaining was not performed on the biopsy specimen. These findings raised suspicion for a malignant phyllodes tumor.

CE-CT demonstrated a heterogeneously enhancing solid mass with a maximum diameter of 11 cm (Fig. 2A). FDG-PET/CT revealed high peripheral uptake with an SUVmax of 7.4 (Fig. 2B). MRI showed low signal intensity on T1-weighted images and high signal intensity on fat-suppressed T2-weighted images (Fig. 2C, 2D). Prominent peritumoral vascular structures were evident, and no distant metastases were identified. The CE-CT, FDG-PET/CT, and MR images shown in Fig. 2 were all obtained in the axial plane at the level of the maximum transverse diameter of the tumor; at this level, the tracer uptake formed a ring-shaped peripheral rim with a photopenic center (Fig. 2B).

The mass demonstrated progressive enlargement, reaching approximately 16 cm by the time of surgery (Fig. 3). A total right mastectomy was performed due to clinical and pathological suspicion of a malignant phyllodes tumor (Fig. 4). Histopathological examination revealed spindle-shaped cells arranged in a patternless architecture surrounding thin-walled, branching staghorn-like vessels, with frequent mitotic figures (32 per 50 high-power fields, corresponding to approximately 6.4 per 10 high-power fields) and extensive necrosis in the central portion of the tumor (Fig. 5). No epithelial components were observed. The plane of the cut surface of the mastectomy specimen (Fig. 4D) corresponded to that of the axial FDG-PET/CT image (Fig. 2B): the ring-shaped peripheral uptake corresponded to the solid, viable peripheral portion of the tumor, whereas the photopenic center corresponded to the central hemorrhagic and necrotic area, which was confirmed histologically (Fig. 5A). Immunohistochemically, the tumor cells exhibited diffuse and strong nuclear positivity for STAT6, along with positivity for CD34, CD99, β-catenin, BCL2, and SMA. They were negative for desmin, AE1/AE3, EMA, and S-100. The Ki-67 index was elevated at 37% (Fig. 5). The surgical margins were tumor-free, and the final pathological diagnosis was malignant SFT. The patient did not receive adjuvant therapy and has remained disease-free for 5 years postoperatively.

This case report was prepared in accordance with the Case Reports (CARE) guidelines. The CARE checklist has been completed and is provided in Supplementary Data (Supplementary Table S1).

A 20-year-old Caucasian female patient, non-smoking, negative for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), and not vaccinated against HPV, was diagnosed with ileocecal stenosing CD (compatible with Montreal classification A2L1B2) (Year 0). Initial treatment involved prednisone, budesonide, mesalamine, and sulfasalazine. After seven years of refractory CD, azathioprine (AZA) was introduced at a 100 mg dose (Year 7).

At Year 9, tumor marker evaluation was requested, revealing an elevated serum CA-125 level (85 U/mL at early Year 9, rising to 262 U/mL by late Year 9).

At Year 10 of the follow-up (three years into AZA therapy), cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 1 (CIN 1) was diagnosed by histopathology and managed via semiannual cytology/colposcopy. Three years later (Year 13), a pterygium-like ocular lesion developed, without episcleritis/uveitis. Biopsy indicated low-grade conjunctival intraepithelial neoplasia (Figure 1A); topical mitomycin was commenced. Eight months later (Year 14), total excision of the lesion revealed well-differentiated CjSCC (Figure 1B). Treatment included topical interferon. AZA was stopped for 10 months, being later resumed at a reduced dose (50 mg).

CD was controlled for two years but then relapsed, and the AZA dose was increased again (125 mg) (Year 17). A cutaneous lesion emerged on the left shoulder with an erythematous papule and central erosion. Histopathology revealed BCC (Figure 1C,D), which was promptly excised surgically. One year later (Year 18), the skin lesion had resolved, CD had remitted, and the AZA dose was maintained. Vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia grade 1 (VIN 1) and cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 (CIN 2) were detected by biopsy. AZA treatment was discontinued, and methotrexate (MTX) therapy was initiated. After 5 months, MTX was suspended due to drug-induced hepatitis, and CD relapse was managed with prednisone (40 mg/day).

In Year 19, the patient underwent cervical conization (Type 1 Transformation Zone Excision). Histopathology revealed moderately differentiated keratinizing CSCC with a measured stromal invasion depth of 3 mm, horizontal extension of 2 mm, circumferential extent of 9 mm, and presence of angiolymphatic invasion (Figure 1E,F). The endocervical surgical margin was involved by carcinoma in situ. Based on the FIGO 2018 staging classification, this lesion was categorized as microinvasive CSCC, FIGO stage IA2. She subsequently underwent a radical hysterectomy and excision of high-grade vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia (VIN 2) lesions. CD treatment commenced with vedolizumab (biologic) 300 mg every 8 weeks and continuous prednisone.

One year later (Year 20), CD persisted with symptoms, including stenosis and ulcerated lesions in the ileo-terminal region. Additionally, perianal condyloma and new vulvar lesions (keratosis, hypo- and hyperpigmented, and ulcerated areas) developed. Imiquimod treatment was effective, with lesion regression after 2 years. One year later (Year 23), at age 43, CD was in remission, with no evidence of new extraintestinal malignant lesions.

Throughout the entire period of clinical follow-up (Table 1; Figure 2), the patient did not present gastrointestinal malignancies. Extraintestinal oncological and tumor marker surveillance evolved progressively over the 23-year follow-up—including serum CA-125 monitoring during active disease in Year 9—shifting from routine diagnostic evaluations at CD onset to targeted gynecological, dermatological, and ophthalmological monitoring as precancerous and cancerous lesions emerged.

To investigate the molecular aspects of this clinical case, immunohistochemistry, PCR and sequencing were performed on samples from the conjunctival and cervical squamous cell carcinomas (see Supplementary Data). HPV 16 DNA was detected using a previously described pair of primers in both tumors, as confirmed by Sanger sequencing analysis (Supplementary Figure S1; Supplementary Table S2). Immunohistochemical analysis of the cervical and conjunctival squamous cell carcinomas revealed Ki-67 and p16 coexpression (Figure 3A–D). Figure 3E,F show an area of moderate cervical dysplasia with nuclear positivity for HPV-L1 in a koilocytic area, along with strong p16 expression involving the lower two-thirds of the dysplastic epithelium. Lymphatic invasion is evidenced by tumor cells within a podoplanin-positive lymphatic vessel (Figure 3G,H). In the cervical squamous cell carcinoma, a discrete CD8+ lymphocytic infiltrate (Figure 3I) and a more prominent CD4+ lymphocytic infiltrate (Figure 3J) were observed in areas of invasive carcinoma.

case_text:
A previously healthy 15-year-old young man presented with 5 weeks of abdominal pain and a 4.5 kg weight loss. The pain started after being punched in the stomach 10–15 times while playing with a friend. The pain was sharp and crampy in nature, mainly localized to his periumbilical region. Initially, the pain was intermittent but had increased in frequency and intensity over the past week. It did not improve or worsen with eating. He reported a bowel movement every day and pain that would sometimes improve after defecation. Review of systems was otherwise negative for fever, vomiting, diarrhea, or bloody stools.

Past medical history was notable for pneumonia at age 6 months and appendicitis at age 10, both treated with antibiotics. He did not take any medications and had a reported penicillin allergy.

Family history was unremarkable with no history of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) or gastrointestinal cancers. His maternal grandfather reportedly died in his early 30s from what was described as “twisting of his bowels.” Social history was notable for parents’ divorce when the patient was 7 years old. He lived in the United States with his mother but occasionally traveled to Italy to visit his father.

On examination, the patient had normal vital signs, weight was 90th percentile, and height was 80th percentile. His abdominal exam was soft, non-distended, and non-tender with audible bowel sounds. There was no hepatosplenomegaly. His cardiac, respiratory, and genitourinary exams were all normal. Complete blood count (CBC), metabolic panel, amylase and lipase, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), and C-reactive protein (CRP) were all within normal limits.

The patient became progressively worse over the next 7 months with multiple hospitalizations for ongoing periumbilical pain associated with significant anorexia but minimal nausea and no vomiting. During this period, he lost an additional 22.7 kg with total weight loss approaching 27.2 kg (37% of his baseline body weight). He underwent an extensive workup (see Table 1). Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) did not identify any mucosal abnormalities along the esophagus, stomach, or duodenum. Colonoscopy was notable for normal-appearing mucosa along the entire colon from the rectum to the cecum. Multiple random biopsies were taken from his upper and lower intestinal tract with no obvious pathology identified. A follow-up capsule endoscopy was performed given the positive fecal occult blood test and noted areas of possible inflammation in the distal small intestine.

The patient subsequently traveled to Italy to visit his father. He continued to experience abdominal pain but also began endorsing additional symptoms including four transient episodes of bright red blood in his stools and occasional episodes of emesis. He was hospitalized in Italy for further evaluation. A magnetic resonance enterography (MRE) was performed and showed an intestinal loop invagination secondary to suspected Meckel’s diverticulum. A repeat enteroscopy procedure showed possible ileitis near the ileocecal valve with suspected lymphoid hyperplasia of the last ileal loop. Biopsies of the ileum showed non-specific inflammation on histology. He subsequently underwent an exploratory laparoscopy that found evidence of ileoileal intussusception approximately 20 cm from the ileocecal valve. Manual reduction was performed and an epiploic appendix was identified as the cause of invagination. Ileal resection and end-to-end anastomosis were performed. Pathology showed erosion of the mucosa, underlying fibroblastic granulation tissue, and hypertrophy of the muscular wall. There were no surgical complications, and he reported doing well at the 2-week follow-up with complete resolution of his abdominal pain.

In the subsequent year following his surgery, the patient continued to do well and eventually gained back all the weight he had lost.

A 65‐year‐old man had been undergoing hemodialysis for 6 years for end‐stage kidney disease secondary to diabetic nephropathy. During pretransplant evaluation for living‐donor kidney transplantation from his spouse, his PSA level was elevated at 26.3 ng/mL, prompting referral to our department. Prostate magnetic resonance imaging revealed no evidence of malignancy. His PSA level subsequently declined; however, prostate cancer could not be excluded, and a systematic prostate biopsy was performed 1 month later. Adenocarcinoma with a Gleason score (GS) of 3 + 3 was detected in 2 of 20 biopsy cores (Figure 1). At the time of biopsy, the PSA level was 3.24 ng/mL, and the patient was diagnosed with low‐risk prostate cancer (cT1cN0M0, GS 3 + 3).

AS was offered and would not have precluded kidney transplantation; however, the patient preferred definitive treatment. Radiotherapy was selected because radical prostatectomy could complicate subsequent transplantation, and SBRT (35 Gy in five fractions) enabled treatment to be completed within a short pretransplant interval. Because the patient was anuric and unable to achieve adequate bladder filling through oral fluid intake, 200 mL of normal saline was instilled intravesically before each fraction to ensure reproducible bladder filling and reduce the risk of radiation‐related genitourinary toxicity.

Two months after the initial visit, the patient underwent SBRT every other day on non‐dialysis days, with intravesical saline administered before each fraction (Figure 2A–C). An absorbable hydrogel rectal spacer was not used. Serial PSA testing showed a decline from 1.39 ng/mL 1 month after SBRT to 0.82 ng/mL immediately before transplantation at 6 months after SBRT (Figure 3); clinical assessment found no severe acute radiation‐related adverse events. Given the low‐risk disease and completion of SBRT, transplantation proceeded without awaiting the final PSA nadir. No marked fibrosis or adhesions were observed in the iliac fossa or around the bladder; perivesical dissection, vascular anastomoses, and ureteroneocystostomy presented no technical difficulties attributable to SBRT. At 2 years after transplantation, the patient remained free of prostate cancer recurrence and severe radiation‐related adverse events, with favorable renal allograft function (Figure 3).

case_text:
A 75‐year‐old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and a 60‐pack‐year smoking history was referred for EBV treatment because of persistent exertional dyspnoea despite dual long‐acting bronchodilator therapy and pulmonary rehabilitation. His modified Medical Research Council (mMRC) dyspnoea grade was 3. Pulmonary function testing showed severe airflow obstruction with marked hyperinflation and reduced diffusing capacity (Table 1). CT demonstrated lower‐lobe‐predominant emphysema, and perfusion scintigraphy showed reduced perfusion of the left lower lung. The left lower lobe was therefore selected as the treatment target.

Under general anaesthesia with neuromuscular blockade and mechanical ventilation, the absence of collateral ventilation between the left upper and lower lobes was confirmed. Bronchoscopic sizing with the dedicated catheter led to placement of size 4.0 Zephyr regular valves (Pulmonx Corporation, Redwood City, CA, USA) in left B8, B9 and B10 (Figure 1C), and a size 5.5 low‐profile valve in left B6. Dyspnoea improved to mMRC Grade 1, although complete left lower‐lobe atelectasis was not achieved. One month later, the patient expectorated an EBV following a coughing episode, and his dyspnoea returned to Grade 3. CT and bronchoscopy confirmed loss of the valve from left B10 (Figure 1B,D). A size 5.5 regular valve was subsequently placed in B10. No further valve migration or expectoration has occurred, although complete left lower lobe atelectasis was not achieved.

Valve undersizing, variation in airway calibre, inadequate landing‐zone length, suboptimal placement and granulation tissue have been associated with EBV migration. As the B10 bronchus had an adequate landing zone and no granulation tissue was observed after expectoration, we investigated whether airway–valve size mismatch had contributed to valve displacement. Preprocedural inspiratory, expiratory and dynamic ventilation CT images were therefore retrospectively analysed to quantify airway lumen dimensions. Cross‐sectional images perpendicular to the bronchial axis were reconstructed along the distal approximately 5 mm of each target bronchus. The airway luminal boundary was determined using the full‐width at half‐maximum method and a perimeter‐derived inner diameter was calculated as luminal perimeter divided by π.

On static CT, the median [range] B10 diameter was 6.20 [6.11–6.42] mm during inspiration and 5.38 [5.33–5.43] mm during expiration (Figure 2C). Dynamic ventilation CT demonstrated substantially greater respiratory variation (Figure 2A,B), with the median B10 diameter changing from 6.55 [6.45–6.59] mm at end inspiration to 4.25 [3.96–4.62] mm at end expiration (Figure 2C). Thus, the B10 lumen approached the lower end of the size 4.0 valve range during expiration but expanded close to the upper end of its recommended 4.0–7.0‐mm working range during inspiration. The replacement size 5.5 valve has a recommended working range of 5.5–8.5 mm.

case_text:
A 21-year-old male presented with persistent unilateral nasal congestion and a recently identified left-sided nasopharyngeal mass. The patient reported unilateral nasal congestion for the past 2-3 years. His otolaryngologist identified a left-sided nasopharyngeal mass approximately one and a half month prior to presentation. He denied significant epistaxis or other symptoms related to the mass. His medical history was notable for asthma, for which he uses an inhaler. He does not smoke and rarely consumes alcohol. Surgical history included tonsillectomy and wisdom teeth extraction without anesthetic complications. Imaging demonstrated an angiofibroma, as shown in Fig. 1. Based on the extent of disease, the tumor was classified as Radkowski stage IIB. Preoperative embolization of the mass was coordinated with the interventional radiology team.Fig. 1Contrast-enhanced axial computed tomography (CT) image of the brain shows a hyperenhancing invasive mass centered in the left sphenoid sinus (A). Axial and coronal T1 fat-saturated contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrate a homogeneously enhancing left sphenoid mass invading adjacent ethmoid air cells and nasopharynx, without intracranial involvement (B and C).Fig 1 – dummy alt text

Angiographic runs of the right internal carotid artery (ICA), right external carotid artery (ECA), and left ICA did not demonstrate branch vessel supply to the tumor. Left posteroanterior (PA) and lateral ECA projection angiograms demonstrated a region of blush posterior to the ECA sphenopalatine artery branch, confirming it to be a contributing branch to the tangle of disorganized vessels making up the nasal angiofibroma, as seen in Fig. 2. No additional branches of the left ECA demonstrated supply to the tumor including the left lingual, facial, occipital, superficial temporal, internal maxillary, and middle meningeal arteries. No aneurysms, arteriovenous malformations, or fistulas were identified. There was no evidence of vasculopathy or vasculitis.Fig. 2Delayed phase conventional angiogram of the left internal maxillary artery branch of the ECA demonstrates the contrast blush of the hypervascular nasopharyngeal mass.Fig 2 – dummy alt text

Selective catheterization and angiography of the sphenopalatine artery branch of the left ECA was performed. Using a roadmap technique and the diagnostic catheter situated in the left ECA, the TRUSELECT microcatheter (Boston Scientific, Marlborough, MA) was advanced over an Aristotle 14 standard microwire (Scientia Vascular, West Valley City, UT) into the left internal maxillary artery. The microwire was then removed. PA and lateral projections demonstrated anterograde flow into the left sphenopalatine artery and its branches with the blush of the angiofibroma again visualized. No appreciable ophthalmic artery branches were evident. HydroPearl PEG particles (Terumo Interventional Systems, Somerset, NJ), 200 micrometers in size, were then injected until there was significant stasis of forward flow and subtle reflux around the catheter tip. Postembolization angiogram demonstrated decreased opacification of the angiofibroma blush consistent with embolization, as seen in Fig. 3. Postembolization left common carotid artery angiogram demonstrated no complications. The patient was then extubated and transferred to the intensive care unit in stable condition. He was transferred to the operating room the day following embolization for surgical resection of the mass.Fig. 3Postembolization conventional angiogram of the left internal maxillary artery shows no enhancement of the tumor.Fig 3 – dummy alt text

Surgical resection was performed with an estimated blood loss of only 50 mL, which is notably very low. The specimen was sent for pathologic evaluation, presented in Fig. 4. Pathology indicated the presence of β-catenin highlights within stromal cells with appropriate control reactivity, further supporting the clinical diagnosis.Fig. 4Biopsy of left sinonasal mass at 2× (A), 4× (B), and 10× (C) magnification demonstrates sinonasal tract angiofibroma with intravascular foreign material consistent with embolizing agent.Fig 4 – dummy alt text

case_text:
A 38-year-old man presented with a longstanding history of recurrent perianal discharge associated with lower urinary tract symptoms. He had no history of anorectal surgery, pelvic trauma, irradiation, inflammatory bowel disease, or other significant medical conditions. Family history was unremarkable, with no known colorectal malignancy or inflammatory bowel disease.

The patient was haemodynamically stable. Perianal examination revealed an external fistulous opening without acute inflammation, abscess, or surrounding cellulitis. Digital rectal examination demonstrated normal anal sphincter tone, with no palpable rectal mass or induration.

Colonoscopy, performed because of the chronic symptoms and suspected complex anorectal fistula, demonstrated cobblestone mucosa, multiple superficial ulcers, and skip lesions, raising suspicion of Crohn's disease. However, multiple biopsies showed no significant pathological abnormalities and did not support inflammatory bowel disease.

Pelvic MRI demonstrated a complex transsphincteric fistulous tract with an internal opening at the 12 o'clock position and a superior extension communicating with the bulbar urethra, confirming an acquired ano-bulbar urethral fistula (Figs 1 and 2). No pelvic abscess, secondary fistulous tract, or fluid collection was identified.

The case was discussed at a multidisciplinary meeting involving colorectal surgeons, urologists, and radiologists. Definitive surgical management was recommended because of the complex fistulous anatomy and urethral communication.

Under general anaesthesia, the patient was placed in the lithotomy position. Examination under anaesthesia confirmed the fistulous tract, and a probe was gently passed through the external opening to delineate its course (Fig. 3). Perineal dissection demonstrated a transsphincteric tract extending superiorly towards the bulbar urethra. Complete fistulectomy was performed, followed by identification and division of the urethral communication. The urethral defect was repaired primarily with interrupted absorbable sutures in a tension-free manner. The anorectal component was subsequently repaired, meticulous haemostasis was achieved, and the wound was closed in layers. A urethral catheter was left in situ for urinary diversion and to facilitate urethral healing.

Postoperative recovery was uneventful, with no urinary leakage, wound infection, or other early complications. At 1-month follow-up, the patient reported complete resolution of urinary and anorectal symptoms. Examination showed satisfactory wound healing, preserved urinary and bowel function, and no clinical evidence of recurrence or postoperative complications (Table 1).

case_text:
Patient information: 35-year-old gentleman who is otherwise fit and well with no significant past medical or surgical history.

Symptomatic right inguinal hernia confirmed on clinical examination.

An elective laparoscopic right inguinal hernia repair was undertaken under general anaesthetic. Open infraumbilical access using the Hasson technique was performed, with insertion of a 10 mm camera port and establishment of pneumoperitoneum.

Immediately following laparoscopy insertion through the infraumbilical port, the camera was observed as being within the lumen of a hollow viscus and, therefore, intraluminal. Conversion to midline laparotomy followed, which revealed a densely adherent MD to the undersurface of the umbilicus (Fig. 1). The diverticulum arose from the anti- mesenteric border of the distal ileum, as proved when the segment was delivered into the operative field, with the port having traversed its wall and caused an iatrogenic enterotomy (Fig. 2). The umbilical attachment was resected via segmental small bowel resection and primary anastomosis (Fig. 3).

The congenital attachment was divided, and the MD was resected. Reconstruction was then performed. The planned laparoscopic hernia repair was abandoned. Following recovery, the patient was scheduled for elective open right inguinal hernia repair.

Microscopic examination confirmed that the small bowel containing a diverticulum had specialized gastric mucosa. There is no significant inflammation and no evidence of malignancy.

Macroscopic examination demonstrated a 70 mm segment of small bowel measuring 30 mm in diameter, containing a diverticulum with an area of wall thickening, and a suspected stricture measuring 17 mm (Fig. 1).

The appearance was in keeping with MD.

The patient spent 3 days in the post-op ward. Upon discharge, he was subsequently listed for elective inguinal hernia repair.

case_text:
A 30‐year‐old male, working as active‐duty soldier presented to our facility with a 6‐year indolent history of progressive skin lesions, recurrent nasal congestion, recurrent epistaxis, and progressive distal sensory neuropathy. He reported no underlying medical history or previous contact with a person known to be affected by leprosy. His symptoms were started as pruritic erythematous macules on the lower limbs, and was attended as atopic dermatitis with topical steroids and antihistamines with suboptimal relief. Over time, the lesions were symmetrically progressing into diffuse plaques and nodules involving the face, trunk, and extremities, accompanied by persistent nasal congestion, then managed as allergic rhinitis at peripheral health facilities.

One year before presentation at our facility, he reported gradual worsening of neurological symptoms characterized by loss of temperature sensation in the toes and fingertips (glove‐and‐stocking pattern), resulting in repeated unnoticed minor trauma and burns‐like lesions, and was managed with Gabapentin and wound dressing without any promising relief. A month prior to admission, he developed painless trophic ulcers over the right medial malleolus and progressive loss of the lateral eyebrows. Furthermore, he was treated with oral Clindamycin and prednisolone for 10 days without relief. There were no constitutional symptoms, respiratory complaints, and/or liver or renal manifestations. He is married with normal sexual activity.

Physical examination revealed bilateral superciliary madarosis without nasal deformity. Dermatological evaluation showed numerous symmetrical hypopigmented erythematous macules, indurated plaques, and firm nodules involving the face, back, and extensor surfaces of the limbs (Figure 1). Arterial pulses were normally palpable in all the four limbs.

Neurological examination showed symmetrical hypoesthesia, analgesia, and loss of temperature sensation in a glove‐and‐stocking distribution extending to the mid‐forearms and mid‐calves with normal cranial nerves and motor system examination. Nerve conduction studies showed mononeuritis multiplex. Two painless non‐healing (trophic) ulcers measuring 2 × 2 cm were noted over the right medial malleolus with evidence of secondary bacterial infection, (Figure 1).

case_text:
A 32-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2, in a consanguineous relationship, underwent transabdominal CVS at 12 + 6 weeks gestation for prenatal diagnosis of ABCA3 deficiency. Her obstetric history included two vaginal deliveries. Her second child died at six years of age from ABCA3-related surfactant dysfunction, an autosomal recessive disorder.

The patient presented with vaginal spotting two days after the procedure and was managed expectantly. Ultrasound at 15 + 4 weeks confirmed a viable intrauterine pregnancy with a SCH measuring 51 × 45 × 20 mm. At 18 + 2 weeks she was admitted with vaginal bleeding. Ultrasound demonstrated appropriate fetal growth, a posterior placenta, normal amniotic fluid volume and enlargement of the SCH to 69 × 12 × 55 mm. Recurrent episodes of vaginal bleeding followed over the next 10 days, accompanied by intermittent lower abdominal cramping (Table 1); the cervix remained closed throughout. Serial ultrasound showed a reduction in haematoma size (45 × 8 × 5 mm at 19 + 2 weeks), and the anomaly scan at 19 + 3 weeks showed normal fetal biometry with a posterior low-lying placenta. She was discharged at 19 + 4 weeks.

She was readmitted at 19 + 5 weeks with further vaginal bleeding and abdominal pain. Fetal cardiac activity was preserved. By 20 + 2 weeks, cumulative estimated blood loss (EBL) had reached 1250 mL. Ultrasound at this stage demonstrated echogenic foci within the amniotic fluid, suggestive of intra-amniotic haemorrhage and a residual SCH of 3 × 3 cm. Inflammatory markers rose progressively over the subsequent 48 h (Table 1).

At 20 + 5 weeks she developed lower abdominal pain and a further 400 mL vaginal bleed, followed by the onset of labour. Speculum examination revealed malodorous, dark brown fluid suggestive of prelabour rupture of membranes, with the cervix 3 cm dilated and a fetal foot at the external os. Intra-amniotic infection was suspected; a septic screen was obtained including high-vaginal swab and empirical intravenous cefuroxime and metronidazole were commenced. Approximately three hours after the onset of contractions, at 20 + 6, the placenta delivered spontaneously, followed by the fetus in breech presentation with large retroplacental clot, suggestive of placental abruption. Cumulative EBL over the pregnancy including miscarriage was 2543 mL. The high-vaginal swab grew Citrobacter braakii, and the placental swab showed no growth. The placenta was submitted for histopathological examination.

The patient was discharged home on oral co-amoxiclav. On the day following discharge, the anaerobic blood culture bottle flagged positive for anaerobic Gram-positive cocci, with identification and antimicrobial susceptibility testing pending. She was advised to return for intravenous (IV) antibiotic therapy but declined. Following discussion with the microbiology team, she continued oral co-amoxiclav 625 mg three times daily.

Three days after discharge, she re-presented feeling unwell, with intermittent passage of clots. By this time, the organism had been identified as F. vaginae, confirming bacteraemia. Following microbiology advice, treatment was escalated to IV co-amoxiclav 1.2 g three times daily and metronidazole 500 mg three times daily. IV therapy was continued for 24 h. Her inflammatory markers then normalised and she remained apyrexial and clinically well, so she was discharged on a 10-day course of oral co-amoxiclav. Repeat blood cultures were negative. On day 19 following the miscarriage, she presented with persistent vaginal bleeding. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrated retained products of conception measuring 35 × 9.2 × 9 mm, and she underwent an uncomplicated evacuation of retained products of conception (ERPC). She was discharged on the same day. Table 1 summarises the key clinical events and microbiology results, and Figure 1 shows the trend in inflammatory markers (white cell count and C-reactive protein) over the clinical course.

Her obstetric history included two vaginal deliveries.
Her second child died at six years of age from ABCA3-related surfactant dysfunction, an autosomal recessive disorder.
The patient presented with vaginal spotting two days after the procedure and was managed expectantly.
Ultrasound at 15 + 4 weeks confirmed a viable intrauterine pregnancy with a SCH measuring 51 × 45 × 20 mm.
At 18 + 2 weeks she was admitted with vaginal bleeding.
Ultrasound demonstrated appropriate fetal growth, a posterior placenta, normal amniotic fluid volume and enlargement of the SCH to 69 × 12 × 55 mm.
Recurrent episodes of vaginal bleeding followed over the next 10 days, accompanied by intermittent lower abdominal cramping (Table 1); the cervix remained closed throughout.
Serial ultrasound showed a reduction in haematoma size (45 × 8 × 5 mm at 19 + 2 weeks), and the anomaly scan at 19 + 3 weeks showed normal fetal biometry with a posterior low-lying placenta.
She was discharged at 19 + 4 weeks.
She was readmitted at 19 + 5 weeks with further vaginal bleeding and abdominal pain.
Fetal cardiac activity was preserved.
By 20 + 2 weeks, cumulative estimated blood loss (EBL) had reached 1250 mL.
Ultrasound at this stage demonstrated echogenic foci within the amniotic fluid, suggestive of intra-amniotic haemorrhage and a residual SCH of 3 × 3 cm.
Inflammatory markers rose progressively over the subsequent 48 h (Table 1).
At 20 + 5 weeks she developed lower abdominal pain and a further 400 mL vaginal bleed, followed by the onset of labour.
Speculum examination revealed malodorous, dark brown fluid suggestive of prelabour rupture of membranes, with the cervix 3 cm dilated and a fetal foot at the external os.
Intra-amniotic infection was suspected; a septic screen was obtained including high-vaginal swab and empirical intravenous cefuroxime and metronidazole were commenced.

The high-vaginal swab grew Citrobacter braakii, and the placental swab showed no growth.
The placenta was submitted for histopathological examination.

case_text:
A 56-year-old male was admitted to our hospital on August 17, 2025, with a 6-month history of postprandial abdominal pain. Before his admission, the patient was evaluated at a local hospital, where contrast-enhanced abdominal computed tomography (CT) suggested possible intestinal adhesions with mild dilation of the proximal intestine and stomach, as well as a suspected gastrojejunal fistula. Despite receiving conservative treatment, the abdominal pain persisted without significant improvement. The patient had no history of foreign body ingestion (such as fruit pits or animal bones), peptic ulcer disease, gastric cancer, or prior abdominal surgery.

Physical examination revealed persistent dull pain and localized tenderness in the mid-upper abdomen, without rebound tenderness or abdominal muscle guarding. The remainder of the abdominal examination was normal. The patient’s vital signs were as follows: body temperature 36.4°C, pulse 75 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and blood pressure 131/80 mmHg. Routine blood examination revealed the following: white blood cell count of 4970/mm3 (normal range 4000–10 000/mm3), proportion of neutrophils of 50.7% (normal range 40–75%), red blood cell count of 4900/mm3 (normal range 3800–5100/mm3), and platelet count of 184 × 103/mm3 (normal range 100–300/mm3). Liver and renal function tests were within normal limits.

An upper digestive tract ioversol angiography showed a normotonic stomach with early opacification of the jejunum, demonstrating a fistulous tract between the gastric fundus and the jejunum. (Fig. 1A and B). Abdominal enhanced CT scan showed a focal disruption of the gastric wall along the greater curvature of the gastric fundus, which communicated with the underlying proximal jejunum via a visible fistulous tract (Fig. 1C). Gastroscopy revealed a depression on the posterior wall of the gastric fundus adjacent to the greater curvature, surrounded by converging gastric folds, indicating a fistulous tract formation (Fig. 1D). Based on the symptoms and the above imaging findings, the diagnosis of a congenital gastrofundic jejunal fistula was suspected.

Following multidisciplinary team discussion and comprehensive preoperative preparation, laparoscopic exploration was performed for the patient. Intraoperatively, due to severe adhesions in the upper abdominal cavity, the fistulous tract could not be identified; therefore, the gastroscopy was underwent during the operation procedure for this case, which successfully revealed the fistula. Additionally, significant anatomical variations were identified in the patient’s abdominal cavity as follows. The ligament of Treitz was found to be absent; a segment of jejunum, approximately 10 cm in length, ascended through the transverse mesocolon and coursed posterior to the pancreas, communicating with the posterior wall of the gastric fundus near the greater curvature, forming a fistulous tract with severe adhesions to the surrounding tissues (Fig. 2A). After separating the fistula tube, an endoscopic linear cutting stapler (EC60A, Ethicon) was used to for the resection and closure of the fistula at the gastric fundus (Fig. 2B). Finally, a drainage tube was routinely placed in the abdominal cavity. The operation time was 128 min and intraoperative blood loss was 72 ml.

The patient had an unremarkable postoperative recovery. Oral feeding was initiated on postoperative day 3 after flatus, and no epigastric pain or other symptoms were mentioned. Subsequently, the patient was discharged on postoperative day 5. During the 6-month follow-up period, no specific symptoms or discomforts were reported, and the findings of upper gastrointestinal radiography and gastroscopy examination were normal (data not shown).

case_text:
A 79-year-old man experienced sudden chest pain while playing golf and visited his primary physician. He was transferred to a local hospital with suspected ACS. Approximately 2 years and 4 months (850 days) earlier, he had undergone mediastinoscopic subtotal esophagectomy and retrosternal gastric conduit reconstruction for thoracic esophageal cancer. The pathological diagnosis was ypT3N0M0, ypStage II according to the 8th edition of the UICC TNM classification. Further evaluation ruled out ACS. CT revealed herniation of the small bowel into the thoracic cavity through a space along the left side of the gastric conduit and decreased enhancement of the small-bowel wall. Consequently, the patient was transferred to our hospital.

Laboratory tests showed the following: white blood cell count, 14.04 × 103/μL; neutrophils, 90.5%; hemoglobin, 14.6 g/dL; platelet count, 19.8 × 104/μL; C-reactive protein, 0.04 mg/dL; serum albumin, 3.12 g/dL; total bilirubin, 0.40 mg/dL; aspartate aminotransferase, 26.6 U/L; alanine aminotransferase, 51.0 U/L; and creatinine, 0.67 mg/dL. His estimated glomerular filtration rate was 85.8 mL/min/1.73 m2. An arterial blood gas analysis indicated metabolic acidosis: pH, 7.363; HCO3⁻, 17.2 mmol/L; lactate, 3.1 mmol/L; and base excess, −6.6 mmol/L.

Plain chest radiography showed diffuse increased opacity in the left lung field (Fig. 1). CT showed extensive herniation of the jejunum near the ligament of Treitz into the left thoracic cavity. Although slight enhancement remained in the herniated bowel, it showed decreased enhancement and edematous changes relative to the intra-abdominal small bowel (Fig. 2A, 2B). Based on persistent chest pain and CT findings suggestive of impaired intestinal blood flow, the patient was diagnosed with an acutely irreducible retrosternal hernia with small-bowel ischemia after retrosternal gastric conduit reconstruction.

Emergency surgery was performed approximately 9 hours after symptom onset for an acutely irreducible retrosternal hernia with suspected small-bowel ischemia. During laparotomy through an upper midline incision, the proximal jejunum was found to have entered the left thoracic cavity through a space along the left side of the narrow gastric conduit elevated via the retrosternal route, consistent with the preoperative CT findings (Fig. 3A). The acutely irreducible bowel was carefully reduced into the abdominal cavity. Approximately 200 cm of the small bowel, originating from the jejunum approximately 30 cm distal to the ligament of Treitz, had herniated into the thoracic cavity. Despite reduction, the dark-red discoloration of the bowel and marked mesenteric congestion did not improve. Irreversible intestinal ischemia was therefore diagnosed, and partial small-bowel resection was performed (Fig. 3B). After resection, approximately 200 cm of the small bowel remained, and intestinal continuity was restored with functional end-to-end anastomosis using linear staplers.

After reduction of the acutely irreducible bowel, examination of the hernia orifice revealed an approximately 2-cm pleural defect on the left side of the gastric conduit (Fig. 3C). The small bowel entered the retrosternal space through the retrosternal inlet and then passed through the approximately 2-cm left pleural defect into the thoracic cavity; this defect was considered the site of acute irreducibility (Fig. 4). While carefully preserving blood flow through the right gastroepiploic artery and vein, the left side of the gastric conduit was sutured to the peritoneum and pleura surrounding the hernia orifice to close the space (Fig. 3D). The operative time was 81 min, and blood loss was 100 mL. Histopathological examination showed ischemic mucosal necrosis and hemorrhage, findings consistent with strangulated small-bowel obstruction.

No postoperative complications occurred. Oral intake was started on POD 4, and the patient was discharged on POD 11. Regular CT follow-up for esophageal cancer surveillance showed no recurrence of the hernia at approximately 1 year after repair.

case_text: A 15‐year‐old boy presented with a history of intermittent right breast pain and spontaneous bloody nipple discharge for 1 month. The patient had a right breast mass since he was five, but it remained asymptomatic until nipple discharge began in recent months (Table 1). The patient had no significant past medical history and took no medications. The patient did not have any family history of breast cancer or other malignancies. Physical examination showed that a firm, relatively fixed, clearly marginated mass was palpated in the right breast (Figure 1). The mass was ~3 cm × 8 cm × 5 cm. Mild skin changes of the nipple were noted, without erythema, warmth, or tenderness. No palpable lymphadenopathy was detected in the axillary, supraclavicular, or cervical regions.

case_text:
A 65-year-old man with a 20-year history of diabetes mellitus and hypertension underwent VP shunt placement for benign hydrocephalus three weeks before presentation. He presented to the emergency department with a 2-day history of abdominal pain, vomiting, progressive abdominal distension, and hiccups. Clinical examination and plain abdominal radiography were consistent with small-bowel obstruction (Fig. 1). Laboratory investigations demonstrated leukocytosis with neutrophilia and mild hypokalaemia.

Given the clinical and radiological evidence of mechanical small-bowel obstruction, emergency exploratory laparotomy was performed. Intraoperatively (Fig. 2), the proximal small bowel was markedly dilated up to the mid-ileum, where the distal VP shunt catheter was found coiled around the bowel, producing a clear mechanical transition point. The bowel distal to the obstruction was collapsed. The involved bowel remained viable, with no evidence of ischaemia, necrosis, or perforation. The catheter was carefully released from the bowel, and the intraperitoneal portion was shortened. No bowel resection was required.

The postoperative course was uncomplicated, with recovery of bowel function and progressive clinical improvement. The patient was subsequently discharged home in stable condition.

case_text: An 80-year-old man with a history of ulcerative colitis treated conservatively with monoclonal antibody therapy underwent CTC for colorectal cancer surveillance. He had no history of previous abdominal surgery. During insertion of the rectal catheter, he experienced mild rectal pain; nevertheless, the procedure was completed. Review of the CTC images subsequently demonstrated extensive extraperitoneal gas, raising suspicion of rectal perforation, and the patient was referred to the emergency department for further assessment. Digital rectal examination revealed blood, but no obvious mucosal defect or gross rectal disruption was identified. The patient reported no abdominal pain and remained hemodynamically stable, with no clinical evidence of peritonitis or sepsis. CT demonstrated extensive extraperitoneal gas surrounding the rectum and extending into the adjacent pelvic soft tissues. The tip of the rectal catheter was in close proximity to the suspected site of rectal injury (Fig. 1). Gas was also identified within the portal venous system (Fig. 2), with branching areas of intrahepatic gas involving both the right and left hepatic lobes (Fig. 3). The patient was admitted to the general surgery department for close observation and conservative management. Treatment consisted of broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, intravenous fluids, and bowel rest. Serial clinical assessments were performed, with particular attention to abdominal pain, peritoneal signs, fever, hemodynamic instability, and other evidence of systemic infection. The patient remained clinically well and afebrile throughout his admission. The white-cell count was 17.7 × 109/L and C-reactive protein was 11.2 mg/dL on admission, with both showing a downward trend from hospital Day 2, and no clinical deterioration occurred. He was discharged home on hospital Day 3 following an uncomplicated clinical course.

case_text:
Early recognition of LD is important for reducing the risk of complications. Early localized infection commonly occurs within weeks of exposure and may be accompanied by nonspecific systemic symptoms, including fatigue, malaise, fever, night sweats, myalgia, and arthralgia. Erythema migrans is the most diagnostically useful early clinical sign. Although it is common in early LD, its reported frequency varies by clinical setting and method of ascertainment. Only approximately 40% of patients with Lyme carditis recall a characteristic erythema migrans lesion. Clinicians should also recognize that the lesion does not always have the classic concentric “bull’s-eye” appearance; it may instead present as a uniformly erythematous or otherwise atypical plaque. Failure to recognize these atypical presentations may delay diagnosis.

Cardiac manifestations generally develop within weeks of the initial skin lesion or other early symptoms, although the interval can vary. Lyme carditis is rarely fatal, but life-threatening presentations have been reported. Importantly, AV block may be the initial or only recognized manifestation of LD. Patients may therefore present with cardiac conduction abnormalities without a typical rash or other preceding symptoms, making a high index of clinical suspicion essential. Autopsy findings and published clinical reports document severe and occasionally fatal cardiac presentations, despite the generally reversible nature of conduction abnormalities with appropriate treatment.

AV block is reported in up to 90% of published Lyme carditis cases, although this estimate is derived largely from selected clinical series. A characteristic feature is rapid fluctuation in the degree of conduction impairment. Within hours or days, a patient’s conduction may deteriorate from first-degree to complete AV block or improve in the opposite direction. Complete (third-degree) AV block has been documented in published Lyme carditis cases, although case-based reviews and selected clinical series cannot establish its population-level frequency. Clinical guidance identifies a PR interval greater than 300 ms as an important risk marker and a reason to consider hospital admission and cardiac monitoring. Other electrocardiographic findings may include left or right bundle-branch block and sinoatrial block. ST-segment depression, particularly in the anterolateral leads, and flattened or inverted T waves, often in the inferolateral leads, have also been reported, although these findings are nonspecific. In severe cases, asystole may occur if an adequate escape rhythm fails to develop. Atypical presentations, including bundle-branch block or atrial fibrillation, have been described but are not specific to Lyme carditis. Uzomah and colleagues examined predictors of pacemaker implantation in a hospitalized cohort of patients with Lyme carditis, whereas Zainal and colleagues described a patient whose initial presentation was atrial fibrillation. Less common forms of cardiac involvement include endocarditis, myocarditis, pericarditis, and pancarditis.

A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis summarized 110 published cases of Lyme carditis with rhythm abnormalities. The review provides a descriptive overview of conduction disturbances and non-AV arrhythmias. However, much of the pooled evidence was derived from case reports and small case series, which limits the reliability of prevalence estimates and comparative effect measures. Its findings should therefore be considered hypothesis-generating rather than definitive estimates of population-level risk.

Lyme endocarditis is extremely rare, and its clinical manifestations are generally indistinguishable from those of endocarditis caused by other pathogens. When endocarditis is the only recognized manifestation of LD, diagnosis can be particularly challenging: serological testing cannot reliably distinguish active infection from previous exposure, and culture has low sensitivity and important practical limitations. In such cases, the possibility of Borrelia infection should be considered in light of the patient’s epidemiological history and clinical presentation, with pathogen-specific testing pursued when appropriate, particularly in endemic regions.

The association between LD and dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) remains controversial, and a causal relationship has not been established. Early reports from Europe raised the possibility of Borrelia-associated myocardial disease, but these reports provide only anecdotal evidence. In 1990, Stanek and colleagues reported isolation of Borrelia burgdorferi from an endomyocardial biopsy specimen obtained from a patient with longstanding cardiomyopathy. Gasser and colleagues subsequently described improvement in cardiac function following ceftriaxone treatment in patients with suspected Borrelia-associated DCM. These individual reports are hypothesis-generating and do not establish an epidemiological association or a causal relationship. Subsequent studies have yielded conflicting findings. A prospective study of patients with severe heart failure in the USA concluded that LD was not a common cause of idiopathic heart failure, while a controlled prospective study in the United Kingdom found no evidence implicating B. burgdorferi in the pathogenesis of DCM. A systematic review of 11 observational studies involving 771 participants found that 7 studies reported evidence of an association between Borrelia infection and DCM; nevertheless, the authors emphasized that further research is required to establish a causal relationship. Accordingly, the potential association remains unresolved. Consistent with this uncertainty, the 2020 guidelines of the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA), American Academy of Neurology (AAN), and American College of Rheumatology (ACR) suggest against routine LD testing in patients with chronic cardiomyopathy of unknown cause.
