Although it is common in early LD, its reported frequency varies by clinical setting and method of ascertainment.
Only approximately 40% of patients with Lyme carditis recall a characteristic erythema migrans lesion.
Clinicians should also recognize that the lesion does not always have the classic concentric “bull’s-eye” appearance; it may instead present as a uniformly erythematous or otherwise atypical plaque.
Failure to recognize these atypical presentations may delay diagnosis.
Cardiac manifestations generally develop within weeks of the initial skin lesion or other early symptoms, although the interval can vary.
Lyme carditis is rarely fatal, but life-threatening presentations have been reported.
Importantly, AV block may be the initial or only recognized manifestation of LD.
Patients may therefore present with cardiac conduction abnormalities without a typical rash or other preceding symptoms, making a high index of clinical suspicion essential.

Autopsy findings and published clinical reports document severe and occasionally fatal cardiac presentations, despite the generally reversible nature of conduction abnormalities with appropriate treatment.
AV block is reported in up to 90% of published Lyme carditis cases, although this estimate is derived largely from selected clinical series.
A characteristic feature is rapid fluctuation in the degree of conduction impairment.
Within hours or days, a patient’s conduction may deteriorate from first-degree to complete AV block or improve in the opposite direction.
Complete (third-degree) AV block has been documented in published Lyme carditis cases, although case-based reviews and selected clinical series cannot establish its population-level frequency.
Clinical guidance identifies a PR interval greater than 300 ms as an important risk marker and a reason to consider hospital admission and cardiac monitoring.
Other electrocardiographic findings may include left or right bundle-branch block and sinoatrial block.
ST-segment depression, particularly in the anterolateral leads, and flattened or inverted T waves, often in the inferolateral leads, have also been reported, although these findings are nonspecific.
In severe cases, asystole may occur if an adequate escape rhythm fails to develop.
Atypical presentations, including bundle-branch block or atrial fibrillation, have been described but are not specific to Lyme carditis.

Uzomah and colleagues examined predictors of pacemaker implantation in a hospitalized cohort of patients with Lyme carditis, whereas Zainal and colleagues described a patient whose initial presentation was atrial fibrillation.
Less common forms of cardiac involvement include endocarditis, myocarditis, pericarditis, and pancarditis.
A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis summarized 110 published cases of Lyme carditis with rhythm abnormalities.
The review provides a descriptive overview of conduction disturbances and non-AV arrhythmias.
However, much of the pooled evidence was derived from case reports and small case series, which limits the reliability of prevalence estimates and comparative effect measures.
Its findings should therefore be considered hypothesis-generating rather than definitive estimates of population-level risk.
Lyme endocarditis is extremely rare, and its clinical manifestations are generally indistinguishable from those of endocarditis caused by other pathogens.

When endocarditis is the only recognized manifestation of LD, diagnosis can be particularly challenging: serological testing cannot reliably distinguish active infection from previous exposure, and culture has low sensitivity and important practical limitations.

In such cases, the possibility of Borrelia infection should be considered in light of the patient’s epidemiological history and clinical presentation, with pathogen-specific testing pursued when appropriate, particularly in endemic regions.
The association between LD and dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) remains controversial, and a causal relationship has not been established.
Early reports from Europe raised the possibility of Borrelia-associated myocardial disease, but these reports provide only anecdotal evidence.
In 1990, Stanek and colleagues reported isolation of Borrelia burgdorferi from an endomyocardial biopsy specimen obtained from a patient with longstanding cardiomyopathy.
Gasser and colleagues subsequently described improvement in cardiac function following ceftriaxone treatment in patients with suspected Borrelia-associated DCM.
These individual reports are hypothesis-generating and do not establish an epidemiological association or a causal relationship.
Subsequent studies have yielded conflicting findings.

A prospective study of patients with severe heart failure in the USA concluded that LD was not a common cause of idiopathic heart failure, while a controlled prospective study in the United Kingdom found no evidence implicating B. burgdorferi in the pathogenesis of DCM.

A systematic review of 11 observational studies involving 771 participants found that 7 studies reported evidence of an association between Borrelia infection and DCM; nevertheless, the authors emphasized that further research is required to establish a causal relationship.
Accordingly, the potential association remains unresolved.

Consistent with this uncertainty, the 2020 guidelines of the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA), American Academy of Neurology (AAN), and American College of Rheumatology (ACR) suggest against routine LD testing in patients with chronic cardiomyopathy of unknown cause.
title: Lyme Carditis: Cardiac Inflammation, Proposed Molecular Mimicry, Diagnosis, and Management

case_text:
A 6‐year‐old left‐hand–dominant female was referred to the pediatric neurology clinic for evaluation of persistent bilateral MM involving the upper limbs. The abnormal movements were first noticed by her mother at approximately 3 years of age and were characterized by involuntary, symmetric movements of the contralateral hand during voluntary unimanual activities. There was no history of other abnormal involuntary movements, seizures, weakness, or loss of motor skills. Over time, the pattern of MM remained stable without progression. At the time of presentation, the child was functioning well in daily activities. She was attending first grade and demonstrated preserved fine motor abilities, including a good pincer grasp, appropriate handwriting for age, and independent feeding. The MM did not significantly interfere with school performance or activities of daily living.

She was born via full‐term normal spontaneous vaginal delivery following an uncomplicated pregnancy. There was no history of perinatal distress or neonatal intensive care unit admission. Growth and nutrition were appropriate for age, and vaccinations were up to date. Developmental milestones were largely age appropriate, except for speech delay. The speech delay was attributed to conductive hearing impairment secondary to recurrent middle ear effusion, which subsequently improved according to parental report. She slept approximately 10 h per night and followed a regular family diet. There was no history of parental consanguinity. The patient had six siblings (four males and two females), all of whom were healthy with normal neurodevelopment. No family history of similar movement disorders, other neurological conditions, or known genetic diseases was reported. The family pedigree and segregation analysis are presented in Figure 1. On clinical examination, the patient appeared well and nondysmorphic. She was alert, interactive, and able to answer simple questions appropriately. No abnormal movements were observed at rest. Neurological examination revealed intact cranial nerve function, with pupils equal and reactive to light and normal extraocular movements. Facial sensation and symmetry were preserved. Muscle bulk, tone, and strength were normal in all extremities, with power graded 5/5 and deep tendon reflexes graded +2 symmetrically. Plantar responses were flexor bilaterally. Gait was normal, and coordination testing, including finger‐to‐nose and heel‐to‐shin maneuvers, was intact. During purposeful voluntary movements of one hand, mild but sustained involuntary mirroring movements were consistently observed in the contralateral hand and were graded as 2/4 on the Woods and Teuber Scale (Supporting Video 1). No other involuntary movements were observed.

Genetic testing was undertaken as part of the diagnostic evaluation. Chromosomal microarray analysis was normal. Whole‐exome sequencing identified a heterozygous missense variant in TUBB NM_178014.4:c.155A > G; p.(Asn52Ser). This variant has previously been reported in ClinVar. Although pathogenic variants in TUBB are known to cause autosomal dominant tubulinopathies, the variant was initially classified as a variant of uncertain significance by the diagnostic laboratory. Parental segregation testing demonstrated that the variant was absent in both parents, supporting a de novo occurrence. Following multidisciplinary genotype–phenotype correlation with the diagnostic laboratory and clinical geneticist, the variant was reclassified as likely pathogenic in accordance with the ACMG criteria PS2, PM2, PP2, and PP4.

Brain MRI demonstrated hypoplasia and abnormal configuration of the pons with mild atrophy of the brainstem and superior cerebellar peduncles. Partial dysgenesis and thinning of the corpus callosum were present. The basal ganglia showed asymmetric configuration with malrotated caudate heads protruding into the lateral ventricles. Additional asymmetry was noted in the insular cortex and Sylvian fissures, which appeared shallow on the left side (Figure 2A–C). No classical malformations of cortical development such as polymicrogyria or heterotopia were identified. Right periventricular parieto‐occipital white‐matter cystic changes and gliosis were observed, likely reflecting a remote prenatal or postnatal insult. Magnetic resonance angiography and venography were unremarkable apart from a fetal origin of the right posterior cerebral artery.

The differential diagnosis initially included isolated familial CMM related to DCC, RAD51, or NTN1 variants; MM secondary to callosal dysgenesis; and motor overflow associated with developmental coordination disorder. Acquired causes such as perinatal stroke, structural corticospinal tract lesions, or epileptic phenomena were considered unlikely given normal strength, absence of seizures, and a stable clinical course. The combination of callosal and brainstem abnormalities on MRI raised suspicion for an underlying tubulinopathy, subsequently supported by the TUBB variant.

Based on the clinical presentation, neuroimaging findings, and genetic results, a diagnosis of CMM associated with TUBB‐related tubulinopathies was established. The imaging abnormalities align with known disruptions of neuronal migration and corticospinal tract development described in tubulin disorders.

The patient has remained clinically stable with preserved fine motor abilities and no progression of symptoms. No pharmacological treatment was initiated. The management plan includes follow‐up in the pediatric neurology clinic every 6 months with monitoring of motor development and surveillance for additional features associated with tubulinopathies.

case_text:
A 57‐year‐old male with no known prior comorbidities presented with imbalance while walking and slurring of speech for three days. The symptoms had a sudden onset and followed a fluctuating course. There was no history of fever, headache, seizures, altered sensorium, limb weakness, or symptoms suggestive of sensory deficits. The patient denied recent alcohol intake.

He was initially evaluated at a health facility where he was diagnosed with acute cerebellar stroke and managed with antiplatelet agents and statins. However, because of persistent symptoms without improvement, he presented to our tertiary care center for further evaluation.

On detailed history, the patient reported an episode of painless genital ulceration two years earlier following unprotected sexual intercourse with a new sexual partner who had multiple sexual partners. The lesion healed spontaneously without medical treatment.

On admission, the patient was conscious and oriented with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of E4V5M6. Vital signs were stable. General physical examination revealed a single well‐defined skin‐colored to pale plaque over the inner aspect of the prepuce without overlying skin changes or inguinal lymphadenopathy. Neurological examination demonstrated dysarthria and prominent cerebellar signs, including dysdiadochokinesia, impaired heel–shin coordination, and broad‐based ataxic gait. Tone, muscle power, deep tendon reflexes, and sensory examination were normal. Romberg test was negative. Other systemic examinations were unremarkable.

MRI of the brain showed a patchy area of altered signal intensity appearing on T2WI/FLAIR and restriction of diffusion noted in the left cerebellum (Figure 1).

Based on the clinical presentation, history of presumed untreated primary syphilis, positive serum TPHA, and reactive CSF VDRL test (Table 1), a diagnosis of neurosyphilis (likely meningovascular with cerebellar involvement) was made. He was managed with injection ceftriaxone for 14 days. He showed marked clinical improvement and discharged home.

case_text:
Initial presentation

A male infant was born to a 33-year-old mother in a nonconsanguineous union. The pregnancy was considered high risk because of maternal hypertension during the third trimester and rapid maternal weight gain; there was no history of maternal diabetes. Prenatal ultrasonography performed at 31 weeks of gestation identified right renal agenesis and ectopia of the left kidney. Delivery occurred vaginally at 40 weeks and five days of gestation. At birth, the infant weighed 3,850 g, measured 50 cm in length, and had a head circumference of 31 cm (below the 3rd percentile). Apgar scores were 8 and 9 at one and five minutes, respectively.

At one month and 10 days of age, the patient was admitted after laboratory testing showed a plasma creatinine level of 58 μmol/L (0.66 mg/dL). Given the right renal agenesis and ectopic left kidney, he was referred to pediatric nephrology and diagnosed with chronic kidney disease (CKD).

Physical examination

Craniofacial examination showed a flat forehead, round low-set ears, preauricular pits, a short neck with skin folds, a high-arched palate, and protrusion of the tongue. No digital or spinal abnormalities were documented. Neurological examination revealed microcephaly with a head circumference of 33.3 cm (below the 3rd percentile), involuntary movements of the upper extremities, limb contractures, and cervical hyperextension. The heart rate was 120 beats/min and blood pressure was 130/90 mmHg. A grade V/VI systolic murmur was audible at the lower left sternal border without radiation.

Imaging studies

Renal Findings

Renal ultrasonography did not visualize the right kidney. The left kidney was ectopic, located in a low lumbar position near the midline, and measured 55 × 30 mm, with a parenchymal thickness of 12 mm. The urinary bladder was normal, with no ureteral dilatation or nephrolithiasis.

Cardiovascular Findings

Doppler echocardiography demonstrated balanced cardiac chambers, a small muscular ventricular septal defect, and a secundum atrial septal defect of approximately 2-3 mm with left-to-right shunting. A ductus arteriosus was not visualized, and the pulmonary trunk and its branches were not dilated (Figure 1).

Neurological Findings

Cranial computed tomography (CT) demonstrated marked ventricular dilatation, predominantly involving the lateral ventricles (right, approximately 23 mm; left, approximately 24 mm), with a rounded third ventricle of approximately 15 mm and a normal fourth ventricle. The supratentorial and infratentorial subarachnoid spaces were increased, particularly at the Sylvian fissures, the cisterna magna, and the periencephalic cistern. Hyperdensity of the thalami and midbrain was also noted and is considered a finding of uncertain significance (Figure 2).

Clinical course and outcome

During hospitalization in the nephrology ward, the patient experienced a sudden aspiration episode while breastfeeding, followed by cardiopulmonary arrest. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation, endotracheal intubation, and mechanical ventilation were performed, and the patient was transferred to the pediatric intensive care unit. Subsequent cardiac assessment documented impaired myocardial contractility, suggestive of myocardial dysfunction, and a small posterior pericardial effusion of approximately 3 mm. The earlier respiratory history was limited to an infectious respiratory episode. Approximately two weeks later, the patient was successfully extubated, with good ventilatory mechanics, and was transferred to the intermediate care unit for continued monitoring and management. The last available clinical documentation corresponded to four months of age. No subsequent follow-up records were available, and the patient's long-term clinical outcome and current vital status could not be determined. The patient was not available for further clinical evaluation.

Based on the overall pattern of congenital anomalies and associated dysmorphic features, a multidisciplinary team made a suspected clinical diagnosis of EYWS. No chest imaging or radiology reports were available to retrospectively assess pulmonary lobation or segmentation. No genetic or molecular testing was performed. This suspected diagnosis was made clinically based on the phenotypic constellation observed in this patient and its correspondence with the limited clinical features previously reported for this rare condition. The principal findings supporting this suspected diagnosis included congenital microcephaly, structural congenital heart defects, and congenital renal abnormalities. However, given the extremely limited number of previously documented cases and the absence of validated diagnostic criteria or an established molecular marker, the diagnosis remains based on clinical and phenotypic assessment and is not molecularly confirmed. No formal diagnostic checklist exists; the diagnosis therefore relies on phenotypic overlap and multidisciplinary clinical reasoning.

case_text:
A 30‐year‐old young woman discovered a mass in the right adnexal area. At that time, she did not experience abdominal pain or vaginal bleeding, so she did not pay attention to it and did not receive any treatment. Fourteen months later, the patient returned to our hospital for a follow‐up examination. Transvaginal ultrasonography of the uterus, adnexa, and pelvis detected a mixed echogenic mass measuring approximately 6.5 × 4.6 × 6.0 cm in the right adnexal region. Irregularly shaped strong echoes were visible inside the mass, which had clear boundaries and regular morphology. Color Doppler flow imaging (CDFI) showed no obvious blood flow signal within the mass. An additional cystic dark area measuring approximately 4.7 × 3.2 × 3.3 cm was also detected in the right adnexal region. The cyst wall was slightly thickened but smooth, with a few spotlike echoes visible inside the cyst, and the lesion had clear boundaries, regular shape, and slight tension. CDFI detected pointlike blood flow signals on the cyst wall (Figure 1). Between the two lesions, the right ovary is visible, with basically normal size and shape. The patient presented to our hospital for treatment because the mass had increased slightly in size compared with prior measurements.

The patient was subsequently admitted to the hospital for further evaluation. Physical examination revealed an approximately 6 × 6 cm mass in the right adnexal area, which was medium in texture, with clear boundaries, good mobility, and no significant tenderness. After ruling out surgical contraindications, the patient underwent laparoscopic right ovarian lesion resection and laparoscopic pelvic adhesion lysis. Intraoperative exploration found the right ovary enlarged to approximately 6 × 8 cm with tumor septation. One portion of the tumor contained fat, hair, and thyroid‐like jellylike tissue, whereas the other portion contained chocolate‐colored cystic fluid. The cyst wall was densely adherent to the ovarian cortex with unclear boundaries and was difficult to separate. The right fallopian tube showed no obvious abnormalities, and no tumors were detected on it. Accordingly, the right fallopian tube and ovary were surgically resected.

Pathological examination revealed multilayered structures within the cyst wall, including skin and its appendages, cartilage, bone, adipose tissue, thyroid tissue, and mature glia (Figure 2A). Additionally, nests and islands of uniformly sized cells were detected in the capsule wall surrounding the thyroid tissue. These cells surrounding the thyroid tissue were uniform in size with a moderate amount of cytoplasm. The nuclei were slightly large, rounded, and centrally located, with homogeneous coarse‐granular chromatin, and no mitotic figures were detected (Figure 2B). Microscopic examination showed the maximum diameter of the lesion was 0.8 cm. Diffuse proliferation of spindle‐shaped Schwann cells could be observed in the local area of the cyst wall, with some lesion foci intermingled with the surrounding adipose tissue. Aggregations of Wagner–Meissner bodies were also observed, interspersed with nerve ganglion cells of varying sizes and quantities (Figure 2C). The wall of the other cyst was mainly composed of fibroblasts and collagen fibers, with prominent fibrosis. The cyst cavity contained a large amount of old hemorrhage and hemosiderin‐phagocytosing macrophages, and a small number of endometrium‐like glands and stroma could also be observed.

Immunohistochemistry results of the strumal carcinoid showed negative expression of CgA and p63 and positive expression of pancytokeratin, CD56, Syn, TG, TTF‐1, with Ki‐67 index of 1%. In the GN component, both Schwann cells and ganglion cells showed positive expression of CD56, Syn, S100, and NSE and negative expression of CgA (Figure 3). The final diagnosis was MCT with strumal carcinoid and focal small GN, with concurrent endometriotic cyst. The entire tumor tissue was processed for histopathological examination, and no neuroblastic component was identified.

The patient had no carcinoid syndrome and other related symptoms and was followed up for 8 months after surgery, with no recurrence or metastasis on vaginal ultrasonography. (Table 1 presents the investigation findings in chronological order.)

In the GN component, both Schwann cells and ganglion cells showed positive expression of CD56, Syn, S100, and NSE and negative expression of CgA (Figure 3).
The final diagnosis was MCT with strumal carcinoid and focal small GN, with concurrent endometriotic cyst.
The entire tumor tissue was processed for histopathological examination, and no neuroblastic component was identified.
The patient had no carcinoid syndrome and other related symptoms and was followed up for 8 months after surgery, with no recurrence or metastasis on vaginal ultrasonography.
(Table 1 presents the investigation findings in chronological order.)
title: Mature Cystic Teratoma With a Strumal Carcinoid and Small Ganglioneuroma: A Case Report

case_text:
A 5‐week‐old female infant, born at another facility presented to us with progressive abdominal distention from birth. She was born at 36 weeks + 1 day of gestation via emergency cesarean section for poor progress of labor. The birth weight was 3.1 kg, and the infant had APGAR scores of 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 min, respectively. Antenatal history was unremarkable except for the detection of fetal ascites on routine obstetric ultrasonography at 36 weeks' gestation.

The early postnatal course was notable for transient tachypnea of the newborn requiring supplemental oxygen for several hours and neonatal jaundice managed with phototherapy. Mild abdominal distension was observed during the initial postnatal period; however, both mother and infant were discharged after 72 h of life. The abdominal distension progressively worsened after the first week of life, associated with recurrent post‐feed vomiting. There was no change in bowel movements and no respiratory complaints.

At presentation to our facility, the infant was alert and hemodynamically stable. Growth parameters were appropriate, with weight for corrected gestational age above the 75th percentile. Abdominal examination revealed gross distension with a positive fluid thrill, consistent with Grade 3 ascites (Figure 1A); there was no hepatosplenomegaly. There was no periorbital, sacral, or lower limb edema. The examination of other systems was unremarkable.

case_text:
A 30‐year‐old female presented with a 10‐year history of anterior neck swelling that had recently become painful and increased in size. She reported no dysphagia, dyspnea, hoarseness, or symptoms of thyroid dysfunction. Thyroid function tests (TSH, free T4, and free T3) were reviewed by the authors at presentation and were within the laboratory reference ranges; the exact numerical values could not be retrieved for this report because the patient was lost to follow‐up. Antithyroglobulin and antithyroid peroxidase antibody results were not available. There was no personal or family history of HHT, vascular malformations, or thyroid disease. Physical examination revealed a palpable, nontender nodule in the right thyroid lobe without an overlying bruit or thrill. The neck swelling (goiter) was attributable to this solitary right‐lobe nodule; the left lobe was normal on imaging, and no other cause, such as diffuse or multinodular enlargement, was identified. The iodine status was not assessed. The cause of the recent painful enlargement could not be established; progressive shunt‐related vascular dilatation or intralesional hemorrhage were possible explanations.

High‐resolution ultrasound of the thyroid gland (Figure 1) demonstrated a well‐defined hypoechoic nodule measuring 1.16 cm × 0.72 cm in the right lobe. The nodule exhibited posterior acoustic enhancement on B‐mode imaging. Color Doppler interrogation revealed intense hypervascularity, with a diffuse, confluent color signal filling the entire nodule, which we describe as a focal “inferno sign” (Figure 1). Within the lesion, a focal, tangled “nidus” of vessels was identifiable. Spectral Doppler analysis of the dominant feeding vessel demonstrated a low‐resistance flow pattern (resistive index < 0.5) (Figure 2), consistent with arteriovenous shunting. Early systolic arterialization of the draining vein was also observed, suggesting direct arteriovenous communication bypassing the capillary bed. Ultrasound did not demonstrate a direct connection between the lesion and a cervical artery; the origin of the feeding vessel was identified only on CTA.

CTA of the neck vessels with multiplanar reformats was performed to characterize the vascular anatomy. A 1.0 cm × 0.9 cm nodule was identified in the right thyroid lobe (Figure 3), with an attenuation of 70 Hounsfield units (HUs) measured in the arterial phase. The nodule exhibited marked heterogeneous enhancement in the arterial phase, mild heterogeneous enhancement in the venous phase, and became isodense to the normal thyroid parenchyma in the delayed phase, a wash‐in/wash‐out pattern typical of high‐flow vascular lesions. The feeding artery was a moderately sized vessel (maximum diameter 0.3 cm and length ~4.9 cm) arising from the innominate artery immediately medial to the origin of the right common carotid artery (Figure 4). It coursed parallel to the right common carotid artery before entering the nidus (Figure 4). Venous drainage occurred directly into the right internal jugular vein (Figure 5). The left thyroid lobe and all major cervical vessels demonstrated a normal anatomy.

The imaging findings were strongly suggestive of an AVM of the right thyroid lobe, supplied by an aberrant branch of the innominate artery with drainage into the right internal jugular vein. Fine‐needle aspiration (FNA) was deferred because of the bleeding risk. The patient was referred for multidisciplinary discussion involving interventional radiology and endocrine surgery to decide between observation with serial imaging, diagnostic angiography with possible preoperative embolization, and surgical resection, but she was lost to follow‐up before a management decision was made.

case_text:
A 72-year-old man presented with anorexia and severe acute onset left-sided epigastric pain. Plain abdominal CT revealed a swollen left kidney with a low-density mass extending from the left renal vein to the IVC, reaching the level of the diaphragm. Subsequent abdominal MRI confirmed these findings.

Renal biopsy revealed renal cell carcinoma with necrosis. Based on these findings, the patient was diagnosed with cT3c renal cell carcinoma with IVC invasion and treated with pembrolizumab plus lenvatinib combination therapy for a total of 5 courses, administered every 3 weeks as neoadjuvant therapy. The extent of the tumor was reassessed preoperatively using CT, MRI, and bone scintigraphy. The imaging revealed a slight reduction in the tumor size (Fig. 1A and 1B) and showed that the tumor thrombus extended from the left renal vein into the IVC up to the level of the diaphragm. The distal IVC was already completely occluded by the tumor thrombus preoperatively. Small pulmonary nodules were also present before surgery, but they could not be definitively diagnosed as metastatic lesions; therefore, no definite metastatic disease was identified. Given the absence of definite metastatic disease, surgery was planned to achieve complete resection. The treatment plan was discussed in a multidisciplinary conference involving urology, gastrointestinal surgery, and cardiovascular surgery specialists, and the neoadjuvant therapy and surgical strategy were determined collaboratively.

The initial surgical plan was tumor resection through an abdominal approach without extracorporeal circulation, with escalation to intrapericardial IVC control and CPB if adequate vascular control could not be obtained. To permit rapid initiation of CPB if required, the right internal jugular vein and the right femoral artery were cannulated prophylactically before laparotomy. A staged strategy to minimize the duration of hepatic inflow interruption was also planned.

A median laparotomy was performed to expose and dissect the IVC. The left renal vein and the hepatic hilar IVC were secured with vascular control tape. Intraoperative findings, including direct ultrasonographic assessment, showed that the tumor was firmly adherent to the IVC wall and could not be sufficiently mobilized. During the Kocher maneuver to mobilize the liver, the right hepatic vein was inadvertently lacerated because the fragile venous wall was weakened by the pre-existing tumor thrombus obstructing the venous lumen. This resulted in massive, uncontrollable hemorrhage (Fig. 2A) and consequent hypovolemic shock. Hemostasis was attempted by clamping the IVC above the diaphragm via a lower sternotomy and at the lower hepatic hilar level, together with total hepatic pedicle occlusion at the hepatic hilum. However, bleeding remained uncontrolled. Using the prophylactically placed cannulas, CPB was promptly established with venous drainage from the right internal jugular vein and lower IVC and arterial return via the right femoral artery.

The laceration progressively enlarged and was nearly detached from the origin of the right hepatic vein. Thus, reconstruction in conjunction with IVC repair, rather than individual repair, was required. To achieve complete tumor removal, the IVC wall was resected extensively because of firm adhesion between the tumor and the vessel (Fig. 2B), and the distal IVC was closed as a blind end. Additional thorough dissection around the IVC and diaphragm was performed to free the IVC from surrounding structures and reposition it closer to the liver. The resulting IVC defect and the right hepatic vein were reconstructed en bloc using an autologous pericardial patch. The upper half of the patch was sutured directly to the liver parenchyma rather than to the right hepatic vein, whereas the lower half was sutured to the residual IVC wall (Fig. 2C and 2D). After vascular reconstruction, the left kidney and associated renal veins were excised (Fig. 3).

Postoperative contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed patent blood flow from the right hepatic vein through the patch to the IVC (Fig. 4), although mild narrowing of the reconstructed IVC was observed. Hepatic blood flow was regularly assessed using ultrasonography, and no apparent abnormalities in hepatic perfusion or venous drainage were detected. The liver enzyme levels returned to near-normal values by POD 14 (Fig. 5). The patient required temporary postoperative dialysis, which was subsequently discontinued following renal function recovery. Lower-body edema was initially observed after surgery but gradually resolved. The small pulmonary nodules noted preoperatively increased in size during the postoperative period and were considered metastatic lesions. The patient died of respiratory failure on POD 120.

case_text:
Clinical data were obtained from the medical records of a patient diagnosed with LAD who was treated at the Department of Dental Medicine, University Hospital of Split, Split, Croatia. The patient underwent a comprehensive oral examination, and relevant clinical, laboratory, and immunopathological findings were retrospectively reviewed. Diagnostic procedures included histopathological examination (HPE), DIF, IIF, and ELISA, all performed according to standard institutional protocols. Information on disease course, treatment, and follow-up was collected and analyzed. Medication exposure (including the timing of drug initiation relative to disease onset, as well as over-the-counter and herbal products), denture history, and oral findings in relation to denture-bearing areas were specifically reviewed. Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for the publication of clinical data and images. The study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and institutional ethical standards.

A structured literature review was conducted from February to July 2026 using the PubMed/MEDLINE (National Library of Medicine, Bethesda, MD, USA; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/), Scopus (Elsevier, Amsterdam, The Netherlands; https://www.scopus.com/), and Web of Science (Clarivate, London, UK; https://www.webofscience.com/) databases. The search strategy combined the terms “linear IgA disease” and “linear IgA bullous dermatosis” with keywords related to oral and laryngeal involvement, including “oral mucosa”, “oral involvement”, “oral lesions”, “oral cavity”, “mucous membrane”, “laryngeal involvement”, and “larynx”, using the Boolean operators AND and OR; the same search terms were adapted to the syntax of Scopus and Web of Science. Articles published in English between January 2016 and July 2026 that described patients with LAD presenting with oral mucosal involvement without cutaneous lesions (i.e., mucosal-predominant disease) were considered eligible for inclusion. The search period was restricted to January 2016–July 2026 to capture recent reports in which the diagnosis was supported by contemporary immunopathological methods; this restriction is acknowledged as a limitation (Section 5.7). Eligible publication types included case reports, case series, and letters to the editor containing original clinical data. Two reviewers (A.G. and A.T.) independently screened titles and abstracts, followed by full-text assessment of potentially relevant studies. Studies lacking sufficient clinical, histopathological, or immunopathological information to support the diagnosis of LAD were excluded. Reports of LAD with concomitant cutaneous involvement were also excluded. Reference lists of included articles were manually screened to identify additional relevant publications.

Data extraction was performed independently by two reviewers (A.G. and A.T.), with disagreements resolved by consensus. Extracted data included patient demographics, clinical presentation, site of oral involvement, presence or absence of laryngeal involvement, histopathological and immunopathological findings, treatment modalities, and clinical outcomes. The study selection process was documented using a PRISMA 2020 flow diagram, generated using the official PRISMA 2020 flow diagram tool (https://www.prisma-statement.org/). Due to the heterogeneity of the available reports, the findings were synthesized qualitatively, with particular emphasis on the clinical characteristics, diagnostic challenges, and management of LAD with oral involvement. The findings of the literature review were then compared with those observed in the present case.

case_text:
A 52-year-old man presented with left flank pain radiating to the lower abdomen and groin and mild gross hematuria. He had no fever, lower urinary tract symptoms, weight loss, smoking history, or occupational carcinogen exposure. His medical and surgical histories were unremarkable, and his Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status was 1. Hemoglobin was 12.8 g/dl, serum creatinine 114 μmol/l, and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) 63.35 ml/min/1.73 m2. Urinalysis showed hematuria without pyuria, and urine culture was negative.

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) showed an 18 × 13-mm, well-defined, avidly enhancing mass in the midportion of the left kidney. The collecting system had grade II hydronephrosis, proximal ureteral dilatation to 12 mm, an 11 × 7-mm upper-ureteral calculus, and irregular thickening and fat stranding of the renal pelvis and proximal ureter (Fig. 1A). Delayed images at 20 min showed impaired left renal enhancement without contrast excretion, whereas the right kidney excreted normally (Fig. 1B).

Because impaired excretion limited upper-tract assessment on CT, contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed. MRI showed an ~5-cm segment of irregularly enhancing renal pelvic and proximal ureteral wall thickening, suspicious for periureteral invasion. A separate 17 × 18-mm renal parenchymal mass showed early enhancement and delayed washout (Fig. 1C, D), raising suspicion of synchronous RCC and UTUC. Staging CT showed no distant metastasis. Voided urine cytology was negative. Preoperative cystoscopy revealed no suspicious bladder lesions; therefore, no biopsy was performed. Left ureteroscopy was attempted but halted by the obstructing 11 × 7-mm proximal ureteral stone, precluding biopsy and selective cytology. Staged lithotripsy followed by repeat ureteroscopy was considered but not pursued because of concerns regarding ureteral injury and MRI-suspected invasive UTUC. Consequently, the absence of preoperative histological confirmation limited diagnostic certainty and risk stratification.

Given MRI-suspected invasive UTUC, laparoscopic radical nephroureterectomy with bladder cuff excision and hilar node sampling was performed after informal interdisciplinary discussion. Kidney-sparing alternatives were discussed with the patient, who consented to radical surgery. Differential renal function was not formally assessed. No gross invasion of adjacent structures was observed. The specimen contained a circumscribed whitish mid-renal mass, dilatation of the renal pelvis and proximal ureter, and a 10 × 8-mm proximal ureteral stone (Fig. 2). Recovery was uncomplicated, and the patient was discharged on postoperative day 6.

Histopathology confirmed a 2-cm WHO/ISUP grade 2 ccRCC (pT1a) and a 2.8 × 2.2-cm low-grade urothelial carcinoma at the ureteropelvic junction, invading the lamina propria (pT1) (Fig. 3). No concomitant carcinoma in situ was identified. The urothelial tumor was adjacent to an impacted calculus, with marked inflammation and fibrosis contributing to MRI-suspected periureteral invasion. No muscular, lymphovascular, or perineural invasion was identified. Surgical margins were negative. Both sampled hilar lymph nodes were negative (0/2; pN0), although nodal assessment was limited.

Neither adjuvant systemic therapy nor postoperative intravesical chemotherapy was administered. At 3 months, cystoscopy showed no bladder tumor. At 6 months, the patient was clinically well; serum creatinine was 94.2 μmol/L and eGFR 79.78 ml/min/1.73 m2. CT showed no recurrence or metastasis but identified focal bladder-wall thickening near the previous cuff site, considered inflammatory or fibrotic (Fig. 4A). Cystoscopy showed no tumor, and biopsies from the cuff site and other bladder locations were negative (Fig. 4B, C).

case_text:
A 36-year-old G1P1001 initially presented to undergo IVF with preimplantation genetic testing for monogenic disorders, given both parents were carriers for galactosemia. The couple elected for the embryos to also undergo PGT-A. The patient and partner were healthy, and fertility evaluation revealed no abnormalities.

The couple underwent IVF with ICSI, which resulted in three euploid embryos that were unaffected by galactosemia. Frozen embryo transfer cycles were initiated and were notably complicated by thin endometrial lining, causing cycle cancellations. The patient's fourth attempt was a natural cycle frozen embryo transfer, which yielded a lining of 5.3 mm, and a transfer of a euploid, female embryo unaffected by galactosemia. This resulted in a positive β-hCG (initial β-hCG was 236 mIU/mL 10 days after transfer and was 1960 mIU/mL when repeated 4 days later ). A clinic ultrasound at 7 weeks of gestation showed a vascular endometrium with a small complex collection that could not be distinguished as within the endometrium (Fig. 1). On the day of this ultrasound, the β-hCG was 85,965 mIU/mL. The next day, a follow-up ultrasound at a specialized obstetrics and gynecology ultrasound clinic showed a 31×27×29 mm hyperechoic mass in the right interstitial portion of the uterus, with moderate-to-marked color flow with appearance suspicious for molar pregnancy (Fig. 2). The patient then underwent an uncomplicated diagnostic hysteroscopy, diagnostic laparoscopy, excision of interstitial ectopic pregnancy from the right uterine cornua, and right salpingectomy. Intraoperative findings were notable for an enlarged bulge of right uterine cornua; upon incision into the cornua, ectopic tissue appeared to be placental-like, consistent with suspected molar pregnancy (Fig. 3). Final pathology revealed chorionic villi with morphological features compatible with partial mole.

case_text:
A 23‐year‐old previously healthy male lifeguard presented with a two‐week history of abdominal pain, vomiting, watery diarrhea, high‐grade fevers (up to 40°C), headache, and widespread arthralgia involving both large and small joints. He also reported the recent development of painful erythematous lesions affecting his hands and feet.

There was no history of intravenous drug use, recent dental procedures, recent travel, freshwater exposure, or contact with unwell individuals.

On admission, the patient appeared acutely unwell and profoundly weak, requiring a wheelchair for mobility. He was confused with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 14 but remained hemodynamically stable. Dermatological examination revealed irregular non‐blanching macular and purpuric lesions involving both the palmar and dorsal aspects of the hands, together with splinter hemorrhages. There was no neck stiffness and both Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs were negative. Neurological examination demonstrated intact cranial nerves, preserved sensation, mild proximal upper limb weakness and generalized hyporeflexia. Cardiovascular examination revealed a regular pulse with no audible murmur initially.

case_text:
A 51‐year‐old man presented in January 2026 with a sudden, painless central scotoma of the left eye of approximately 3 hours′ duration. He had treated systemic arterial hypertension. No precipitating event could be identified: on direct and repeated questioning the patient recalled no lifting, coughing, vomiting, straining or other Valsalva‐type manoeuvre preceding the onset of symptoms. There was no history of ocular trauma, intraocular surgery, high myopia or anticoagulant use, and no personal or family history of bleeding diathesis.

Uncorrected visual acuity was 20/25 in the right eye and counting fingers in the left.

Pupils were reactive, no RAPD, IOP normal in both eyes; anterior segment and lens are also normal.

Dilated fundoscopy of the left eye showed a dense, well‐circumscribed premacular haemorrhage overlying the fovea with an associated intraretinal component (Figure 1A). The right fundus was normal, with no hypertensive retinopathy and no macroaneurysm (Figure 1E).

Review at one and 3 weeks showed no change: visual acuity remained counting fingers and the haemorrhage was unchanged in extent, with no dependent layering.

OCT (Optovue iVue, 6 × 6 mm Retina Map) on January 14, 2026 showed a large, dome‐shaped, homogeneously hyperreflective lesion centred on the fovea, elevating the inner retinal surface and shadowing the outer retina and retinal pigment epithelium. Central subfield thickness was 571 μm (superior 606, inferior 333, nasal 403, temporal 436 μm) against 223 μm in the fellow eye. The foveal architecture was not assessable (Figure 2A).

Fluorescein angiography (Kowa VX‐20) on 26 January 2026 showed hypofluorescence corresponding to blocking by the haemorrhage, with subtle foveal and perifoveal hyperfluorescence and juxtapapillary and optic nerve head staining in both eyes. In the retina not obscured by blood, there was no aneurysmal filling, no arteriolar abnormality, no capillary nonperfusion or venous staining, and no late leakage (Figure 1). Because the haemorrhage blocked the fovea itself, a macroaneurysm lying directly beneath it could not be excluded on angiography alone. Systemic workup was performed and was unremarkable: CBC, platelets, coagulation profile, Hba1C and blood pressure measurement were within normal.

case_text:
An 8‐year‐old Black South African male with chronic liver disease of unknown aetiology was referred for genomic investigation following an extensive but inconclusive diagnostic evaluation. His clinical course began at approximately two years of age with recurrent episodes of hypoglycaemia and hepatic encephalopathy, leading to a provisional clinical diagnosis of glycogen storage disease. Treatment with uncooked cornstarch resulted in resolution of the hypoglycaemic episodes; however, the diagnosis remained unconfirmed despite continued metabolic evaluation.

At three years of age, he developed his first episode of acute‐on‐chronic liver failure associated with hepatic encephalopathy and hypoglycaemia. Comprehensive investigations, including viral, autoimmune, toxicological, Wilson disease, and α1‐antitrypsin deficiency screening, as well as plasma and urine metabolic analyses, failed to identify an underlying cause. Plasma amino acid analysis demonstrated elevated alanine, methionine, phenylalanine, and tyrosine, although this pattern was considered nonspecific for an inherited metabolic disorder. Liver biopsy performed in October 2018 demonstrated mild portal triaditis, portal tract oedema, bile ductular proliferation, bile plugs, and mild hepatocellular necrosis. These findings were interpreted as consistent with cholestatic liver injury and did not demonstrate histopathological features supporting glycogen storage disease or Wilson disease. At the time of biopsy, a metabolic storage disorder was the principal diagnostic consideration, and protoporphyria was not suspected as the underlying cause of the liver disease. Fluorescence examination for protoporphyrin deposition was not performed, and examination for characteristic birefringent deposits under polarised light was not documented in the available histopathology findings. Retrospective examination was not possible because the archived biopsy material could not be retrieved.

Over the following years, the patient progressed to advanced chronic liver disease complicated by portal hypertension, splenomegaly, recurrent oesophageal variceal haemorrhage requiring multiple endoscopic band ligation procedures, hypersplenism, and recurrent hepatic encephalopathy. Episodes of metabolic decompensation persisted, including an episode of encephalopathy associated with hyperammonaemia and lactic acidosis requiring intensive care, although hypoglycaemia was not consistently documented later in the disease course. His clinical course was further complicated by pulmonary tuberculosis, which was treated, but this did not provide an explanation for the underlying multisystem phenotype.

At around seven years of age, the patient developed multiple atraumatic fractures involving both humeri, both radii, ribs, and the femur, with radiographic evidence of osteopenia. Biochemical evaluation demonstrated severe hyperparathyroidism, adding a significant skeletal manifestation to the otherwise unexplained multisystem disease. Despite repeated multidisciplinary assessments involving hepatology, metabolic specialists, and transplant services, no unifying diagnosis was established during his lifetime. Owing to progressive end‐stage liver disease, he underwent evaluation for liver transplantation.

Characteristic photosensitivity was not reported by the family or documented in the clinical records. Although sunlight‐induced symptoms were specifically enquired about during the clinical evaluation for porphyria, none were elicited. Cutaneous thickening and scarring were observed but were clinically attributed to skin trauma associated with pruritus in the context of chronic cholestatic liver disease. Porphyria was considered during the investigation of abdominal pain but was not suspected to be the underlying cause of the progressive liver disease. A historical porphyria investigation was reported as negative; subsequent clarification with the performing laboratory established that this comprised a qualitative porphobilinogen‐based screen. Quantitative erythrocyte protoporphyrin analysis, including differentiation of metal‐free and zinc‐bound fractions, and stool protoporphyrin testing were not performed. The patient died on 6 October 2024 following progressive liver disease, without a definitive molecular diagnosis having been established during his lifetime. Figure 1 summarises the patient’s clinical course.

case_text: A 41-year-old Qatari woman was transferred to our tertiary center for management of suspected CS. Her history included a moderately differentiated NET of the left supraglottis, surgically resected in the United Kingdom in 2022. She initially presented to the weight management clinic in July 2025 with significant weight gain, first noticed in May 2025, with an increase from 68 to 80 kg over 2 months. Associated symptoms included increased hunger, nervousness, hyperpigmentation of the face, palms, and knuckles, generalized fatigue, and elevated blood pressure. On examination, blood pressure was 140/88 mmHg, height 155.1 cm, and weight 80 kg (body mass index 33 kg/m2). Examination showed a round face, supraclavicular fat pads, acanthosis nigricans on the posterior neck, and mild proximal muscle weakness, without striae, bruising, or lower limb edema.

case_text:
A 55-year-old postmenopausal woman presented on 21 June 2026 with intermittent right lower abdominal pain for one month, associated with low-grade fever, intermittent non-bilious vomiting, and loss of appetite. She reported intermittent mild-to-moderate abdominal pain for ~4 years. Her surgical history included open myomectomy 25 years earlier, with no other significant medical history.

Repeated ultrasonography at other centers demonstrated bilateral bulky ovaries and a bulky fibroid uterus. On examination, she was hemodynamically stable with an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status of 1 and body mass index of 21 kg/m2. A firm-to-hard, non-tender ~6 × 6 cm mass was palpable in the right iliac fossa. Laboratory investigations showed normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL), while leukocyte count, eosinophil count, renal function tests, carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), and cancer antigen 125 (CA-125) were largely within normal limits. Hepatic transaminases were mildly elevated (aspartate aminotransferase 48 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 72 U/L) (Table 1). Because hydatid disease was not clinically or radiologically suspected preoperatively, Echinococcus serology immunoglobulin G ELISA was not performed prior to surgery. Postoperative serological testing was also withheld given that complete surgical excision was achieved and histological confirmation had already established the diagnosis.

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) demonstrated an ill-defined 68.7 × 50.5 mm mildly enhancing lesion posterior to the cecum and ileocecal junction, containing coarse calcification with surrounding fat stranding and adjacent omental and mesenteric thickening (Fig. 1). Multiple calcified mesenteric and retroperitoneal nodules were also identified. Both ovaries were enlarged without solid components or mural nodules. No hepatic or pulmonary hydatid cysts were identified. The radiological impression favored a low-grade appendiceal mucinous neoplasm with peritoneal dissemination, with chronic appendiceal inflammatory pathology as an alternative diagnosis.

Diagnostic laparoscopy revealed multiple calcified and cystic lesions involving the appendix, right tubo-ovarian complex, parietal peritoneum, and greater omentum. Because of the extensive disease and the need to prevent cyst rupture and spillage, conversion to laparotomy was performed (Fig. 2). Following multidisciplinary consultation, total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, appendectomy, and excision of all visible peritoneal and omental lesions were completed using meticulous no-spillage techniques. Because hydatid cyst dissemination was not suspected preoperatively, intraoperative scolicidal irrigation or hypertonic saline packing was not routinely applied prior to excision; however, strict surgical isolate protocols and gentle non-traumatic handling were maintained throughout the procedure. No intraoperative features of acute anaphylactoid reaction occurred.

Gross examination showed an appendiceal specimen measuring 9 × 3.2 × 2.2 cm with an area of focal wall disruption containing thick gelatinous material, representing a pre-existing chronic micro-rupture or leak rather than intraoperative spillage. Similar calcified and gelatinous deposits were present in the omentum and peritoneum. One ovary contained a cystic lesion with thick gelatinous contents.

Histopathology demonstrated abundant acellular eosinophilic laminated ectocyst membranes with characteristic concentric, undulating, and folded lamellations, surrounded by fibrocollagenous tissue with mild chronic inflammation (Fig. 3). No epithelial lining, dysplasia, mucin-producing epithelium, or evidence of appendiceal mucinous neoplasia was identified. Similar laminated hydatid membranes were present in the peritoneal and omental deposits and on the ovarian and uterine serosal surfaces, confirming primary appendiceal hydatid disease with disseminated peritoneal, ovarian serosal, and uterine serosal involvement.

Following histopathological confirmation, epidemiological history was revisited. Although she denied direct dog contact, she reported daily exposure to cattle, buffaloes, and goats in a rural household environment.

The postoperative course was complicated by ileus, which resolved conservatively by postoperative day 3. A superficial surgical-site infection and subsequent bacteremia were successfully treated with culture-directed antibiotics. Albendazole 400 mg twice daily was initiated on postoperative day 10 and continued for four weeks (a standard 28-day cycle for localized/completely resected disease without ongoing cyst spillage). The patient was discharged in stable condition on postoperative day 14. At the 3-month follow-up evaluation, the patient remained asymptomatic, and follow-up abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated no evidence of disease recurrence or residual pelvic/peritoneal lesions.

case_text:
The clinical features reported in Iranian patients are broadly consistent with the classical presentation of mycetoma. Infection usually follows minor trauma and initially appears as a painless subcutaneous nodule. The lesion may enlarge slowly over months or years, eventually developing multiple sinus tracts and discharge containing grains. Pain may remain minimal despite progressive disease, allowing infection to extend into the subcutaneous tissues, fascia, and, in advanced cases, bone. Delayed recognition and diagnosis therefore contribute substantially to the morbidity associated with the disease in Iran.

Diagnosis requires integration of clinical findings with laboratory and imaging studies. Direct examination of discharged grains can provide useful preliminary information, with fungal hyphae generally observed in eumycetoma and fine, branching bacterial filaments in actinomycetoma. Culture remains an important method for confirming the etiological agent and may be performed on media including Sabouraud dextrose agar, blood agar, and brain–heart infusion agar. Because many causative organisms grow slowly, cultures may require prolonged incubation, sometimes for 6–8 weeks. Histopathological examination, including hematoxylin and eosin and periodic acid–Schiff staining, can demonstrate grains and provide additional evidence of the infectious etiology.

Molecular identification is particularly useful when culture or morphological examination does not provide a definitive species‐level diagnosis. In reported Iranian cases, PCR followed by sequencing of fungal targets such as the internal transcribed spacer and β‐tubulin regions has been used to identify unusual or difficult‐to‐characterize isolates, including A. flavus. Imaging is important for assessing disease extent, particularly when deeper tissue or bone involvement is suspected. Plain radiography, computed tomography, and magnetic resonance imaging can help define the extent of osseous and soft‐tissue disease and may influence surgical planning and treatment selection. Overall, the Iranian literature supports a stepwise diagnostic approach beginning with clinical assessment and grain examination, followed by culture and histopathology and, where available, molecular identification for species confirmation.

case_text:
A 37‐year‐old G2P2 woman initially presented in October 2024 with acute right‐sided chest pain. Imaging obtained at that time was interpreted as negative, and she was discharged with a diagnosis of anxiety. Retrospective review later identified subtle, non‐enhancing right diaphragmatic densities on that scan, representing an early and missed diagnostic opportunity (Figure 1A).

In October 2025, she was readmitted on Day 5 of menstruation with a confirmed right‐sided pneumothorax (Table 1). Repeat imaging demonstrated interval enlargement of diaphragmatic nodules, raising suspicion for TES (Figure 1A,B). Of note, the patient reported a prior diagnosis of endometriosis made in her country of origin; however, no supporting records were available for review, and formal pelvic re‐evaluation had not been performed. Gynecological consultation was obtained during this admission, and the patient was initiated on norethindrone at a suppressive dose for menstrual suppression and empiric treatment of possible pleural endometriosis. She remained asymptomatic with no further pneumothorax recurrence while adherent to therapy. Norethindrone was discontinued during a subsequent hospitalization for supraventricular tachycardia, after which she developed recurrent dyspnea presented with the third pneumothorax episode in April 2026. Despite recommendations for surgical evaluation, follow‐up was deferred due to insurance‐related barriers to specialist access. This resulted in a six‐month timeline delay between the initial recommendation and her eventual operation.

In April 2026, now age 38, she presented a third time with recurrent right‐sided chest pain and a large right‐sided pneumothorax on chest x‐ray (Figure 1D). Notably, this episode occurred outside the perimenstrual window, a variation from her prior catamenial pattern. Previous outpatient records had raised the possibility of emphysema; however, repeat high‐resolution CT clarified the absence of emphysematous change and confirmed persistent pleural‐based nodularity.

Preoperatively, the combination of perimenstrual symptom onset, progressive diaphragmatic nodularity on serial imaging, and the patient's reported prior diagnosis of endometriosis led to characterization of the nodular lesions as highly suspicious for thoracic endometriosis with diaphragmatic implants. Intraoperatively, the nodular protrusions were noted to have a fleshy, non‐cystic appearance inconsistent with the characteristic chocolate‐colored cysts of endometriosis, prompting intraoperative frozen section analysis of the first excised specimen to confirm tissue identity prior to determining the reconstructive approach.

Given recurrent disease and unresolved diagnostic uncertainty, she underwent robotic‐assisted thoracoscopic surgery. Intraoperative findings were as follows: extensive fenestrations were identified at the junction of the muscular diaphragm and central tendon, spanning approximately 8 cm in aggregate, with multiple nodular protrusions through the defects into the pleural cavity and dense adhesions involving the right lower lobe.

The intraoperative impression was immediately redirected when frozen section analysis of the nodular lesions returned hepatic parenchyma, confirming transdiaphragmatic liver herniation rather than endometrial implants (Figure 1A–C), an unexpected finding that altered the reconstructive approach in real time. Three separate nodular lesions were excised from the right hemidiaphragm, the largest measuring approximately 3 cm. Two specimens were submitted for formal pathological analysis; intraoperative frozen section of the first specimen returned unremarkable liver tissue, a finding communicated to the surgeon intraoperatively and confirmed on permanent sections. Final histopathologic analysis of both specimens demonstrated hepatic parenchyma with central vein ectasia and mild nonspecific chronic portal triaditis. No endometrial tissue was identified in either specimen. Given the unusual presentation, the case was referred for external pathologic second opinion. A single dense lower lobe pleural adhesion was identified and lysed, considered a possible contributing source of traction‐related pneumothorax in addition to diaphragmatic fenestrations. Intercostal nerve cryoablation from T3 through T7 was performed for postoperative pain management. The diaphragm was repaired primarily and reinforced with a 9 cm composite mesh. Chemical pleurodesis with doxycycline was performed.

The postoperative course was complicated by a persistent air leak requiring repeat bedside pleurodesis. At discharge, gynecologic follow‐up was arranged for consideration of hormonal suppression therapy. At her most recent follow‐up appointment 1 month post discharge, the patient's repeat imaging demonstrated a small right pleural effusion with compressive atelectasis, both expected postoperative findings. No further recurrences of her right‐sided pneumothorax were documented. Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this case report and accompanying images in accordance with institutional policy.
sentences: A 37‐year‐old G2P2 woman initially presented in October 2024 with acute right‐sided chest pain.
Imaging obtained at that time was interpreted as negative, and she was discharged with a diagnosis of anxiety.
Retrospective review later identified subtle, non‐enhancing right diaphragmatic densities on that scan, representing an early and missed diagnostic opportunity (Figure 1A).
In October 2025, she was readmitted on Day 5 of menstruation with a confirmed right‐sided pneumothorax (Table 1).
Repeat imaging demonstrated interval enlargement of diaphragmatic nodules, raising suspicion for TES (Figure 1A,B).

Of note, the patient reported a prior diagnosis of endometriosis made in her country of origin; however, no supporting records were available for review, and formal pelvic re‐evaluation had not been performed.

Gynecological consultation was obtained during this admission, and the patient was initiated on norethindrone at a suppressive dose for menstrual suppression and empiric treatment of possible pleural endometriosis.
She remained asymptomatic with no further pneumothorax recurrence while adherent to therapy.

Norethindrone was discontinued during a subsequent hospitalization for supraventricular tachycardia, after which she developed recurrent dyspnea presented with the third pneumothorax episode in April 2026.
Despite recommendations for surgical evaluation, follow‐up was deferred due to insurance‐related barriers to specialist access.

The diaphragm was repaired primarily and reinforced with a 9 cm composite mesh.
Chemical pleurodesis with doxycycline was performed.
The postoperative course was complicated by a persistent air leak requiring repeat bedside pleurodesis.

At her most recent follow‐up appointment 1 month post discharge, the patient's repeat imaging demonstrated a small right pleural effusion with compressive atelectasis, both expected postoperative findings.

title: Menstrual‐Associated (Catamenial) Pneumothorax With Hepatic Herniation Through an Advanced Porous Diaphragm

case_text:
A 49-year-old woman with dilated cardiomyopathy associated with pathogenic LMNA and SCN5A variants was referred to our centre for repeat CA because of recurrent ventricular tachycardia (VT) resulting in implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) shocks. A CRT-D (Rivacor 3 HF-T QP, Biotronik, Berlin) had been implanted in May 2025.

The patient had previously undergone endocardial VT ablation. During that procedure, the presumed VT substrate was localized to the lateral left ventricle in close proximity to the mitral annulus. Endocardial voltage mapping, however, did not demonstrate relevant areas of low voltage, raising suspicion of a predominantly epicardial substrate.

The patient’s medical history was additionally notable for AF and atrial tachycardia. The CHA2DS2-VA score was 1. In addition, multiple previous left atrial ablation procedures, including electrical isolation of the left atrial appendage (LAA), were carried out. This was followed by percutaneous LAA occlusion (27-mm Watchman FLX Pro, Boston Scientific, Marlborough, Massachusetts) in 2025.

After recurrence of symptomatic VT with subsequent ICD therapies and no significant substrate endocardially during the initial VT ablation, an epicardial mapping and ablation strategy was intended. Venous and arterial femoral access was obtained, followed by percutaneous epicardial access. High-density epicardial substrate mapping was performed (HDGridX mapping catheter, Abbott, Abbott Park, IL, USA) in conjunction with electroanatomical mapping (EnSiteX, Abbott, Abbott Park, IL, USA). In contrast to the findings during the previous endocardial procedure, epicardial voltage mapping demonstrated extensive areas of low voltage (Figure 1) with distinct late potentials. Pace mapping identified the best morphological match to the clinical VT at the basal lateral left ventricle, consistent with an epicardial arrhythmogenic substrate.

Epicardial ablation was subsequently performed using a dual-energy ablation catheter (TactiFlex Duo catheter, Abbott; Abbott Laboratories) with both RF energy up to 40 W and repetitive PFA (monopolar biphasic waveform, 2400 V, Figure 2). Following PFA application in close vicinity to the LV lead and/or the laterally implanted CRT-D generator, sudden onset of DDD pacing was observed (immediately after the PFA train, DDD pacing started, Figure 3). Attempts to interrogate the CRT-D were initially unsuccessful despite multiple attempts. Several resets of the device interrogation system were required before communication with the CRT-D could be re-established permanently.

After successful interrogation, the CRT-D was found to have reverted to factory settings. The device parameters could subsequently be reset and reprogrammed to the intended settings. After restoration of device communication and programming, the ablation procedure was continued and successfully completed but omitting PFA applications in close vicinity to LV lead or generator.

The final lead parameters, including sensing, pacing thresholds, and impedances, were unchanged from baseline. No further device malfunction occurred during the procedure.

case_text:
A 74‐year‐old male presented with complaints of neck swelling along with difficulty in swallowing. No symptoms suggestive of hypothyroidism/hyperthyroidism were present. The patient did not report any voice changes or breathing difficulties. Neck ultrasonography (USG) confirmed a large nodule, occupying the entire right lobe, characterized as solid, hypoechoic, with indistinct boundaries, and measuring 48 mm × 62 mm × 80 mm. The nodule exhibited a heterogeneous sound structure, increased peripheral blood flow, and a firm texture with localized soft areas on elastographic analysis. It appeared to extend beyond the thyroid capsule. Enlarged lymph nodes with clear margins, smooth contours, and a subround shape were observed in the right parapharyngeal chain (level II), measuring 24.5 mm × 9.5 mm, and were suspected to be infiltrated. Additional lymph nodes at level III on both sides of the neck were considered inflammatory. Finally, on USG, a tumor thrombus was found present within the right IJV. Fine‐needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) of the right level II lymph node and the thyroid mass indicated characteristics suggesting a papillary carcinoma with characteristics of low differentiation, while FNAC of the remaining lymph nodes suggested lymphoid hyperplasia. Routine blood investigations and thyroid function tests were performed within normal limits.

During the course of preoperative workup, the patient gradually presented with voice change. Preoperative laryngoscopy revealed reduced mobility of the right vocal cord. After thorough counseling and obtaining informed consent, the surgery was performed. Intraoperative findings confirmed the imaging report, with an enlarged right lobe of the thyroid (Figures 1 and 2). A tumor thrombus was also identified arising from the upper pole of the right lobe of the thyroid gland and progressing within the right superior thyroid vein along the right IJV, partially occluding the vessel. A right central neck dissection and right lateral neck dissection of levels II–V were performed. During the dissection, resection of the tumor from the right IJV was performed, followed by vein reconstruction (Figure 3). The right carotid artery was not involved in the tumor, and the right vagus nerve was preserved on the right side. Thyroidectomy was initiated. During right lobectomy, the upper and lower parathyroid glands were identified and preserved. The recurrent laryngeal nerve was monitored with the use of intraoperative intermittent neuromonitoring. The nerve did not have an electromyographical response after vagal stimulation, a finding compatible with the findings of preoperative laryngoscopy. After dissection, it was found to be infiltrated in the tracheoesophageal groove as well as in its entrance in the trachea. Tracheal surface infiltration was also identified. As the recurrent laryngeal nerve was nonfunctioning and extensively infiltrated by the tumor, resection of the involved segment was performed. Primary closure of the defect was performed, and strap muscles reinforced the closure. The procedure was not extended to the left side until a definite pathological diagnosis could be obtained, as there was an absence of macroscopic disease on the left lobe and the risk of bilateral vocal cord palsy was not justified without proper pathological diagnosis. Drains were placed, and the wound was closed. The patient continued to have hoarseness in the postoperative period. Other than that, the postoperative course was uneventful.

Histopathological examination revealed a poorly differentiated carcinoma of the thyroid with extracapsular and IJV invasion. 3 out of 80 lymph nodes were positive for metastasis. In view of the diagnosis, completion thyroidectomy was performed 6 weeks after the initial surgery to allow subsequent adjuvant radioactive iodine treatment. The patient recovered without further complications and subsequently received adjuvant radioactive iodine therapy.

Despite adjuvant treatment, intratracheal tumor recurrence was diagnosed during follow‐up. A tracheostomy was required 4 months postoperatively to secure the airway, followed by external beam radiotherapy to the cervical region. Disease progression continued, and the patient died 7 months after the first surgical intervention.

Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for the publication of his clinical information and accompanying images. The completed CARE Checklist is available as File S1.

case_text:
A 29-year-old Sudanese male presented to the emergency department with a one-day history of suprapubic abdominal pain and three episodes of non-bloody, non-bilious vomiting. He subsequently developed abdominal distension and an inability to pass flatus. Otherwise, he denied fever, dysuria, previous similar episodes, or a preceding history of constipation.

His past medical history was unremarkable. Six years earlier, laparoscopic cholecystectomy at another institution was converted to open surgery because of intraoperative bleeding. Bile duct injury and leakage subsequently required exploratory laparotomy and hepaticojejunostomy. Approximately 6 months later, he underwent endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography with biliary stent placement, followed by another laparotomy for postoperative intra-abdominal collections. Details of the stents, intended duration, and planned removal or follow-up were unavailable.

On presentation, blood pressure was 98/62 mmHg, heart rate 97 beats/min, and temperature 36.8°C. The abdomen was initially tender suprapubically without peritonitis but became progressively distended and diffusely tender. Initial investigations showed a white blood cell count of 7.1 × 103/μl, C-reactive protein of 2.5 mg/l, lactate of 0.9 mmol/l, and normal renal and liver function.

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated dilated small bowel loops with fecalization and distal ileal narrowing, consistent with partial small bowel obstruction. A tubular, hyperdense intraluminal structure was seen distally in the small bowel, raising suspicion for a migrated biliary stent (Fig. 1).

Initial management included bowel rest, nasogastric decompression, intravenous fluids, antibiotics, analgesia, and antiemetics. Colonoscopy demonstrated a large, hard fecaloma measuring ~7–8 cm within the ileum (Fig. 2). Attempts at retrieval with a cold snare, grasping forceps, and irrigation were unsuccessful, prompting operative removal.

At exploratory laparotomy, a large intraluminal obstructing mass was identified ~60–70 cm proximal to the ileocecal junction. Following proximal milking, a 1-cm antimesenteric enterotomy revealed migrated biliary stent material completely encased within a large, hardened fecaloma (Fig. 3). The mass was extracted and the enterotomy was closed primarily. The involved bowel was viable, without ischemia, perforation, or serosal injury.

Pathological examination identified two separate pieces of foreign material consistent with biliary stents, measuring 11.0 × 2.0 × 2.0 cm and 11.0 × 0.5 × 0.5 cm, respectively, surrounded by stony-hard fecal material consistent with a fecaloma.

Postoperatively, transient hypotension responded to intravenous fluids without vasopressor support. He subsequently remained stable, bowel function returned, and diet was advanced as tolerated. No wound infection, intra-abdominal collection, or recurrent obstruction occurred. He was discharged home on postoperative day 9, with outpatient follow-up with General Surgery arranged.
