case_text:
A 13‐year‐old boy, weighing 50 kg, sustained a direct epigastric impact against a bicycle handlebar after falling from his bike. The patient showed hemodynamic stability at first assessment in a peripheral hospital, where he had symptoms of exclusively abdominal pain and vomitting. At clinical evaluation, an epigastric circular hematoma was well visible on the abdomen. The first abdominal ultrasound was unremarkable, although laboratory tests showed early elevation of hepatic and pancreatic enzymes (AST: 250 U/L, ALT: 150 U/L, GGT: 30 U/L, amylase: 110 U/L).

As abdominal pain, associated to guarding and abdominal distension, increased and persisted over the following hours, a repeat ultrasound demonstrated a large amount of free intraperitoneal fluid. A contrast‐enhanced CT scan subsequently revealed massive intra‐ and retroperitoneal hemorrhage together with ectasia of the infrarenal abdominal aorta, highly suggestive of a traumatic dissection.

Concurrently, hemoglobin levels showed a significant decline (from 13 g/dL to 9 g/dL), prompting transfer, the following day, to a tertiary pediatric center for advanced management.

On arrival, Doppler ultrasound confirmed dilation of the infrarenal aorta with an intimal flap, turbulent flow, and preserved distal arterial perfusion (Figure 1). Additional findings included a sizeable (10 × 7 cm) hematoma between the left hepatic lobe and the pancreas, diffuse echogenic (corpuscular) free fluid, and a hepatic laceration along the falciform ligament.

Subsequent imaging demonstrated mild progression of aortic dilation and persistence of the spiral‐shaped dissection flap. A dedicated angio‐CT confirmed infrarenal aortic ectasia measuring up to 17 × 16 mm, with the flap extending approximately 20 mm (Figure 2). CT evaluation also documented a deep hepatic laceration, marked distortion of the pancreatic head and proximal body, and multiple peripancreatic and perivisceral fluid–blood collections reaching up to 13 cm in craniocaudal extension (Figure 3).

Given the risk of hemorrhagic, ischemic, and aneurysmal complications, a multidisciplinary team composed by vascular surgeons and interventional radiologists, recommended EVAR.

This approach was considered safer and less invasive in comparison with an open surgical repair (OSR), in particular in a trauma scenario.

On seventh post‐traumatic day, the patient underwent successful exclusion of the dissection via placement of a covered Viabahn stent (13 × 5 mm) [Gore Inc., USA], with preservation of renal artery perfusion on final angiographic assessment (Figure 4).

Initially, the postoperative course was stable and the boy recovered well.

However, the patient later developed recurrent abdominal pain and bilious vomiting.

Follow‐up ultrasound revealed enlargement of the peripancreatic collection, and MRCP demonstrated disruption of the main pancreatic duct at the mid‐body, with a large communicating fluid–blood collection compressing the stomach, consistent with the formation of a post‐traumatic pancreatic pseudocyst.

Endoscopic ultrasound‐guided drainage was therefore performed on the twentieth‐one post‐traumatic day, with placement of a 15 × 10 mm lumen‐apposing metal stent (LAMS) and evacuation of approximately 650 mL of pancreatic fluid.

The patient demonstrated progressive clinical improvement afterward, with decreasing inflammatory markers, resumption of oral feeding, discontinuation of parenteral nutrition, and discharge in good general condition. The LAMS was removed 22 days after placement.

At 6‐month follow‐up, Doppler ultrasound showed a normal‐caliber abdominal aorta with regular flow patterns both proximal and distal to the stent, without residual intimal flaps or aneurysmal dilatation (Figure 5). Flow in the common iliac arteries remained antegrade, and the renal arteries and veins were unremarkable.

case_text:
A 68‐year‐old postmenopausal female presented with a recently enlarged and mildly tender left cervical mass, initially discovered incidentally. There was no redness or swelling of the overlying skin, and the patient experienced discomfort and pain with movement of the mass, and the mass showed a gradual increase in recent months. Her menarche occurred at age 14. She is postmenopausal and has a history of childbearing. She had no known gynecologic pathology. She had a long‐term history of hypertension, which was well controlled with oral antihypertensive drugs, and a history of renal insufficiency requiring hemodialysis three times weekly.

A left cervical mass measuring approximately 5 × 5 × 5 cm was palpable, with hard consistency, poor mobility, and mild tenderness on palpation; no obvious enlargement of superficial lymph nodes was found in the neck.

Serum tumor markers including carcinoembryonic antigen, alpha‐fetoprotein, carbohydrate antigen 19–9, carbohydrate antigen 125, and squamous cell carcinoma‐related antigen were all within the normal reference range.

Ultrasound examination: Two‐dimensional ultrasound showed a hypoechoic mass in the left cervical region, with a clear boundary, irregular contour, and heterogeneous internal echotexture. Color Doppler flow imaging showed visible blood flow signals inside and around the mass (Figure 1). Contrast‐enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) showed that the contrast agent presented heterogeneous hyperenhancement from the periphery toward the center (Figure 2). A previously well 15-year-old female presented with a 2-day history of right iliac fossa pain associated with anorexia, nausea, vomiting, and a documented fever of 38°C at home. She had a known stable right ovarian cyst and a background of polycystic kidney disease. She attained menarche at age 14 and reported irregular, occasionally heavy but non-painful menstrual periods. She had never been sexually active.

On examination, she had focal peritonism in the right iliac fossa with a temperature of 37.6°C. Laboratory investigations demonstrated leukocytosis (white cell count 16.5 × 109/l; neutrophils 12.2 × 109/l) and an elevated C-reactive protein of 45.7 mg/l. Transabdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a thick-walled, hyperaemic appendix measuring 7 mm in diameter with surrounding inflammatory fat stranding, consistent with acute appendicitis (Figs 1 and 2). A simple 34 mm right ovarian cyst was noted, with both ovaries appearing normal (Figs 3 and 4).

The patient was commenced on intravenous amoxicillin-clavulanic acid and underwent diagnostic laparoscopy with planned appendicectomy the following morning.

At laparoscopy, the appendix appeared inflamed, and laparoscopic appendicectomy was performed routinely (Figs 5 and 6). During routine inspection of the pelvis, a haemorrhagic structure adjacent to the right uterine cornu prompted intra-operative gynaecology review. This was identified as the right fallopian tube, torted four complete turns around an associated parafimbrial cyst (Figs 7 and 8). Laparoscopic detorsion restored normal tubal colouration and salpingectomy was avoided. The parafimbrial cyst was left in situ. The uterus, both ovaries and the left fallopian tube appeared normal.

Recovery was uncomplicated, and the patient was discharged day one post-operatively.

Histopathological examination demonstrated no neutrophilic infiltration of the appendiceal wall, excluding acute appendicitis and supporting a reactive inflammatory process secondary to the adjacent torsed fallopian tube.

Follow-up ultrasonography at 6 weeks demonstrated preserved right adnexal vascularity without hydrosalpinx and complete resolution of the parafimbrial cyst. The patient declined hormonal therapy and was counselled regarding the uncertain long-term function of the salvaged tube, the possibility of recurrent torsion, and the need for early obstetric assessment in future pregnancies because of a potential increased risk of ectopic pregnancy.

case_text:
In April 2022, a 70-year-old woman presented with a one-day history of sudden-onset lower abdominal pain. She had a medical history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hyperlipidemia and had no prior history of abdominal surgery. Abdominal computed tomography (CT) demonstrated findings suggestive of perforated sigmoid diverticulitis. The patient subsequently underwent emergency Hartmann’s procedure. Histopathological examination confirmed a diverticulum with abscess formation. Her postoperative course was uneventful, and she was discharged on postoperative day 10.

In August 2022, ~4 months after the initial surgery, the patient was readmitted for colostomy reversal. Preoperative ACT demonstrated two well-defined hyperattenuating lesions with bone attenuation along the previous midline incision. The first lesion was an ~21-mm inverted V-shaped ossified lesion located near the superior aspect of the incision (Fig. 1). The second lesion was an ~70-mm inverted J-shaped ossified lesion involving the periumbilical region and extending toward the inferior aspect of the incision (Fig. 2).

A laparoscopic stoma reversal was initially attempted but was converted to an open procedure because of severe postoperative adhesions. The abdominal cavity was entered through the previous midline incision. Intraoperatively, two mature bony structures were grossly identified along the incision line and were completely resected (Fig. 3).

The superior HO lesion was identified within the fascial layer, measuring 21 × 14 mm and located ~ 120 mm distal to the xiphoid process. The inferior HO lesion measured 70 × 14 mm and was situated immediately superficial to the fascial layer, with its inferior margin ~45 mm cephalad to the superior border of the pubic symphysis.

Histopathological examination of the resected specimens demonstrated mature heterotopic bone formation associated with fibrosis and fat necrosis (Fig. 4).

The postoperative course was uneventful, and no significant abnormalities were detected during outpatient follow-up after discharge.

case_text:
A 71-year-old woman underwent abdominal ultrasonography for urinary tract stones and was incidentally found to have multiple liver nodules predominantly in the right hepatic lobe (Fig. 1A–1C). She reported mild diarrhea and abdominal discomfort. Physical examination findings were unremarkable. Laboratory data, including liver function tests, endocrine tests, and tumor markers, were within normal ranges. MRI revealed 4 liver tumors ranging from 11 to 36 mm in diameter, including a lesion adjacent to the middle hepatic vein (Fig. 1D–1F). Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a calcified tumor in the pancreatic tail with enlarged regional lymph nodes (Fig. 2A, 2B); the liver lesions were not clearly detected on CT. The pancreatic tumor showed faint contrast enhancement and diffusion restriction on MRI (Fig. 2C, 2D). Percutaneous US-guided biopsy of the superficial liver tumor confirmed a well-differentiated NET G2, with immunohistochemical results of synaptophysin [+], CD56 [+], and a Ki-67 index of 10% (Fig. 3). The patient was diagnosed with a nonfunctioning PanNET with multiple liver metastases (T2N1M1, Stage IV, according to the 8th edition of the Union for International Cancer Control staging system). Contrast-enhanced MRI revealed 4 liver metastases, including a 28-mm lesion in segment 4/8 abutting the middle hepatic vein, whereas the remaining lesions were confined to the right hepatic lobe. Complete clearance of all hepatic disease at that time would have required at least an extended right hepatectomy, and limited parenchyma-sparing resection was not considered feasible. The multidisciplinary team considered the disease not amenable to upfront curative-intent resection. First, a single session of TACE was performed to control the dominant liver metastasis and abdominal symptoms. Angiography identified the tumor feeder from hepatic artery A5, and intra-arterial infusion of a Lipiodol-based emulsion containing epirubicin (15 mg) was administered, followed by embolization using Gelpart (Nippon Kayaku, Tokyo, Japan). Epirubicin was selected as part of our institution’s conventional Lipiodol-based TACE protocol. The patient’s abdominal symptoms improved after the TACE. Subsequently, lanreotide was administered as systemic therapy (120 mg every 4 weeks) for approximately 2 years. The treatment was well tolerated, with only mild cutaneous rash. Serial contrast-enhanced MRI revealed a marked and sustained hepatic response. The number of MRI-detectable liver lesions decreased from 4 at baseline to 1 before surgery. The size of the residual segment 5 lesion decreased from 36 to 19 mm, whereas the other lesions were no longer detectable. Retrospective assessment according to the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) version 1.1 showed that the sum of target lesion diameters decreased from 87 to 19 mm representing a 78% reduction. The best overall response was a partial response. The primary pancreatic tumor and regional lymph node metastases remained stable, and no new intrahepatic or extrahepatic lesions developed during approximately 18 months of sustained disease control (Fig. 4).

Given the sustained therapeutic response, which was maintained for approximately 18 months, the patient’s case was reassessed at a multidisciplinary conference. Residual hepatic disease was limited to a solitary lesion in segment 5 that was amenable to complete resection by minor parenchyma-sparing hepatectomy. There was no evidence of new metastatic disease. The primary pancreatic tumor and regional lymph node metastases remained technically resectable by distal pancreatectomy with lymphadenectomy. Based on these anatomical and oncological findings, curative-intent conversion surgery was considered a reasonable treatment option. After shared decision-making with the patient, robot-assisted simultaneous resection was performed, including hepatectomy of the residual solitary lesion in segment 5 and distal pancreatectomy with regional lymphadenectomy. The operation was completed using 5 ports, and the docking position of the ports was changed between the pancreatic and hepatic phases of the procedure (Fig. 5). After precise delineation of the tumor contours using ICG fluorescence imaging, H5′ hepatectomy was performed. The operative time was 8h 2 min, and blood loss was 5 mL. No intra-operative transfusions were required. The postoperative course was complicated by a Grade B postoperative pancreatic fistula, as defined by the International Study Group of Pancreatic Fistula; however, there was no bile leakage or other major complications. The patient was discharged on POD 35. Final pathological examination showed that the resected liver lesion was largely replaced by scar tissue without viable tumor cells (Fig. 6A). In contrast, the pancreatic tumor and metastatic lymph nodes were viable (Fig. 6B, 6C). The pancreatic tumor corresponded to NET G1 with a Ki-67 index of 1% (Fig. 6D). The surgical margins were negative. Of the 7 lymph nodes examined, 4 were positive. The patient has been followed up without adjuvant therapy and remains alive without recurrence at postoperative month 15.

case_text:
In December 2023, an 18-year-old male, with no history of congenital vascular malformations, trauma, or invasive vascular procedures, presented to the emergency department with a 10-day history of respiratory symptoms suggestive of an acute respiratory tract infection, accompanied by dyspnea and cough. Notably, this prolonged acute respiratory infection had led to a recent period of reduced mobility prior to admission. Admission laboratory investigations revealed a marked increase in inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein 148 mg/L, reference range <5 mg/L) and, notably, a significantly elevated D-dimer level (8432 µg/L, reference range 0–500 µg/L). Given the respiratory manifestations and marked edema of the left lower limb, computed tomography angiography (CTA) was performed, demonstrating complete thrombosis of the left iliofemoral veins extending into the proximal inferior vena cava (Figure 1), together with a pulmonary embolism (PE) involving a lobar branch of the right lower lobe. Baseline CTA and vascular evaluations did not reveal extrinsic venous compression syndromes, such as May–Thurner syndrome. Subsequent color DUS also demonstrated complete occlusion of the left popliteal vein. Anticoagulant therapy was immediately initiated with fondaparinux (7.5 mg once daily subcutaneous injection). Following clinical stabilization, the patient was transitioned to rivaroxaban according to standard therapeutic protocols and discharged with a prescription for a class II thigh-length elastic compression stocking.

At evaluation at our outpatient clinic three months after the acute event, the patient was in excellent general condition and completely free of signs or symptoms suggestive of PTS. Follow-up DUS demonstrated a favorable yet complex pattern of evolution: partial recanalization of the left popliteal vein, with a small residual thrombus measuring 3.0 mm in maximum thickness. Of note, color Doppler ultrasonography evaluation revealed no evidence of an AVF. Partial recanalization was also observed in the left common femoral vein, with persistent patency and continuous flow at the saphenofemoral junction (Figure 2). The external iliac vein remained occluded, whereas complete recanalization of the left common iliac vein was maintained through internal iliac collateral pathways and associated suprapubic venous collaterals. During thrombophilia screening, the patient demonstrated markedly reduced antithrombin (AT) III activity (52%). Given the possibility of hereditary AT III deficiency, repeat testing was performed during follow-up, after the acute phase, and confirmed persistently reduced AT III activity. Furthermore, cascade screening was extended to first-degree relatives, revealing AT III deficiency in the patient’s father and thus further supporting a hereditary pattern of the defect. Considering these findings, the therapeutic plan was adjusted. Long-term therapeutic-dose anticoagulation with rivaroxaban (20 mg once daily) was maintained. The class II thigh-length compression stocking was replaced with a class II knee-high compression stocking, and a micronized purified flavonoid fraction (MPFF, 500 mg twice daily) was added to support venous circulation, given its pleiotropic effects, including the reduction of venous remodeling, inhibition of inflammatory cascades, and improvement in venous tone and stasis.

During subsequent scheduled six-monthly follow-up visits, the patient demonstrated excellent adherence to both pharmacological and compression therapies, which remained unchanged over time. Clinically, no signs or symptoms of PTS were recorded (Villalta score = 0). Periodic DUS examinations documented progressive and encouraging recanalization of the deep venous system: complete restoration of the lumen was achieved in the left popliteal vein, alongside partial recanalization of the femoral and common femoral veins, whereas occlusion of the external iliac vein persisted. During the routine evaluation performed in July 2026, approximately 31 months after the onset of DVT, the patient remained in excellent clinical status and remained free of post-thrombotic complications. However, the follow-up DUS revealed the new onset of a popliteal AVF (Figure 3, Video S1 in Supplementary Material), with no evidence of a direct communication with the main popliteal artery trunk. The AVF was considered likely to originate from adventitial neovessels, as the main popliteal artery consistently demonstrated normal high-resistance, triphasic arterial waveforms, without a reduction in the resistive index. The patient also underwent a cardiological evaluation with echocardiography, which revealed no signs of cardiac overload or alterations in the pulmonary-to-systemic flow ratio (Qp/Qs). Given the absence of cardiac alterations and symptoms suggestive of venous hypertension, significant deep venous reflux on color DUS, or limb edema, a conservative management strategy consisting of close DUS surveillance without further diagnostic procedures was adopted.

The class II thigh-length compression stocking was replaced with a class II knee-high compression stocking, and a micronized purified flavonoid fraction (MPFF, 500 mg twice daily) was added to support venous circulation, given its pleiotropic effects, including the reduction of venous remodeling, inhibition of inflammatory cascades, and improvement in venous tone and stasis.
During subsequent scheduled six-monthly follow-up visits, the patient demonstrated excellent adherence to both pharmacological and compression therapies, which remained unchanged over time.
Clinically, no signs or symptoms of PTS were recorded (Villalta score = 0).

Periodic DUS examinations documented progressive and encouraging recanalization of the deep venous system: complete restoration of the lumen was achieved in the left popliteal vein, alongside partial recanalization of the femoral and common femoral veins, whereas occlusion of the external iliac vein persisted.

During the routine evaluation performed in July 2026, approximately 31 months after the onset of DVT, the patient remained in excellent clinical status and remained free of post-thrombotic complications.
However, the follow-up DUS revealed the new onset of a popliteal AVF (Figure 3, Video S1 in Supplementary Material), with no evidence of a direct communication with the main popliteal artery trunk.

The AVF was considered likely to originate from adventitial neovessels, as the main popliteal artery consistently demonstrated normal high-resistance, triphasic arterial waveforms, without a reduction in the resistive index.
The patient also underwent a cardiological evaluation with echocardiography, which revealed no signs of cardiac overload or alterations in the pulmonary-to-systemic flow ratio (Qp/Qs).

Given the absence of cardiac alterations and symptoms suggestive of venous hypertension, significant deep venous reflux on color DUS, or limb edema, a conservative management strategy consisting of close DUS surveillance without further diagnostic procedures was adopted.
title: Late Arteriovenous Fistula After Deep Vein Thrombosis in a Young Patient: A Case Report

case_text:
A 50‐year‐old man presented with progressively worsening right distal femoral/knee pain for approximately 6 months, accompanied by difficulty bearing weight and walking. Anteroposterior radiography demonstrated bilateral distal femoral lesions (Figure 1), initially considered possibly benign cystic bone lesions. According to the treating orthopedic surgeon, the right‐sided lesion extended to the articular cartilage surface, whereas the left‐sided lesion was farther from the cartilage surface. The available radiograph does not permit a more confident characterization of lesion margins or internal matrix.

Physical examination revealed no remarkable findings.

At presentation, the radiological differential diagnosis included a benign cystic bone lesion; given the atypical osseous appearance, other considerations included a primary bone tumor and chronic osteomyelitis.

Persistent right‐sided pain with impaired weight‐bearing and walking, together with the extension of the right‐sided lesion to the articular cartilage surface, prompted operative management. Curettage of the right‐sided lesion and right knee arthroplasty were performed in the same operative session. The left‐sided lesion was managed without surgery based on clinical and radiological assessment. Histopathological examination of the curettage specimen demonstrated diffuse fibrosis with numerous lipid‐laden (foamy) histiocytes (Figure 2). These unexpected findings raised suspicion for a histiocytic disorder and prompted immunophenotypic investigation and expert pathological consultation.

case_text:
A 60‐year‐old woman presented for left ureteroscopy with laser lithotripsy, ureteral stent exchange, and kidney stone extraction. The day of presentation and admission is designated Day 0. Her history included recurrent calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis requiring multiple ureteral stent placements, for which she used tamsulosin 0.4 mg orally nightly; potassium citrate extended‐release 10 mEq orally twice daily had recently been stopped. She had Type 2 diabetes mellitus in remission following Roux‐en‐Y gastric bypass and was prescribed semaglutide (Ozempic) 1 mg subcutaneously once weekly; hypertension treated with lisinopril 10 mg orally daily; a prior transient ischemic attack with aspirin 81 mg orally daily; hyperlipidemia treated with rosuvastatin 5 mg orally daily; and obsessive‐compulsive disorder treated with clomipramine 50 mg orally nightly. Her history also included nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, obstructive sleep apnea without CPAP use, thalassemia trait, and gastroesophageal reflux disease, with omeprazole 20 mg orally daily listed but not recently taken. Other listed medications were ferrous sulfate 325 mg orally every other day and cholecalciferol 1000 units orally daily. Semaglutide was held during hospitalization, and lisinopril was held because of concern for acute renal dysfunction. During preoperative evaluation, SpO2 was 88% on room air. Despite escalation to 8 L/min supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula, SpO2 improved only to 92%, prompting cancellation of the procedure and hospital admission for further evaluation.

She had completed a 14‐day course of phenazopyridine 200 mg orally three times daily for dysuria after ureteral stent placement. She reported medication adherence and took her last dose on Day −1. Stent placement was estimated to have occurred on Day −15 by subtracting 14 days from the last dose; the procedure date was not independently verified. She had felt unwell for approximately 1 week and reported intermittent dizziness and bilateral upper extremity tingling, particularly with deep inspiration. She denied dyspnea, chest pain, cough, wheezing, fever, orthopnea, lower extremity edema, or decreased exercise tolerance. She had no history of chronic pulmonary disease and denied smoking or vaping. After ascorbic acid was started in the emergency department on Day 0 for suspected methemoglobinemia, oxygen was reduced to 4 L/min by nasal cannula. At subsequent inpatient assessment, she was comfortable and hemodynamically stable, with SpO2 of 93%–94%, respiratory rate of 14/min, heart rate of 64 beats/min, and blood pressure of 134/73 mmHg. Her lungs were clear, and neurological examination showed no focal deficits.

case_text:
A 7‐year‐old fully vaccinated female child with a history of atopy presented to the emergency department (ED) with 3 days of fever, right otalgia, and upper respiratory symptoms, including significant nasal congestion. She was evaluated in the ED, without otolaryngology consultation. On examination, she was febrile to 38.1°C (100.6 °F), tachycardic, and noted to have clear rhinitis with an otherwise normal head and neck examination. She was discharged with supportive care including acetaminophen; however, she returned the following day with new right‐sided facial and oral swelling (Figure 1A,B). Vital signs in the ED were significant for a fever of 38.5°C (101.3 F). Head and neck examination was pertinent for right acute otitis media, right infraorbital and periorbital erythema with soft edema, premaxillary fullness with induration, a right fluctuant hard palatal lesion without auto‐drainage, purulence in bilateral sinonasal cavities with a swollen right middle turbinate, intact extraocular movements and vision, and absence of meningeal signs. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis with neutrophilic predominance and leftward shift and elevated inflammatory markers including C‐reactive protein (CRP) (Table 1).

Additional imaging was pursued to further evaluate the extent of bony and soft tissue involvement and the etiology of the palatal mass. Computed tomography (CT) with contrast of the sinuses revealed a right palatal abscess with bony erosion of the hard palate and extensive pansinusitis, right greater than left, involving the maxillary and ethmoid sinuses (Figure 2A–D). Other findings included pre‐ and postseptal right orbital cellulitis with a focal defect in the right medial orbital wall but without intracranial extension and associated right malar cellulitis. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated a 3‐cm, partially subperiosteal abscess along the right hard palate with extension anteriorly along the maxillary alveolar cortex and frontal process of the maxilla, posteriorly toward the pterygoid plates, and superiorly toward the greater palatine foramen (Figure 3). Additionally, MRI was consistent with pansinusitis with orbital cellulitis and superficial infection of the periorbital, anterior maxillary, and right nasolabial soft tissues.

The patient was admitted and started on intravenous ampicillin–sulbactam (50 mg/kg every 6 h) and a nasal sinus regimen including saline rinses, intranasal fluticasone spray, and a three‐day course of oxymetazoline hydrochloride intranasal decongestant spray. After 24 h of intravenous antibiotics without improvement, the patient underwent CT‐guided functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) with maxillary antrostomy, right anterior ethmoidectomy, right partial posterior ethmoidectomy, and incision and drainage of the right hard palate and right premaxillary region. Postoperatively, the patient clinically improved but had persistently increasing CRP levels (Day 5: 47.0 mg/L; Day 6: 54.9 mg/L). Two days after the surgery, the palatal abscess reaccumulated. Thus, the patient returned to the operating room for a repeat intraoral incision and drainage of the right hard palate abscess with Penrose drain placement. Operative cultures produced Streptococcus mitis and Streptococcus constellatus with sensitivity to ampicillin–sulbactam.

The patient demonstrated clinical improvement with downtrending inflammatory markers (CRP Day 7: 40.0 mg/L; Day 8: 27.8 mg/L; Day 9: 24.3 mg/L) and stable vitals and was discharged on hospital day nine. She was discharged with oral amoxicillin–clavulanate (40 mg/kg/day) three times daily for six weeks, per the pediatric infectious disease team, and a nasal sinus regimen including saline rinses and intranasal fluticasone spray. At a follow up otolaryngology clinic visit 2 months later, the patient had mild right soft palate fullness without residual fluctuance or erythema. Anterior rhinoscopy showed resolution of sinusitis with only scant rhinorrhea.

case_text:
A 49‐year‐old male sustained multiple burns due to an alcohol explosion at work on October 23, 2021. After initial management including internal jugular vein catheterization and tracheal intubation at a local hospital, he was transferred to our burn emergency department 7 h after the accident. On admission, he was conscious but complained of breathlessness. Physical examination showed cold extremities, undetectable pulse oximetry, and reduced respiratory mobility due to thoracic eschars. Fluid resuscitation and anti‐shock therapy were started. Indwelling catheter drained 200 mL dark brown urine, suggesting myoglobinuria. Due to dyspnea, escharotomy, and tracheotomy were performed.

Examination revealed multiple burn wounds covering 93% TBSA. Most skin was peeled off, both eyes swollen, nasal hair burnt, lips deformed with eversion resembling a fish mouth. Face and buttocks showed red‐and‐white wound bases with large exudate. Black, tough eschars were present on neck, trunk, and limbs. Distal blood flow was poor, skin temperature low. Complications included severe inhalation injury, right pneumothorax, hypoproteinemia, coagulopathy, and acute renal dysfunction. ABSI score was 13, indicating high mortality risk.

case_text:
A 76-year-old man had undergone surgical bioprosthetic mitral valve replacement and coronary artery bypass grafting in 2014. Serial echocardiography showed stable valve function. In 2022, he was diagnosed with systemic sclerosis-associated interstitial lung disease and subsequently underwent regular follow-up by the Allergy and Clinical Immunology service, including serial chest computed tomography (CT) using an interstitial lung disease protocol. In September 2022, echocardiography demonstrated normal bioprosthetic mitral valve function, with a mean transmitral gradient of 4.01 mmHg (Figure 1A). Echocardiography in March 2023 showed preserved prosthetic valve haemodynamics, with a mean transmitral gradient of 5.14 mmHg (Figure 1B). No echocardiography was performed in May 2024.

In August 2024, he was admitted with a three-month history of progressive dyspnoea, which had advanced to minimal activity and orthopnoea (New York Heart Association functional class III–IV). Physical examination revealed crackles and peripheral oedema. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated severe bioprosthetic mitral stenosis, with peak and mean transmitral gradients of 30.8 and 21.6 mmHg, respectively, a pressure half-time of 296 ms, and an estimated mitral valve area of 0.7 cm2 (Figure 1C,D). Left ventricular systolic function was preserved. Moderate tricuspid regurgitation and pulmonary hypertension were present, with an estimated systolic pulmonary artery pressure of 57 mmHg.

After severe bioprosthetic mitral stenosis was diagnosed, the preceding chest CT series was retrospectively reviewed because the original reports had not described the prosthetic valve. Longitudinal comparison showed a relatively thin leaflet region in September 2022 (Figure 2A), mild interval thickening in March 2023 (Figure 2B), and diffuse thickening with increased attenuation and an appearance suggestive of commissural fusion in May 2024 (Figure 2C). Repeat chest CT during the August 2024 admission showed a similar appearance of the bioprosthesis to that in May 2024 (Figure 2D). Table 1 summarizes CT, echocardiographic, and clinical findings.

TEE demonstrated marked leaflet thickening, with near-immobility of the basal and mid-portions and limited motion of the free edges. A thin layer of echogenic material on the ventricular aspect suggested a superimposed thrombotic component (Supplementary Videos 1 and 2). No vegetation or periprosthetic abscess was identified, and blood cultures were negative.

Management was challenging because of progressive interstitial lung disease, previous coronary artery bypass grafting with a patent left internal mammary artery-to-left anterior descending artery graft, and acute kidney injury limiting preoperative coronary angiography. Given the suspected superimposed thrombotic component, therapeutic enoxaparin was initiated. Four days later, recurrent acute pulmonary oedema requiring non-invasive ventilatory support occurred. Given severe obstruction and instability, the Heart Team proceeded with redo mitral valve replacement and tricuspid valve repair.

Examination of the explanted bioprosthesis showed diffuse leaflet thickening and rigidity with commissural fusion and markedly restricted opening. Pannus was present but was not considered by the surgeon to be the predominant mechanism of obstruction. Thin thrombotic material was identified within the leaflet sinuses on the ventricular aspect. No histopathological examination was available (Figure 3).

The patient recovered uneventfully. At the most recent follow-up in June 2026, approximately 22 months after surgery, he remained free of heart failure symptoms, with normal mechanical mitral prosthesis function on echocardiography.

case_text:
A 73-year-old woman underwent elective right TKA for advanced primary osteoarthritis (Fig. 1). Relevant comorbidities included obesity (body mass index 44.2 kg/m2), type 2 diabetes mellitus, arterial hypertension, chronic kidney disease, atrial fibrillation treated with edoxaban, and a DDD pacemaker for sick sinus syndrome. She was classified as American Society of Anesthesiologists physical status III. No medication, latex, cement, or implant allergy was documented preoperatively.

General anaesthesia was induced with sufentanil 25 micrograms, propofol 200 mg, and rocuronium 30 mg. Cefazolin 2 g and dexamethasone 20 mg were administered. A posterior-stabilized prosthesis was implanted using 60 g of gentamicin-loaded polymethyl methacrylate cement (Palacos MV+G).

Approximately 1.5 h after the start of surgery and within minutes of cementation, oxygen saturation and blood pressure fell abruptly. Peripheral oxygen saturation reached 74%, blood pressure fell to a recorded nadir of 57/43 mmHg before invasive monitoring, and end-tidal carbon dioxide fell from 35 to 22 mmHg. Systolic blood pressure decreased by more than 40%. Peak airway pressure increased from ~20 to 30 cmH2O with reduced tidal volume. New bronchospasm and diffuse flushing were documented.

The treating team initiated emergency treatment for severe perioperative anaphylaxis while considering BCIS and pulmonary embolism. Repeated intravenous epinephrine 0.1 mg boluses were administered to a documented cumulative dose of 1 mg, together with norepinephrine and epinephrine infusions, prednisolone 500 mg, dimetindene 8 mg, cimetidine 200 mg, high inspired oxygen, fluids, and invasive monitoring. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation was not required, and haemodynamics and oxygenation improved.

Computed tomography (CT) showed no macroscopic pulmonary embolism or right-heart strain but demonstrated soft-tissue swelling around the proximal endotracheal tube. Repeated cuff-leak testing remained negative. No cuff leak was detected on repeated testing. The patient was transferred to intensive care and remained intubated until postoperative Day 2 while the airway swelling regressed. She subsequently returned to the orthopaedic ward and completed rehabilitation. Early postoperative radiographs showed the components in situ without an acute periprosthetic fracture (Fig. 2).

Neither acute nor baseline serum tryptase was obtained. At allergology assessment 3 months later, no reaction was documented to benzoyl peroxide, gentamicin, propofol, ropivacaine, or latex. The assessment did not identify a culprit. At 5 months, the patient rated recovery of the operated knee as good, although the event had somewhat affected her confidence regarding future anaesthesia.

case_text:
A 62‐year‐old male with past medical history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, obesity, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, coronary artery disease, and prior bilateral inguinal hernia repair presented to the ED with acute right testicular pain.

The patient reported sudden onset of right testicular pain, followed by nausea, diaphoresis, and shortness of breath while lifting a 300‐lb generator into his truck. He denied previous episodes of similar testicular pain but did report a history of an undescended testis in childhood, which did not require surgical intervention.

On physical examination, the patient was diaphoretic and in acute distress. Examination of the genitalia revealed an easily palpable left testicle but no palpable right testicle within the scrotum. A palpable, tender mass was noted within the right inguinal canal.

The patient was treated with IV analgesia and antiemetics. A testicular ultrasound was obtained, which demonstrated the right testis in the inguinal canal with good perfusion, and no evidence of testicular torsion (Figure 1). Urology was consulted for testicular dislocation. Manual reduction was attempted at bedside by the urology team using IV analgesia with successful reduction to the upper hemiscrotum.

The patient was admitted to the observation unit for a repeat testicular ultrasound, urology evaluation in the morning, and pain control. The repeat ultrasound redemonstrated adequate perfusion. He was discharged home with urology follow‐up as there was no acute surgical intervention needed. He was counseled on expectant management and informed of the risks of testicular atrophy and abnormal testicular positioning.

Following discharge, the patient was seen at multiple facilities within the surrounding area with persistent testicular discomfort. Two days after discharge, the patient was seen at two different facilities for continued testicular pain with associated nausea and vomiting. CT of the abdomen and pelvis was completed and revealed no acute testicular pathology. He was subsequently discharged with antiemetics and urology follow‐up. Nine days after the initial encounter, he presented to another facility with persistent groin pain. A repeat CT abdomen and pelvis and ultrasound of the testicles were performed. The ultrasound was remarkable for a right testicle superiorly displaced in the upper scrotal sac with normal perfusion. Urology at that facility recommended that he be discharged with a muscle relaxer and outpatient follow‐up.

The patient had three more subsequent ED visits to area hospitals for testicular pain, and he had no significant changes to his testicular ultrasound other than possible decrease in size of testis, concerning for potential development of testicular atrophy. The patient reported sudden onset of right testicular pain, followed by nausea, diaphoresis, and shortness of breath while lifting a 300‐lb generator into his truck.
He denied previous episodes of similar testicular pain but did report a history of an undescended testis in childhood, which did not require surgical intervention.
On physical examination, the patient was diaphoretic and in acute distress.
Examination of the genitalia revealed an easily palpable left testicle but no palpable right testicle within the scrotum.
A palpable, tender mass was noted within the right inguinal canal.
The patient was treated with IV analgesia and antiemetics.
A testicular ultrasound was obtained, which demonstrated the right testis in the inguinal canal with good perfusion, and no evidence of testicular torsion (Figure 1).
Urology was consulted for testicular dislocation.
Manual reduction was attempted at bedside by the urology team using IV analgesia with successful reduction to the upper hemiscrotum.
The patient was admitted to the observation unit for a repeat testicular ultrasound, urology evaluation in the morning, and pain control.
The repeat ultrasound redemonstrated adequate perfusion.
He was discharged home with urology follow‐up as there was no acute surgical intervention needed.
He was counseled on expectant management and informed of the risks of testicular atrophy and abnormal testicular positioning.
Following discharge, the patient was seen at multiple facilities within the surrounding area with persistent testicular discomfort.
Two days after discharge, the patient was seen at two different facilities for continued testicular pain with associated nausea and vomiting.
CT of the abdomen and pelvis was completed and revealed no acute testicular pathology.
He was subsequently discharged with antiemetics and urology follow‐up.
Nine days after the initial encounter, he presented to another facility with persistent groin pain.
A repeat CT abdomen and pelvis and ultrasound of the testicles were performed.
The ultrasound was remarkable for a right testicle superiorly displaced in the upper scrotal sac with normal perfusion.
Urology at that facility recommended that he be discharged with a muscle relaxer and outpatient follow‐up.

case_text:
A 56‐year‐old Tanzanian man presented to Southern Zone Referral Hospital in Mtwara, Tanzania, with a 1‐week history of recurrent twitching around the right eye. The twitching lasted approximately 20–25 s and occurred several times daily without an identifiable trigger. Several days after symptom onset, he developed recurrent episodes of transient mouth deviation and right cheek numbness. He also reported intermittent headache. The episodes resolved spontaneously without residual weakness or altered awareness. He reported no limb weakness, speech impairment, visual loss, generalized convulsions, or recent head trauma. He had no known history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, cardiovascular disease, stroke, or epilepsy. There was no known family history of hereditary vascular or neurological disorders.

On admission, he was alert and fully oriented, and his vital signs were within normal limits. Neurological examination between episodes revealed no persistent cranial nerve deficit, limb weakness, or limb sensory deficit. Coordination and gait were normal. No episode was observed during the assessment.

The abrupt onset and spontaneous resolution of the facial symptoms initially raised concern for a transient ischemic attack. The brief, recurrent, stereotyped episodes, particularly the right periocular twitching, subsequently raised suspicion for focal seizures.

case_text:
A 7 year old boy presented with a 1‐month history of progressively worsening headache and recurrent non‐bilious vomiting. The headache was severe, constant, and throbbing in character, exacerbated by valsalva maneuvers, and not associated with photophobia or tinnitus. Vomiting occurred multiple times daily, predominantly in the early morning, and was unrelated to food intake. There was no history of chronic systemic illness or regular medication use.

At age six, he had experienced a similar episode characterized by headache and vomiting and was treated with therapeutic lumbar punctures followed by acetazolamide and furosemide, with subsequent clinical improvement. Ophthalmologic documentation from that episode was unavailable, and therefore the presence or absence of papilledema at that time could not be confirmed.

He remained symptom‐free for approximately 1 year before the current presentation. 10 days after the onset of the current illness, the patient developed medial deviation of the left eye, which progressively involved the right eye over subsequent days (Figure 1). Given the clinical presentation, initial differential diagnoses included an intracranial space‐occupying lesion, obstructive hydrocephalus, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, central nervous system (CNS) infection, and idiopathic intracranial hypertension.

Abnormalities in markers of hepatocellular injury such as aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase, and lactate dehydrogenase are almost always noted. Biliary injury may also be detected by elevations in gamma glutamyl transferase, alkaline phosphatase, and less commonly bilirubin. Close to 80% of adults and children with either pHLH or sHLH have liver enzyme elevation as part of presentation and a small subset of these patients meet ALF clinical criteria (36, 72). Coagulation derangements may be affected by both liver dysfunction and endothelial activation that may occur concurrently with HLH (73). Children suffering from HLH–PALF have higher incidence of hypoalbuminemia, splenomegaly and clinical findings of capillary leak (69).

Liver biopsy is an important tool to assist with diagnosis of HLH-hepatitis/ALF. Technical advances improving safety of liver biopsy in ALF allow for liver biopsy to add information to other noninvasive testing to assist with diagnosis (74, 75). Ultimately, decision for needle biopsy should be determined by the severity of coagulation and platelet derangements and availability of other diagnostics clinically. Typical histological findings include features of infiltration of CD3+/CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes as well as histiocytes (markers such as CD68+ or CD163+) that at times show hemophagocytosis and sinusoidal tracts (Fig. 3) (76, 77). In more severe cases in patients that underwent liver transplantation or postmortem examination, the lymphocytic infiltrate extends to bile ducts and to the hepatic lobule with resulting massive hepatic necrosis and parenchymal collapse on cytokeratin stain (Fig. 3) (68, 77).

HLH accounted for 3% of cases of PALF in patients under the age of 3 in data from PALF-Study Group (78). In the largest cohort to date, 30 children <2 years of age who met HLH-2004 diagnostic criteria as well as PALF criteria underwent genetic testing retrospectively. 66.7% had at least one pathogenic variant in HLH-related genes with PRF1 mutations being most common (33%) (65). More recently, a separate group found that pHLH in infancy presents with liver failure in 30% of cases (66). sHLH is most often seen in children/adults with ALF above age of 3, although sHLH due to infection still may present with liver failure in infancy (66). The National Institutes of Health–funded PALF-Study Group found that in 4–17 year-olds, HLH accounted for only 1.7% of PALF cases, and there was no information on the genetic testing performed (78). The adult literature on sHLH ALF is scarce with primarily case reports, series, and limited retrospective clinical data (67, 79, 80, 81, 82). In the adult ALF-Study group, HLH accounted for only 0.14% of cases (82). sHLH ALF in adults is commonly triggered by malignancy or infection. Despite liver injury being common in HLH, the more severe manifestations of liver failure are quite rare above the age of 3. However, this diagnosis should be considered in patients with predisposing conditions such as malignancy, rheumatologic disorders, and certain infections.

ALF can be the dominant manifestation of HLH, especially in young children (73). In some patients, the severity of the liver involvement can overshadow other aspects of the presentation that are consistent with HLH, most commonly fevers, cytopenias, and splenomegaly, and the diagnosis of HLH can be delayed. These systemic features can be initially attributed to an infectious or toxin-related liver injury instead of HLH. Rarely, patients may initially present with ALF and then go on to develop other HLH-related manifestations later in the disease course (83). The index of suspicion for HLH in patients with ALF needs to be high, especially in population under the age of 3 years, so that HLH-directed treatment can be initiated earlier in the disease course to prevent organ damage and mortality. Further, the diagnosis of HLH-PALF needs to be considered for liver transplant, as there is a lower transplant-free survival in HLH-PALF compared with other causes of PALF (65, 68, 69).

A 57‐year‐old woman with a 4‐month history of chronic cough managed by an outside pulmonologist presented with acute kidney injury. Evaluation revealed acute kidney injury with proteinuria and microscopic hematuria with dysmorphic red blood cells, consistent with a glomerular source.

Serologic workup was notable for MPO‐ANCA positivity, while PR3‐ANCA, complement (C3 and C4), anti‐GBM antibody, anti‐dsDNA, ANA, and infectious serologies (hepatitis B/C, HIV, syphilis, and coccidioidomycosis) were negative. Kidney biopsy showed pauci‐immune necrotizing and crescentic glomerulonephritis (Figure 1) with ∼70% globally sclerosed glomeruli (Figure 2), consistent with ANCA‐associated glomerulonephritis with marked chronicity. The absence of significant glomerular inflammation on immunofluorescence refers to the absence of immune‐complex deposition and endocapillary proliferation, consistent with a pauci‐immune process (Figure 1). Chest CT revealed localized cystic densities and ground‐glass opacities.

Following the institutional preimmunosuppression protocol, QuantiFERON testing and AFB cultures were obtained; because active mycobacterial infection had to be excluded before cyclophosphamide or rituximab, these agents were withheld pending culture results. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage grew M. abscessus complex, with susceptibility testing demonstrating multidrug resistance.

The patient was started on pulse IV methylprednisolone 500 mg daily × 3 days and then oral prednisone 1 mg/kg daily with a subsequent taper. Weeks 2–4: BAL culture returned M. abscessus complex. Multidrug antimicrobial therapy was initiated per infectious diseases. Serum creatinine improved to ∼2.2 mg/dL.

Months 2–6: Renal function further improved to ∼1.9 mg/dL and stabilized. ESR and CRP normalized. Hematuria resolved; proteinuria decreased. Quantitative MPO‐ANCA showed a downtrend but remained detectable.

The patient received pulse intravenous methylprednisolone 500 mg daily for 3 days followed by oral prednisone 1 mg/kg daily with a subsequent taper. Given the active M. abscessus infection, cyclophosphamide and rituximab were withheld. Antimicrobial therapy for the multidrug‐resistant M. abscessus isolate was directed by susceptibility testing and designed in collaboration with infectious diseases. The isolate demonstrated no inducible (erm(41)‐mediated) or mutational macrolide resistance; accordingly, a macrolide‐containing multidrug regimen was used, consistent with the 2020 ATS/ERS/ESCMID/IDSA NTM guideline recommendation of a macrolide‐containing regimen with at least three active drugs in the initial phase for macrolide‐susceptible disease. The regimen comprised oral azithromycin 250 mg once a day, intravenous imipenem 500 mg every 24 h with a renally adjusted dose, oral omadacycline 300 mg daily, clofazimine 100 mg daily, and inhaled amikacin 590 mg daily.

Over ∼6 months, serum creatinine improved from a peak of 3.9 mg/dL to 2.2 mg/dL and then 1.9 mg/dL, ESR and CRP normalized, hematuria resolved, and proteinuria decreased (Table 2). No cytotoxic immunosuppression was administered.

A 48-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a pancreatic tail cyst detected during a routine health checkup. Initial contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) revealed a 23-mm cyst with thin internal septations (Fig. 1a). MCN was suspected, and follow-up was recommended; however, the patient discontinued surveillance.

Five years later, repeat imaging revealed enlargement of the cyst to 43 × 36 mm and thickening of the cyst wall (Fig. 1b). Serum CA19–9 was elevated to 53.28 U/ml. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated high signal intensity on T2-weighted images and low signal intensity on T1-weighted images, with faint peripheral diffusion restriction (Fig. 2a–c).

Endoscopic ultrasonography (EUS) showed internal septa and a mural nodule-like structure. On contrast-enhanced EUS, the septa enhanced, whereas the mural nodule did not (Fig. 2d–e). Despite this atypical finding for MCN, interval growth and CA19–9 elevation led to a preoperative diagnosis of MCN.

Laparoscopic spleen-preserving distal pancreatectomy was performed. The operative time was 4 h 6 min, and blood loss was 50 ml. Gross examination revealed brownish tissue suggestive of splenic tissue adjacent to the pancreas. Histopathology showed a cyst lined by stratified squamous epithelium positive for p63, with abundant subepithelial lymphoid tissue positive for CD8, consistent with ECIPAS (Fig. 3).

A 66‑year‑old woman was admitted to our hospital with a 9-day history of persistent fever and chills, accompanied by palpitations and chest tightness. She had a history of hypertension and coronary heart disease, with no prior myocardial infarction or PCI, and no regular examinations or therapy. Laboratory examinations revealed elevated C‑reactive protein and neutrophil counts. Electrocardiography showed atrial premature beats accompanied by junctional escape beats. TTE and TEE both demonstrated a 74 × 65 mm round mass located between the left atrium and the pulmonary artery. On TTE, the mass could be visualized on the parasternal short-axis view. On TEE, the giant mass was well visualized at the mid-esophageal level at approximately 57°. The lesion manifested as an aneurysmal sac filled with fluid, containing internal spontaneous echo contrast (dot-like echoes) and peripheral hypoechoic material consistent with mural thrombus. The aneurysm exerted significant extrinsic compression on the left atrium. At a TEE angle of approximately 112°, the left atrium appeared obviously compressed with reduced volume. On the parasternal short‑axis view, the LMCA was dilated with an internal diameter of approximately 9 mm. Color Doppler revealed low‑velocity swirling flow signals within the mass, with communication to the left coronary arterial system (Figs. 1A and B). Contrast-enhanced echocardiography showed contrast agent perfusion into the lesion via the left coronary system, although the exact origin could not be fully delineated due to acoustic limitations. The study demonstrated homogeneous opacification within the aneurysm lumen, with a small peripheral filling defect corresponding to non‑perfused thrombotic tissue (Fig. 1C).Fig. 1Imaging findings in a 66-year-old female with giant coronary artery aneurysm. TEE and TTE revealed a coronary artery aneurysm (CAA) located adjacent to the left atrium (A). A white arrow indicates the dilated left circumflex coronary artery (LCX) (B). Left-heart contrast echocardiography showed contrast filling within the CAA (C).Abbreviations: AO, aorta; LA, left atrium; LV, left ventricle; RVOT, right ventricular outflow tract; M, aneurysm; TEE, transesophageal echocardiography; TTE, transthoracic echocardiography.Fig 1 – dummy alt text

CTA demonstrated a giant true aneurysm arising from one branch of the left circumflex artery. The maximum dimensions were 79 mm × 69 mm × 88 mm on three orthogonal planes. The aneurysm neck measured approximately 8 mm. The proximal segment connected to the branch of the left circumflex artery, while the distal coronary segment continued from the aneurysm sac. Partial mural thrombus was identified within the aneurysm lumen. No mural calcification was detected. The giant aneurysm exerted significant extrinsic compression on the left atrium, without direct anatomical contact with the pulmonary artery, pulmonary veins or mitral valve. The LMCA and proximal left circumflex artery were dilated. The distal left circumflex artery remained patent (Figs. 2A–E). Other modalities including conventional coronary angiography, cardiac magnetic resonance and positron emission tomography (PET) were also useful for coronary artery aneurysm evaluation, but were not performed in this case because adequate diagnostic data had been obtained from echocardiography and coronary CTA.Fig. 2CTA of the giant left circumflex coronary artery (LCX) aneurysm. Axial CTA demonstrates the narrow neck of the aneurysm (A). Multiplanar reformatted images (B, C, D) allow multidimensional size measurements of the giant aneurysm.Abbreviations: AO, aorta; M, aneurysm.Fig 2 – dummy alt text

The patient was transferred to an external cardiac surgery center for surgical repair. The individualized surgical strategy was formulated by the multidisciplinary cardiac team at that center—including cardiac surgeons, cardiologists, and cardiovascular imaging specialists—after comprehensive review of the transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography and coronary CTA findings. Given the giant aneurysm measuring approximately 80 mm arising from a branch of the left circumflex artery, intraluminal thrombus formation, and substantial compression of the left atrium due to mass effect, surgical repair was chosen over conservative medical management or percutaneous interventional therapy. The operation was performed using an on‑pump beating‑heart technique. Intraoperative findings showed significant dilatation of the LMCA and proximal left circumflex artery. A giant aneurysm (80 mm in diameter) was found to arise from a branch of the left circumflex artery, with intraluminal thrombus. Temporary test occlusion of the left circumflex branch produced no electrocardiographic changes. The inflow ostium of the aneurysm was closed with 3‑0 Prolene sutures, and the aneurysmal sac was partially resected. No coronary artery bypass grafting was required. No perioperative complications including aneurysm rupture, pericardial tamponade, myocardial ischemia, major bleeding or arrhythmia were observed in this patient.

The operation was performed using an on‑pump beating‑heart technique.
Intraoperative findings showed significant dilatation of the LMCA and proximal left circumflex artery.

case_text:
A male infant, the only child of healthy, nonconsanguineous parents, was delivered at term via elective cesarean section for breech presentation. The Apgar scores were 4 and 8 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively, with a delayed cry necessitating admission to the neonatal intensive care unit. He received supplemental oxygen but did not require mechanical ventilation, and no perinatal hypoxic-ischemic event was identified. Neurological examination during the neonatal stay was unremarkable, and he was discharged on day 7, alert, feeding well, and vitally stable. Early developmental milestones up to 2 months of age were reported by the parents as age-appropriate, although no formal developmental assessment had been performed before symptom onset.

At 2 months of age, the parents reported recurrent paroxysmal episodes characterized by lateral head deviation, generalized limb rigidity, and subtle myoclonic jerks that lasted 5 to 10 seconds, often accompanied by hiccup-like vocalizations. These spells occurred multiple times a day and were stereotypical. There was no preceding fever, infection, or trauma.

The full sequence of events, from birth through the 20-month assessment, is summarized in Table 1.

A neurological evaluation was undertaken shortly after seizure onset. Routine metabolic screening was reportedly unremarkable, although the specific tests performed were not documented in the available case record. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed no overt structural abnormalities. The first EEG was performed shortly after seizure onset at approximately 2 months of age. Interictal EEG demonstrated a characteristic SB pattern, featuring alternating high-amplitude sharp wave bursts and generalized attenuation, present in both wakefulness and sleep – highly suggestive of early infantile epileptic encephalopathy, consistent with OS. The patient’s original EEG tracing is not reproduced in this report; Figure 1A is an educational illustration of this type of pattern and is not the patient’s recording. EME was considered in the differential diagnosis; however, the predominance of tonic spasms and the persistence of the SB pattern during both wakefulness and sleep favored OS over EME. Routine metabolic screening was unremarkable; however, because the specific tests were not documented and more extensive metabolic testing was not performed, this finding was not regarded as excluding a metabolic cause. Genetic analysis could not be performed due to resource limitations.

The patient was initially treated with oral sodium valproate; the exact dose, dosing frequency, and duration of monotherapy were not documented in the available case record. Breakthrough tonic seizures, showing cephalocaudal propagation, continued while the child was receiving valproate. Adjunctive brivaracetam was subsequently initiated; the exact age at initiation and dose/dosing frequency were not documented in the available case record. No other antiseizure medications were trialed before brivaracetam, adrenocorticotropic hormone, and vigabatrin were considered but were not available at our center. Following the addition of brivaracetam, the patient achieved seizure freedom. The therapeutic response was monitored clinically and with serial EEGs. The exact dates or ages of the follow-up EEGs were not documented in the available case record. These follow-up studies showed persistent SB activity that was qualitatively reduced in amplitude and frequency compared with the initial tracing. Figure 1B is an educational illustration of this type of finding and is not the patient’s recording.

At 20 months, the child presented to our center with a 3-day history of productive cough and fever. He was diagnosed with community-acquired bronchopneumonia and hospitalized. The developmental assessment revealed global delays: he was unable to sit independently, exhibited hypotonia, had no expressive language, and showed only rudimentary motor skills, including a delayed pincer grasp (a fine motor milestone). He responded to auditory stimuli, and otoacoustic emissions confirmed normal peripheral hearing.

Anthropometric measurements were within normal limits (60th percentile for weight, length, and head circumference). The neurological examination demonstrated generalized hypotonia, with preserved deep tendon reflexes and sustained visual tracking. The patient remained seizure-free on the existing dual antiseizure medication regimen. The exact duration of seizure freedom at the 20-month assessment and the presence or absence of medication-related adverse effects were not documented in the available case record.

He was discharged after resolution of pneumonia and was enrolled in a structured follow-up program with monthly pediatric neurology evaluations. The available case record does not document whether he received physiotherapy, occupational therapy, or other early developmental interventions prior to or during follow-up. The family was counseled on the natural history of OS, the risk of respiratory complications, potential syndromic evolution (e.g., West syndrome), and the importance of promptly recognizing disease progression.

case_text:
A 43-year-old Saudi man, an ex-smoker, had a 5-year history of intermittent anxiety, palpitations, episodic anger, and recurrent elevated clinic blood pressure despite normal home readings. These episodes had initially been attributed to emotional stress. Over the preceding year, he developed chest tightness and was found to have blood pressure of 200/120 mmHg, prompting evaluation for aortic dissection.

A computed tomography (CT) aortogram excluded dissection but incidentally revealed a right adrenal mass. Dedicated adrenal CT showed a 5.2-cm heterogeneous right adrenal lesion suspicious for pheochromocytoma. He was referred to our tertiary center for further evaluation.

At presentation, he was normotensive and clinically stable. Plasma metanephrine and normetanephrine were markedly elevated, confirming catecholamine excess. Testing for hyperaldosteronism and Cushing syndrome was negative (Table 1). Repeat imaging approximately 7 months later showed further enlargement to 5.9 cm (Fig. 1), which, together with the biochemical findings, was consistent with pheochromocytoma. I-123 metaiodobenzylguanidine scanning showed no evidence of metastatic disease, and genetic testing for pheochromocytoma-paraganglioma-associated mutations, including RET, VHL, NF1, SDHA, SDHB, SDHC, SDHD, SDHAF2, TMEM127, and MAX, was negative. Preoperative preparation was initiated with doxazosin 1 mg daily, later titrated to 2 mg daily—the maximum tolerated dose given his baseline normotension—followed by β-blockade after 1 week. Blood pressure and heart rate remained well controlled during follow-up.

case_text:
A male neonate born at 32 weeks of gestation was the first twin delivered via cesarean section due to maternal severe preeclampsia and failed tocolysis. Antenatal corticosteroid therapy with dexamethasone was administered four times to promote fetal lung maturity. The amniotic fluid, placenta, and umbilical cord appeared normal. The birth weight was 1540 g, and Apgar scores were 10 at both 1 and 5 min. However, within 10 min of birth, the infant developed grunting and progressively worsening respiratory distress, necessitating continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP). The infant exhibited no seizures or abnormal cries and received surfactant, caffeine therapy, and neuroprotective treatment.

The patient′s medical, personal, and family histories were unremarkable..

The infant displayed good responsiveness, respiratory rate of 62 breaths per minute, nasal flaring, and mild cyanosis. Facial features were normal. Anterior fontanelle was flat, muscle tone was adequate, and pupils were equal, round, and reactive to light (3 mm bilaterally). Auscultation revealed coarse lung sounds with mild rales. The heart sounds were strong and regular, with no murmurs. The abdomen was soft, with no hepatosplenomegaly. Peripheral cyanosis was observed, and neonatal reflexes were incomplete.

Routine blood gas analysis, biochemistry, procalcitonin, TORCH screening, urinalysis, and bacterial cultures were unremarkable. Chest and abdominal X‐rays showed no abnormalities. Ultrasonography of the liver, gallbladder, spleen, and adrenal glands was normal. Brain MRI suggested preterm brain changes. Thyroid function tests on Day 7 showed marginally low free triiodothyronine (2.29 pg/mL), which normalized after one week.

On postnatal Day 33, after weaning from oxygen therapy at corrected gestational age (CGA) of 36+5 weeks, ROP screening revealed a white circular lesion below the optic disc and macula in the left eye, surrounded by vascular patterns (Figure 1a). Further evaluation at a higher level hospital was recommended.

The neonate required CPAP for 26 days due to respiratory distress.

Cefotaxime, ampicillin, and meropenem were administered for 21 days.

Formula feeding was initiated due to unavailability of breast milk, supplemented by 30 days of parenteral nutrition.

On Day 33 (CGA 36+5 weeks), ROP screening revealed abnormalities in the left eye. Despite being advised to seek specialized care, the parents returned to the hospital one week later for reevaluation. The lesion had become more prominent (Figure 1a), prompting further referrals.

At CGA 37+4 weeks (postnatal Day 46), ultrasonography and optical coherence tomography (OCT) at a tertiary hospital in Shenyang indicated a solid mass in the left temporal retina and incomplete regression of the vitreous artery in both eyes (Figure 1b).

By CGA 56 weeks, ultrasonography at Shanghai Jiao Tong University Hospital confirmed a retinal mass in the left eye, measuring 12.84 × 12.52 × 6.36 mm, suggestive of retinoblastoma (RB). MRI findings corroborated the diagnosis (Figure 1c). The results of genetic testing are as follows: No single nucleotide variants, small insertion or deletion variants, or copy number variations significantly related to the patient’s clinical phenotype were detected. MLPA analysis did not reveal any large fragment deletions or duplications in the exon regions of the patient’s RB1 gene. The child subsequently underwent arterial interventional therapy, utilizing a combination of melphalan, topotecan, and carboplatin. Under general anesthesia, a fundus reexamination was performed, and based on the fundus photographs, laser therapy, intravitreal injections, and cryotherapy were administered.

case_text:
A woman in her mid-50s was referred in March 2025 with a solid left lateral abdominal-wall mass and intermittent left abdominal and back discomfort. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in January 2025 demonstrated a lobulated 7 × 7 × 3 cm heterogeneously enhancing mass centred within the left transversus abdominis muscle. Desmoid tumour and soft-tissue sarcoma were considered. Fluorodeoxyglucose positron-emission tomography/computed tomography (FDG PET/CT) showed heterogeneous moderate uptake with central photopenia, but no nodal or distant FDG-avid disease. Small non-avid pulmonary nodules were noted, whilst diagnostic chest CT showed no concerning thoracic findings (Fig. 1).

Ultrasound-guided core biopsy demonstrated fascicles of bland spindle cells without atypia, mitoses, or necrosis. The cells showed nuclear beta-catenin expression and were negative for epithelial, neural, vascular, and myogenic markers; Ki-67 was below 2%. The findings were reported as desmoid-type fibromatosis. As symptoms had improved and were not functionally limiting, active surveillance was selected after discussion of observation, medical therapy, and surgery.

A planned surveillance MRI was abandoned because of severe claustrophobia, and the patient initially declined both MRI and CT. Abdominal ultrasonography in January 2026 demonstrated interval enlargement to 13.4 × 12.4 × 6.0 cm with protrusion into the abdomen. The patient could palpate progressive enlargement and reported increasing abdominal pain. She subsequently agreed to cross-sectional imaging.

Repeat FDG PET/CT in March 2026 showed marked enlargement of the abdominal-wall mass and a new left intra-abdominal component with a similar metabolic signature. There was no FDG-avid metastatic disease, although bilateral sub-centimetre lung nodules remained below PET resolution (Fig. 2). Given rapid progression and intra-abdominal extension, operative management was recommended.

In April 2026, the patient underwent laparotomy, en bloc excision of the abdominal-wall tumour, resection of involved small bowel with primary anastomosis. The remaining abdominal-wall musculofascial layers were re-approximated primarily without formal reconstruction. The resection specimen weighed 2110 g and contained a 200-mm lobulated haemorrhagic and myxoid spindle-cell tumour. Histology demonstrated sweeping hypercellular fascicles, focal herringbone architecture, 10 mitoses per 10 high-power fields, calcification and ~10% necrosis. Tumour cells expressed TLE1, EMA, BCL2, CD56, and nuclear beta-catenin. Fluorescence in situ hybridisation demonstrated SS18 rearrangement, confirming FNCLCC grade 3 monophasic synovial sarcoma (Fig. 3). The tumour involved the small bowel muscularis propria. The posterior margin was microscopically involved; all other margins were less than 1 mm clear.

Next-generation sequencing of the resection specimen identified no clinically significant CTNNB1 or APC variant in the exons sequenced. The original core biopsy was re-reviewed and remained morphologically and immunophenotypically consistent with desmoid-type fibromatosis. Specialist pathological review favoured sampling of a relatively bland component within a morphologically heterogeneous synovial sarcoma. Postoperative CT showed no nodal or distant metastatic disease and demonstrated a wide-necked abdominal-wall hernia. The patient was referred to medical and radiation oncology. At the latest documented review, she was clinically well without obstructive symptoms; restaging and consideration of systemic therapy were planned.

case_text: An 80‐year‐old man, with no known prior comorbidities, current daily cigarette smoker with 70 pack‐years, presented to the emergency department with acute‐onset right‐sided chest pain and shortness of breath of 2 days duration. At presentation, he was tachypneic, with a respiratory rate of 36/min, a resting oxygen saturation of 82% at room air, a heart rate of 110 beats/min, and a blood pressure of 150/90 mm Hg. On examination of right hemithorax, percussion was hyperresonant and breath sounds were absent. On left hemithorax, expiratory wheeze was heard. His chest radiograph revealed a large right‐sided pneumothorax (Figure 1a), and arterial blood gas analysis showed moderate hypoxemia with Type I respiratory failure. Subsequently, a 24F intercostal chest drain was inserted in the right hemithorax and connected to water seal drainage, which showed bubbling of air during expiration only (Cerfolio Grade 2) (Table 1). His HRCT thorax showed residual small pneumothorax (Figure 2a), subcutaneous emphysema, along with significant bilateral emphysematous lungs, and multiple bullae (Figure 2b). After 10 days of chest drainage, air leak persisted. Thoracic surgeon opinion was taken for consideration of surgical intervention (VATS). He had risk factors such as advanced age, baseline functional status (ECOG PS‐3), underweight (BMI: 17.26 kg/m2), poor nutritional status (serum albumin: 2.3 g/dL, Hb: 10.8 g/dL), significant bilateral emphysema with multiple bullae and severe pulmonary hypertension (ePASP: 65 mm Hg). Considering these risk factors, he was deemed unfit for thoracic surgery. In a resource‐limited setting, pleurodesis was the only viable medical management option therefore, we proceeded with ABPP.

He had risk factors such as advanced age, baseline functional status (ECOG PS‐3), underweight (BMI: 17.26 kg/m2), poor nutritional status (serum albumin: 2.3 g/dL, Hb: 10.8 g/dL), significant bilateral emphysema with multiple bullae and severe pulmonary hypertension (ePASP: 65 mm Hg).
Considering these risk factors, he was deemed unfit for thoracic surgery.
In a resource‐limited setting, pleurodesis was the only viable medical management option therefore, we proceeded with ABPP.
title: Management of a Spontaneous Secondary Pneumothorax Complicated by Persistent Air Leak With Autologous Blood Patch Pleurodesis: A Case Report

case_text: This case report was prepared in accordance with the CARE reporting guidelines. A 58‐year‐old woman was admitted after 4 h of exertion‐triggered sudden chest tightness with transient visual blackout. She denied chest pain, back pain, recent upper respiratory or gastrointestinal infection, and had no history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, smoking or family history of sudden cardiac death. On admission, vital signs were: temperature 36.5°C, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, pulse 36 beats/min, blood pressure 158/76 mmHg. Physical examination revealed clear bilateral lung fields, no obvious cardiac murmur, and markedly slow regular heart rhythm. Electrocardiography showed sinus rhythm with complete AVB and ventricular escape rhythm (Figure 1). Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated only mild tricuspid regurgitation without significant structural heart disease. Chest CT showed mild patchy pulmonary changes plus small pericardial and pleural effusion. Laboratory tests revealed elevated cardiac troponin‐I (4.49 ng/mL), alanine aminotransferase (174.5 U/L) and aspartate aminotransferase (222.9 U/L). Given complete AVB accompanied by myocardial injury raising suspicion for acute coronary syndrome (especially inferior myocardial infarction compromising atrioventricular nodal perfusion), emergency coronary angiography was performed. No significant stenosis was seen in the left main, left circumflex or right coronary artery; only mild 30%–40% stenosis was noted in the mid‐left anterior descending artery without a culprit lesion (Figure 2A,B). Ischaemic coronary disease was therefore unlikely to explain the severe conduction abnormality. Further autoimmune work‐up showed a speckled‐pattern ANA (titer 1:1000), strongly positive anti‐SSA (> 400), anti‐SSB (35.21) and anti‐Ro52 (> 400), together with multiple cardiac autoantibodies: anti‐ADP/ATP carrier (129.23 ng/mL), anti‐β1‐adrenergic receptor (137.9 ng/mL), anti‐calcium channel (5.38 ng/mL) and anti‐myosin heavy‐chain antibody (177.16 ng/mL). Tests for lupus anticoagulant, Coombs test, anti‐β2‐glycoprotein antibody, complement C3/C4 and erythrocyte sedimentation rate were negative. Targeted history‐taking uncovered long‐standing xerostomia and xerophthalmia. Schirmer's test showed decreased tear secretion (2 mm bilaterally). Minor salivary‐gland biopsy revealed acinar and periductal lymphocytic‐plasma cell infiltration, with a focus score satisfying diagnostic criteria for pSS. Integrating clinical, serological and pathological findings, we diagnosed primary Sjögren's syndrome with immune‐mediated cardiac involvement manifesting as complete AVB and myocardial injury. The clinical timeline is summarized in Table 1. After rheumatology consultation, immunomodulatory therapy was initiated with methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg/day plus hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily. Given symptomatic cerebral hypoperfusion from complete AVB and unpredictable conduction recovery, a dual‐chamber permanent pacemaker was implanted. The patient's chest tightness and transient loss of consciousness resolved, and troponin‐I gradually normalized. At 3‐week outpatient follow‐up, ECG showed VAT‐mode ventricular pacing, with no recurrent syncope or chest discomfort.
