case_text:
A 22‐year‐old male with poorly controlled T1DM (A1c 12.7%) presented with a 6‐month history of diffuse hyperpigmented, pruritic skin lesions involving the face, trunk, extremities, palms, fingers, and genitalia, accompanied by erosive oral and ocular mucositis and nail dystrophy (Figure 1). Skin biopsy with direct immunofluorescence was consistent with paraneoplastic pemphigus. CT imaging revealed a pelvic mass, which was surgically resected with regional lymph nodes; pathology confirmed Castleman disease.

During hospitalization, he was treated with high‐dose systemic corticosteroids (IV methylprednisolone 40–50 mg daily, later converted to prednisone, with a 20 mg taper at discharge), tocilizumab, rituximab, and IVIG. Glycemic management was complicated by glucocorticoid‐induced hyperglycemia and difficulty obtaining fingerstick POC BG measurements due to severe digital involvement. Glucose levels were highly labile, ranging from the 70s to the 400s mg/dL despite multiple insulin adjustments (Figure 2).

A Dexcom G7 CGM was initiated to minimize skin trauma and facilitate CGM (Figure 3). A single earlobe POC BG measurement was obtained at the time of CGM initiation as a reference blood glucose value. CGM data were manually integrated into the electronic medical record (EMR) Epic by the nursing staff. Available CGM readings were generally similar to the corresponding POC BG and laboratory plasma glucose measurements (Figure 2).

Glycemic control remained challenging due to fluctuating corticosteroid dosing, intermittent patient refusal of steroids, and variable dietary patterns. CGM data facilitated daily insulin titration, including adjustments to basal insulin, insulin‐to‐carbohydrate ratios, and insulin sensitivity factors, particularly in response to nocturnal glycemic variability. His basal insulin requirements fluctuated substantially, ranging from 20 to 15 units and occasionally requiring a reduction to as low as 3 units. During the first 14 days of CGM use, average glucose was 187 mg/dL, glucose management indicator (GMI) was 7.8%, time in range (TIR) (70–180 mg/dL) was 53%, with 22% of readings in the high range (181–250 mg/dL), 22% in the very high range (>250 mg/dL), 2% in the low range (54–69 mg/dL), and 1% in the very low range (<54 mg/dL) (Figure 2). After 1 month of CGM use, GMI was 8.9%, with 30% TIR and 2% time below the range (TBR) (<70 mg/dL). CGM was continued for nearly 3 months during the hospitalization, supporting CGM when POC testing remained challenging. No diabetic ketoacidosis was seen. The patient was discharged; however, 6 days later, he was readmitted with complicated respiratory failure, likely secondary to bronchiolitis obliterans. He was intubated in the ICU and subsequently passed away.

case_text: A 40‐year‐old female patient presented to Universidad del Valle de México, Hermosillo, Mexico, seeking improvement in the esthetic appearance of her smile (Figure 1). The patient was systemically healthy, denied smoking and alcohol consumption, and was classified as ASA I. She reported a history of composite restorations on the incisal edges of the anterior teeth, which exhibited signs of wear at the time of examination. Clinical evaluation revealed incisal wear extending from the maxillary right canine to the maxillary left canine, spacing between the maxillary left central and lateral incisors, and open gingival embrasures (“black triangles”) in the anterior region. Clinical examination and radiographic assessment also revealed reduced posterior support associated with missing posterior teeth. No alteration in the vertical dimension of occlusion was observed.

case_text:
A 48‐year‐old man with hypertension, atrial fibrillation, asthma, smoking history, and documented myxomatous mitral valve degeneration presented with progressive dyspnea, intermittent cough, and occasional low‐grade fever. A right upper lobe opacity had been observed before surgery and treated with multiple antibiotic courses for presumed pneumonia. No available interval images document clearance and subsequent recurrence of the opacity.

Examination demonstrated an apical holosystolic murmur and bilateral crackles. White blood cell count was 8500/μL (reference range 4000–11,000/μL), procalcitonin was 0.025 ng/mL (reference < 0.1 ng/mL), and BNP was elevated at 250 pg/mL (reference < 100 pg/mL). Blood cultures were negative.

Chest radiography demonstrated focal right upper lobe airspace opacity/consolidation (Figure 1). Contrast‐enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated unilateral right upper lobe smooth interlobular septal thickening with associated ground‐glass opacities and patchy consolidation predominantly distributed along the minor fissure without pleural effusion or substantial cardiomegaly (Figures 2 and 3).

Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) demonstrated severe MR associated with myxomatous mitral valve degeneration and a left atrial diameter of 58 mm. The original TTE report described an eccentric, posteriorly directed MR jet and stated that the regurgitant jet was directed toward the right pulmonary veins. This documented orientation provided patient‐specific support for the possibility of preferential right pulmonary venous hypertension underlying the right upper lobe opacity. The original echocardiographic images were not available for independent review; regional pulmonary venous flow abnormalities were not established by the available documentation.

The patient underwent mechanical mitral valve replacement with a concomitant MAZE procedure. Sinus rhythm was restored postoperatively. A chest radiograph 3 months after surgery demonstrated resolution of the right upper lobe opacity (Figure 4), and the patient reported symptomatic improvement. Both correction of MR and restoration of sinus rhythm may have contributed to the clinical improvement (Table 1).

case_text:
A 46‐year‐old para 7 woman presented with a one‐week history of right breast swelling, initially appearing as a small ulcerated mass in the upper outer quadrant.

Two days after ulceration, the lesion extended to the right axilla on Day 3 and the right chest on Day 4. Over the following 3 days, pain became severe, with purulent wound discharge. Her initially low‐grade fever progressed to high‐grade fever, accompanied by anorexia and myalgia.

At presentation, she was breastfeeding her 1‐year‐2‐month‐old son and using injectable contraception. All seven children were alive and she reported no previous similar illness.

She appeared acutely ill and in significant pain. Vital signs were: blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, pulse 120 beats/min, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min, temperature 38.7°C, and oxygen saturation 96%. Examination revealed a swollen, darkened, ulcerated right breast with purulent discharge (Figure 1). Other systemic examinations were unremarkable.

With an initial diagnosis of necrotizing breast infection, intravenous access was established, and resuscitation commenced with one unit of normal saline. Intramuscular diclofenac (75 mg) was administered for analgesia. Empirical antibiotics included intravenous ceftriaxone (1 g twice daily) and metronidazole (500 mg three times daily). She was kept NPO and started on maintenance fluids. Diagnostic evaluation included targeted serological tests, available imaging, and microbiological cultures, guided by her clinical presentation.

Initial investigations showed elevated BUN (29 mg/dL), likely due to dehydration, hypoalbuminemia (2.4 g/dL), possibly related to inflammation, and mildly reduced serum calcium (2.14 mmol/L). Postoperatively, BUN and calcium normalized to 17 mg/dL and 2.43 mmol/L, respectively. Albumin remained low at 2.7 g/dL but subsequently normalized to 3.8 g/dL at outpatient follow‐up, supporting an inflammatory cause of the initial hypoalbuminemia.

Laboratory findings and corresponding reference ranges are presented in Table 1.

Bedside breast ultrasonography showed diffuse hypoechoic breast tissue, skin and fascial thickening, and multiple septated collections containing internal debris, suggestive of right breast mastitis with multiple abscesses. Although MRI and CT were indicated, they were unavailable because of resource and equipment limitations.

Wound culture identified Streptococcus pyogenes , which was susceptible to ceftriaxone; therefore, the same antibiotic regimen was continued.

Following discussion of the findings, treatment plan, and potential need for mastectomy depending on intraoperative findings with the patient and her family, written informed consent was obtained. She was subsequently transferred to the operating room for excision and debridement.

Intraoperatively, the entire right breast was necrotic, with active purulent discharge (Figure 2), while the pectoralis fascia and underlying muscle remained normal. A simple mastectomy was therefore performed (Figure 3), and tissue samples were submitted for histopathological examination. Histopathology confirmed the initial diagnosis, with microscopic findings supporting the clinical and preliminary diagnosis (Figure 4).

case_text:
A 29‐year‐old woman with no significant past medical history had fever in October 2019, without chest pain, chest tightness, or dyspnea. Echocardiography at another hospital showed a pericardial effusion. The fever resolved after approximately 5 days of treatment, and repeat echocardiography in November showed a marked reduction in the effusion. On December 3, a workplace health examination identified a pericardial mass on echocardiography, prompting referral to our hospital. She was admitted on December 13 with a temperature of 36.5°C and no signs of heart failure.

Transthoracic echocardiography showed a giant mass within the pericardial space, predominantly located over the left atrium (Figure 1). Contrast‐enhanced computed tomography revealed a mixed‐density mass measuring 101 × 76 × 96 mm, extending from the left margin of the main pulmonary artery to the left atrioventricular groove, with compression of the left atrium and left lower pulmonary vein (Figure 2). Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a heterogeneous intrapericardial mass surrounding the ascending aorta and main pulmonary artery, with partial invasion of the left atrial cavity (Figure 3).

An ultrasound‐guided pericardial biopsy was performed. Histopathological examination showed a densely cellular spindle‐cell neoplasm with a monophasic pattern. The tumor cells were arranged in fascicles and short bundles on hematoxylin and eosin staining (Figure 4A).

Immunohistochemically, the tumor cells showed focal weak positivity for pancytokeratin and epithelial membrane antigen, positivity for vimentin and D2‐40, weak positivity for CD99, and focal positivity for h‐caldesmon. The tumor cells were negative for smooth muscle actin, desmin, CD34, CD56, MyoD1, CK5/6, calretinin, WT‐1, PLAP, CD3, CD20, CD45, and myeloperoxidase. The Ki‐67 labeling index was approximately 15%.

Fluorescence in situ hybridization using an SS18 break‐apart probe demonstrated split red and green signals in tumor‐cell nuclei, consistent with SS18 gene rearrangement (Figure 4B). Taken together, the monophasic spindle‐cell morphology, immunohistochemical profile, and SS18 rearrangement supported the diagnosis of monophasic synovial sarcoma.

Surgical resection and adjuvant therapy were recommended; however, the patient declined further treatment. She died 22 months after the initial diagnosis.

case_text:
A 54‐year‐old man with a long‐standing history of gastroesophageal reflux disease, treated with proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) and metoclopramide, presented to the emergency department with chest pain and recurrent vomiting.

On admission, the patient was hemodynamically stable, and physical examination revealed no signs of peritoneal irritation. An electrocardiogram, obtained because of chest pain, showed no abnormalities. Contrast‐enhanced computed tomography (CT) demonstrated a giant type III hiatal hernia with approximately two‐thirds of the stomach, including the gastroesophageal junction and fundus, herniated into the thoracic cavity and causing gastric obstruction (Figure 1).

Laboratory investigations are summarized in Table 1. Based on the clinical presentation and CT findings, a complicated giant type III hiatal hernia with gastric obstruction and suspected volvulus or strangulation was diagnosed. Given the risk of gastric ischemia, the patient was taken urgently to the operating room.

Initial exploration revealed a severely twisted stomach with extensive necrotic areas involving the fundus and greater curvature. Because of the intrathoracic position of the stomach and suboptimal exposure of the hiatal region, safe laparoscopic dissection could not be achieved. Therefore, strategic conversion to an open approach through a left subcostal laparotomy was decided (Figure 2).

The pars flaccida was opened, allowing mobilization of the right diaphragmatic crus and access to the posterior epiploic cavity. The short gastric vessels were sealed and divided with a vessel‐sealing device, followed by mobilization of the left diaphragmatic crus. Circumferential dissection of the distal esophagus was completed, enabling reduction and excision of the hernia sac and complete repositioning of the stomach into the abdominal cavity. Gastric viability was assessed macroscopically, as indocyanine green(ICG) fluorescence imaging was not available.

A longitudinal atypical gastrectomy was performed using four 80‐mm GIA stapler reloads, resecting ~60% of the stomach, including the nonviable fundus and greater curvature segment, while preserving a healthy, well‐perfused gastric remnant (Figure 3).

The hiatal defect was then repaired by anterior cruroplasty. Given the large and distorted hiatus, posterior approximation was considered likely to create excessive suture tension and anterior displacement of the distal esophagus; anterior closure was therefore selected to preserve an adequate esophageal axis and avoid luminal angulation (Figure 4). Neither fundoplication nor gastropexy was technically feasible because the fundus and a substantial portion of the greater curvature had been resected (Figure 5).

Staple line integrity was confirmed by an intraoperative methylene blue test administered through the nasogastric tube, with no evidence of leakage. A closed‐suction drain was positioned along the gastric remnant. Operative time was 2 h 40 min, and estimated blood loss was 80 mL.

The patient spent 2 days in the intensive care unit, followed by 3 days in the surgical ward. He remained nil per os for three postoperative days, with a nasogastric tube maintained for decompression. The tube was then removed, and a clear liquid diet was gradually introduced.

The postoperative course was uneventful, with no clinical or biochemical evidence of staple‐line leakage, gastric fistula, or intra‐abdominal sepsis. In our institution, we do not routinely perform postoperative contrast imaging in clinically uncomplicated patients; therefore, oral intake was resumed based on clinical assessment. The abdominal drain was removed on postoperative Day 4, and the patient was discharged on postoperative Day 5.

At a 3‐year follow‐up, the patient remained clinically well, with no symptoms suggestive of recurrent hiatal hernia. Mild residual gastroesophageal reflux was adequately controlled with PPI therapy. Metoclopramide was administered for 4 months postoperatively. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy performed at 6 months showed no evidence of recurrent hiatal hernia and demonstrated only mild gastritis. No additional radiological or endoscopic assessment was performed thereafter; therefore, the long‐term absence of recurrence was assessed clinically rather than anatomically.

Gastric viability was assessed macroscopically, as indocyanine green(ICG) fluorescence imaging was not available.

A longitudinal atypical gastrectomy was performed using four 80‐mm GIA stapler reloads, resecting ~60% of the stomach, including the nonviable fundus and greater curvature segment, while preserving a healthy, well‐perfused gastric remnant (Figure 3).
The hiatal defect was then repaired by anterior cruroplasty.

Given the large and distorted hiatus, posterior approximation was considered likely to create excessive suture tension and anterior displacement of the distal esophagus; anterior closure was therefore selected to preserve an adequate esophageal axis and avoid luminal angulation (Figure 4).
Neither fundoplication nor gastropexy was technically feasible because the fundus and a substantial portion of the greater curvature had been resected (Figure 5).
Staple line integrity was confirmed by an intraoperative methylene blue test administered through the nasogastric tube, with no evidence of leakage.
A closed‐suction drain was positioned along the gastric remnant.
Operative time was 2 h 40 min, and estimated blood loss was 80 mL.
The patient spent 2 days in the intensive care unit, followed by 3 days in the surgical ward.
He remained nil per os for three postoperative days, with a nasogastric tube maintained for decompression.
The tube was then removed, and a clear liquid diet was gradually introduced.
The postoperative course was uneventful, with no clinical or biochemical evidence of staple‐line leakage, gastric fistula, or intra‐abdominal sepsis.
In our institution, we do not routinely perform postoperative contrast imaging in clinically uncomplicated patients; therefore, oral intake was resumed based on clinical assessment.
The abdominal drain was removed on postoperative Day 4, and the patient was discharged on postoperative Day 5.
At a 3‐year follow‐up, the patient remained clinically well, with no symptoms suggestive of recurrent hiatal hernia.
Mild residual gastroesophageal reflux was adequately controlled with PPI therapy.
Metoclopramide was administered for 4 months postoperatively.
Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy performed at 6 months showed no evidence of recurrent hiatal hernia and demonstrated only mild gastritis.
No additional radiological or endoscopic assessment was performed thereafter; therefore, the long‐term absence of recurrence was assessed clinically rather than anatomically.
title: Challenges in the Management of Giant Strangulated Hiatal Hernia: A Case Report

case_text: A Rhesus Macaque NHP weighing ~5-kg underwent heterotopic renal allo-transplantation under an IACUC-approved protocol. The graft was re-vascularized to the recipient infra-renal aorta and inferior vena cava, and urinary continuity was restored by a spatulated uretero-ureterostomy between the graft and native ureter over a 3.7-Fr stent. Immediate graft function was observed. On postoperative Day 6 the animal developed reduced urine output, rising BUN and creatinine and abdominal distension. Urgent surgical abdominal exploration was performed, and a urine leak was confirmed by an ascitic creatinine markedly exceeding the serum value. The urinoma was evacuated. The distal graft ureter at the anastomosis was necrotic and dehisced, whereas the proximal ureter and renal pelvis were viable. The ureter was debrided to briskly bleeding tissue, leaving a shortened graft ureter with a deficit that precluded tension-free primary repair. The bladder was mobilized and distended with saline. Rather than a full-thickness Boari flap, a broad-based flap of bladder mucosa (urothelium with a thin layer of lamina propria), with its base-oriented postero-laterally to preserve perfusion and a length-to-width ratio kept at or below:1. The flap was tubularized, urothelium inward, over a 4.7-Fr ×12 cm stent with running 6–0 Maxon suture, creating a urothelial-lined neo-ureter in continuity with the bladder. The shortened graft ureter and the neo-ureter were each spatulated and joined by a tension-free, uretero-ureterostomy over the indwelling stent (Fig. 1). No detrusor approximation, nor psoas hitch were performed. Watertight suture line was confirmed via foley distention of the bladder and neo-ureter with sterile normal saline. Recovery was uneventful. Serum creatinine normalized to 1 mg/dL. At the planned terminal timepoint, ~1-month later, the neo-ureter was grossly intact, patent, with a healed anastomosis and no urine leak or obstruction.

case_text:
A 76-year-old woman with hypertension and no other conventional coronary risk factors was referred for evaluation of a cardiac murmur. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated severe mitral regurgitation caused by prolapse of the P3 segment. Preoperative coronary angiography showed no significant coronary artery stenosis (Figure 1A), and minimally invasive mitral valve repair was planned after informed consent.

Under general anaesthesia and single-lung ventilation, the patient was positioned in an approximately 45° left lateral decubitus position. A 6-cm right fourth-intercostal mini-thoracotomy was performed. Cardiopulmonary bypass was established with right femoral venous drainage and right femoral arterial perfusion, with an additional superior vena caval cannula after pericardiotomy. The patient was cooled to 30°C. After external aortic cross-clamping, antegrade cardioplegia was delivered through the ascending aorta and cardiac arrest was achieved.

The left atrium was opened through the interatrial groove, confirming P3 prolapse. Because exposure of the posterior papillary muscle was limited, the Wakka technique was used with a plastic measuring strip.4 The posterior papillary muscle was grasped with a ValveGate PRO forceps (Geister, Tuttlingen, Germany), and a pledgeted CV-4 expanded polytetrafluoroethylene neochord was placed. The neochord was secured to the prolapsing P3 segment with a figure-of-eight suture, adjusted using a saline test, and tied. A 29-mm St. Jude Medical Flexible Band (Abbott, Chicago, IL, USA) was implanted.

After left atrial closure and aortic unclamping, spontaneous cardiac activity resumed; however, lead II showed ST-segment elevation. Coronary air embolism was initially suspected. Repeated intracardiac de-airing produced transient improvement, followed by recurrent ST-segment elevation. Transoesophageal echocardiography did not clearly demonstrate a new regional wall-motion abnormality. Cardiac index, mixed venous oxygen saturation, pulmonary artery pressure, and central venous pressure remained stable. The patient was therefore transferred to the intensive care unit under close electrocardiographic and haemodynamic monitoring.

Two hours after intensive care unit admission, marked inferior ST-segment elevation persisted in leads II, III, and aVF (Figure 2B). Serum creatine kinase was 2490 U/L, creatine kinase–myocardial band was 167 U/L, and troponin I was 18 585 pg/mL (institutional upper reference limit 26.2 pg/mL). Transthoracic echocardiography showed mild lateral wall hypokinesis. Emergency coronary angiography demonstrated complete occlusion of the posterolateral branch of the left circumflex coronary artery (segment 14PL; Figure 1B). The differential diagnosis at this point included air embolism, iatrogenic circumflex injury, coronary spasm, thromboembolism, and tissue embolism.

Aspiration thrombectomy was performed with a THROMBUSTER PRO aspiration catheter (Kaneka Medix Corporation). Intravascular ultrasound and optical coherence tomography were not performed. Coronary flow was immediately restored to TIMI grade 3 (Figure 1C), and the ST-segment elevation resolved (Figure 2C). No additional antithrombotic agent was administered during or immediately after aspiration thrombectomy. Histopathological examination of the aspirated material with haematoxylin and eosin staining showed that all identifiable tissue fragments consisted of striated cardiac muscle (Figure 3), supporting coronary embolization of papillary muscle tissue.

Postoperatively, warfarin was administered for three months according to the institutional anticoagulation protocol after mitral valve repair, and aspirin 100 mg daily was initiated and continued during follow-up. The patient was extubated on postoperative day 1 and discharged on postoperative day 10. Echocardiography at discharge showed no residual mitral regurgitation, a left ventricular ejection fraction of 63%, and no residual regional wall-motion abnormality. At two-year follow-up, she remained asymptomatic, with no recurrent mitral regurgitation or apparent left ventricular regional wall-motion abnormality.

case_text:
An 18‐year‐old white male presented to the local emergency department via EMS after his motorized scooter was hit by a car in early July 2025. Upon arrival, the patient was uncooperative, incoherent, and somewhat combative with a GCS of 9. He was intubated to prevent further injury, and history could not be obtained at the time. The initial CT scan was significant for acute subdural and subarachnoid hemorrhages and a left temporal bone fracture. The patient was then transferred for a higher level of care, including neurosurgical services.

As part of the trauma workup, an MRI of the head and cervical spine was obtained. The brain MRI revealed significant findings, including round and oval‐shaped foci throughout the left cerebrum in the frontal and frontal insular regions, which were intraaxial with susceptibility artifacts and exhibited faint areas of linear T1 intrinsic shortening (Figure 1). The largest lesion measured 3.2 cm. T2/FLAIR hyperintensity diffusely throughout the cortical, subcortical, periventricular, and posterior fossa regions supported concern for demyelination (Figure 2). Cervical spine MRI was significant for nonenhancing, multifocal, scattered, faint foci of T2 intramedullary signal hyperintensity of the cervical cord, including the C2 level, which measured 1.2 cm, and the C4‐C5 level, which measured 1.6 cm. All lesions were nonenhancing and considered incidental findings.

A neurology consult was obtained based on the concern for a demyelinating process, specifically MS. Upon obtaining history from family and the patient, it was determined that the patient experienced right upper extremity weakness in mid‐2021. Extensive workup, including EMG, was performed in November of that year and was negative, with a central cause ruled out and the weakness self‐resolving. The patient denied any other history of transient neurological symptoms, including vision changes, vertigo, weakness, or ataxia. Visual changes were difficult to assess given legal blindness in his right eye due to an accident in childhood. Family history was insignificant for neurologic pathologies, including MS. The neurologic physical exam was unremarkable. Further neurologic workup included MRI of the thoracic spine in addition to the previously obtained head and cervical spine images. Thoracic spine MRI was significant for a focus of nonenhancing T2/STIR hyperintensity at the T4 level, with additional small, scattered foci of nonenhancing high signal versus artifact. Along with the intracranial findings, these were thought to represent additional sequelae of demyelinating disease. Since no gadolinium‐enhancing lesions were found, the patient was cleared from a neurologic perspective to be followed as an outpatient after he recovered from his head trauma.

Upon initial evaluation by outpatient neurology, a lumbar puncture was performed in mid‐August 2025 to further investigate a diagnosis of MS. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was significant for OGBs, and MOG and AQP‐4/NPG antibodies were negative, further supporting the diagnosis of MS.

At a follow‐up visit in early September 2025, treatment options were discussed, and it was decided he would begin ocrelizumab as DMT. No new neurologic symptoms were identified on physical exam at either outpatient visit, and right upper extremity weakness 4 years prior was insignificant. It has been determined that this is a RIS. The patient was seen in clinic 6 months after the decision was made to begin ocrelizumab, and he has been doing well. He denies adverse effects from the two ocrelizumab infusions thus far and denies any new neurological symptoms. The patient and his family wish to continue DMT for RIS to prevent disease progression.

case_text:
A 74-year-old man with arterial hypertension and a body mass index of 26 kg/m2 presented to the emergency department with sudden abdominal pain and pronounced recurrent vomiting. He reported no smoking or alcohol consumption. Approximately one month earlier, he had fallen down stairs but had not sought medical attention. An asymptomatic interval separated the injury from the acute presentation. Consequently, no contemporaneous examination or imaging from the original trauma was available to establish when the diaphragmatic defect or visceral herniation developed.

On admission, the abdomen was distended and bowel sounds were absent. Breath sounds were diminished over the right hemithorax, particularly at the base. These findings indicated an acute obstructive abdominal presentation accompanied by a thoracic abnormality. Initial laboratory results showed a C-reactive protein (CRP) concentration of 28 mg/L, a leukocyte count of 9.8 × 109/L, and hemoglobin of 142 g/L.

Chest radiography demonstrated a colonic loop within the right hemithorax, without pneumothorax (Figure 1). Multiphase CT of the chest and abdomen subsequently demonstrated a right hemidiaphragmatic defect with herniation and incarceration of the transverse colon into the right thoracic cavity (Figure 2). There was no mediastinal compression or displacement. CT established the anatomical explanation for the obstructive presentation, and operative exploration was undertaken.

The patient received a single preoperative dose of cefazolin 2 g and metronidazole 500 mg for antibiotic prophylaxis. He was placed supine in the reverse Trendelenburg position, with the legs apart, to allow the bowel to fall towards the pelvis. The surgeon stood between the legs and the assistant on the patient’s left. Carbon dioxide pneumoperitoneum was maintained at 12 mmHg. Laparoscopy was performed using four ports: a 10 mm supraumbilical camera port, working ports in the left and right hypogastrium, and an additional assistant port. An approximately 4 cm defect was identified in the right hemidiaphragm, containing incarcerated transverse colon and greater omentum (Figure 3). Exposure did not require liver mobilization.

The herniated contents were gently reduced into the abdomen. A macroscopically identified hernial sac was present, without adhesions to the lung; it was completely withdrawn into the abdominal cavity and resected. After reduction, the transverse colon was edematous but judged viable on visual assessment of the bowel wall and visible pulsation of the mesenteric vessels. No indocyanine green fluorescence angiography or instrument-based perfusion measurement was used. The colon was preserved without resection. The gangrenous portion of the greater omentum was resected using an ultrasonic scalpel and removed en bloc together with the 12 mm port, with the specimen engaged in the port cannula. No extraction bag was used.

The diaphragmatic margins were robust and approximated readily without tension. The defect was closed with interrupted 2-0 non-absorbable monofilament polypropylene sutures (Prolene), without pledgets or mesh (Figure 4). Pledget reinforcement was not considered during the operation. Before the final closure was completed, the anesthesiologist re-expanded the right lung using positive-pressure ventilation while residual gas was simultaneously evacuated from the right hemithorax with suction through the remaining diaphragmatic opening. No chest drain was inserted. Reduction, omental resection, and diaphragmatic repair were completed laparoscopically without conversion.

The postoperative course was uneventful. The patient was mobilized on the day of surgery and tolerated a normal diet from postoperative day one. A chest radiograph obtained 24 h after surgery showed no pneumothorax, and the patient had no dyspnea. On the first postoperative day, CRP was 112 mg/L and the leukocyte count was 12 × 109/L. By postoperative day three, these values had decreased to 60 mg/L and 7.6 × 109/L, respectively; no further inflammatory marker measurements were obtained. The rise was clinically interpreted as reactive to the underlying disease and surgery. No pneumonia or other postoperative complication was identified. No postoperative antibiotic treatment was administered. The patient was discharged in good condition on postoperative day five.

At three-month follow-up, the patient was clinically well, without pain, dyspnea, or gastrointestinal symptoms. Follow-up included clinical assessment and chest radiography, which showed no radiographic signs of recurrence.

case_text:
A 17‐year‐old competitive football player was referred for breathlessness, fatigue, left‐sided chest discomfort and bilateral calf muscle cramps during high‐intensity training and competition. He is a never smoker with childhood asthma managed with inhaled bronchodilators (combined budesonide/formoterol), and a leukotriene antagonist, as well as SCT manifesting as microcytosis without anaemia. His medical history also included hay fever, eczema and possible Raynaud's phenomenon.

Initial workup included serial normal chest radiographs and a normal ventilation‐perfusion scan. Post‐bronchodilator spirometry and diffusion capacity were within normal limits, with FEV1 4.51 L (104% predicted), FVC 4.78 L (94% predicted) and DLCO 98%.

In view of the patient's persistent breathlessness during intensive training despite inhaler treatment, CPET was performed (Figure 1a) on a cycle ergometer using a continuous 15 W/min ramp to volitional termination. Data were analysed using SentrySuite software, with predicted values derived from the Wasserman et al. reference values. This demonstrated peak VO2 64.3 mL/min/kg (134% predicted), anaerobic threshold (AT) at 69% predicted VO2 max, VE/VCO2 slope at AT 23, oxygen pulse response 24.6 mL (154% predicted), dynamic hyperinflation (Figure 1b) and adequate breathing reserve at end exercise (29%). Peak workload was 282 W (115% predicted). Oxygen saturations, heart rate and blood pressure responses remained normal throughout exercise. Although a left ventricular hypertrophy pattern was noted on ECG, a transthoracic echocardiogram did not reveal ventricular hypertrophy. Exercise was terminated by leg fatigue rather than his presenting symptoms of chest discomfort or muscle cramps, though he did report a cough affecting his breathing near peak exercise. These findings suggested physiological evidence of asthma without significant respiratory limitation, and with no evidence of cardiac or metabolic exercise limitation (Table 1).

He reported greater symptomatic relief with ipratropium compared to combined budesonide/formoterol, and was advised to continue inhaled bronchodilator therapy alongside montelukast and loratadine. He was counselled on adequate hydration during intensive exercise to reduce the risk of SCT‐related complications, and advised to seek urgent review if experiencing persistent chest pain, palpitations, musculoskeletal pain or left upper quadrant abdominal pain suggestive of splenic infarction. Surveillance included 3‐monthly blood tests and a repeat echocardiogram at 1 year to monitor for ventricular hypertrophy.

He was counselled on adequate hydration during intensive exercise to reduce the risk of SCT‐related complications, and advised to seek urgent review if experiencing persistent chest pain, palpitations, musculoskeletal pain or left upper quadrant abdominal pain suggestive of splenic infarction.
Surveillance included 3‐monthly blood tests and a repeat echocardiogram at 1 year to monitor for ventricular hypertrophy.
title: The Challenges in Investigating and Managing Dyspnoea in a Young Athlete With Asthma and Sickle Cell Trait

case_text:
A 79-year-old male patient with a significant medical history of heavy smoking, arterial hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and rheumatoid arthritis underwent triple coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery, which included right great saphenous vein graft harvesting. Postoperatively, the patient developed a deep surgical site infection along the right thigh caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The wound was subsequently opened, evacuated, debrided, and left to heal by secondary intention.

Following debridement, severe lymphorrhea became apparent. Due to the profuse exudation of clear lymphatic fluid, clinical identification of the leakage source was impossible. Application of an elastic compressive bandage for two weeks failed to improve the lymphorrhea. Once the wound infection was clinically controlled, the wound was closed using three heavy sutures (Figure 1). However, the patient still required frequent dressing changes as they became profusely soaked, prompting further diagnostic evaluation via hybrid SPECT/CT to localize the exact source of the leak.

Initially, lymphoscintigraphy was performed following the intradermal injection of four 0.10 mL aliquots, each containing 7.2 MBq (28.8 MBq in total) of 99mTc-labelled human albumin nanocolloid (Lymphoscan), into the first and second interdigital spaces of both lower extremities. The radiopharmaceutical was prepared according to the manufacturer’s specifications. Following a 2 min massage of the injection sites, sequential planar and SPECT/CT imaging was performed for up to 2 h after injection, following dressing removal. Imaging was performed using a SPECT/CT system (Infinia GE) equipped with low-energy high-resolution (LEHR) collimators. The system was configured in H mode, with the patient lying supine on the examination table. Static images were acquired using a 128 × 128 matrix, an acquisition duration of 3 min per view, and a 10% energy window. SPECT acquisition (360°) was performed with 30 angular sampling steps and 15 s per projection. Reconstruction was performed using ordered-subset expectation maximization (OSEM), with two iterations and 10 subsets. CT was performed with helical acquisition at 140 kVp and 2.5 mA, with a slice thickness of 5 mm.

Lymphatic drainage of the left lower extremity was unremarkable. In contrast, the right lower extremity exhibited delayed lymphatic drainage compared to the contralateral side, along with the visualization of collateral lymphatic vessels below the knee. A small, localized area of dermal lymphatic backflow was noted at the mid-portion of the anterior aspect of the right tibia, likely secondary to regional surgical trauma or inflammation. Crucially, foci of increased radiotracer accumulation were detected in the medial region of the right femur distally, which progressively expanded and intensified over time, strongly suggesting an active lymphatic leak (Figure 2). On hybrid SPECT/CT imaging, the dominant focus was localized predominantly within the superficial medial soft tissues, approximately 3.5 cm proximal to the medial femoral condyle and slightly distal to the inferior margin of the surgical scar (Figure 3).

Guided by these imaging findings, a new heavy suture was placed slightly distal to the wound edge to ligate the presumed leaking site within the subcutaneous tissue (Figure 4). Following ligation, the lymphorrhea immediately subsided, and the patient was discharged the following day wearing elastic compression stockings.

Six months postoperatively, the patient underwent percutaneous transluminal tibial angioplasty with stent placement in the right lower extremity due to critical limb ischemia. Four months later, progressive forefoot and heel gangrene necessitated a below-knee amputation. Three years following the initial surgery, the patient succumbed to an acute myocardial infarction.

case_text:
A 25‐year‐old previously healthy male presented with a 2 month history of progressively worsening headaches. The pain was of sudden onset, diffuse in distribution and gradually intensified over time. In the days preceding the presentation, the headache became associated with episodes of nausea and non‐projectile vomiting. He denied any antecedent trauma, including sports impacts, minor slips, domestic falls, alcohol consumption, a history of chronic medical conditions, loss of consciousness or use of anticoagulant or antiplatelet medications. His past medical and surgical history was unremarkable.

Neurological examination revealed a fully conscious, cooperative and oriented individual with intact cranial nerves and normal motor and sensory findings. Deep tendon reflexes were symmetrical, and no focal neurological deficits were identified. Routine laboratory investigations, including the coagulation profile, were within the normal limits.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain (Figure 1) demonstrated a crescentic extra‐axial collection measuring ~2 cm thick over the left fronto‐parietal‐temporal convexity and right parietal convexity. The lesion appeared hyperintense on both T1‐weighted and T2/FLAIR sequences with different intensities indicating acute‐on‐chronic intra‐cystic haemorrhage, consistent with an acute intra‐cystic haemorrhage with SDH. Additionally, a well‐circumscribed, loculated lesion was identified in the anterior portion of the left temporal lobe, suggestive of an AC exerting a mass effect on the adjacent temporal lobe parenchyma. Notably, there was radiological evidence of communication between the cystic cavity and the adjacent SDH. The overall findings were indicative of a subdural haemorrhage involving the left frontoparietotemporal and right parietal regions with associated intra‐cystic acute‐on‐chronic haemorrhage in the setting of an underlying AC. The main differential diagnosis considered was an epidermoid cyst; however, this was excluded based on the absence of diffusion restriction on imaging. Consequently, a diagnosis of AC with associated haemorrhage and rupture was established. The AC was completely unknown prior to this presentation; the patient had no previous neuroimaging. Neuroepithelial cysts and porencephalic cysts were excluded due to their extra‐axial location without parenchymal cell communication. Cystic neoplasms were also excluded by the absence of solid mural nodules.

In view of several high‐risk anatomical factors such as the significant volume of the left frontoparietotemporal subdural collection of more than 2 cm thickness, localised mass effect on the left temporal lobe and 6 mm midline shift and radiological evidence of intra‐cystic communication. The patient underwent surgery due to the high risk of sudden clinical deterioration from re‐bleeding within an unstable cyst–haematoma complex. An elective left pterional craniotomy was performed with evacuation of the left frontoparietotemporal SDH and marsupialisation of the AC was done.

Intra‐operative findings revealed an ~8 cm × 6 cm AC occupying the left temporal region. The outer cyst membrane was found to have fistulous communication connecting it directly to the subdural space. Around 150 mL of thick, xanthochromic fluid, ‘machinery‐oil‐like appearance’, was evacuated from the subdural space, along with fresh/dark‐altered blood clots within the cystic cavity, confirming intra‐cystic haemorrhage. The right parietal thin SDH was managed conservatively. On the left side, an RV (Redivac) drain was placed intra‐operatively. The post‐operative recovery was uneventful. The patient was managed with standard post‐operative antibiotics and analgesics. The RV drain output remained minimal and was removed on the second post‐operative day. A follow‐up non‐contrast CT scan of the head on the second post‐operative day (Figure 2) demonstrated no haematoma without new complications. Histopathology of cyst with haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) stain (Figure 3) revealed the epithelial cuboidal cells, evidence of distant haemorrhage and haemosiderin pigment deposition. Hence, pure cystic changes related to chronic SDH were excluded by histopathology, where a true arachnoid epithelial cell lining was found. The patient remained neurologically intact and was discharged on the fifth post‐operative day in stable condition.

At follow‐up on post‐operative day 14, a repeat CT scan of the head (Figure 4) confirmed continued resolution of the haematoma and decompression of the cyst. At 1 year post‐surgery, the patient remained asymptomatic, with no recurrence of symptoms and a modified Rankin Scale (mRS) score of 0, indicating full functional recovery.

case_text:
A 10‐year‐old boy with no relevant medical history was referred to the Department of Pediatric Dentistry, CCTD, for the management of recurrent sinus tracts associated with the maxillary central incisors (Teeth 11 and 21). His dental history revealed a previous traumatic injury resulting from a fall. Written informed consent was obtained from the patient′s parents before treatment in accordance with current ethical guidelines.

Clinical examination revealed complicated crown fractures (Ellis Class III) involving both maxillary central incisors, defective temporary restorations, and active sinus tracts adjacent to the corresponding apices. Based on the clinical and radiographic findings, a diagnosis of pulp necrosis was established.

Periapical radiographs revealed open immature apices in both teeth, corresponding to Nolla Stage 8, together with periapical radiolucencies and enlarged root canals (Figure 1). The roots exhibited thin, parallel dentinal walls. Radiographically, the apical diameter was greater in Tooth 11 than in Tooth 21.

Under rubber dam isolation, the access cavities of teeth 11 and 21 were refined, followed by root canal debridement without aggressive mechanical instrumentation. The canals were irrigated with 2% sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl) using a closed‐end irrigation needle positioned 2 mm short of the apical foramen, followed by saline irrigation. Copious intracanal exudate was observed in both canals during this visit (Figure 2), indicating persistent periapical exudation. Calcium hydroxide [Ca(OH)2] was placed as an intracanal medicament, and the access cavities were sealed with glass ionomer cement.

At the subsequent appointment, in the absence of residual intracanal exudation, the root canals of teeth 11 and 21 were obturated with calcium hydroxide [Ca(OH)2]. The quality of the canal filling was confirmed radiographically (Figure 3).

At the 6‐month follow‐up, periapical radiographs showed a reduction in the periapical radiolucencies associated with both teeth. Initial formation of a thin calcified apical barrier was observed in Tooth 11, whereas no apical barrier was visible in Tooth 21 (Figure 4). Calcium hydroxide [Ca(OH)2] was renewed in both root canals.

At the 9‐month follow‐up, periapical radiographic assessment using a gutta‐percha master cone confirmed the presence of a newly formed calcified apical barrier in Tooth 11 (Figure 5). In contrast, Tooth 21 continued to exhibit an open apex despite 9 months of calcium hydroxide [Ca(OH)2] therapy, although it had presented with comparable initial conditions and a narrower apical diameter than Tooth 11. Consequently, a 4‐mm MTA apical barrier (ProRoot MTA; Dentsply Sirona, York, Pennsylvania, United States) was placed in tooth 21 during the same appointment (Figure 6).

Root canal obturation was performed in teeth 11 and 21 using gutta‐percha and the lateral condensation technique, followed by coronal restoration with direct composite resin (Figure 7). No pathological clinical signs were observed at the immediate postoperative follow‐up.

The chronological summary of the clinical and radiographic follow‐up for Case 1 is presented in Table 1.

case_text:
A 12‐year‐old boy was referred to our department for evaluation of depigmented lesions in the elbow and popliteal fossae that had worsened despite topical therapy for atopic dermatitis (AD). At the first visit, mild erythema, papules, and excoriations were observed on the trunk. The antecubital and popliteal fossae showed erosions and whitish macules (Figure 1A,B). His EASI score was 20.9, IGA 3, and pruritus NRS 2.

Laboratory findings revealed slight elevation of IgE. A skin biopsy was obtained from an excoriated, depigmented lesion on the left elbow flexure. Histology showed spongiosis with superficial lymphocytic infiltration, consistent with AD (Figure 2A). Melan‐A‐positive basal melanocytes were present, whereas Fontana‐Masson staining revealed no melanin pigment (Figure 2B,C). These findings suggested that melanocytes were present, but melanin synthesis was impaired, compatible with post‐inflammatory hypopigmentation (PIH). Functional impairment of melanocytes, possibly due to inflammation or mechanical stress, was suspected.

Because topical corticosteroids alone were insufficient to control the disease activity, upadacitinib 15 mg/day was initiated. After 5 weeks, the patient showed marked improvement: the EASI score decreased to 8.4, the IGA score to 1, and the pruritus NRS to 0. Importantly, the hypopigmented macules in the elbow and popliteal fossae showed marked repigmentation (Figure 1C).

case_text:
A 30‐year‐old Nepali man, recently returned from the United States after 18 months, presented with a 4‐month history of chronic diarrhea, diffuse abdominal pain, and unintentional weight loss of 10 kg over 4 months. His symptoms included watery, foul‐smelling stools with undigested food particles after meals, subjective febrile sensation (without documented fever), and fatigue. There was no history of oral ulcers, jaundice, nausea, vomiting, hematemesis, melena, hematochezia, or pain during defecation. He had no known comorbidities and no history of sick contacts. He was a smoker for the past 10 years and stopped 4 months ago, and consumed alcohol, which he stopped 6 months back. He had tattoos and piercings; however, he did not give any history of high‐risk sexual behavior. He did not give any history of illicit drug use and has not received any blood transfusions in the past.

On examination, he appeared cachectic and pale, with no cyanosis, clubbing, lymphadenopathy, or edema. His blood pressure was 90/60 mmHg, temperature was 100°F, and heart rate was 125 beats per minute (sinus tachycardia). Chest examination revealed decreased air entry over the left lung, bronchial breath sounds, and bilateral crepitations. His abdomen was soft and non‐tender without hepatosplenomegaly; neurological and cardiovascular examinations were unremarkable.

case_text:
A 4‐year‐old girl, weighing 16 kg, born to consanguineous parents, was referred to the pediatric gastroenterology department for evaluation of persistently elevated liver enzyme levels. These abnormalities were initially detected during routine annual health evaluations at the age of 1 year and remained consistently elevated on subsequent follow‐up assessments.

The patient was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery, with no significant past medical history. She remained clinically asymptomatic despite the persistent biochemical abnormalities. There was no history of previous illnesses, surgical procedures, or exposure to herbal or indigenous medications. The child was the only offspring of healthy parents, and there was no family history of liver disease or similar conditions. No exposure to hepatotoxic drugs or environmental toxins was reported.

A comprehensive review of systems was unremarkable. The patient had no gastrointestinal symptoms, including abdominal pain, gastrointestinal bleeding, vomiting, or changes in bowel habits. Neurological review revealed no history of seizures, altered mental status, or developmental delay. There were no dermatological manifestations, including jaundice, rash, petechiae, or ecchymosis. Additionally, there was no history of arthralgia, arthritis, fever, weight loss, or fatigue.

On physical examination, the patient appeared well and in no distress. She was afebrile, conscious, and alert, with stable vital signs. There were no stigmata of chronic liver disease, including jaundice or palmar erythema. Abdominal examination revealed a soft, nontender abdomen with no hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, or ascites. Examination of the extremities showed no edema, clubbing, or bleeding manifestations. Ophthalmologic evaluation, including slit‐lamp examination for Kayser–Fleischer rings, was normal. Neurological examination revealed no abnormalities.

Laboratory investigations are summarized in Table 1. Autoimmune and viral markers were negative. Hepatic copper concentration was 1605 μg/g. Abdominopelvic ultrasonography and echocardiography results were normal.

Whole‐exome sequencing identified a homozygous mutation in the ATP7B gene, with both parents confirmed as carriers. The liver biopsy revealed a chronic active hepatitis pattern with interface activity, steatosis, and vacuolization of hepatocyte nuclei, consistent with WD.

The patient was started on zinc therapy at a dose of 25 mg twice daily, alongside trientine 20 mg/kg twice daily. Liver enzyme levels returned to the normal range within 3 months of treatment initiation. After a one‐year follow‐up period, the patient demonstrated significant improvements in laboratory test results, as summarized in Table 1.

A 51-year-old woman (gravida 1, para 0) presented in 2025 for neuropelveological evaluation of long-standing, intractable right-sided pelvic and predominantly gluteal neuropathic pain, partly radiating to the lower limb along the S1–S2 dermatomes, with an intensity of 7–8 on the visual analog scale (VAS). The pain worsened with prolonged sitting or standing and resolved when she was lying down. She reported pelvic pain of visceral character since the age of 16 years, which over time became somatic, and coccygeal pain radiating to the right lower limb since 2005. At presentation, she also reported dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia and dyschezia (each rated 10 on a numeric rating scale, NRS), dysuria (NRS 6) and urinary incontinence. Her medications included relugolix combination therapy, pregabalin (225–300 mg), duloxetine and etoricoxib (60 mg).

According to the 2009 hospital record, she had been treated for back pain for 15 years. Between 2005 and 2012, she underwent five lumbosacral spinal procedures in other centers (Table 1). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in 2005 showed a right-lateralized L5–S1 disc herniation compressing neural elements, and percutaneous laser disc decompression (PLDD) was performed at L5–S1 and, later the same year, at L4–L5 and L5–S1. In 2006, an interspinous device (DIAM) was implanted at L4–L5 for chronic lumbosacral pain with L4–L5 instability on MRI and right foot weakness. In 2009, bilateral L5–S1 stenosis was treated by open revision and decompression, during which extensive epidural scar tissue compressing the neural structures was removed; the operating surgeons considered it probably related to the previous laser procedures. In 2012, recurrent pain radiating to the right calf was treated by right L4–L5 decompression with removal of the interspinous device; medialized articular processes and hypertrophic scar tissue and joint capsule were found, and the compressing elements were removed, freeing the dural sac and the L5 root. Each procedure was followed by improvement documented at discharge, but the symptoms recurred, and the patient later reported no lasting benefit. Her course was therefore consistent with failed back surgery syndrome, now termed persistent spinal pain syndrome type 2.

In 2014, she underwent laparoscopic excision of endometriosis (revised American Society for Reproductive Medicine, rASRM, stage II). Within 24 h after this operation, the right gluteal pain worsened acutely.

On neuropelveological examination, the finger–nose test and diadochokinesis were normal, thigh and calf circumferences were symmetrical, patellar reflexes were present and symmetrical, active movements of the feet and toes were symmetrical with normal strength, and cutaneous sensation in the L1–S2 dermatomes was normal and symmetrical. The right Achilles reflex was brisk, with tremor. While lying, the gluteal muscles were asymmetric, smaller on the right side, and on voluntary contraction of the anal sphincter the perineum deviated to the left, suggesting weakness of the right side of the pelvic floor. Pain was reported in the projection of the SGN and of the S1–S2 roots. Bimanual pelvic examination revealed marked hypertonicity of the pelvic floor muscles in the anterior and middle compartments and tenderness on palpation of the right sacral plexus region, whereas the left side was not tender; the uterus and adnexa were normal in size, mobile and non-tender.

Transvaginal ultrasonography (TVUS) with mapping for deep endometriosis showed a normal uterus without features of adenomyosis, normal ovaries without endometriomas, positive sliding signs and no deep endometriotic lesions (#Enzian P0, O0/0, T0/0, A0, B0/0, C0, F0); the post-void residual urine volume was 100 mL. High-resolution pelvic MRI performed before surgery was unremarkable, with no structural abnormality, deep endometriosis or retroperitoneal mass. Electrodiagnostic studies (electromyography or nerve conduction studies), diagnostic nerve blocks and dedicated Doppler assessment of the pelvic veins were not part of the documented work-up.

The combination of posture-dependent pain, right gluteal muscle asymmetry, asymmetric pelvic floor contraction and focal tenderness over the right sacral plexus on vaginal palpation suggested involvement of the proximal sacral plexus rather than isolated spinal root pathology. The working diagnosis was neurogenic pain involving the right S1 root and the SGN, with suspected compression by endometriosis or fibrosis, and diagnostic and therapeutic laparoscopy with exploration of the right sacral plexus was planned. The differential diagnosis is summarized in Table 2.

Retroperitoneal laparoscopic exploration of the right sacral plexus was performed in March 2026. The right SGN was compressed and entrapped in the suprapiriform part of the greater sciatic foramen by an engorged, aberrant superior gluteal vein (Figure 1a); the remaining elements of the sacral plexus appeared unaffected. The vein was isolated, coagulated with bipolar energy and transected, releasing the nerve (Figure 1b–d). The operative time was 100 min, and estimated blood loss was 5 mL. The postoperative course was uneventful with no complications, and the patient was discharged on postoperative day 4.

No neurological deficit was present at discharge. At 7-month follow-up, the patient reported sustained complete resolution of gluteal and radicular pain (VAS 0) and no other complaints. She had returned to her normal daily activities and to work and had discontinued regular intake of the analgesic and neuromodulatory medication (pregabalin, duloxetine and etoricoxib). The other preoperative symptoms (dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, dyschezia and urinary symptoms) were not scored separately, and no physical examination was performed at this consultation. The timeline of the clinical course is shown in Table 1.

case_text:
A 31-year-old man with obesity (BMI 32.6) and polysubstance use presented with syncope and acute dyspnoea (blood pressure 93/61 mmHg; heart rate 136 b.p.m.). PESI was 91 (class III), and sPESI was 2. CT pulmonary angiography showed bilateral pulmonary arterial filling defects (Figure 1C), right-heart strain, and contrast reflux into the inferior vena cava (IVC). Venous ultrasonography demonstrated occlusive left popliteal, peroneal, and posterior tibial deep-vein thrombosis, a probable embolic source. There was no leukocytosis or clinical evidence of sepsis; blood cultures were not obtained. No definitive provoking factor was established from the available records.

After intravenous heparin and placement of bilateral pulmonary arterial infusion catheters, catheter-directed alteplase began at 02:37 on hospital day 1. Echocardiography demonstrated an elongated, mobile thrombus extending from the IVC into the right atrium and intermittently across the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, without a definite attachment point (Figure 1A,B). Right-ventricular dysfunction was present (TAPSE 8 mm; tricuspid annular S′ 7.2 cm/s). Persistent haemodynamic concern in the setting of syncope, right-ventricular dysfunction, and a mobile thrombus-in-transit prompted escalation to systemic fibrinolysis. One catheter-directed alteplase infusion was recorded at 0 ml/h at 11:35; the second infusion's status at that time was not documented. Systemic tenecteplase (50 mg IV, off-label for pulmonary embolism) was administered at 11:46. The catheter infusion system was documented as turned off and disconnected at 13:40.

Follow-up pulmonary angiography showed improved bilateral flow and a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 18 mmHg (initially 34 mmHg). Repeat echocardiography on hospital day 3, ∼46 h after systemic tenecteplase, reported no definite residual intracardiac thrombus (Figure 1D). He was discharged ambulatory on apixaban.

Right-heart thrombus-in-transit is a recognized high-risk pulmonary embolism finding. Management is individualized.1–3 This case illustrates sequential multimodality imaging during treatment and follow-up.

case_text:
Our patient is a 56-year old nonverbal male with a history of diastolic heart failure, type 2 diabetes mellitus, cerebral palsy with developmental delay, and a remote history of omphalocele with surgical repair in childhood. He had recurrent admissions for small bowel obstructions and on 11/8/2024 had a computed tomography (CT) abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast demonstrating medial displacement of the liver from right colon volvulus. A repeat CT scan on 11/11/24 showed resolution of this liver medialization after colonic decompression. He was discharged without surgical intervention. He then presented on 5/28/26 with abdominal pain reported by group home staff. A CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast was notable for volvulus of the liver into the left hemiabdomen and transverse colon and gastric dilation secondary to hepatic volvulus. A nasogastric tube was placed. His abdominal exam was benign; thus he was admitted for observation.

On morning rounds 4 h later, he had worsening tenderness. He was hemodynamically normal and labs within normal limits though given change in physical exam, we proceeded to the operating room 9 h after admission. Intraoperatively his stomach was noted to be massively dilated presumed to be secondary to chronic obstruction from intermittent hepatoptosis (Fig. 1). The liver was exceedingly mobile without ligaments anchoring it to the diaphragm or abdominal wall (Fig. 2). The was apparent transverse colon dilatation and redundancy, secondary to chronic, intermittent colon volvulus. The descending colon was relatively normal though with lax attachments to the retroperitoneum, the sigmoid colon was redundant.

We performed a hepatopexy by suturing the ligament teres to the right lateral abdominal wall with 2-0 silk horizontal mattress sutures. A total of 5 cm of the falciform ligament was removed to correct its laxity and fixed to the anterior abdominal wall with 2-0 silk sutures in Cannell fashion, ensuring that fascia was included in the stitch (Figs 3 and 4). Decision was made to perform an extended right hemicolectomy. The splenic flexure was mobilized and a side-to-side stapled ileocolic anastomosis using 80 3.8 mm gastrointestinal anastomosis (GIA)stapler was completed. An open gastrostomy tube was placed to pexy the stomach using Stamm fixation with 3-0 silk sutures. Postoperatively he remained nothing by mouth as we awaited return of bowel function. On postoperative day three he was distended; G tube was vented for decompression. He had return of bowel function on postoperative day four and increasing tenderness on day five. A CT abdomen and pelvis with IV and PO contrast to evaluate for an underlying intra-abdominal process. The liver was in appropriate anatomic position with residual small bowel and colonic dilation. There was evidence of pneumoperitoneum, secondary to his postoperative state, no contrast extravasation was noted. Decision was made to monitor his exam.

On postoperative day six he was acutely hypotensive, tachycardic and somnolent. Labs demonstrated leukopenia of 0.2 and elevated lactate of 4.3. He was persistently hypotensive despite intravenous fluids with systolic blood pressures between 72 and 89, and subsequently dropped to systolics 51 and 58. Norepinephrine was started and he was upgraded to the Intensive Care Unit. A kidneys, ureter, bladder (KUB) film and upright chest XR were obtained, demonstrating gastric distention below the left hemidiaphragm and a displaced and dilated colon under the right hemidiaphragm. His health care proxy was contacted, who elected to make him comfort measures only with no escalation in care. He passed away on postoperative day seven. The family declined an autopsy.

case_text:
A 74‐year‐old female experienced cardiac arrest after complaining of back pain. After approximately 2 min of chest compressions and a single defibrillation, circulation spontaneously returned, and the patient was transferred to our emergency department. Her medical history included right‐sided breast cancer, Type B aortic dissection, hypertension, and hyperuricemia. Her vital signs upon arrival included a Glasgow Coma Scale of E1V1M2, blood pressure of 125/85 mmHg, heart rate of 153 bpm, body temperature of 36.3°C, oxygen saturation of 93%, and respiratory rate of 38/min. Her pupils were 2.0 mm in diameter with a loss of light reflex. Her jugular vein was distended; however, respiratory sounds were clear bilaterally, without lower extremity oedema. Electrocardiography (ECG) revealed atrial fibrillation and Q waves in Leads III and aVF; however, no significant ST changes or SIQIIITIII patterns were observed.

Laboratory data on admission showed troponin T at 71 ng/L, creatine kinase‐MB at 31 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase at 164 U/L, and D‐dimer at 3.55 μg/mL. Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) showed no left ventricular (LV) asynergy, and neither the LV nor the left atrium was dilated. In contrast, the RV was significantly dilated in the presence of moderate tricuspid regurgitation (TR). However, her TR peak gradient was within normal limits, suggesting the absence of pulmonary hypertension (PH). In addition, midbasal RV wall motion showed McConnell′s sign (hypokinesis with intact wall motion in the RV apex; Figure 1A–D and Supplementary Material 1). Immediate contrast‐enhanced computed tomography revealed no findings suggestive of PE.

Emergency coronary angiography was subsequently performed, which demonstrated left‐dominant coronary circulation with an occlusion detected in the proximal right coronary artery (RCA), which was estimated to supply a relatively limited myocardial territory (Figure 2A). Additional occlusion was identified in the middle of the left anterior descending (LAD) artery; however, substantial collateral flow originating from the circumflex artery was noted in the delayed phase (Figure 2B). Based on ECG and TTE findings, RCA occlusion was considered the culprit lesion, and percutaneous coronary intervention targeting this area was initiated. However, the procedure was discontinued due to minor procedural complications and angiographic features indicative of a chronically progressive lesion. Although the patient exacerbated right‐sided heart failure after the intervention, her hemodynamic status, including RV wall motion, McConnell′s sign, and TR, gradually improved with conservative medical management. Retrospective quantitative assessment of RV–pulmonary artery (PA) coupling was also performed using the tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE)/systolic pulmonary artery pressure (sPAP) ratio. On hospital Day 1, the TAPSE/sPAP ratio was 0.21 mm/mmHg, indicating marked RV–PA uncoupling. Follow‐up echocardiography at approximately 1 month demonstrated an improvement in the ratio to 0.58 mm/mmHg, accompanied by recovery of RV wall motion and resolution of McConnell′s sign.

case_text: A 23-year-old woman with a 46,XY karyotype and classic 17OHD presented to our clinic for management of CAH with severe hypertension. She was initially diagnosed at age 8 years after evaluation for severe hypertension. She subsequently underwent gonadectomy and received estrogen replacement therapy for pubertal induction and long-term management of hypogonadism. At presentation to our clinic, her blood pressure was 160/130 mmHg. Her body mass index (BMI) was 27.2 kg/m2 (Table 1). Her antihypertensive regimen consisted of spironolactone 200 mg daily, valsartan 320 mg daily, metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, and amlodipine 5 mg daily (Fig. 1). Previous glucocorticoid therapy included hydrocortisone 17.5 mg/day in 3 divided doses until age 17 years, followed by dexamethasone 0.25 mg daily for 2 years to simplify treatment. She was subsequently transitioned to prednisone but developed cushingoid features with persistent evidence of mineralocorticoid excess. For hypertension management she required multiple antihypertensive medications. Amlodipine was discontinued because of gingival bleeding, metoprolol was switched to carvedilol which was titrated from 25 mg daily to 50 mg/day and spironolactone was progressively increased over 12 months to 600 mg/day (Fig. 1) to improve blood pressure control.

case_text:
A woman in her 70s was referred to our hospital after an abnormal chest shadow was detected during routine screening. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a well-circumscribed posterior mediastinal tumor measuring approximately 10 cm. Surgical resection was recommended, but the patient preferred observation. During the 6 years of follow-up, the tumor gradually enlarged to 13 cm, and an FDG-PET showed increased uptake, with a maximum standardized uptake value of 9.2 at 60 min and 10.4 at 120 min after tracer injection (Fig. 1).

CT demonstrated that the tumor extended from the T9 to the L2 level. The mass displaced the right kidney posteriorly, compressed the hepatic portion of the IVC anteriorly, and shifted the descending aorta to the left (Figs. 2 and 3; Supplementary Video 1).

Because malignancy could not be completely excluded and further growth was considered likely to increase the risk of symptoms and make complete resection technically more challenging, surgical resection was planned.

Preoperatively, the surgical strategy was discussed in a multidisciplinary setting involving orthopedic, vascular, and hepatobiliary-pancreatic surgeons, with particular attention to the surgical approach and the risk of spinal cord ischemia associated with division of the tumor-feeding segmental arteries. The planned strategy was to begin with a thoracotomy and, if adequate visualization of the caudal portion of the tumor could not be obtained, to extend the incision to the abdomen. For vascular management, the strategy was to minimize the number of segmental arteries requiring division by obtaining adequate exposure and to divide the feeding arteries as close to the tumor capsule as possible.

The patient was placed in a left semi-lateral decubitus position under single-lung ventilation. A right thoracotomy was performed through the eighth intercostal space. Intraoperative biopsy revealed a spindle-cell tumor consistent with a neurogenic tumor. Based on these findings, resection was performed with the intention of dissecting as close to the tumor capsule as possible.

To expose the caudal aspect of the tumor and secure the adjacent major vessels before deep retrocrural dissection, the thoracotomy was extended to the abdominal midline, followed by midline laparotomy to the xiphoid process and diaphragmatic incision. The liver and right kidney were mobilized anteriorly and laterally, respectively, to access the retroperitoneal space, and the IVC and right renal artery were secured before tumor dissection.

The caudal aspect of the tumor was exposed along the vertebral bodies, and dissection proceeded laterally toward the descending aorta to carefully expose the tumor–aorta interface. case_text:
A 58-year-old woman of Turkish descent presented with a 4-month history of rapidly progressive hirsutism and virilization. She had no family history of hyperandrogenism or virilization. Her medical history included asthma and hypercholesterolemia. She reported regular menstrual cycles during her reproductive years and had 2 children, both conceived spontaneously. Menopause occurred at the age of 53.

She reported progressive coarse hair growth involving the face, abdomen, and thighs, accompanied by voice deepening over the preceding 3 months. She was obese and had central adiposity (body mass index of 31.3 kg/m2). She denied exogenous androgen exposure or testosterone-containing products. The virilization caused significant cosmetic and psychological distress.

case_text:
This case report has been prepared in accordance with the CARE 2023 guidelines for reporting surgical case reports. A 46‐year‐old male with a history of well‐controlled Type 1 diabetes mellitus presented to the emergency department with worsening lower abdominal pain and a progressively enlarging lump beneath the umbilicus for 6 days prior to presentation. He denied urinary symptoms, fever, weight loss or gastrointestinal complaints. His regular medication included isophane insulin only. He had no history of previous abdominal surgery and no known history of urachal abnormalities.

On clinical examination, the patient was haemodynamically stable and afebrile. Abdominal examination revealed a localised, tender, approximately 5 × 5 cm palpable mass beneath the umbilicus without overlying skin erythema or discharge at the time of admission. There was no guarding or peritonism. Examination of the external genitalia and hernial orifices was unremarkable.

Laboratory investigations demonstrated an elevated white blood cell (WBC) count of 16.3 × 109/L and a C‐reactive protein level of 322 mg/L, consistent with an inflammatory or infectious process. Renal function, liver function tests and electrolytes were within normal limits. Glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c) was 40 mmol/mol, confirming good diabetic control.

Contrast‐enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis was performed using standard portal venous phase imaging. This demonstrated a 5.4 × 4.8 × 6.2 cm lobulated fluid collection located in the midline, deep to the umbilicus and anterior to the bladder, with peripheral enhancement and surrounding inflammatory stranding, consistent with an infected urachal remnant or abscess (Figure 1A,B).

A conservative approach was initially adopted because of the absence of peritonitis, haemodynamic instability or radiological evidence of bladder involvement. The patient was started on empiric intravenous broad‐spectrum antibiotics while further management options, including drainage or surgical excision, were considered. He received intravenous co‐amoxiclav 1.2 grams every 8 hours according to local institutional guidelines for intra‐abdominal infection. Following spontaneous drainage of the collection and sustained clinical improvement, intravenous therapy was transitioned to oral co‐amoxiclav 625 mg every 8 hours after 3 days to complete a total antimicrobial course of 7 days. Image‐guided drainage was considered; however, this was deferred after spontaneous rupture of the collection with drainage through the umbilicus, resulting in immediate clinical improvement.

On the second day of admission, purulent discharge was noted from the umbilicus. Gentle expression of the area allowed drainage of residual pus. A sample of the spontaneously draining fluid was obtained through the nonsterile umbilical opening and sent for microbiological culture. This demonstrated heavy growth of Streptococcus intermedius, reported as sensitive to penicillin and clindamycin. Blood and urine cultures were negative, with no pathogenic organisms identified.

The patient improved clinically following spontaneous drainage and antibiotic therapy. He remained afebrile after Day 2 of admission. His WBC count decreased from 16.3 × 109 to 6 × 109/L and a C‐reactive protein level from 322 to 38 mg/L. Total hospital stay was 3 days. He completed the prescribed course of antibiotics and remained asymptomatic at follow‐up 3 months later. The clinical course, management and follow‐up are summarised in Table 1.

He was advised to seek urgent medical assessment if he developed recurrent pain, umbilical discharge, fever, urinary symptoms, haematuria or a new abdominal mass. The absence of repeat imaging, histological confirmation and longer term follow‐up limits certainty regarding complete resolution of the remnant and exclusion of occult malignancy.
