case_text:
We report the case of a 69-year-old woman with a history of stenting of the right renal artery, peripheral arterial disease, and a history of 50 pack-years of active smoking, with no history of smoking cessation. She was admitted for an acute-on-CMI, presenting as postprandial abdominal pain that had been progressing for 6 months. This cramp-like pain following meals, combined with early satiety, had led to a gradual reduction in food intake, resulting in marked weight loss and a current weight of 32 kg.

On admission, the patient was emaciated, with normal blood pressure, a soft abdomen, mild abdominal tenderness, and no rigidity. Laboratory tests revealed mild normochromic, normocytic anemia, with a major inflammatory syndrome (C-reactive protein [CRP] of 291 mg/L), elevated lactate levels, hypoalbuminemia, hypophosphatemia, and hypocalcemia, as well as normal renal function.

Abdominal computed tomography angiography (CTA) demonstrated severe multivessel mesenteric occlusive disease involving all 3 mesenteric arteries. The celiac trunk and the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) were occluded at their origins. Moderate atherosclerotic calcification was noted at the origins of the celiac trunk and SMA. The SMA occlusion extended for approximately 40 mm, with distal reconstitution and preserved distal opacification through a well-developed collateral network, indicating the presence of a suitable distal target for revascularization. CTA also demonstrated bowel wall thickening involving the ascending colon and distal ileal loops, associated with minimal free fluid in the right paracolic gutter; findings consistent with acute bowel ischemia superimposed on chronic mesenteric arterial occlusive disease. No preoperative conventional angiography was performed, as CTA provided sufficient anatomical information to assess the feasibility of mesenteric revascularization and to plan the surgical strategy (Fig. 1).

The multidisciplinary consultation recommended exploratory abdominal surgery, which revealed segmental necrosis of the terminal ileal loops and necrotic changes in the jejunum, justifying the performance of a revascularization procedure as the first-line treatment.

Conventional antegrade endovascular recanalization was considered technically unfeasible because of the flush ostial occlusion of the SMA, which precluded antegrade catheterization. Although a primary mesenteric bypass was considered, bowel necrosis requiring intestinal resection and the contaminated intra-abdominal operative field were deemed to increase the risk of prosthetic graft infection. Consequently, hybrid revascularization by ROMS was selected as the initial treatment strategy. After exposing the artery during a laparotomy, an arteriotomy was performed, allowing for retrograde catheterization. Angioplasty was then carried out using a 6-mm covered stent. Intraoperative assessment revealed good patency of the device from the ostium. The procedure was completed by closing the arteriotomy using an arterial patch (Fig. 2). Subsequently, a resection of the terminal ileum and ascending cecum was performed due to ischemic lesions of the intestinal walls of mesenteric origin. The remaining length of the small intestine was estimated at 180 cm. A terminating ileostomy was created in the right iliac fossa, in conjunction with a terminating colostomy in the right subcostal region (Fig. 3).

Six months after ROMS, the patient presented with recurrent postprandial abdominal pain, which brought her weight to 29 kg. CTA demonstrated thrombosis of the SMA stent (Fig. 4). The patient had poor adherence to the prescribed medical therapy and continued heavy smoking despite repeated smoking cessation advice. Although the exact mechanism of stent thrombosis could not be determined, these factors may have contributed to stent failure, together with the severity of the underlying diffuse atherosclerotic disease. In view of the stent occlusion and recurrent mesenteric ischemia, the multidisciplinary team decided to perform definitive open revascularization with an aorto-mesenteric bypass. This involved retracting the small intestine to the right, and the left lobe of the liver after its release, followed by dissection of the supra-celiac aorta with clamping for 45 minutes. After assessment and clamping of both renal arteries, the mesenteric artery, and the primary iliac arteries, a 2-cm longitudinal arteriotomy was made at the level of the celiac aorta, followed by the placement of an 8-mm polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) graft and anastomosis at the upper end via an end-to-side suture using 2 hemistitches. The graft was then tunnelled pre-pancreatically and trans-mesocolically, followed by an lower end-to-side anastomosis onto the SMA trunk (Figs. 5 and 6).

The postoperative course was uneventful from both a hemodynamic and gastrointestinal perspective. The patient experienced gradual clinical improvement, with complete resolution of postprandial abdominal pain within the first few weeks after surgery.

Oral feeding was progressively reintroduced and was well tolerated, resulting in an improvement in nutritional status. Ileostomy output was satisfactory, with no evidence of severe short-bowel syndrome. Restoration of intestinal continuity was planned following nutritional optimization. However, the patient was subsequently lost to follow-up; therefore, no long-term clinical or imaging assessment of graft patency, nutritional status, or stoma outcome was available (Table 1).

case_text:
A 79‐year‐old male presented with gross hematuria. Contrast‐enhanced computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed an infiltrative bladder tumor involving the left bladder wall, with perivesical invasion. He was diagnosed with locally advanced muscle‐invasive bladder cancer (cT3bN0M0) (Figure 1:A,B). The tumor was initially considered potentially unresectable at a departmental conference.

Transurethral resection of the bladder tumor (TURBT) revealed invasive high‐grade urothelial carcinoma (Grade 3) (Figure 1:E). As systemic therapy for potentially unresectable disease, he received four courses of EV (1.25 mg/kg Days 1 and 8) plus pembrolizumab (200 mg, Day 1) every 3 weeks. Treatment was tolerated, and serial CT scans showed marked tumor regression, with the residual lesion radiologically corresponding to cT2 (Figure 1:D).

Following tumor downstaging, the decision to proceed with consolidative radical cystectomy was made at a departmental conference. He subsequently underwent RARC with IC. Intraoperatively, minimal adhesions were observed, and the left bladder wall was dissected from the pelvic wall without difficulty. The surgical specimen showed no residual carcinoma, and the final pathological stage was ypT0N0 consistent with a pathological complete response (CR) (Figure 1:F). His postoperative course was initially uneventful. Oral intake was resumed on postoperative Day (POD) 3, and ureteral stents were removed between POD 13 and 15. He developed mild anorexia and a low‐grade fever on POD 18. Laboratory testing showed sodium 134 mmol/L, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, C‐reactive protein 10.5 mg/dL, and white blood cell count 15 180/μg. His symptoms improved promptly with intravenous antibiotics and fluid therapy. He was discharged on POD 23.

On POD 25, he was readmitted because of persistent fever, anorexia, and progressive fatigue. Laboratory tests revealed a normal serum potassium level (3.9 mmol/L), Na 137 mmol/L, eGFR 45.3 mL/min/1.73 m2 and blood glucose of 57 mg/dL, but markedly decreased plasma adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH: 2.4 pg/mL; baseline: 63.2 pg/mL) and cortisol levels (6.68 μg/dL; baseline: 16.3 μg/dL). Based on these endocrine abnormalities and the temporal association with prior exposure to ICI therapy, he was diagnosed with adrenal insufficiency as an irAE.

Intravenous hydrocortisone sodium phosphate was initiated at 100 mg/day for 2 days, followed by 50 mg/day for an additional 2 days. His symptoms rapidly improved, with resolution of anorexia and fatigue, accompanied by resolution of hypoglycemia. Treatment was then switched to oral prednisolone at 40 mg/day, which was tapered to 30 mg/day and 20 mg/day at approximately 2‐week intervals, followed by further reductions to 15 mg/day and 10 mg/day (Figure 2). He was discharged in stable condition on Day 16 after hydrocortisone initiation, and no recurrence of adrenal insufficiency has been observed during steroid tapering. Since the patient achieved a pathological CR and developed an irAE, adjuvant therapy was withheld, and he remained under observation. Follow‐up CT at 2 months showed no disease recurrence.

case_text:
A 56‐year‐old woman was referred for evaluation of severe anemia detected during routine laboratory testing. The patient reported only mild asthenia and denied dyspnea, palpitations, bleeding, weight loss, gastrointestinal symptoms, or neurological complaints. On physical examination, she appeared pale. Cutaneous evaluation revealed areas of vitiligo, suggesting an underlying autoimmune predisposition. No lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly was detected, and vital signs were stable. Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated severe anemia, with a hemoglobin level of 70 g/L and marked macrocytosis, as indicated by a mean corpuscular volume of 137 fL; platelets count was 80 × 103/μL. Biochemical analysis revealed markedly elevated LDH levels, increased bilirubin concentrations, and undetectable haptoglobin. These findings initially suggested hemolytic anemia.

However, further evaluation revealed inconsistencies with this diagnosis. The reticulocyte count was only mildly elevated and not proportional to the severity of anemia, indicating an inadequate bone marrow response. Peripheral blood smear examination showed pronounced macrocytosis without schistocytes or fragmented erythrocytes, effectively excluding thrombotic microangiopathy (Figure 1). Subsequent investigations demonstrated markedly reduced serum vitamin B12 levels, associated with elevated homocysteine concentrations. Autoimmune testing revealed high titers of anti‐parietal cell antibodies, supporting the diagnosis of pernicious anemia (Figure 2).

case_text:
A 29-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of a right-breast lump. The mass, in the upper-outer quadrant (10 o’clock), was superficial, mobile, well-circumscribed, and non-tender, measuring approximately 3cm on clinical examination. Clinical examination of the contralateral breast and both axillae was unremarkable. She had no personal breast history or family history of breast/ovarian cancer. Menstrual/reproductive history was unremarkable; she had not used hormonal contraception. Ultrasound showed a lobulated, hypoechoic nodule with mild heterogeneity and vascularity, measuring 2.8 cm (previously 1.9 cm 4 months earlier), compatible with a suspicious fibroadenoma (Fig. 1). Ultrasound-guided core biopsy demonstrated a fibroadenomatous lesion with proliferative changes, including foci of adenosis, without atypia or malignancy. The combination of interval growth, mild heterogeneity, vascularity, and adenosis on core raised suspicion for a complex fibroadenoma or a fibroepithelial tumor, and surgical excision was advised. Wide local excision yielded a well-circumscribed, ovoid mass (3.0 × 2.5 × 1.9 cm) with a rubbery, whitish cut surface and lobulated architecture.

Histopathologic examination confirmed a complex fibroadenoma containing foci of DCIS (Fig. 2). Microscopically, typical fibroadenoma architecture (stromal proliferation with benign glands) coexisted with atypical epithelial proliferations ranging from atypical ductal hyperplasia (ADH) to low-grade cribriform DCIS. The DCIS comprised monomorphic cells forming sieve-like cribriform spaces without necrosis or marked pleomorphism (nuclear grade 1). The foci measured only a few millimeters and were completely confined within the fibroadenoma, without extension into surrounding breast tissue. Margins were negative; DCIS was > 2 mm from the closest inked margin. No invasive carcinoma was identified on extensive sampling. Adjacent non-lesional tissue showed fibrocystic change only.

Immunohistochemistry showed strong estrogen-receptor positivity (100% nuclei) and complete loss of cytokeratin (CK)5/6 expression in the neoplastic cells, supporting a clonal process and aiding distinction from usual ductal hyperplasia. These findings confirmed low-grade DCIS arising within a complex fibroadenoma.

Following multidisciplinary review and counselling, axillary surgery was not indicated for pure in-situ disease. No adjuvant radiotherapy or endocrine therapy was recommended given the very small volume of low-grade DCIS, clear margins, and the patient’s fertility plans. Comprehensive germline multigene testing was negative. Following multidisciplinary review, an individualized surveillance plan was adopted, consisting of clinical examination every 6 months for 2 years, annual ultrasound, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) every 1–2 years, and initiation of mammography at age 30. This strategy reflected an institution-specific multidisciplinary decision in the absence of established surveillance guidelines for carcinoma arising within a fibroadenoma. At the most recent follow-up, 3 months after surgery, the patient remained disease-free.

case_text:
A 59‐year‐old Albanian woman presented with fatigue, malaise, nausea, vomiting, epigastric pain, and intermittent syncope persisting for approximately 1 month and acutely worsening on the day of admission. Her history included arterial hypertension treated with Losartan 50 mg daily, a symptomatic hiatal hernia diagnosed about 1 year earlier (surgical repair planned), prior radical hysterectomy, and cholecystectomy. Her mother had diabetes mellitus. She was a non‐smoker, reported no alcohol use or history of alcohol abuse, and had no known allergies.

Initial blood glucose was markedly elevated at 19.5 mmol/L. Given this finding, together with nonspecific abdominal symptoms (epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting) and no prior history of diabetes, she was admitted to Endocrinology with a working diagnosis of abdominal colic and suspected new‐onset type 2 diabetes mellitus.

On the ward, she was disoriented, hypothermic (32.5°C), tachycardic with muffled heart sounds, and borderline hypotensive (100/70 mmHg), with cold extremities and diffuse abdominal tenderness.

case_text:
Written informed consent for publication was obtained from the patient.

A 67‐year‐old man was scheduled for elective right thyroid lobectomy with isthmectomy due to progressive compressive symptoms secondary to structural thyroid disease.

The patient had been diagnosed with cold agglutinin autoimmune haemolytic anaemia. Haematologic evaluation at the time demonstrated positive direct and indirect antiglobulin tests, panagglutination, high antibody titres and broad thermal amplitude consistent with clinically significant cold agglutinin disease. Given baseline anaemia and anticipated crossmatch complexity, the haematology team recommended reserving red blood cell transfusion for exceptional circumstances.

Relevant comorbidities included Type 2 diabetes mellitus, arterial hypertension, dyslipidaemia, obesity (body mass index of 30 kg m−2), severe obstructive sleep apnoea treated with continuous positive airway pressure and chronic corticosteroid therapy with prednisolone 20 mg daily. Preoperative haemoglobin concentration was 8.7 g·dL−1. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a mildly reduced left ventricular systolic function with an ejection fraction of 46%. The patient was classified as American Society of Anesthesiologists Physical Status III.

Given the risk of haemolysis associated with peripheral cooling, perioperative management focused on limiting redistribution hypothermia and maintaining a thermal safety margin above the presumed antibody activation range.

Preoperative planning involved coordination among the surgical, anaesthesia and transfusion medicine teams. The blood bank was notified in advance, and compatible blood products were prepared with warming capability available if required. The procedure was scheduled as the first case of the day, and a multimodal thermal management strategy was implemented. This included active prewarming for 30 min before arrival in the operating room, transport on a prewarmed stretcher, ambient temperature maintained between 22°C and 24°C, warmed intravenous and irrigation fluids and continuous dual‐site temperature monitoring.

Standard monitoring was applied together with continuous central and peripheral temperature monitoring using an oesophageal temperature probe and a skin thermistor placed at the temporal region. Baseline core temperature was 37.4°C. An arterial catheter was not inserted because a short‐duration procedure with limited expected blood loss and stable haemodynamic conditions was anticipated. Continuous noninvasive monitoring was considered sufficient, and serial blood sampling was not expected to alter intraoperative management. General anaesthesia was induced with fentanyl, propofol and rocuronium and maintained with sevoflurane in an oxygen–air mixture. Hydrocortisone was administered intraoperatively in view of the patient’s chronic corticosteroid therapy. Mechanical ventilation was performed using pressure‐controlled ventilation with volume guarantee. Ventilatory parameters were adjusted throughout the procedure to maintain normocapnia and normoxaemia, guided by end‐tidal carbon dioxide monitoring and pulse oximetry.

Prewarming was applied for 30 min using forced‐air warming set to 43°C. Intraoperatively, active warming was maintained at the same setting, and intravenous fluids were administered via a fluid warmer set to 37°C. Following induction, the lowest recorded core temperature was 37.2°C. During the 87‐min procedure, central temperature remained between 37.2°C and 38.1°C, while peripheral temperature ranged from 37.4°C to 37.7°C (Figure 1). The central–peripheral temperature gradient (ΔT) remained ≤ 0.4°C throughout the procedure.

Haemodynamic stability was maintained without vasopressor support. No additional blood‐sparing measures were used, with blood conservation relying on meticulous surgical haemostasis. Estimated blood loss was 150 mL, and transfusion was not required. Recovery and extubation were uneventful. At operating room exit, central temperature was 38.0°C, and peripheral temperature was 37.6°C.

Upon arrival in the postanaesthesia care unit, peripheral temperature was 37.6°C. Active warming was continued to avoid delayed hypothermia, and temperature at discharge from recovery was 37.2°C.

On postoperative day one, haemoglobin concentration remained stable at 8.8 g·dL−1, bilirubin levels were unchanged, and no clinical evidence of haemolysis was observed. The postoperative course was uneventful, with no signs suggestive of acute haemolytic exacerbation.

case_text: A 56‐year‐old woman with histologically confirmed oral LP, previously followed at another hospital, was referred to our dermatology unit for patch testing because of suspected contact dermatitis. Her medical history was otherwise unremarkable, and she was not taking any medications. Dermatological examination showed known white reticular oral LP lesions and erythematous hyperkeratotic papules on her back, sacral region, and dorsum of the feet, with a perifollicular distribution on the back. Patch testing with the SIDAPA 2023 standard series and supporting dental and orthopedic series revealed mild positive reactions to Myroxylon pereirae, nickel sulfate, palladium chloride, and benzoyl peroxide, none of which were considered clinically relevant. A biopsy of a follicular hyperkeratotic papule on the back showed histopathological findings consistent with LPP. Routine blood tests, including hepatitis B and C serology, were normal or negative. Treatment with heliotherapy and a Class III topical corticosteroid led to resolution of the skin lesions with residual brownish hyperpigmentation. Approximately 1 year later, multiple grouped comedones developed in the patient’s pubic area, with fewer similar lesions on the abdomen and thighs (Figures 1a and b). Relevant differential diagnoses, including acneiform eruptions, hidradenitis suppurativa, steatocystoma multiplex, Favre–Racouchot syndrome, nevus comedonicus, and drug‐ or environmentally induced comedonal eruptions, were considered unlikely based on features such as adult onset, clinical morphology and distribution, absence of typical associated features, and absence of relevant drug or environmental exposures. Moreover, the clinical presentation was not considered consistent with LP follicularis tumidus (LPFT), as the patient lacked the characteristic tumid or erythematous‐violaceous plaques with superimposed cysts and comedones, and the lesions were not distributed in the typical retroauricular location. Histopathological examination showed epidermoid cysts with chronic perilesional lichenoid inflammation involving the epithelial–stromal junction (Figure 1c). Topical adapalene and clindamycin resulted in partial improvement.

case_text:
A married elderly male former smoker with no documented alcohol misuse was followed over several decades for melanoma originating from the medial aspect of the right lower leg. Past medical history was significant for Type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with oral hypoglycemic agents, aortic stenosis, aortic sclerosis, and hyperlipidemia. No family history of malignancy was documented.

In 1992, he underwent a diagnostic excision of a pigmented lesion from the right lower extremity where histopathological examination demonstrated a superficial spreading melanoma with Breslow thickness of 1.0 mm and Clark Level III. Wide local excision was subsequently performed with free margins. One year later, in 1993, a local recurrence developed which was treated with repeat wide excision with a 2 cm margin. Histopathological examination confirmed recurrent melanoma, and tumor‐free surgical margins were achieved.

The patient remained clinically disease‐free for approximately 20 years. In April 2013, a 4‐cm in‐transit melanoma metastasis was detected medial to the right knee and completely excised with clear margins. Sentinel lymph node biopsy from the right inguinal basin showed no metastatic involvement. Histopathological examination confirmed metastatic melanoma, and molecular analysis showed no BRAF mutation. Serum S‐100 was mildly elevated at 0.13 μg/L (reference < 0.11 μg/L). At a regional melanoma conference on May 28, 2013, no additional treatment was recommended.

case_text:
A 41-year-old woman with recently diagnosed CLE presented with severe acute retrosternal chest pain radiating to the left arm, accompanied by diaphoresis and nausea. She had no history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, smoking, dyslipidaemia, or premature coronary artery disease in the family. CLE had been diagnosed three months earlier, limited to photosensitive inflammatory skin lesions involving the face, neck, and scalp. Antiphospholipid antibodies were negative. Treatment with hydroxychloroquine had been initiated as first-line therapy, with subsequent stabilization of cutaneous symptoms. On examination, she was haemodynamically stable with blood pressure 118/72 mmHg and heart rate 84 bpm. Cardiopulmonary examination was normal, and there were no signs of heart failure. The initial electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with ST-segment elevation in leads V1–V5 and aVL, accompanied by reciprocal ST depression in leads II, III, and aVF (Figure 1A). A repeat ECG shortly afterwards demonstrated normalization of ST segments but persistent T-wave inversion in aVR and V1–V4 (Figure 1B). Despite transient ST elevation, the patient experienced ongoing angina despite treatment with intravenous morphine, nitrates, and aspirin. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated apical hypokinesia with mildly reduced left ventricular systolic function (left ventricular ejection fraction approximately 45%).

Given persistent chest pain and dynamic ECG changes, emergency coronary angiography was performed via right radial access. Angiography revealed a thrombotic lesion in the proximal left anterior descending artery (LAD) at the bifurcation with the first diagonal branch (RD1), with preserved distal coronary flow (Figure 1C).

Thrombus aspiration was considered but deferred because of the risk of embolization into the LCX. Pre-intervention OCT imaging demonstrated a large, irregular intraluminal thrombus with a partly ‘cauliflower-like’ morphology, protruding into the lumen and appearing attached to the vessel wall. Signal attenuation behind the mass suggested erythrocyte-rich (red) thrombotic material. Only subtle luminal surface irregularities were visible, raising the possibility of focal superficial vessel wall injury or very early atherosclerotic alteration, without definitive OCT features of plaque rupture or erosion (Figure 2A). Nevertheless, concealed plaque rupture cannot be completely excluded, as the substantial thrombotic burden may have obscured the underlying vessel wall. During advancement of a 6 French Extra Back-Up (EBU) catheter for OCT imaging via the radial access, the patient developed sudden pain and swelling in the proximal forearm. Angiography demonstrated contrast extravasation consistent with proximal radial-brachial artery perforation (Figure 3A). Immediate external compression using a blood pressure cuff was applied, and the procedure was completed via femoral access. OCT was used to assess the reference vessel dimensions and to exclude LCX ostium involvement. Given the substantial thrombotic burden and the bifurcation anatomy, a drug-eluting stent was implanted in the LAD using a bifurcation strategy with final kissing balloon inflation and proximal optimization technique (Figure 2B). Post-intervention OCT confirmed adequate stent expansion and apposition, with no relevant stent edge dissection, significant malapposition, or tissue protrusion. The following day, duplex ultrasound of the access site showed a small haematoma without active bleeding, evidence of compartment syndrome, or neurological deficit (Figure 3B). Conservative management was sufficient.

The patient was discharged on dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin 100 mg once daily and prasugrel 10 mg once daily, in addition to beta-blocker, an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor, statin therapy, and continued hydroxychloroquine treatment. At one-month follow-up, she remained asymptomatic with recovery of the left ventricular function and no residual vascular complications.

case_text:
A 66‐year‐old female was brought to the emergency department at Gargash Hospital, Dubai, UAE, in July 2025 with sudden aphasia and left‐sided weakness. Before reaching the hospital, the neurological deficits were resolved spontaneously, with a total duration of approximately 30 min. She was initially admitted as a case of transient ischemic attack (TIA). On examination, she was conscious and oriented (Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15/15). Neurological examination was unremarkable, with normal tone, power, reflexes, and intact sensation. However, general examination revealed pallor and multiple ecchymotic patches over the trunk and limbs. Cardiovascular, respiratory, and abdominal examinations were unremarkable.

Initial laboratory investigations (Table 1) showed severe anemia (hemoglobin 7.8 g/dL) and significant thrombocytopenia (platelet count of 15,000/μL) on admission, both of which remained low by Day 5. The white blood cell count was normal. Renal function and electrolyte levels were also within normal ranges throughout the observation period. C‐reactive protein was within the reference range, whereas D‐dimer was high and showed a rising trend during follow‐up (Table 1).

The high total bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase, and reticulocyte count were consistent with hemolysis. The presence of schistocytes in peripheral blood smears supports the diagnosis of MAHA. The coagulation indicators were normal, and blood cultures were negative, helping to exclude disseminated intravascular coagulation and infectious etiologies, respectively.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed no evidence of ischemic changes. Chest X‐ray and abdominal ultrasound were unremarkable.

The calculated PLASMIC score was 6, indicating a high probability of severe ADAMTS13 deficiency. Based on the high clinical suspicion of iTTP, laboratory findings, and PLASMIC score, treatment with corticosteroids (prednisolone) and therapeutic plasma exchange (plasmapheresis) was initiated without waiting for the ADAMTS13 results. Subsequent testing showed markedly reduced ADAMTS13 activity (< 5%), confirming the diagnosis of iTTP.

The patient also received one unit of packed red blood cells because of severe anemia, and a platelet transfusion because of severe thrombocytopenia and concern for sudden severe bleeding. Although platelet transfusion is generally not recommended in iTTP and is typically reserved for life‐threatening bleeding, the treating team decided to give platelets because of the multiple ecchymotic patches over the trunk and limbs in addition to the very low platelet count (15,000/μL). The patient responded well to the treatment and demonstrated progressive improvement, with complete resolution of neurological symptoms and a steady rise in platelet count. She was discharged in stable condition after 2 weeks with hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL and platelet count of 194000/μL. Arrangements were made for close outpatient follow‐up.

A postmenopausal woman in her late 70s was reviewed in breast clinic with recurrent left breast pain and a gradually enlarging palpable breast mass. Family history included two maternal relatives with breast cancer. Her past history included hysterectomy for pelvic organ prolapse and left thyroid lobectomy with parathyroidectomy for follicular thyroid adenoma and parathyroid adenoma.

Over ~5 years, she underwent multiple breast clinic assessments for left breast pain and a palpable lump. Examination initially identified a soft, smooth, mobile mass with benign features. Mammography and ultrasound repeatedly showed no suspicious abnormality, and the finding was attributed to a large, benign-appearing fatty lesion described as a prominent fat lobule or lipoma. She was discharged after reassuring assessment on more than one occasion.

She re-presented because the mass had enlarged and become increasingly symptomatic. Examination demonstrated a soft palpable mass in the left lower breast. Mammography was again reported as normal (M1) and ultrasound as benign (U2; Fig. 1). Interval ultrasound confirmed gradual enlargement, eventually measuring ~65 mm. Contrast-enhanced breast magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated a posterior fat-containing lesion (~27 × 61 × 39 mm) that suppressed evenly on fat-suppressed sequences, with no suspicious post-gadolinium enhancement and no significant lymphadenopathy (Fig. 2). Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the chest also demonstrated the fat-attenuation lesion in the left anterior chest-wall/breast region (Fig. 3).

Because the lesion continued to enlarge despite benign imaging, ultrasound-guided percutaneous core biopsy was undertaken. FISH demonstrated MDM2 amplification (MDM2/CEP12 ratio 3.71), supporting ALT/WDL.

The case was discussed at local breast and sarcoma multidisciplinary team meetings, with input from a tertiary sarcoma centre; consensus favoured ALT/WDL and local excision. The patient underwent marginal excision with the capsule intact, achieving breast conservation. Intraoperatively the lesion was found in a deep plane, appearing to arise from the interpectoral fascia/fat pad.

Histology confirmed mature adipose tissue without atypia or dedifferentiation. Margin assessment was limited because lesional fat was difficult to distinguish from background fat, although the lesion appeared macroscopically clear of all margins. The patient recovered well and entered a 5-year patient-initiated follow-up pathway for local recurrence surveillance.

case_text: A 46‐year‐old male pedestrian sustained blunt abdominal trauma following a road traffic accident. The mechanism of injury involved being struck from behind by a motorcycle, which precipitated a forward fall onto the roadway surface, resulting in direct abdominal impact. He was immediately managed conservatively elsewhere, where ultrasonography of abdomen showed splenic injury, moderate hemoperitoneum and left mild pleural effusion with partial collapse of basal segments (Figure 1). A chest x‐ray showed a mild left‐sided pleural effusion with no rib fractures. The patient received multiple blood transfusions for correction of anemia and was empirically treated with intravenous amoxicillin–clavulanate for 1 week, prior to referral to our center 3 weeks following the road traffic accident. Given persistent pain in abdomen and drop in hemoglobin, Triphasic Computerized Tomography (CT) scan of abdomen was done which showed Grade 4 splenic laceration with subcapsular hypodensities, multiple splenic pseudoaneurysms involving splenic artery and its branches, high density ascites suggestive of moderate hemoperitoneum and trace bilateral pleural effusions, with no evidence of biliary tree injury or obstruction, or abnormal communication between pleural space and biliary tree (Figure 2). Liver was normal with no intrahepatic biliary duct dilatation or focal lesions or hepatic capsular disruption. Common bile duct was normal in caliber. Gall bladder wall thickness was normal with no evidence of intraluminal calculi or pericholecystic fluid. Pancreas was normal in size, shape and attenuation, with no evidence of ductal dilatation or parenchymal calcifications or peripancreatic fluid collection. Following initial stabilization with transfusions and supportive care, the patient and family were counseled regarding therapeutic options, with emphasis on spleen‐preserving strategies such as selective splenic artery embolization, which are generally preferred over splenectomy. However, financial constraints ultimately led to elective splenectomy 1 month post‐trauma reflecting real‐world practice in many settings. In the absence of such constraints, spleen‐preserving alternatives could have been considered. Adapting management to local realities while prioritizing patient safety remains an important clinical lesson. Intra operative findings during laparotomy revealed lacerated spleen, large splenic hematoma, mild hemoperitoneum, and adhesiolysis of fundus of stomach and colon to spleen was done. No additional intra‐abdominal injuries or visible diaphragmatic lesions were identified.

case_text:
A 33-year-old right-handed male manual laborer presented 15 days after sustaining a sharp machinery-related injury to the left palm and middle finger caused by an electric saw. Initial wound care and skin closure had been performed at another healthcare facility. His medical history was otherwise unremarkable, with no history of diabetes mellitus, peripheral vascular disease, neuropathy or other comorbidities that could adversely affect wound healing or nerve regeneration. He was a non-smoker and reported no alcohol or recreational drug use. The injury involved the non-dominant left hand, and he presented with persistent inability to flex the middle finger and sensory loss in the adjacent digital nerve distribution.

On examination, a healed longitudinal laceration extended from the palm toward the base of the middle finger, corresponding clinically to the zone II–III region. The middle finger showed complete loss of active flexion at the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints, while passive range of motion was preserved without fixed joint contracture. Sensory examination demonstrated loss of sensation along the ulnar aspect of the middle finger and the radial aspect of the ring finger, consistent with injury to the common digital nerve of the third web space. Capillary refill and digital perfusion were preserved.

Given the delayed presentation, preserved passive motion, suspected tendon retraction and associated sensory deficit, operative exploration with single-stage tendon reconstruction and digital nerve repair was planned. Written informed consent was obtained for treatment and for publication of anonymized clinical details and accompanying clinical images/video-derived stills.

case_text:
A 42‐year‐old woman, not known to have any chronic medical problems, presented to a general medical clinic, complaining of new‐onset abnormal facial hair growth and acne. She noticed increased hair growth mainly on her face but also on her upper and lower back and upper chest. She also reported mild acne, a problem she had not previously encountered, even during adolescence. Menstrual irregularity had developed only recently after previously regular cycles. Her initial investigations were reported to show an elevated total testosterone level (the numerical result and assay details were unavailable for review), and pelvic ultrasound (US) demonstrated multiple small follicles in both ovaries, suggesting a polycystic ovarian morphology. Consequently, the patient was diagnosed with PCOS and was prescribed a combined oral contraceptive pill (COCP).

The patient remained on therapy for 3 years, during which she experienced transient improvement in hirsutism and acne. A few months after discontinuing the COCP, the symptoms recurred and became progressively more prominent. She therefore sought a second medical opinion. At that time, she reported increased terminal hair growth involving the face, chest, back, and abdomen, worsening acne, and significant scalp hair loss; the specific pattern of scalp hair loss was not documented. She denied weight gain, deepening of the voice, galactorrhea, headaches, visual disturbances, fatigue, abdominal pain, or abdominal distention. Menarche occurred at age 13 years, and her menstrual cycles had been regular until a few months before her initial presentation when menstrual irregularity developed. Her obstetric history included five pregnancies and five deliveries. Records from the initial evaluation were unavailable; therefore, the degree of initial testosterone elevation and whether earlier investigation for an ovarian tumor was indicated could not be determined. The later onset and progressive course of hyperandrogenic symptoms after years of regular cycles were considered atypical for a straightforward presentation of PCOS and prompted a reassessment of the original diagnosis.

Physical examination showed a weight of 72 kg and a height of 156 cm. Her BP was 115/70 mmHg. She exhibited a normal female body habitus with normal breast development. She had mild facial acne. Hirsutism was notably present on the face, especially the upper lip, chin, and cheeks. It was also noticed on the chest, back, and abdomen. Her Ferriman–Gallwey score was 16. There were no clinical signs of virilization apart from hirsutism and acne, and clitoral examination did not reveal clitoromegaly. Her abdominal examination was normal, with no masses appreciated.

Repeat laboratory evaluation demonstrated marked biochemical hyperandrogenism: total testosterone was 5.83 nmol/L (reference range 0.5–2.0), and dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEAS) was mildly elevated at 14 µmol/L (reference range 1.7–10). LH was 19.78 mIU/mL, FSH 3.84 mIU/mL, prolactin 339 (reported reference interval 80–450; unit requires confirmation), TSH 1.3 mIU/L (reference range 0.8–4.5), and HbA1c 6%. In view of the progressive clinical course and the degree of testosterone elevation, the diagnosis of PCOS was reconsidered, and an androgen‐secreting ovarian or adrenal lesion was investigated.

CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a 5.1 × 4.2 × 4.0 cm isodense mass adjacent to the right ovary (Figure 1). The adrenal glands were normal, without any nodules or hyperplasia. Although DHEAS was mildly elevated at 14 µmol/L, the elevation was not strongly suggestive of an adrenal tumor; thresholds around 700 µg/dL (~19–20 µmol/L) have historically been used to prompt investigation for an adrenal source, while interpretation should also account for age, assay methodology, and laboratory‐specific reference ranges. The combination of predominant testosterone elevation, normal adrenal imaging, and a right adnexal mass therefore favored an ovarian source of androgen excess.

An androgen‐secreting right ovarian tumor was considered the most likely diagnosis, and the patient was referred to gynecology for surgical management. Following discussion of the surgical options and fertility considerations, she underwent a right oophorectomy. Histopathological examination demonstrated a fibrothecoma composed of spindle‐shaped stromal cells arranged in fascicles with focal luteinization. The nuclei were mildly hyperchromatic without pleomorphism or mitotic activity. Immunohistochemistry showed positive staining for inhibin and calretinin and negative staining for epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), supporting a sex cord‐stromal tumor.

Three months after surgery, the patient reported marked clinical improvement, with the resolution of acne and a noticeable reduction in hirsutism. Total testosterone decreased to 0.50 nmol/L. DHEAS and sex hormone‐binding globulin (SHBG) were reported to have normalized, although the numerical postoperative values were not available. The available biochemical results before and 3 months after surgery are summarized in Table 1.

case_text:
A 55‐year‐old man, known to have diabetes mellitus Type 2, hypertension and kidney stones, presented to the emergency department with left flank pain that started 10 days ago. The pain was tolerable until the day of his presentation. At presentation, the left flank pain was severe and radiated to the back; it was associated with exertional dyspnea, diaphoresis, fatigue and haematuria. He also revealed that he has been experiencing chronic chest pain for 3 years. Prior medical history revealed recurrent kidney stones, for which he underwent transurethral lithotripsy.

On examination, vital signs revealed blood pressure of 104/88 mmHg, heart rate of 105 beats/min, respiratory rate of 25 breaths/min, oxygen saturation of 88% on room air, and temperature of 37.2°C.

The patient was in mild pain distress and diaphoretic with cold peripheries. Chest auscultation revealed basilar crepitations bilaterally along with a harsh pansystolic murmur at the left sternal border.

case_text:
A 43‐year‐old lifelong non‐smoker with no relevant occupational exposure was evaluated for chronic productive cough, progressive dyspnoea, and recurrent respiratory tract infections. He had experienced frequent upper and lower respiratory tract infections since childhood. Since 2017, symptoms had progressively worsened, with daily yellow‐green sputum production, intermittent low‐grade fever, and occasional haemoptysis. Bilateral bronchiectasis and situs inversus totalis were identified in 2017, when a clinical diagnosis of Kartagener syndrome was considered. Confirmatory PCD testing, including genetic testing, was not performed at that time because of technical and financial constraints, and the diagnosis remained presumptive until molecular testing became available. A formal PICADAR score was not recorded, as this screening tool was not routinely incorporated into the diagnostic pathway at our centre at that time. In 2021, microbiologically confirmed pulmonary tuberculosis was diagnosed and successfully treated. During the preceding 12 months, he had experienced five respiratory exacerbations, three requiring hospitalisation. He had fathered six biological children conceived without assisted reproductive techniques. There was no family history of bronchiectasis, laterality abnormalities, or infertility.

His medical history also included bilateral nasal polyposis, chronic pansinusitis, sinus tachycardia, and persistent non‐reversible airflow obstruction. He had been repeatedly evaluated by ENT specialists since 2017. In 2022, functional endoscopic sinus surgery, septoplasty, and polypectomy were recommended during separate assessments, but the patient declined the proposed procedures despite counselling. Conservative management included intranasal corticosteroid therapy. With subsequent deterioration in respiratory status, elective ENT surgery was considered high risk.

He was receiving long‐term oxygen therapy at 1.5–2 L/min. During an acute exacerbation, oxygen saturation was approximately 60% on room air and improved to 86%–90% with supplemental oxygen. Laboratory testing showed mild leukocytosis (12 × 109/L), neutrophilia (84%), and a C‐reactive protein level of 15 mg/L. Arterialised capillary blood gas analysis demonstrated hypoxemic respiratory failure without hypercapnia (pO2 6.17 kPa; pCO2 5.67 kPa). Post‐bronchodilator spirometry showed severe non‐reversible airflow obstruction, with FEV1 37% predicted, FVC 51% predicted, and an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.64. Residual volume was 164% predicted, indicating marked air trapping, while diffusing capacity was preserved.

Chest imaging demonstrated dextrocardia, situs inversus totalis, diffuse bilateral mosaic attenuation, and extensive cystic and tubular bronchiectasis. Changes were most pronounced in the left upper lobe and lingula and posterior right lower lobe, with bronchial wall thickening, intraluminal secretions, and adjacent fibrotic and inflammatory parenchymal abnormalities (Figures 1 and 2).

Bronchoalveolar lavage performed in 2017 yielded mucoid Pseudomonas aeruginosa . An initial eradication attempt with intravenous ceftazidime and amikacin was followed by long‐term inhaled colistin. P. aeruginosa was repeatedly recovered from subsequent respiratory specimens, consistent with chronic airway infection. Follow‐up sputum smear microscopy, mycobacterial culture, and Xpert MTB/RIF showed no evidence of recurrent or active mycobacterial infection. Sweat chloride was < 30 mmol/L, making cystic fibrosis unlikely, and Aspergillus fumigatus sensitisation was negative.

The combination of childhood‐onset sinopulmonary disease, chronic sinonasal disease, extensive bronchiectasis, and situs inversus totalis remained strongly suggestive of PCD with a Kartagener phenotype. In September 2025, whole‐exome sequencing identified a homozygous pathogenic frameshift variant in DNAH5 (NM_001369.3:c.5563dup; p.(Ile1855Asnfs*6)), exon 34, establishing the molecular diagnosis of DNAH5‐associated PCD.

Management included airway‐clearance therapy, inhaled hypertonic saline, long‐term oxygen therapy, inhaled colistin, and susceptibility‐guided systemic antibiotics during exacerbations. Long‐term azithromycin 500 mg three times weekly was introduced during the most recent year because of recurrent bronchiectasis exacerbations. Triple inhaled therapy (ICS/LABA/LAMA), previously initiated for severe persistent non‐reversible airflow obstruction under a working diagnosis of COPD, was continued; no concomitant asthma had been documented. During 9 months of follow‐up after molecular diagnosis, lung function remained stable, although exacerbation frequency did not decrease in the context of inconsistent adherence to inhaled colistin. Lobectomy was considered but not undertaken because bilateral disease, severe airflow obstruction, and chronic hypoxemic respiratory failure conferred a high perioperative risk.

case_text:
Proximal MCN neuropathy has several potential causes; its presence should not automatically be attributed to a CBM variant. Pećina and Bojanić reported exercise-related symptoms attributed to the CBM region that improved after activity cessation. Structural lesions represent another potential cause, as illustrated by a proximal humeral osteochondroma and a later report of humeral osteophyte compression. Such cases support investigation of a focal lesion when the clinical course is persistent or atypical; they do not establish a morphology-specific entrapment risk.

A proximal MCN lesion may cause weakness or wasting of the biceps and brachialis muscles, together with sensory disturbances in the lateral forearm. Severe pain may occur, as in the traumatic case reported by Yilmaz et al.. Swain distinguished mixed motor–sensory presentations from distal lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve symptoms. In a larger retrospective series, O’Gorman et al. identified 32 MCN neuropathies and five isolated lateral antebrachial cutaneous neuropathies; pain and sensory disturbance were more common presenting complaints than weakness. Preserved gross elbow flexion therefore does not exclude MCN dysfunction.

Although anatomical variation may plausibly modify the mechanical environment of the nerve, current clinical evidence does not demonstrate that any specific CBM type or R1–R3 route independently predicts entrapment. The Type–Route framework should therefore be used to describe anatomy and generate mechanistic hypotheses rather than to assign an established neuropathy risk.

Such cases support investigation of a focal lesion when the clinical course is persistent or atypical; they do not establish a morphology-specific entrapment risk.
A proximal MCN lesion may cause weakness or wasting of the biceps and brachialis muscles, together with sensory disturbances in the lateral forearm.
Severe pain may occur, as in the traumatic case reported by Yilmaz et al..
Swain distinguished mixed motor–sensory presentations from distal lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve symptoms.

In a larger retrospective series, O’Gorman et al. identified 32 MCN neuropathies and five isolated lateral antebrachial cutaneous neuropathies; pain and sensory disturbance were more common presenting complaints than weakness.
Preserved gross elbow flexion therefore does not exclude MCN dysfunction.

Although anatomical variation may plausibly modify the mechanical environment of the nerve, current clinical evidence does not demonstrate that any specific CBM type or R1–R3 route independently predicts entrapment.
The Type–Route framework should therefore be used to describe anatomy and generate mechanistic hypotheses rather than to assign an established neuropathy risk.
title: Coracobrachialis Morphology and Musculocutaneous Nerve Course: A Type–Route Framework for Imaging, Entrapment, and Coracoid Surgery— A Structured Narrative Review

case_text:
Candida chorioamnionitis is difficult to diagnose, because clinical findings are nonspecific and maternal fever is uncommon. In the review by Maki et al., preterm labour was the most frequent manifestation and fever was recorded in only 13% of cases. The main diagnostic task is not detecting Candida but determining whether it has crossed the maternal–fetal barrier and is associated with inflammation. Vaginal culture is useful for exploring colonization or vulvovaginal candidiasis, but has poor positive predictive value for intra-amniotic infection because Candida in the vagina is common and the prevalence of invasive disease is infrequent. A positive result (e.g., after PPROM) should therefore be interpreted as a possible source rather than proof of ascending infection. PCR and other nucleic-acid tests increase the analytical sensitivity, but do not distinguish colonization from invasive disease. Vaginal Candida deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) cannot verify upper-genital-tract infection, and even amniotic-fluid DNA requires interpretation alongside viability, anatomical localization and inflammatory findings.

Therefore, investigating co-colonization is of much greater importance, particularly with regard to Str. agalactiae, Ureaplasma, and Mycoplasma.

Amniotic-fluid assessment can provide direct evidence of intra-amniotic infection and may include culture, microscopy, leukocytes, glucose and inflammatory biomarkers such as IL-6, IL-8 and MMP-8, however, amniocentesis is an invasive procedure; it cannot be repeated indefinitely due to the risk of superinfection and miscarriage. Microbial invasion and sterile intra-amniotic inflammation are distinct entities, so microbiological evaluation and inflammatory assessment should be interpreted together.

Amniotic-fluid culture confirms the presence of viable microorganisms because it confirms the presence of viable microorganisms, allows species identification and can support susceptibility testing. Limitations include prior antimicrobial exposure, low pathogen load and delayed results. Species identification is particularly relevant for non-albicans Candida species.

Direct microscopy can provide rapid evidence of fungal elements, but this requires trained personnel. Historical reports depict prenatal diagnosis of Candida chorioamnionitis by amniocentesis and direct examination, including potassium hydroxide preparation. Candida hyphae have also been illustrated in amniotic-fluid sludge, particularly in pregnancies with PPROM and intrauterine devices. Amniotic-fluid sludge near the internal os of the uterine cervix is associated with intra-amniotic infection and preterm delivery. Although not Candida-specific, fungal elements within sludge may provide an important clue in a high-acuity clinical setting. Ultrasound examination cannot give the microbiological diagnosis. IL-6, MMP-8 and related amniotic-fluid biomarkers can indicate intra-amniotic inflammation, but no Candida-specific thresholds have been implemented. They should therefore be regarded as measurements of inflammatory activity rather than fungal-specific tests. Placental histopathology can point to acute chorioamnionitis, fetal inflammatory response and fungal invasion. Periodic acid–Schiff (PAS) or Grocott–Gömöri’s methenamine silver (GMS) stains can highlight yeast and hyphal structures. Candida in the umbilical cord with funisitis is particularly strong evidence of fetal exposure. However, umbilical cord sampling before the labor is not a routinely available diagnostic method in most obstetric centers and the risk of complications is also high. Publications cited in the literature reference are postnatal histopathological analyses and studies.

Histological and microbiological inflammation entails varying degrees of severity and different clinical significance. The placenta may show chorioamnionitis without recoverable organisms, whereas microorganisms may be detected with limited histological inflammation. The strongest diagnosis is therefore the presence of Candida in an appropriate compartment, inflammation compatible with this phenomenon and the characteristic pathology (Figure 3).

Microbiological culture and histology present diagnostic challenges (Table 4) when the microbial load is low or prior treatment has reduced the viability, as the detection of contamination and non-viable DNA can confound the findings.

The sensitivity of clinical criteria based on fever, tachycardia, uterine tenderness, and leukocytosis is very low for microbiologically confirmed intra-amniotic infection.. The low frequency of fever in reported Candida chorioamnionitis indicates that clinical suspicion should not depend on maternal fever alone. Suspicion should increase in very early preterm labor or PPROM when retained IUCD, cervical cerclage, IVF/embryo transfer, recent invasive procedures, recurrent Candidiasis, amniotic-fluid sludge, unusual placental lesions or neonatal fungal infection are present. These factors lower the threshold for targeted testing but do not establish causality. The management of suspected intra-uterine fungal infections follows a structured, step-by-step clinical approach to differentiate simple colonization from active, high-risk upper-genital tract disease (Figure 4).

case_text: A 32-year-old female with NF1 has been followed at a tertiary cancer center for locally recurrent PCC. At age 22, she had an adrenalectomy for a 5 cm symptomatic PCC. At age 28, she underwent a second surgery—right adrenalectomy and a retroperitoneal lymph node dissection for a 4.5 cm recurrent PCC with extra-adrenal extension, positive margins, and lymphovascular invasion with 23 positive lymph nodes. Within a year after the second surgery, she had a 1.9 cm mass in the right adrenalectomy bed adjacent to the liver and abutting the inferior vena cava and duodenum. Surgery was deemed not feasible due to multiple prior surgeries with consequential adhesions in the surgical bed and the inability to achieve negative surgical margins. External beam radiation therapy was not recommended due to the risk of collateral damage to adjacent structures, especially the duodenum. The MIBG therapy was not available, despite MIBG uptake in the recurrent lesion. Neither DOTATATE positron emission tomography/computed tomography (CT) nor somatostatin receptor scintigraphy was performed. Systemic therapy was discussed; however, given potential toxicity, the patient elected surveillance. The patient was treated with terazosin 2 mg once daily, resulting in improvement in adrenergic symptoms.

case_text:
The patient was a 14‐year‐old female with a body mass index (BMI) in the obese range who had no known family history of thrombosis. Two months prior to the current presentation, she had been hospitalized for right lower extremity deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and acute pulmonary embolism (PTE), and was discharged on warfarin. During the same hospitalization, a positive lupus anticoagulant (LA) test was reported once, and the test was scheduled to be repeated after 13 weeks to confirm the diagnosis of antiphospholipid syndrome (APS).

Six days prior to the current presentation, despite the positive LA test result, the patient's treatment was inappropriately changed from warfarin and low‐dose aspirin to rivaroxaban without adequate specialist supervision. Following the alteration in medication, the patient exhibited a progressive exacerbation of dyspnea, weakness, dizziness, fever, and a worsening cough. This indicated an absence of efficacy in the anticoagulant therapy and the occurrence of recurrent thrombosis.

Upon admission, the patient exhibited tachycardia (pulse rate of 130 beats per minute), fever (temperature of 37.7°C), and severe respiratory distress. The patient's blood pressure was documented at 100/60 mmHg. The patient was promptly admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU).

case_text:
A 49-year-old perimenopausal woman presented with a painless palpable mass in the right breast that she had first noticed one month earlier. She denied nipple discharge or use of hormonal therapy, and her family history was negative for breast and gynecologic malignancies. Eight years prior, the patient underwent surgical excision of a fibroadenoma of the left breast. Her medical history was otherwise unremarkable. Clinical examination revealed a firm mass, approximately 1 cm in diameter, at the border of the inner quadrants of the right breast, without overlying skin changes, nipple retraction, or discharge. No axillary lymphadenopathy was detected, and the contralateral breast was unremarkable.

MMG demonstrated an ACR breast density category B. A round mass measuring 1.1 × 0.8 cm, with partially obscured margins and a density similar to the surrounding fibroglandular tissue, was identified at the border of the inner quadrants of the right breast (Figure 1). No associated microcalcifications, architectural distortion, or skin thickening were observed. The MMG examination was assigned a BI-RADS 0.

Seven days later, the multiparametric breast US was performed using a Logiq Fortis system (GE Healthcare, Chicago, IL, USA) with a 6–15 MHz linear transducer. It revealed an oval hypoechoic mass measuring 1.1 × 0.8 cm, located at the 3 o’clock position, approximately 2 cm from the nipple. The lesion exhibited a non-parallel orientation, microlobulated to angular margins, and mixed posterior acoustic features, comprising both shadowing and enhancement (Figure 2a). No suspicious axillary lymph nodes were found. Strain elastography demonstrated a soft mass, corresponding to a Tsukuba elasticity score of 1; however, quantitative assessment (strain ratio and E/B ratio) was not performed (Figure 2b). Color (CDI) and power Doppler imaging (PDI) showed peripheral vascularity (Figure 3a,b), while microvascular imaging (MVI) and B-flow imaging identified a penetrating intralesional vessel (Figure 3c,d). Based on these sonographic features, the lesion was upgraded to BI-RADS 4, and breast MRI was performed after 10 days.

Breast MRI was performed on a 1.5T uMR 570 system (United Imaging Healthcare Co., Shanghai, China). It demonstrated a 1.1 × 0.8 cm oval mass with irregular margins. The mass was isointense relative to fibroglandular tissue on fat-suppressed (FS) T1-weighted (T1W) images and T2-weighted (T2W) images, without signs of perifocal edema (Figure 4a,b). Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) demonstrated restricted diffusion (b values 50 and 600), with an apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) value of 1.04 × 10−3 mm2/s (Figure 4c,d). Following gadolinium administration (12 mL of gadoterate meglumine), marked background parenchymal enhancement attributable to fibrocystic changes was present. The mass showed heterogeneous, rapid initial enhancement and delayed washout, consistent with a type III kinetic curve (Figure 5). Application of the Kaiser score algorithm yielded a score of 8 (absent spiculations, delayed phase washout, heterogeneous internal enhancement). No suspicious non-mass enhancement or additional suspicious lesions were identified in either breast. The MRI examination was classified as BI-RADS 5.

A US-guided core needle biopsy was subsequently performed with a 14-gauge needle, yielding six tissue specimens, clip placement, and no post-biopsy complications. Histopathological examination established the diagnosis of a breast ductal adenoma (B2 lesion) (Figure 6). Following multidisciplinary evaluation, conservative management with routine imaging surveillance was recommended. The mass remained stable at 6-month follow-up.

case_text:
A 47‐year‐old woman, married and multiparous, presented with 1‐month postmenopausal bleeding. ThinPrep cytology test (TCT) revealed atypical glandular cells of undetermined significance (AGC‐NOS) and positivity for HPV Type 18. She had a history of hypertension, with no family history of malignancy. Colposcopy identified a 1‐cm cervical nodule, which was confirmed as adenocarcinoma on biopsy (Figure 1A). The serum carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) level was elevated to 14.2 ng/mL, whereas all other tumor markers were within the normal range. Contrast‐enhanced MRI revealed multiple small cystic structures without a definite mass in the cervix (Figure 2A). Contrast‐enhanced CT demonstrated a heterogenous cervix and circumferential wall thickening at the descending‐sigmoid junction, with mesenteric fat blurring and an enlarged mesenteric lymph node (LN) (Figure 2B). For financial reasons, the patient declined to undergo a positron emission tomography–computed tomography (PET‐CT) scan. The fecal occult blood test was positive. Colonoscopy identified a mass at 35 cm from the anal verge causing significant luminal narrowing (Figure 1B), confirmed as colon adenocarcinoma on biopsy (Figure 3A). Immunohistochemistry (IHC) revealed diffuse positive expression of p16, CK7, and PAX8 in cervical tumor cells, whereas colorectal cancer markers, including CK20, CDX2, and SATB2, were negative (Figure 4B–D). Colon adenocarcinoma cells were positive for CK20, but negative for CK7 and PAX8 (Figure 3B–D). Collectively, these findings confirm the diagnosis of synchronous primary malignancies with UAC at FIGO 2018 Stage IB1 (clinical T1b1N0M0) and CRC at clinical stage T3N1M0. Following the MDT discussion, simultaneous laparoscopic radical hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo‐oophorectomy, pelvic lymphadenectomy, and radical left hemicolectomy were performed. Figure 5 shows the distribution of surgical TROCAR. Operative time was 240 minutes with 50 mL of blood loss. Postoperatively, bowel function returned on Day 1. The patient was discharged on Day 5, and no postoperative complication meeting Clavien–Dindo Grade I or higher occurred. Macroscopic examination revealed a 0.5‐cm ulcer on the anterior wall of cervical canal (Figure 6), and a grayish‐white, firm mass within the lumen, measuring 5.0 × 3.5 × 1.0 cm on the resected colon, respectively (Figure 7). Final pathology revealed moderately differentiated HPV‐associated UAC with a Silva Type A pattern, invading the inner third of the stroma without lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI) or LNs metastasis (pT1b1N0M0), and moderately differentiated colon adenocarcinoma with mucinous component penetrating the muscularis propria with LVSI, nerve invasion, and 4/13 positive LNs (pT3N2aM0). Peritoneal washing cytology was negative. The surgical margins of both the cervical and colon specimens were negative.

We performed IHC staining for PD‐L1 and mismatch repair (MMR) proteins on both tumors. PD‐L1 showed negativity with a combined positive score (CPS) of < 1, and both tumors exhibited proficient mismatch repair (pMMR) with intact expression. HER‐2 in IHC staining was negative in UAC, moderately positive (2+) in CRC but subsequent fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) proved negative with an amplification score of < 2.2. Genetic testing revealed a germline nonpathogenic KIT p.T304A mutation. No significant somatic mutations were detected in UAC, whereas CRC harbored KRAS p.A146T, TP53 p.R282W, and APC p.E1322 mutations. Given the absence of high‐ or medium‐risk factors, adjuvant therapy was not indicated postoperatively for UAC. For CRC, the patient received eight cycles of the CapeOX regimen, consisting of capecitabine 1000 mg/m2 orally twice daily for 14 days combined with oxaliplatin 130 mg/m2 intravenously on Day 1, repeated every three weeks. The regimen was well‐tolerated, without significant adverse events. At the 12‐month follow‐up after treatment completion, no evidence of recurrence was observed for either malignancy. Written informed consent for publication of the clinical details and images was obtained from the patient.

case_text:
A 35‐year‐old woman was referred for evaluation of a progressively symptomatic right inguinal swelling present for approximately 3 months. She reported intermittent discomfort and a sensation of local pressure, exacerbated by prolonged standing and physical activity. She denied fever, gastrointestinal symptoms, urinary complaints, or prior similar episodes.

Her medical history was unremarkable. She had no previous abdominal or pelvic surgeries, no known drug allergies, and was not taking regular medications. Menstrual cycles were regular, and obstetric history was noncontributory.

On gynecological examination, the uterus was anteverted and normal in size, with no adnexal tenderness or pelvic masses. Inspection and palpation of the right inguinal region revealed a soft, nonreducible, mildly tender cystic mass measuring ~3 cm in diameter along the course of the inguinal canal. The overlying skin was normal, and the mass did not enlarge during the Valsalva maneuver.

Doppler ultrasonography demonstrated a well‐defined anechoic cystic lesion measuring 30 × 22 × 30 mm3 in the right inguinal region without internal septations, solid components, or vascular flow (Figure 1). No pelvic abnormalities were identified. Dynamic ultrasonography during the Valsalva maneuver was not performed.

For further anatomical characterization, contrast‐enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis was performed. CT demonstrated a thin‐walled fluid‐attenuation lesion measuring 4.0 cm in transverse diameter, 2.2 cm in anteroposterior diameter, and 5.0 cm in craniocaudal extension along the right inguinal canal, without bowel herniation or radiological communication with the peritoneal cavity (Figure 2). CT was selected to define the lesion’s extent and relationship with the inguinal canal for surgical planning; because it provided adequate anatomical characterization, additional magnetic resonance imaging was not considered necessary. Based on the clinical and imaging findings, a cyst of the canal of Nuck was suspected preoperatively.

Given the patient’s symptoms and the risk of diagnostic uncertainty with conservative management, surgical treatment was recommended.

The operation was performed by the gynaecological team in collaboration with a general surgeon under general anesthesia through an ~2‐cm right inguinal incision. Layered dissection allowed the identification of the internal inguinal ring and an ~4‐cm cyst containing clear citrine fluid (Figure 3).

The cyst was completely enucleated and sent for histopathological examination. The peritoneum and fascia were closed, followed by subcutaneous approximation and absorbable intradermal skin closure. No mesh repair was performed, as no associated inguinal hernia requiring prosthetic repair was identified.

The postoperative course was uneventful, and the patient was discharged on postoperative day one. Histopathological examination of the excised specimen, completed after discharge, demonstrated a benign cystic lesion lined by mesothelial cells, confirming the diagnosis of a cyst of the canal of Nuck (Figure 4). No endometriosis, significant inflammation, hemorrhage, atypia, or malignancy were identified. At a 1‐month follow‐up, clinical examination and ultrasonography showed complete symptom resolution and no evidence of recurrence.

She reported intermittent discomfort and a sensation of local pressure, exacerbated by prolonged standing and physical activity.
She denied fever, gastrointestinal symptoms, urinary complaints, or prior similar episodes.
Her medical history was unremarkable.
She had no previous abdominal or pelvic surgeries, no known drug allergies, and was not taking regular medications.
Menstrual cycles were regular, and obstetric history was noncontributory.
On gynecological examination, the uterus was anteverted and normal in size, with no adnexal tenderness or pelvic masses.
Inspection and palpation of the right inguinal region revealed a soft, nonreducible, mildly tender cystic mass measuring ~3 cm in diameter along the course of the inguinal canal.
The overlying skin was normal, and the mass did not enlarge during the Valsalva maneuver.

Doppler ultrasonography demonstrated a well‐defined anechoic cystic lesion measuring 30 × 22 × 30 mm3 in the right inguinal region without internal septations, solid components, or vascular flow (Figure 1).
No pelvic abnormalities were identified.
Dynamic ultrasonography during the Valsalva maneuver was not performed.
For further anatomical characterization, contrast‐enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis was performed.

CT demonstrated a thin‐walled fluid‐attenuation lesion measuring 4.0 cm in transverse diameter, 2.2 cm in anteroposterior diameter, and 5.0 cm in craniocaudal extension along the right inguinal canal, without bowel herniation or radiological communication with the peritoneal cavity (Figure 2).

case_text:
A 77-year-old man presented to a tertiary teaching hospital in Australia with less than a day of severe epigastric pain, diaphoresis, and vomiting. His background included hypertension, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, and diverticular disease. There was no history of previous abdominal surgeries, cholelithiasis, biliary symptoms, or alcohol use.

On presentation, he was haemodynamically stable (blood pressure 146/102, heart rate 67) but was tachypnoeic (respiratory rate 30/min) requiring 4 l/min of supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs to maintain saturation of 95%. He was afebrile. Abdominal examination revealed a soft abdomen, with tenderness localized to the epigastrium and left upper quadrant but without signs of peritonism.

Initial laboratory investigations revealed a lipase of 11 827 U/l, white cell count 17.9 × 109/l, C-reactive protein 6 mg/l, total bilirubin 26 umol/l, lactate 3.2 mmol/l, glucose 8.2 mmol/l, AST 50 U/l, and LDH 2.7 mmol/l. An admission Ranson score of 2 stratified his condition as unlikely to be severe pancreatitis. There was no pleural effusion on admission chest X-ray. Admission Bedside Index of Severity for Acute Pancreatitis (BISAP) score of 2 identified him as at increased risk of severe disease and mortality. Despite the low Ranson score, an early ICU referral was made due to the overall clinical picture.

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen at ~3.5 h from onset of symptoms demonstrated imaging features of acute pancreatitis, with pancreatic enlargement and peripancreatic inflammatory changes (Fig. 1). The imaging was in keeping with acute interstitial oedematous pancreatitis with no necrosis. Based on the initial imaging findings, the pancreas demonstrated features consistent with Balthazar grade C, corresponding to a modified CT severity index of 2 (mild disease).

Evidence-based management for acute pancreatitis was instituted comprising close haemodynamic monitoring, aggressive crystalloid fluid resuscitation, protein pump inhibitor therapy, analgesia, antiemetics, and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with early surgical and intensive care unit review, as well as involving the hepatobiliary surgical team. Despite an initially low predicted risk of severe pancreatitis, the patient was admitted to the ICU given his early presentation and potential for deterioration. Subsequently, clinical concern for abdominal compartment syndrome, evolving respiratory failure, and a rising lactate prompted endotracheal intubation.

Overnight, the patient developed severe systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) contributing to worsening multiorgan failure with circulatory shock requiring escalating vasopressor support, acute kidney injury (with a peak creatinine of 189 umol/l and an eGFR of 29 ml/min/1.73 m2), and rising lactate (peaking at 7.7 mmol/l). Hyperbilirubinemia (149 umol/l) prompted investigation with an abdominal ultrasound which demonstrated a distended gallbladder containing sludge, mild gallbladder wall thickening (4 mm), and concern for intramural gas and possible emphysematous cholecystitis. No definite cholelithiasis or biliary duct dilatation was identified.

The patient’s significant clinical deterioration prompted a repeat CT scan which was performed less than 24 h after the initial study. This demonstrated severe necrotizing emphysematous pancreatitis with gas locules replacing almost all the pancreatic parenchyma, widespread pelvic free fluid, and significant pneumoperitoneum (Fig. 2). Despite the presence of significant pneumoperitoneum, contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated no contrast extravasation to suggest an associated gastrointestinal perforation or fistula. The intra-abdominal gas appeared to originate within the pancreatic parenchyma, with subsequent extension into the peritoneal cavity accounting for the pneumoperitoneum. This likely reflected the progression of pancreatic necrosis accompanied by gas production from intra-abdominal anaerobic organisms. The CT findings were in keeping with a Balthazar grade E with almost 95% necrosis that yielded a modified CT severity index 10 and re-classified his disease as severe.

Following discussion with the hepatopancreatobiliary service, the patient was transferred to a quaternary referral centre with the capacity to provide both image-guided drainage and emergency surgical intervention. In view of the patient’s progressive deterioration despite maximal intensive care support, characterized by escalating inotropic requirements, worsening lactic acidosis, deteriorating pH and progressive multiorgan failure, emergency exploratory laparotomy, and pancreatic necrosectomy were undertaken as salvage treatment, with the aims of achieving sepsis source control and excluding additional intra-abdominal pathology not evident on CT. Worsening abdominal compartment syndrome provided a further indication for urgent operative intervention, as percutaneous drainage alone would not adequately address this complication. Following discussion with the patient’s family, the decision to proceed with surgery was made collaboratively, with the aim of maximizing the patient’s chance of survival in the context of his previously good premorbid health.

Intra-operative findings included a necrotizing haemorrhagic pancreas (predominantly involving the body and tail), a gangrenous gallbladder, extensive pancreatic ascites, and retroperitoneal fluid. No gastrointestinal perforation or fistula was identified. Cholecystectomy, evacuation of retroperitoneal fluid, and extensive pancreatic necrosectomy were undertaken (Fig. 3). A laparostomy was performed with an AbThera™ dressing.

Postoperatively the patient remained critically unwell with worsening multiorgan failure, increasing noradrenaline requirements to 18 ml/h and a serum lactate reaching 13 mmol/l. Despite maximal ICU support, the patient unfortunately continued to deteriorate and he died ~48 h after presenting to hospital.

Clinical evidence, though more limited than preclinical data, has shown promising outcomes. However, the translation of these results into standardized medical practice faces significant hurdles. Unlike standard pharmacology, where active ingredients are precisely quantified, clinical trials for Shilajit are complicated by the inherent heterogeneity of the source material. Variations in altitude, purification methods, and geographic origin result in vastly different concentrations of fulvic acid and minerals between study cohorts, making cross-study comparisons difficult. Furthermore, dosage protocols remain highly variable, ranging from 100 mg to 2000 mg daily, often without established pharmacokinetic profiles for different populations. Recent randomized control trials have demonstrated that Shilajit supplementation can enhance overall sexual function in women, improving desire and arousal without significant adverse effects. In middle-aged women, supplementation was found to improve skin microperfusion and upregulate genes linked to extracellular matrix (ECM) maintenance, suggesting its potential for vascular health and skin aging. Furthermore, its use has been linked to the retention of muscular strength and improved adaptation to exercise in human subjects. However, robust clinical trials for many traditional indications, such as diabetes and Alzheimer’s, are still required to establish definitive therapeutic efficacy.

In addition to standard clinical trials, published case reports provide critical insights into the real-world safety and tolerability profile of Shilajit. Notably, Losa et al. reported a unique case where Shilajit served as a potential cofactor in exercise-induced anaphylaxis, highlighting that while hypersensitivity reactions to purified Shilajit remain exceptionally rare, individual susceptibility and physiological triggers like exertion must be considered during clinical risk assessment. Furthermore, regarding organ-specific safety, current clinical evidence demonstrates a reassuring lack of direct hepatotoxicity associated with isolated, purified Shilajit preparations. This stands in stark contrast to clinical findings for several other widely used traditional herbal supplements, such as ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) and Tinospora cordifolia (Giloy), which have been increasingly documented in drug-induced liver injury (DILI) registries and case series. The distinct safety profile of Shilajit regarding liver function underscores the importance of proper purification and standardization to eliminate toxic contaminants while maintaining its therapeutic safety.
