case_text:
A 9‐year‐old boy of Northern European ancestry presented with recurrent episodes of polyarthralgia involving multiple joints, including the shoulders, wrists, elbows, hips, and knees, accompanied by high‐grade fever. Each episode lasted 7–10 days, began with mild symptoms, resolved spontaneously, and was unresponsive to acetaminophen or NSAIDs. He also experienced intermittent small, nonerythematous, nonpruritic bumps on his abdomen, but no other systemic symptoms such as swelling in the joints, morning stiffness, rashes, Raynaud’s phenomenon, mouth sores, or serositis. He had no significant family history of autoimmune or autoinflammatory disease.

During attacks, C‐reactive protein was elevated and normocytic anemia was present; both improved between attacks (Table 1). Mild leukocytosis (11.6 × 109/L) was documented during one attack. Antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, and cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody were negative. Ferritin measured during an attack was 123 mcg/L. A cytokine panel, including Interleukin‐18, was not performed.

Clinical germline testing used the “MAYO Autoinflammatory Disorders—Custom Analysis,” performed and reported by Variantyx, Inc. on the Genomic Unity® Custom Analysis platform; Mayo Clinic Laboratories extracted and stored the DNA. Short‐read whole‐genome sequencing data (Genomic Unity® Whole Genome Analysis, platform Version 3.17.5.1) were interpreted against a clinician‐selected custom list of approximately 114 genes, including TNFRSF1A and MEFV; genes outside the list were masked, and off‐list coverage was not guaranteed. The laboratory specified a minimum on‐target depth of 30x and did not report variant calls below 8x. Whole‐genome sequencing‐based structural and copy‐number analysis included deletions, duplications, mobile‐element insertions, and inversions, with reduced sensitivity for 50–300 bp events. Sanger sequencing was not used; the report states that orthogonal confirmation, when required, is performed using Oxford Nanopore Technologies PromethION 24 long‐read sequencing. Testing identified heterozygous TNFRSF1ANM_001065.4:c.305G > A (NP_001056.1:p.Cys102Tyr) and MEFV NM_000243.3:p.(Glu148Gln). No other affected family member was reported, and segregation testing was not available.

Given the recurrent inflammatory attacks, clinically compatible phenotype, and molecular findings, canakinumab was initiated. The patient achieved complete symptom control and normalization of inflammatory markers. At 6 months, he remained flare‐free, with resolution of the prior anemia and C‐reactive protein elevation.

To place genotype–phenotype variability in context, we reviewed two additional patients from our Autoinflammatory Clinic who carried TNFRSF1A cysteine substitutions (Table 2). One patient carried p.(Cys125Gly), an extracellular cysteine‐rich Domain 2 substitution, and had intermittent fever and gastrointestinal symptoms; the other carried p.(Cys395Trp), which lies in the intracellular death domain, and had recurrent infections, intermittent fever, and night sweats. Because these substitutions affect different structural regions, they should not be interpreted as mechanistically equivalent to p.(Cys102Tyr). We also observed a separate 6‐year‐old girl with severe persistent asthma and TNFRSF1A p.(Arg121Gln); after TRAPS was diagnosed and canakinumab monotherapy was started, asthma symptoms resolved and treatment was de‐escalated (Figure 1).

case_text: A 60‐year‐old gentleman presented with cryptogenic cirrhosis in January 2013. In March, he was admitted with refractory ascites & hepatorenal syndrome, a presentation consistent with decompensated (Child‐Pugh class C) cirrhosis. He underwent living‐donor liver transplantation outside Pakistan in April 2013, receiving a graft from a living related donor. As the transplant surgery itself was performed abroad, formal pre‐transplant quantification of the Model for End‐Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score, serum albumin, and the exact volume of pre‐transplant ascites were not part of the records transferred to our institution for this retrospective report. Postoperative course was uneventful. He was started on tacrolimus and prednisolone initially. Later on he was switched to cyclosporine and mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) with a suspicion of graft rejection on deranged liver function tests (LFTs). His LFTs improved, i.e., this immunosuppressive switch and its associated LFT derangement resolved before, rather than after, the onset of ascites. Dose adjustments were made empirically against serial LFTs rather than by fixed protocol; the exact trough levels and cumulative dosing from this period could not be retrieved given the decade‐long interval since the index admission, but the temporal sequence argues against delayed wound healing from this switch as a major contributor to the later ascites. In June 2013, he presented with ascites. Ascitic fluid detailed report (D/R) showed high serum‐ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) high protein lymphocytic ascites.

case_text:
A 74-year-old woman was referred to our hospital after a pelvic mass in the pouch of Douglas was incidentally detected during a preoperative examination for orthopedic surgery at another hospital. She was asymptomatic. Laboratory investigations revealed a mildly elevated serum cancer antigen 125 (CA125) level of 37.2 U/mL, whereas carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA; 2.5 ng/mL) and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 (CA19-9; 2.0 U/mL) levels were within the normal ranges.

MRI revealed a cystic lesion in the pouch of Douglas associated with localized peritoneal thickening, raising suspicion for ovarian cancer or primary peritoneal carcinoma with peritoneal dissemination (Fig. 1A, 1B). Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a 46-mm pelvic mass adjacent to the uterus accompanied by a moderate amount of pelvic ascites (Fig. 1C). No enlargement or cystic lesion of the appendix was identified on CT (Fig. 1D). The appendiceal primary lesion was not identified on preoperative MRI. Upper and lower gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed no evidence of a primary gastrointestinal malignancy.

Diagnostic laparoscopy was performed to establish a definitive diagnosis. Intraoperatively, gelatinous mucin was found predominantly within the pelvis, with a small amount surrounding the appendix (Fig. 2A). No obvious lesions were identified on the liver surface, omentum, small bowel, or small-bowel mesentery. A peritoneal biopsy obtained at the beginning of the procedure was submitted for frozen-section examination; however, no tumor was identified. Because ovarian cancer or primary peritoneal carcinoma was suspected preoperatively and a uterine leiomyoma was also present, a total hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy had been planned and were subsequently performed. During the hysterectomy, a peritoneal nodule was identified in the pouch of Douglas and was excised for a second frozen-section examination (Fig. 2B). Histopathological examination revealed a mucinous tumor, and if the lesion was of gynecologic origin, a tumor of at least borderline malignancy was suspected. Therefore, a partial omentectomy was additionally performed. Subsequent careful inspection of the appendix revealed a grossly unremarkable appendix with a small amount of adherent gelatinous mucin (Fig. 2C). Further inspection of the appendiceal tip identified a fistulous opening with adherent mucin (Fig. 2D), raising suspicion of an appendiceal origin of the disease. An intraoperative consultation with the general surgery team was requested, and an appendectomy was subsequently performed during the same operation. Ascitic fluid was also collected for cytological examination.

Histopathological examination of the appendix revealed a LAMN (Fig. 3A, 3B). At the appendiceal tip, perforation of the appendiceal wall was identified, corresponding to the fistulous opening observed intraoperatively (Fig. 3C). The neoplasm extended into the subserosal tissue, and mucin was present on the serosal surface. Based on the presence of serosal mucin, the appendiceal lesion was classified as pT4a. Histopathological examination of the peritoneal lesion revealed mucin-containing low-grade neoplastic mucinous epithelial cells. According to the Peritoneal Surface Oncology Group International classification, the peritoneal lesion was classified as low-grade mucinous carcinoma peritonei (Fig. 3D). Ascitic fluid cytology demonstrated atypical glandular cell clusters in abundant extracellular mucin and was reported as suspicious for malignancy. No tumor involvement was identified in the uterus, bilateral adnexa, or omentum. The postoperative course was uneventful. The patient was followed postoperatively by both the Department of Gynecology and the Department of Surgery. Gynecologic follow-up was completed 3 months after surgery, while surveillance was continued by the Department of Surgery without additional treatment. Follow-up CT and tumor marker measurements showed no evidence of disease progression during the 8 months after surgery. The patient was subsequently referred to another hospital for continued surveillance.

case_text:
A 46‐year‐old female presents with chronic right lower back and buttock pain. She previously had adequate temporary relief from previous facet joint blocks but returned for lumbar medial branch nerve ablation secondary to recurring pain. Initial lumbar MRI demonstrates severe facet degenerative changes at L4–L5 and L5–S1, including joint space narrowing, facet hypertrophy, and subchondral cystic changes without any significant disc or endplate pathology (Figure 1a,b). On July 7, 2023, the patient successfully received her first treatment of right L4–L5 and L5–S1 medial branch nerve ablation with no complications (Table 1). Before the procedure, the patient rated her pain 8/10 and postprocedure rated her pain 0 with ambulation. On November 27, 2024, she returned with the same recurring episodes of pain, which she rated 8/10 (Table 1). After a significantly less effective second lumbar medial L4 and L5 branch nerve ablation compared with the first, she rated her pain 3/10 with ambulation. This shows that the patient had a diminished response with repeat RFA. On physical examination, the patient demonstrated right lumbar paraspinal tenderness to palpation with lumbar extension and rotation; however lower extremity strength and sensation were intact bilaterally without evidence of any focal neurological deficit. The source of the patient′s pain could be because of an altered lesion, scar formation, or worsening facet arthropathy. In addition, fascial and musculoskeletal sources can be considered as possible pain generators. The main fascial layer that surrounds the lumbar region is the thoracolumbar fascia as it is densely innervated with nociceptors. Patients with low back pain show reduced fascial shear‐strain, increased thickness, and decreased sliding mobility; this produces longer lasting and intense pain when stimulating the muscle or subcutaneous tissue within the thoracolumbar fascia, making this a possible pain generator. Furthermore, muscles, fascia, and ligaments can be a cause of low back pain when it comes to muscle guarding, spasm, atrophy, or referred posterior thigh pain. From this, it was decided that the next step in her plan of care would be cryoneurolysis. The patient is a perfect candidate for medial branch ablation, as shown by a previous L‐spine MRI. MRI depicts no significant disc or endplate pathology but shows an isolated degeneration of the facet degenerative changes at L4–L5 and L5–S1. When seeking a longer pain relief option, the patient returned on May 9, 2025, with 8/10 and underwent CT‐guided cryoneurolysis of the right L4 and L5 medial branch nerves (Table 1). After the patient was sterilely prepped, CT fluoroscopic guidance was utilized, and two Boston Scientific IceSphere probes (17‐gauge) were appropriately positioned at the corner of the superior articular process and transverse process junction at left L4 and L5 (Figure 2). The patient was administered Ketolag 40 mg mixed with 15 cc 0.25% bupivacaine delivered to three spots. Each location was cryoablated utilizing two cycles: 8‐minute freeze and 3 minutes of passive thaw and subsequently a 3‐minute freeze and 3‐minute passive thaw. After successful ablation, the probes were removed, and hemostasis was achieved with manual compression. The patient tolerated the procedure well with no complications. She rated her pain 3/10 with ambulation. The patient was not taking medication before or after cryoneurolysis procedure.

It is important to note that the patient had complete relief in 2023, but has had recurring worsening pain postprocedurally, with a consistent 3/10 pain with ambulation (Table 1). After receiving an incomplete RFA, cryoablation was able to achieve a meaningful pain reduction. On follow‐up visit after 1‐year postcryoneurolysis, the patient reports still having good pain relief and is able to go back to the gym without any complications. Furthermore, the procedure was well tolerated and reproducibly effective. This depicts how cryoneurolysis may serve as a viable alternative option for patients who have a history of repetitive RFA treatments.

The patient was born in Egypt at 40 weeks of gestation by cesarean delivery, with a birth weight of 2.4 kg. Her parents are consanguineous, and there were no perinatal complications. The family lives in the United Arab Emirates (UAE). In 2017, at age 8 years, she was referred to pediatric endocrinology at Dubai Hospital with short stature and primary hypothyroidism. Examination showed triangular facies, a high-arched palate, and periorbital puffiness. There was no goiter, and she was prepubertal (Tanner stage 1). Before 2017, she had attended several centers sporadically for financial reasons. No earlier endocrine results or hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) values were available. No faltering weight or diarrhea was documented in early childhood, although the limited records cannot exclude them.

Mid-parental target height was 159 cm (mother 155 cm, father 176 cm). In October 2024, at age 15 years 9 months, her height was 132.3 cm (Z = −4.69), which is far below her genetic target range. Her weight was 28.1 kg, and her body mass index was 16.05 kg/m2 (Z = −2.04) (Fig. 1). Z-scores were calculated with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 2000 growth reference. Bone age was 12 years at a chronological age of 15 years, a delay of approximately 3 standard deviations. Levothyroxine was started at age 12 years. Puberty was induced at the same age with estradiol and progesterone, and menarche occurred at age 15 years. Abdominal ultrasound showed no hepatosplenomegaly or evidence of enteropathy, and developmental milestones were not delayed. Both findings contrast with most reported ADMFD cases. Persistent pubertal delay prompted genetic panel testing in 2024.

In March 2025, at age 16 years, she presented with DKA. She was admitted to the intensive care unit and treated with intravenous insulin. After recovery, she continued on high-dose insulin therapy, consistent with new-onset T1DM. Pancreatic autoantibodies were positive, confirming an autoimmune basis (Table 1). Type 1 diabetes mellitus was her second autoimmune endocrine disease, after Hashimoto thyroiditis.

case_text:
This 3-year-old girl had no known genetic disorder or long-term health issue. The patient presented to our pediatric orthopedic clinic, and the family reported concerns regarding the abnormal shape of both thumbs, first noticed when she was one year old. The patient’s bilateral thumb deformity progressed over time, making it difficult to actively flex, oppose, or pinch using her thumbs. Figure 1 illustrates hyperextension at the interphalangeal joints and radial deviation in both thumbs.

Radiographs showed subluxation of the thumb interphalangeal joint on both sides, a nearly complete epiphyseal bracket of the proximal phalanx, and a C-shaped epiphysis. In the proximal phalanx, the epiphysis ossified in a proximal-to-distal direction. The lateral deviation angle was defined as the angle between the longitudinal axes of the distal thumb phalanx and the first metacarpal. The preoperative deviation measured approximately 63° in the left thumb and 65° in the right thumb (Figure 2). The findings were considered consistent with a stage III longitudinal epiphyseal bracket bilaterally in the four-stage radiographic scheme summarized by Choo and Mubarak. There was no family history of similar digital deformities, and no other anomalies or syndromic features were identified on clinical assessment.

Preoperative antimicrobial prophylaxis consisted of intravenous cefazolin 500 mg (30 mg/kg), administered 30 min before skin incision. The operation was performed under general anesthesia with the patient in the supine position. We began with the right thumb. An incision was made on the ulnar aspect of the thumb at the dorsal edge of the flexion crease (Figure 3).

The incision was deepened to expose the proximal phalanx; the periosteum was identified; and the neurovascular structures were protected during deeper dissection (Figure 4).

Based on preoperative X-ray planning and the estimation of angulation deformity, two K wires were inserted on the intended osteotomy site (Figure 5).

The osteotomy was planned with preoperative radiographs, and two Kirschner wires were placed as guides; intraoperative fluoroscopy was used to confirm their position relative to the ends of the longitudinal bracket (Figure 5). A powered saw was used to remove a bone wedge from the proximal thumb phalanx (Figure 6). The closing-wedge osteotomy was performed in the proximal phalanx of the thumb at the planned site localized fluoroscopically between the proximal and distal extent of the longitudinal epiphyseal bracket. An ulnar-based bone wedge was fashioned, with the osteotomy cuts oriented perpendicularly as planned to correct the radial lateral-deviation angle while avoiding disruption of the adjacent metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal articular surfaces. Following resection of the planned bone wedge, the osteotomy was closed by approximating the opposing osseous surfaces to achieve correction of the angular deformity. The corrected alignment was subsequently stabilized using transphalangeal Kirschner-wire (1.0 mm) fixation, with no residual osteotomy gap at definitive fixation.

Next, we performed physiolysis on the radial side of the phalanx using the osteotomy window (Figure 7).

Limited physiolysis was performed on the radial side of the proximal phalanx through the osteotomy window (Figure 7). The planned correction and extent of bone/physeal resection were estimated from preoperative radiographs and the angular deformity (approximately 63° in the left thumb and 65° in the right thumb). Intraoperative fluoroscopy guided the placement of localization K-wires and confirmed the proximal and distal boundaries of the longitudinal, C-shaped epiphyseal bracket. Within these localized boundaries, a limited section of the abnormal epiphysis and physeal-cartilage bridge was removed using a 2-mm curette or fine rongeur. This targeted approach was intended to minimize unnecessary disturbance of the remaining physis and adjacent articular surface; the exact depth of excision was not recorded. No fat, muscle, polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA), bone graft, or other interposition material was placed within the physiolysis defect following excision of the abnormal physeal bridge; this defect was left unfilled. The separate closing-wedge osteotomy was nevertheless definitively closed by approximation of its cut osseous surfaces, with alignment maintained by transphalangeal Kirschner-wire fixation. Definitive fixation was achieved with one Kirschner wire per thumb, introduced retrograde from the distal phalanx across the interphalangeal joint into the proximal phalanx (Figure 8).

After phalanx alignment was corrected, the osteotomy surfaces were approximated to close the wedge and secured with trans-phalangeal Kirschner-wire fixation (Figure 8). Final inspection showed a properly aligned phalanx without additional angulation or displacement. The operated thumb was dressed with soft bandages. The left thumb underwent the same procedure as the right thumb.

Postoperative follow-up was performed at three weeks (Figure 9), six weeks, and three months (Figure 10), the last recorded visit. Both Kirschner wires and the sutures were removed three weeks after surgery. Mobilization commenced after K-wire removal at three weeks following physiotherapy referral, with assisted, passive, and active range-of-motion exercises. Using the angle between the longitudinal axes of the thumb distal phalanx and first metacarpal, deviation improved from approximately 63° to 16.4° on the left and from approximately 65° to 19.1° on the right on the three-month postoperative radiographs (Figure 10D). At the final three-month clinical assessment, thumb movement and object grasp were observed clinically, and the parents reported satisfactory hand use and appearance. Interphalangeal range of motion, opposition, and pinch were not assessed with recorded quantitative measurements or a standardized functional instrument.

case_text:
The median age at presentation varies slightly between subtypes, with GCTs presenting earlier (median age of 42.5 years, range 27–77) compared to pituicytomas and SCOs, which occur predominantly at a median age of 58 (range 31–76). SCO and pituicytomas appear to affect both genders equally, while GCT show a slight female predilection (57% of 88 reported cases).

Due to their slow growth, PPTs are often incidentally diagnosed or present with non-specific symptoms resulting from progressive compression of adjacent structures. Exceptionally rare are functioning PPT with symptoms of hypercortisolism or acromegaly.

The clinical presentation of PPTs closely mimics that of non-functioning PAs. The most frequent symptoms are visual field deficits (present in 50–60% of the patients), including bitemporal hemianopia, and chronic headache (present in 25–40% of the patients). Hypopituitarism is common (22–40% of patients), resulting from direct compression of the anterior pituitary gland or the portal vessels within the pituitary stalk. Central hypogonadism is the commonest pituitary deficiency, but central adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism, and growth hormone deficiency can also be observed.

A striking clinical hallmark of PPTs is the low incidence of preoperative arginine vasopressin deficiency (AVP-D), despite the tumors originating directly within the neurohypophysis or the infundibular stalk. In large systematic reviews and patient series, preoperative AVP-D is reported in less than 5% of patients. Arginine vasopressin (AVP) is synthesized in the cell bodies of magnocellular neurons located in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus. The posterior pituitary consists merely of the terminal axons of these neurons. Progressive tumor growth in the sellar region causes gradual compression of these axonal terminals, while the proximal axonal segments and hypothalamic cell bodies remain functionally intact. AVP is released en-passant from axonal terminals within the internal zone of the median eminence, thereby preserving vasopressin secretion and preventing hormonal deficiency. However, AVP-D is a frequent postoperative complication, occurring in up to 30% of patients following transsphenoidal or transcranial surgical resection due to intraoperative traction on the infundibulum or surgical disruption of the proximal pituitary stalk.

case_text:
A 51‐year‐old male with hypertension had been quadriplegic and unable to communicate since a brainstem hemorrhage 6 years earlier. He had bilateral renal calculi and recurrent left pyelonephritis requiring ureteral stent exchange every 3 months for 2 years and 7 months. Eight months before death, he developed septic shock due to P. aeruginosa urinary tract infection; computed tomography at that time showed a single 1.5‐cm left upper‐pole calculus.

One month before death, scheduled stent exchange failed because the proximal coil of the stent was encrusted and fixed to left renal pelvic calculi. Preoperative computed tomography was not performed, and the size of the calculi was not assessed. Urine culture 2 weeks before surgery grew P. aeruginosa . Neither therapeutic antibiotics nor antibiotic prophylaxis was given before surgery.

On the day of death, he had no fever or abnormal vital signs. Ureteroscopy showed an approximately 1.3‐cm calculus adherent to the stent near the ureteropelvic junction and an upper‐pole calculus whose size could not be measured. Lithotripsy (0.4 J, 6 Hz) of the adherent calculus was performed with a holmium:yttrium‐aluminum‐garnet laser through a semirigid ureteroscope with a 6.7/8.4‐Fr tip‐to‐shaft diameter (OES Elite, WA2UR11A; Olympus Medical Systems) without an access sheath. Irrigation was manually pressurized with a hand pump (SAPS Single Action Pumping System; Boston Scientific); its pressure was not measured. A guidewire was inserted before and after lithotripsy, and the stent was exchanged for the same Tria Firm 6‐Fr × 26‐cm stent over a Sensor guidewire (Boston Scientific) under fluoroscopy without apparent complications or substantial blood loss. Because of the bacteriuria, the procedure was limited to 30 min, and piperacillin/tazobactam was planned postoperatively.

Shivering and fever (39°C) developed immediately after surgery, followed by hypotension requiring catecholamines, and piperacillin/tazobactam was initiated. Progressive hematuria required continuous bladder irrigation. Hemoglobin remained stable (preoperative, 12.3 g/dL; 12.5 and 11.8 g/dL at 3 and 7.5 h, respectively) despite systolic blood pressure below 90 mmHg. Cardiac arrest occurred 7.5 h after surgery, and death was confirmed at 8 h.

Postmortem computed tomography (Figure 1) showed left perirenal fluid with multiple high‐density fragments extending into the retroperitoneal fat, while the stent tip remained in the renal pelvis. Postmortem blood cultures grew Citrobacter koseri , Proteus mirabilis , and Enterococcus faecalis , all susceptible to piperacillin/tazobactam.

Autopsy performed 11 h after death with the family's consent revealed extensive retroperitoneal hemorrhage continuous with left renal subcapsular hemorrhage (Figure 2), without intraperitoneal hemorrhage. The left renal pelvis contained a 2.5‐cm calculus and multiple stone fragments. A 6‐mm perforation extended from the dorsal upper‐pole calyx through the renal parenchyma, and stone fragments within the subcapsular hemorrhage indicated migration through the perforation.

Histology showed bacterially colonized calculi, acute‐on‐chronic left pyelonephritis, and neutrophilic infiltration around the perforation and in the perirenal retroperitoneum with extrarenal stone fragments, indicating retroperitoneal extension of infection. Slight degeneration at the perforation margins (Figure 3) favored a mechanical cause. Absence of clot formation at the hemorrhage site and glomerular fibrin thrombi supported disseminated intravascular coagulation. The heart was unremarkable, with no pulmonary embolism.

The cause of death was considered to be septic shock rather than hemorrhage, as hemoglobin remained stable: bacteria in the infected renal pelvis likely entered the bloodstream through the RPP, which developed during lithotripsy, and extruded infected stone fragments caused retroperitoneal infection.

Lithotripsy (0.4 J, 6 Hz) of the adherent calculus was performed with a holmium:yttrium‐aluminum‐garnet laser through a semirigid ureteroscope with a 6.7/8.4‐Fr tip‐to‐shaft diameter (OES Elite, WA2UR11A; Olympus Medical Systems) without an access sheath.
Irrigation was manually pressurized with a hand pump (SAPS Single Action Pumping System; Boston Scientific); its pressure was not measured.

A guidewire was inserted before and after lithotripsy, and the stent was exchanged for the same Tria Firm 6‐Fr × 26‐cm stent over a Sensor guidewire (Boston Scientific) under fluoroscopy without apparent complications or substantial blood loss.
Because of the bacteriuria, the procedure was limited to 30 min, and piperacillin/tazobactam was planned postoperatively.
Shivering and fever (39°C) developed immediately after surgery, followed by hypotension requiring catecholamines, and piperacillin/tazobactam was initiated.
Progressive hematuria required continuous bladder irrigation.
Hemoglobin remained stable (preoperative, 12.3 g/dL; 12.5 and 11.8 g/dL at 3 and 7.5 h, respectively) despite systolic blood pressure below 90 mmHg.
Cardiac arrest occurred 7.5 h after surgery, and death was confirmed at 8 h.
Postmortem computed tomography (Figure 1) showed left perirenal fluid with multiple high‐density fragments extending into the retroperitoneal fat, while the stent tip remained in the renal pelvis.
Postmortem blood cultures grew Citrobacter koseri , Proteus mirabilis , and Enterococcus faecalis , all susceptible to piperacillin/tazobactam.

Autopsy performed 11 h after death with the family's consent revealed extensive retroperitoneal hemorrhage continuous with left renal subcapsular hemorrhage (Figure 2), without intraperitoneal hemorrhage.
The left renal pelvis contained a 2.5‐cm calculus and multiple stone fragments.
A 6‐mm perforation extended from the dorsal upper‐pole calyx through the renal parenchyma, and stone fragments within the subcapsular hemorrhage indicated migration through the perforation.

Histology showed bacterially colonized calculi, acute‐on‐chronic left pyelonephritis, and neutrophilic infiltration around the perforation and in the perirenal retroperitoneum with extrarenal stone fragments, indicating retroperitoneal extension of infection.
Slight degeneration at the perforation margins (Figure 3) favored a mechanical cause.
Absence of clot formation at the hemorrhage site and glomerular fibrin thrombi supported disseminated intravascular coagulation.
The heart was unremarkable, with no pulmonary embolism.

The cause of death was considered to be septic shock rather than hemorrhage, as hemoglobin remained stable: bacteria in the infected renal pelvis likely entered the bloodstream through the RPP, which developed during lithotripsy, and extruded infected stone fragments caused retroperitoneal infection.
title: Fatal Sepsis With Renal Parenchymal Perforation During Ureteroscopic Removal of an Encrusted Ureteral Stent: An Autopsy Case Report

case_text:
A man in his 60s was referred following an incidental abnormality identified on transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) performed as part of pre-operative assessment for a pulmonary nodule. He had a background of previous coronary artery bypass graft surgery with one graft and a tissue aortic valve replacement (AVR) 5 years earlier for a bicuspid aortic valve with severe stenosis and regurgitation. Approximately 2 years before the current presentation, he had been admitted with a left middle cerebral artery stroke, possibly embolic in nature, during which a PPM was implanted for complete heart block. The chronology of the patient’s clinical course, investigations, diagnosis and management is summarized in Fig. 1.

Over the preceding several years, the patient had experienced non-specific symptoms, including fatigue, dyspnoea, myalgia and weight loss. He reported no fever. On presentation, he was afebrile with stable clinical observations and no significant abnormalities on respiratory or neurological examination. No peripheral stigmata of IE were identified.

A pulmonary nodule had been identified on computed tomography (CT) and positron emission tomography (PET) several months earlier, demonstrating low-grade avidity. He was considered a candidate for curative surgical resection or radiotherapy once his cardiac status had been clarified. The pre-operative TTE revealed abnormal, independent rocking motion of the bioprosthetic aortic valve relative to the aortic root, with severe paravalvular leak and findings suggestive of partial prosthetic valve dehiscence. Doppler assessment demonstrated a dimensionless velocity index of 0.11, maximum aortic valve velocity of 4.0 m s−1 and a maximum pressure gradient of 65 mmHg. The aortic root appeared echogenic and thickened, raising suspicion of prosthetic valve endocarditis. Additional findings included a low left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) velocity–time integral (9 cm) and a dilated left ventricle with preserved overall systolic function. CT coronary angiography demonstrated an occluded bypass graft, with incidental dilatation of the aortic root also noted.

Six sets of blood cultures were obtained before initiation of antimicrobial therapy. A single blood culture bottle grew Kocuria rosea, which was considered a possible contaminant, while the remaining cultures were negative. Empirical intravenous vancomycin, gentamicin and rifampicin were initiated at the referring hospital for suspected prosthetic valve endocarditis.

He was transferred to a tertiary cardiac centre for surgical management and underwent emergency redo sternotomy, AVR and aortic root replacement (Day 0). Intraoperative transoesophageal echocardiography confirmed prosthetic aortic valve dehiscence and raised suspicion of anterior mitral valve leaflet perforation, with a possible communication between the LVOT and the left atrium (Fig. 2). At surgery, the aortic bioprosthesis was markedly dehisced, with small deposits suggestive of IE and evidence of circumferential infection involving the native aortic annulus. However, direct inspection of the mitral valve revealed no perforation or macroscopic evidence of infection. A prominent lymph node superior to the right axillary artery was also excised for histological examination and was negative for malignancy.

case_text:
A 42-year-old woman with class II obesity (weight 98.7 kg, height 164.5 cm, body mass index 36.4 kg/m2), essential hypertension controlled with amlodipine 5 mg daily, and vitamin D insufficiency treated with cholecalciferol presented to an obesity medicine clinic for pharmacological weight management. Over the preceding 18 months, a structured lifestyle program of dietitian-guided caloric restriction and at least 150 minutes of weekly moderate-intensity exercise had produced <2% weight loss, falling short of the 5% target. She had no personal history of psychiatric illness, epilepsy, migraine, cerebrovascular or autoimmune disease, substance use, or cognitive impairment, and no family history of schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, dissociative disorders, or epilepsy. Baseline examination and laboratory studies were unremarkable, including a fasting plasma glucose of 91 mg/dL (SI: 5.1 mmol/L; reference range, 70-99 mg/dL [SI: 3.9-5.5 mmol/L]), a glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) of 5.4% (SI: 36 mmol/mol; reference range, 4.0-5.6% [SI: 20-38 mmol/mol]), and normal renal function and liver enzyme levels.

Semaglutide was initiated at 0.25 mg subcutaneously once weekly following multidisciplinary counseling. She tolerated the initial dose with only mild transient nausea. After 4 weeks, having lost 4.8 kg, the dose was escalated to 0.5 mg weekly per standard titration. Approximately 7 days after the second 0.5 mg dose, she developed sudden episodes of feeling detached from herself while at work, describing a sensation of “watching myself from outside my body,” accompanied by a pervasive sense that her surroundings were unreal, distant, and dreamlike. Throughout these episodes, she remained fully oriented and retained clear insight that the experiences were abnormal. She denied experiencing loss of consciousness, memory impairment, hallucinations, paranoia, or delusional content.

The episodes initially occurred once daily, lasting 15 to 20 minutes, but over the following 10 days increased to 3 to 4 episodes daily, each lasting 20 to 45 minutes, with marked associated distress despite coherent speech and behavior. There were no autonomic symptoms, headache, focal neurological signs, incontinence, tongue biting, or postictal confusion, and no preceding panic attacks, psychosocial stressors, sleep deprivation, alcohol use, or recreational drug use. As the episodes affected her occupational functioning, she presented to the emergency department for evaluation.

case_text:
A 71‐year‐old male with diabetes, history of partial right foot amputation in 2022 due to methicillin‐susceptible Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) osteomyelitis, and dialysis‐dependent end‐stage kidney disease (ESKD) due to diabetic nephropathy underwent deceased‐donor kidney transplant in August 2023. His donor was a 40‐year‐old female with a kidney donor profile index (KDPI) of 51%. Cold‐ischemic time was 21 h and 16 min. Calculated panel reactive antibody (CPRA) was 0%, and he received thymoglobulin 1.5 mg/kg induction for three doses. His posttransplant period was complicated by delayed graft function requiring hemodialysis for hyperkalemia and Escherichia coli sepsis after removal of his indwelling ureteral stent. Treatment was further complicated by pancytopenia attributed to myelosuppressive effects and antimicrobials.

In July 2025, he completed a 5‐week course of antibiotics for MSSA bacteremia from recurrent osteomyelitis of his residual right foot. His tacrolimus dose was reduced, and mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) was held because of the infection. In September 2025, he was admitted as an interfacility transfer for nonoliguric AKI with serum creatinine 2.74 mg/dL, increased from his posttransplant baseline of 1.4–1.6 mg/dL. A complete record of his antecedent clinical course, including precise onset of allograft dysfunction, laboratory timeline, and serial immunosuppression adjustments was not available to the authors. Transplant ultrasound at our facility was normal. His tacrolimus trough level was subtherapeutic at < 1.0 ng/mL. Repeat blood cultures were negative, and neither transthoracic nor transesophageal echocardiogram showed vegetations. He had pancytopenia and BK viremia of 726 IU/mL (Table 1). Renal transplant biopsy revealed acute TCMR (Banff 2A), C3‐dominant IRGN, and BKVAN (Figure 1).

His immunosuppressive regimen at time of transfer included tacrolimus 1 mg every 12 h, MMF 500 mg every 12 h, and prednisone 5 mg daily. After excluding endocarditis and ensuring eradication of MSSA bacteremia, his tacrolimus was increased, and he received three doses of intravenous methylprednisolone 250 mg followed by oral prednisone taper. Thymoglobulin for treatment of TCMR was deferred because of infectious risk and pancytopenia. His hospital course was complicated by Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteremia due to transplant pyelonephritis, hyperkalemia warranting intermittent hemodialysis, and pancytopenia supported by transfusions. MMF was temporarily discontinued. Tacrolimus troughs were maintained between 4 and 6 ng/mL. His BK viremia peaked at 5280 IU/mL but improved with reduced immunosuppression to an undetectable viral load several weeks later. Prior to discharge, his renal function recovered to near baseline. He remains off hemodialysis with recovering cell lines and has restarted maintenance immunosuppression.

case_text: In the majority of patients diagnosed with ARSA, the condition remains asymptomatic indefinitely. If present, symptoms generally occur in adult patients, largely due to compression of the adjacent mediastinal structures, in particular the oesophagus and trachea. Dysphagia lusoria is the most frequently observed clinical picture, characterised by difficulty swallowing solid food due to the retroesophageal position of the artery which compresses the oesophagus. The latter symptom is mainly reported in the presence of either Kommerell’s diverticulum or age-related atherosclerotic stiffening of the vessel. Symptoms observed less frequently include dyspnoea, chronic cough, retrosternal pain, and, rarely, hoarseness from recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement or upper limb ischemia. Recent case reports have emphasized how ARSA may represent an underdiagnosed cause of atypical chest pain and dyspepsia, even, on endoscopic examination, at times simulating the behaviour of an oesophageal tumour featuring a pulsatile, extrinsic compression.

case_text:
A 76‐year‐old male with a history of permanent AF, chronic heart failure, and hypertension presented with symptomatic bradycardia and exertional dyspnea. Approximately 1 month before admission, the patient developed exertional dyspnea that gradually worsened and was accompanied by bilateral lower leg edema. At admission, his medications included warfarin and diuretics.

Electrocardiography demonstrated AF with bradycardia and a heart rate of 35 beats/min. Chest radiography showed signs of congestive heart failure. Echocardiography revealed a marked biatrial enlargement and ventricular hypertrophy (Figure 1). The left ventricular (LV) ejection fraction was preserved at 61% and no significant valvular disease was observed. Laboratory evaluation showed elevated levels of high‐sensitivity troponin I and B‐type natriuretic peptide (BNP), while renal function was preserved, and no proteinuria was detected.

case_text:
A 79‐year‐old man was brought to the emergency department after a fall left him unable to walk. During the preceding several days, he had developed progressive dyspnea, fever, rigors, and severe low back pain. His medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidemia, atrial fibrillation, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, and severe aortic stenosis treated with TAVR in 2023. He reported five falls during the preceding year, including the event that prompted admission. He had undergone no recent dental procedures and knew of no oral infection.

At presentation, his temperature was 38.6°C; he was tachycardic and appeared ill. He was unable to ambulate normally but had no focal neurologic deficits. The white blood cell count was 20 × 109/L, with 92% neutrophils; C‐reactive protein was 121 mg/L, and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 77 mm/h. High‐sensitivity troponin was 292 ng/L, and B‐type natriuretic peptide was 321 pg/mL.

Both sets of blood cultures grew G. haemolysans, identified by matrix‐assisted laser desorption/ionization time‐of‐flight mass spectrometry (MALDI‐TOF). The isolate was susceptible to the antimicrobial agents tested.

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a 0.6 × 0.6 cm vegetation at the aortic valve annulus and a left ventricular ejection fraction of 40%–45%. Subsequent transesophageal echocardiography confirmed involvement of the prosthetic valve and better characterized the perivalvular structures (Figures 1 and 2). Neither a perivalvular abscess nor a fistula was identified.

Abdominal MRI demonstrated a 6.2 cm wedge‐shaped splenic signal abnormality consistent with infarction (Figure 3). Fluid adjacent to the right psoas muscle was interpreted as a psoas abscess. Cross‐sectional imaging of the chest showed no pulmonary emboli or additional infectious foci.

The severity of the back pain and the inability to walk prompted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the lumbar spine. Fluid signal in the L4–L5 and L5–S1 intervertebral discs, together with adjacent vertebral marrow edema, was consistent with discitis and osteomyelitis. Anterior epidural thickening posterior to L5 measured up to 5.5 mm and contributed to moderate‐to‐severe canal stenosis at L5–S1 and moderate stenosis at L4–L5. Moderate bilateral foraminal stenosis was also present at both levels (Figure 4).

The positive blood cultures and echocardiographic vegetation met the 2023 Duke–International Society for Cardiovascular Infectious Diseases criteria for definite IE. Vertebral infection, epidural abscess, a right psoas collection, and splenic infarction demonstrated extensive extracardiac involvement.

Empiric treatment with intravenous vancomycin and ceftriaxone was begun at admission. Once the organism had been identified and susceptibility results were available, vancomycin was discontinued and ceftriaxone continued at 2 g intravenously every 24 h. A peripherally inserted central catheter was placed to allow a planned 6‐week course, in view of the prosthetic valve and concomitant vertebral infection.

The treating team considered the patient a poor operative candidate because of his age, comorbidities, and clinical course. During hospitalization, fever resolved and inflammatory markers declined. He developed no focal neurologic deficits attributable to the epidural abscess and was discharged to complete intravenous treatment with outpatient infectious disease follow‐up.

case_text:
A 22-year-old woman attended the medical assessment unit on day 1 following an episode of presyncope, preceded by three days of fever, sore throat, nausea, vomiting and lower abdominal pain. She was generally fit and well and worked as an air hostess. She denied any new medications or supplements and drank minimal alcohol. She was found to have a borderline temperature of 37.9 degrees Celsius, with observations otherwise normal. Her abdomen was soft with mild suprapubic tenderness, and she was jaundiced. Her bloods showed a significant LFT derangement. She was initially reviewed by the surgical team; no surgical cause identified and referred to the medical team. A monospot test was positive, and she was discharged with a plan for repeat blood tests and abdominal ultrasound.

She re-attended on day 5 with worsening liver function tests (LFTs) and anaemia. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated splenomegaly, with her spleen measuring 15.7 cm, and the liver, kidneys and gallbladder appeared normal. She was then admitted for further monitoring and investigation. At this point, she reported increased fatigue, a generalised itch and dark urine. She appeared visibly more jaundiced.

Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated significant hyperbilirubinaemia and deranged LFTs (Table 1). Blood tests showed a mixed hepatic and cholestatic liver injury picture with worsening hyperbilirubinaemia. Total bilirubin 291 umol/L, conjugated 138 umol/L and unconjugated 153 umol/L. Bilirubin increased from 179 umol/L to a peak of 344 umol/L, while ALT peaked at 579 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) at 535 U/L and alkaline phosphatase (ALP) at 319 U/L. Concurrently, her haemoglobin (Hb) fell from 125 g/L to 64 g/L, with a rising reticulocyte count, supporting ongoing haemolysis.

LDH was significantly elevated at 802U/L (reference range: 80-240U/L), haptoglobin was reduced to 0.22 g/L (reference range: 0.3-2.0g/L) and her blood film showed red cell agglutination, strongly suggesting AIHA. The DAT was IgG positive (1+) and C3d strongly positive (3+). A blood film showed normocytic red cells with mature neutrophils and lymphocytes, with occasional reactive forms, in keeping with a viral infection. Other investigations were undertaken for acute liver injury and haemolysis, including viral serology, autoimmune screenings and assessment of haemolytic markers. HIV, CMV and hepatitis A/B/C/E screening were negative. ANA was negative. EBV serology on day 2 demonstrated positive VCA immunoglobulin G and VCA immunoglobulin M, and EBNA immunoglobulin G (EBV) was not detected, supporting acute or recent EBV infection.

Following discussions with haematology, as the patient was asymptomatic, haemodynamically stable and there was no evidence of tissue hypoxia, corticosteroids were not advised, as her haemoglobin was expected to improve with resolution of the acute underlying infection. Transfusion was reserved for symptomatic anaemia. Her haemoglobin and liver biochemistry subsequently improved without specific treatment for the haemolysis including corticosteroids or blood transfusions as she remained asymptomatic of her anaemia.

A summary of the patient’s course, including key investigations, disease progression and follow-up, is presented in Table 2. By day 14, her bloods were improving, and clinically, she had improved. She was discharged home with a plan for haematology follow-up. In clinic a month later, she was asymptomatic and bloods improving. One month later, her bloods had normalised. Follow-up ultrasound abdomen six months after her admission demonstrated resolution of the splenomegaly, with a spleen measuring 12 cm. She was subsequently discharged from any further haematology follow-up.

She was found to have a borderline temperature of 37.9 degrees Celsius, with observations otherwise normal.
Her abdomen was soft with mild suprapubic tenderness, and she was jaundiced.
Her bloods showed a significant LFT derangement.
She was initially reviewed by the surgical team; no surgical cause identified and referred to the medical team.
A monospot test was positive, and she was discharged with a plan for repeat blood tests and abdominal ultrasound.
She re-attended on day 5 with worsening liver function tests (LFTs) and anaemia.
Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated splenomegaly, with her spleen measuring 15.7 cm, and the liver, kidneys and gallbladder appeared normal.
She was then admitted for further monitoring and investigation.
At this point, she reported increased fatigue, a generalised itch and dark urine.
She appeared visibly more jaundiced.
Initial laboratory investigations demonstrated significant hyperbilirubinaemia and deranged LFTs (Table 1).
Blood tests showed a mixed hepatic and cholestatic liver injury picture with worsening hyperbilirubinaemia.
Total bilirubin 291 umol/L, conjugated 138 umol/L and unconjugated 153 umol/L.
Bilirubin increased from 179 umol/L to a peak of 344 umol/L, while ALT peaked at 579 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) at 535 U/L and alkaline phosphatase (ALP) at 319 U/L.
Concurrently, her haemoglobin (Hb) fell from 125 g/L to 64 g/L, with a rising reticulocyte count, supporting ongoing haemolysis.

LDH was significantly elevated at 802U/L (reference range: 80-240U/L), haptoglobin was reduced to 0.22 g/L (reference range: 0.3-2.0g/L) and her blood film showed red cell agglutination, strongly suggesting AIHA.
The DAT was IgG positive (1+) and C3d strongly positive (3+).
A blood film showed normocytic red cells with mature neutrophils and lymphocytes, with occasional reactive forms, in keeping with a viral infection.
Other investigations were undertaken for acute liver injury and haemolysis, including viral serology, autoimmune screenings and assessment of haemolytic markers.
HIV, CMV and hepatitis A/B/C/E screening were negative.
ANA was negative.
EBV serology on day 2 demonstrated positive VCA immunoglobulin G and VCA immunoglobulin M, and EBNA immunoglobulin G (EBV) was not detected, supporting acute or recent EBV infection.

Following discussions with haematology, as the patient was asymptomatic, haemodynamically stable and there was no evidence of tissue hypoxia, corticosteroids were not advised, as her haemoglobin was expected to improve with resolution of the acute underlying infection.
Transfusion was reserved for symptomatic anaemia.
Her haemoglobin and liver biochemistry subsequently improved without specific treatment for the haemolysis including corticosteroids or blood transfusions as she remained asymptomatic of her anaemia.
A summary of the patient’s course, including key investigations, disease progression and follow-up, is presented in Table 2.
By day 14, her bloods were improving, and clinically, she had improved.
She was discharged home with a plan for haematology follow-up.
In clinic a month later, she was asymptomatic and bloods improving.
One month later, her bloods had normalised.
Follow-up ultrasound abdomen six months after her admission demonstrated resolution of the splenomegaly, with a spleen measuring 12 cm.
She was subsequently discharged from any further haematology follow-up.
title: A Case Report of Autoimmune Haemolytic Anaemia and Acute Hepatitis Associated With Epstein-Barr Virus Infection

case_text:
A 25-year-old male patient born and living in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) presented with episodic neurological symptoms. In September 2021 (at age 24), he developed acute right spastic hemiparesis and ipsilateral paresthesia, with an initial Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) score estimated at 3.0. Following physical therapy and symptomatic treatment (vitamins, pregabalin, aspirin), symptoms improved within two weeks to an EDSS of 2.0. In December 2021, he developed dizziness, gait ataxia, and nystagmus (estimated EDSS 3.5). General medical workup (EEG, cervicodorsal MRI, blood counts, renal, hepatic, and inflammatory panels) was unremarkable. Brain MRI performed with standard protocol (millimetric 3D T1, millimetric 3D FLAIR, axial/coronal T2, axial DWI + ADC, and post-contrast axial/sagittal T1) revealed two primary findings:

Multiple T2/FLAIR hyperintense nodular lesions located within the subependymal and subcortical white matter, predominating in the centrum semiovale (7–12 mm diameter) (Fig. 1A), along with similar hyperintense T2/FLAIR lesions in the left brainstem and left cerebellopontine cistern (16–18 mm diameter) (Fig. 1B).

An extra-axial left basitemporal space-occupying mass (10 cc volume; 2.78 × 2.74 × 2.67 cm) displaying intense homogeneous enhancement typical of a meningioma (Fig. 2A and B).

Based on clinical presentation and radiological evidence meeting McDonald 2017 criteria, a diagnosis of relapsing–remitting multiple sclerosis concomitant with a temporal meningioma was established. Maintenance therapy with oral methotrexate (2.5 mg/week) was initiated due to limited availability of first-line disease-modifying therapies in our setting. Over follow-up, the patient experienced no further relapses, with clinical recovery corresponding to an EDSS score of 1.0. Follow-up brain MRI performed in March 2023 demonstrated complete resolution of the brainstem lesion (Fig. 3). The patient declined neurosurgical resection of the extra-axial temporal tumor.

case_text:
A 40‐year‐old male with a history of childhood asthma, tobacco use (7 cigarettes per day for 15 years), heroin use, and occupational exposure to industrial waste—including possible heavy metals such as cadmium—while working as a trash collector for 10 years, presented with 1 week of progressive right flank pain and mild dyspnea at rest and with exertion. Imaging revealed multiple large, multiloculated, peripherally enhancing cystic masses occupying the majority of the right hemithorax with marked leftward mediastinal shift (Figures 1 and 2). Additional findings included a right upper lobe segmental pulmonary embolism, diffuse narrowing of the right pulmonary arterial tree, and severe compression of the pulmonary venous vasculature with a slitlike inferior vena cava (IVC). Severe apical‐predominant bullous emphysema was present bilaterally. Multifocal consolidation in the left lung raised concern for bronchopneumonia, and imaging findings were also suggestive of hepatic congestion.

Laboratory studies demonstrated elevated lactate, alpha‐fetoprotein (AFP), and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), raising concern for an underlying neoplastic process. The patient rapidly developed obstructive shock and respiratory failure requiring endotracheal intubation and vasopressor support.

case_text:
A 20-year-old systemically healthy man presented with difficulty chewing in the mandibular right posterior region and requested functional replacement. He reported no spontaneous pain, swelling, drainage, fever, or other acute symptoms. He smoked approximately one pack of cigarettes daily and continued smoking during follow-up. The mandibular right second molar (FDI 47) showed extensive subgingival destruction extending below the cementoenamel junction, furcation involvement, and insufficient remaining tooth structure for predictable restoration. The tooth was non-mobile and non-tender to percussion or palpation and did not respond to cold, heat, or electric pulp sensibility testing. Panoramic radiography showed a periapical radiolucency. Pulp necrosis with asymptomatic apical periodontitis was diagnosed. The mandibular right third molar (FDI 48) was asymptomatic, mesioangular, and soft-tissue impacted, with approximately three-quarters root development and open apices (Figs 1 and 2).

Options of extraction with subsequent implant-supported replacement, removable partial denture, and autotransplantation were discussed; the patient selected autotransplantation. Local anesthesia was achieved with 2% lidocaine containing 1:100 000 epinephrine and 0.5% bupivacaine containing 1:200 000 epinephrine using an inferior alveolar nerve block and buccal infiltration. Tooth 47 was extracted. The socket was thoroughly curetted to remove visible granulation tissue and irrigated with sterile saline. Because donor-root morphology did not correspond precisely to the recipient socket, the interradicular septum was carefully reduced before donor extraction.

Tooth 48 was exposed through a buccal full-thickness flap with a vertical releasing incision, and limited buccal and mesiobuccal bone removal was performed under saline irrigation. The donor was removed intact without sectioning, handled only by the crown, and immediately transferred to the prepared socket. Extra-alveolar time was <30 s. The tooth was seated on the first attempt without removal, reinsertion, or further socket modification (Fig. 3). It was positioned slightly infraocclusally with no occlusal contact. Stabilization was achieved with two 0.3-mm stainless-steel wires and a 4-0 nylon suture around the transplanted tooth; the flap was closed with interrupted 3-0 silk sutures (Fig. 4). Immediate postoperative periapical radiography documented tooth position (Fig. 5).

Amoxicillin 500 mg every 8 hours for 7 days, ibuprofen 600 mg every 6 h as needed with food, and 0.12% chlorhexidine rinse twice daily for 14 days were prescribed. At 14 days, the patient was asymptomatic, soft-tissue healing was satisfactory, and the tooth remained stable after removal of the wires and sutures. Percussion and palpation were negative, while cold, heat, and electric pulp sensibility tests remained negative. The clinical appearance was documented photographically (Fig. 6), and periapical radiography showed maintained transplant position (Fig. 7).

At 6 months, the patient reported normal mastication. The tooth was stable and in functional occlusion, with healthy gingiva, probing depths within normal limits, and no tenderness, swelling, sinus tract, or drainage. Cold, heat, and electric pulp sensibility responses were positive and comparable with adjacent and contralateral control teeth. Periapical radiography showed progressive surrounding bone formation, continued root development, and apical narrowing (Fig. 8).

At 12 months, the patient remained asymptomatic, reported normal mastication, and was satisfied with the outcome. The tooth remained stable, with healthy periodontal tissues, no tenderness, positive thermal and electric pulp sensibility responses, and no crown discoloration. The clinical appearance was documented photographically (Fig. 9). Periapical radiography showed surrounding bone healing, continued root development, and apical narrowing (Fig. 10).

case_text:
A 76-year-old man presented with 6–7 months of intermittent painless hematochezia, without abdominal, constitutional, or respiratory symptoms. Hemoglobin was 14.5 g/dL (baseline 15.5). Computed tomography angiography suggested possible rectosigmoid extravasation. Colonoscopy revealed a normal-appearing terminal ileum (not biopsied), a 4 mm cecal polyp with a depressed center (Figure 1), a 4 mm rectosigmoid polyp, and nonbleeding hemorrhoids. Histology of the cecal polyp showed suppurative necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with acid-fast bacilli (Figure 2); the rectosigmoid polyp was a tubular adenoma. His wife, an Indonesian immigrant, was treated for pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) 12 years earlier. Chest radiography showed right upper lobe infiltrates, and induced sputum grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex. He started directly observed 4-drug therapy.

Hematochezia is usually attributed to benign anorectal disease, diverticulosis, or neoplasia; infectious etiologies are unexpected.1 Necrotizing granulomas in colonic tissue have a broad differential, including Crohn's disease, fungal infection, and mycobacteria.2 Demonstrating acid-fast bacilli is highly specific but uncommon in tissue.3 Here, hemorrhoids likely explained the bleeding, but the polyp's histology prompted an exposure history that revealed household TB contact and led to the diagnosis of pulmonary TB in a patient without respiratory symptoms.4 Incidental granulomatous inflammation in a polyp warrants infectious evaluation, especially with exposure risk.

case_text:
A 68‐year‐old male with a history of APKD, polycystic liver disease, and type 2 diabetes mellitus, and a history of chronic smoking presented with severe left upper quadrant (LUQ) pain for 2 days, associated with fever, chills, anorexia, scleral icterus, clay‐colored stools, and dark urine. He denied any trauma, recent travel, or significant weight loss.

The patient’s medical history included a previous hepatic abscess requiring percutaneous drainage. His family history was remarkable for APKD in his daughter, though no genetic testing had been conducted. There was no known history of pre‐existing splenic cysts, splenic lesions, or vascular abnormalities.

On examination, the patient was alert and hemodynamically stable, with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 15. LUQ tenderness was noted without guarding or rebound tenderness, and the Murphy’s sign was negative.

Laboratory investigations revealed leucocytosis with a white blood cell count of 14.0 × 103/uL, low hemoglobin (11.8 g/dL), and low hematocrit (34.9%). Inflammatory markers were markedly elevated, with C‐reactive protein of 328.9 mg/L and procalcitonin of 2.67 ng/mL. Liver function tests demonstrated an obstructive pattern, with alkaline phosphatase of 143 U/L, total bilirubin of 7.23 mg/dL, and direct bilirubin of 5.36 mg/dL.

Contrast‐enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen was performed, as shown in Figures 1–3. CT demonstrated splenomegaly with multiple splenic lacerations and contusions, associated with perisplenic and intra‐abdominal hematoma, consistent with a high‐grade splenic injury, likely American Association for the Surgery of Trauma (AAST) grade III–IV. No history of trauma was reported, supporting the diagnosis of spontaneous splenic injury. Hepatobiliary findings included acute cholecystitis with possible intraluminal calculi or polyps, a distal common bile duct (CBD) calculus causing mild biliary obstruction, and mild intrahepatic biliary dilatation. Multiple calcifications were also noted along the walls of hepatic cysts, in keeping with the underlying polycystic liver disease. Renal findings included bilateral multiple renal cysts and calculi, consistent with the patient’s known APKD. Mild free fluid was present in the pelvis. Overall, the clinical, laboratory, and CT findings supported a diagnosis of sepsis secondary to acute cholangitis and choledocholithiasis, Tokyo Classification grade II, with concurrent spontaneous high‐grade splenic injury.

On the day of admission, empiric broad‐spectrum antibiotics were initiated, and endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) with sphincterotomy, CBD stone extraction, and biliary stent placement was performed. The high‐grade splenic injury was initially managed nonoperatively because the patient was hemodynamically stable, had no peritonitic signs, and had no immediate evidence of uncontrolled active arterial hemorrhage, making close monitoring with serial clinical assessment and hemoglobin measurements appropriate despite the presence of splenomegaly.

On the third day of admission, the patient developed a sudden drop in hemoglobin, prompting urgent repeat imaging. Repeat imaging demonstrated an abnormally dilated peripheral intrasplenic vessel with minimal contrast pooling on the delayed phase, suggestive of slow‐flow venous oozing rather than brisk arterial extravasation. Selective splenic angiography was subsequently performed and demonstrated abnormal vascularity with suspected contrast extravasation arising from segmental splenic artery branches, as shown in Figure 4, corresponding to the suspected bleeding site. Super‐selective catheterization of the feeding arterial branch was achieved, followed by embolization. Postembolization angiography confirmed complete occlusion of the feeding arteries with no further contrast pooling, indicating a technical success. Following embolization, the patient’s hemoglobin stabilized.

Following an extended hospital stay and multidisciplinary management, including targeted antibiotics, ERCP, and SAE, the patient was discharged in stable condition. At discharge, he was clinically well, afebrile, with improving bilirubin and inflammatory markers, and stable hemoglobin.

case_text:
A 74-year-old woman was diagnosed as having SIT since childhood. Following a positive fecal occult blood test, rectal cancer was detected through colonoscopy, and she was referred to our hospital for treatment. The patient suffered from hypertension and was obese, with a height of 152.4 cm, weight of 73.0 kg, and BMI of 31.4 kg/m2. Chest X-ray showed dextrocardia, suggesting situs inversus (Fig. 1A). Colonoscopy revealed a tumor in the upper rectum, and biopsy confirmed diagnosis of moderately differentiated tubular adenocarcinoma (Fig. 1B). Contrast-enhanced CT with 3D angiography showed wall thickening with contrast enhancement in the upper rectum, and complete left–right transposition of the abdominal viscera and vessels (Fig. 1C). No abnormalities in the branching or course of the abdominal vessels and ureters were observed, except for left–right transposition (Fig. 1D). Blood tests showed carcinoembryonic antigen and carbohydrate antigen 19–9 levels within the normal range. Based on the above findings, the patient was diagnosed as having T3N2aM0 Stage IIIB (UICC 8th edition) cancer. Four cycles of CAPOX chemotherapy were administered preoperatively. Although the tumor shrank, residual tumor was detected, and robot-assisted curative resection using the hinotori was planned. Given that the patient had SIT, we determined that careful consideration of the robot’s roll-in direction, port placements, and instruments to be used, as well as information sharing across disciplines, would be necessary. Therefore, we conducted simulations using the hinotori, instruments, monitors, and a dry box in collaboration with surgical nurses and clinical engineers to ensure thorough preparation before proceeding with the surgery (Fig. 2).

During the surgery, the patient was placed in the Trendelenburg position at 17-degree and 7-degree tilted left-side-down. Port placements were performed by completely reversing the port configuration used for robot-assisted rectal resection in our department (Fig. 3A and 3B). A 7 cm Lap Protector and E-Z ACCESS cap (both, Hakko, Chikuma, Nagano, Japan) were attached to the umbilicus, and a 10 mm robotic metal port for a 30-degree camera and 12 mm assist port were placed. Three robot ports were placed from the left lower abdomen to the right upper abdomen in a straight line. For the patient-side surgeons, 12 and 5 mm assist ports were placed at the left upper abdomen and right lower abdomen, respectively. After rolling in the hinotori from the patient’s right side, the arm base of the hinotori was tilted 7-degree left-side-down. We performed pivoting of Arm 3 for the camera, adjusting the arm positions automatically, and pivoting of the other arms to set the fulcrum. During the abdominal phase, which included the medial approach, mesenteric vessel division, left-sided colon mobilization, and dissection around the rectosigmoid junction, we attached croce grasping forceps to Arm 1, MCS to Arm 2, the camera to Arm 3, and bipolar fenestrated forceps to Arm 4. These instruments were also placed in completely left–right reversed positions from our standard configuration. During the pelvic phase, which included rectal dissection, division of the mesorectum, we intentionally changed the instrument configuration by placing the bipolar fenestrated forceps on Arm 2 and the MCS on Arm 4 (Fig. 3C). In the operating room, a monitor displaying the left–right flipped image was placed alongside the original-image monitor (Fig. 4). During the abdominal phase, the cockpit surgeon carefully operated the MCS with his non-dominant left hand while performing surgical maneuvers in a fully reversed configuration including forceps manipulation and tissue retraction (Fig. 5A and 5B). This procedure minimized interference between the instruments and operational constraints. The surgery was performed while the patient-side surgeons confirmed that the anatomical orientation matched that of a standard procedure by checking a flipped monitor. For the pelvic phase, we attached bipolar fenestrated forceps to Arm 2 and the MCS to Arm 4 and performed the surgery with the cockpit surgeon using his dominant right hand as the primary manipulator because the anatomy is bilaterally symmetrical in the pelvis (Fig. 5C). As the hinotori does not have sealing devices or linear staplers, the patient-side surgeons inserted these devices through the assist port to divide the mesorectum and perform rectal transection (Fig. 5D and 5E). After roll-out of the hinotori, the specimen was extracted through the umbilical incision. Finally, end-to-end anastomosis was laparoscopically completed with double stapling technique (Fig. 5F). A Supplementary Video 1 is provided to demonstrate the surgical procedure, including the left–right flipped image and the corresponding modifications in instrument configuration and surgical maneuvers. The total operative time was 332 minutes, with 206 minutes spent at the console. Blood loss was minimal. Although a Clavien–Dindo grade I surgical site infection occurred at the umbilicus, the patient was discharged on the 11th POD. Postoperative pathological diagnosis revealed T3N1aM0 Stage IIIB cancer. The patient underwent 4 additional cycles of CAPOX chemotherapy and remains recurrence-free at 6 months postoperatively.

No abnormalities in the branching or course of the abdominal vessels and ureters were observed, except for left–right transposition (Fig.
Blood tests showed carcinoembryonic antigen and carbohydrate antigen 19–9 levels within the normal range.

Given that the patient had SIT, we determined that careful consideration of the robot’s roll-in direction, port placements, and instruments to be used, as well as information sharing across disciplines, would be necessary.

Therefore, we conducted simulations using the hinotori, instruments, monitors, and a dry box in collaboration with surgical nurses and clinical engineers to ensure thorough preparation before proceeding with the surgery (Fig.
During the surgery, the patient was placed in the Trendelenburg position at 17-degree and 7-degree tilted left-side-down.
Port placements were performed by completely reversing the port configuration used for robot-assisted rectal resection in our department (Fig.
3A and 3B).
A 7 cm Lap Protector and E-Z ACCESS cap (both, Hakko, Chikuma, Nagano, Japan) were attached to the umbilicus, and a 10 mm robotic metal port for a 30-degree camera and 12 mm assist port were placed.
Three robot ports were placed from the left lower abdomen to the right upper abdomen in a straight line.
For the patient-side surgeons, 12 and 5 mm assist ports were placed at the left upper abdomen and right lower abdomen, respectively.
After rolling in the hinotori from the patient’s right side, the arm base of the hinotori was tilted 7-degree left-side-down.
We performed pivoting of Arm 3 for the camera, adjusting the arm positions automatically, and pivoting of the other arms to set the fulcrum.

During the abdominal phase, which included the medial approach, mesenteric vessel division, left-sided colon mobilization, and dissection around the rectosigmoid junction, we attached croce grasping forceps to Arm 1, MCS to Arm 2, the camera to Arm 3, and bipolar fenestrated forceps to Arm 4.

In the operating room, a monitor displaying the left–right flipped image was placed alongside the original-image monitor (Fig.

5A and 5B).

The surgery was performed while the patient-side surgeons confirmed that the anatomical orientation matched that of a standard procedure by checking a flipped monitor.

For the pelvic phase, we attached bipolar fenestrated forceps to Arm 2 and the MCS to Arm 4 and performed the surgery with the cockpit surgeon using his dominant right hand as the primary manipulator because the anatomy is bilaterally symmetrical in the pelvis (Fig.

5D and 5E).
After roll-out of the hinotori, the specimen was extracted through the umbilical incision.
Finally, end-to-end anastomosis was laparoscopically completed with double stapling technique (Fig.

Blood loss was minimal.

case_text:
A multidisciplinary Cleft‐Craniofacial Team performed clinical assessments as described in the Methods. All eight recruited families were simplex ones with no reported family history of craniosynostosis, whether syndromic or nonsyndromic (Supporting Information 1: Figure S1). Clinically, the probands of four of the families were diagnosed with Crouzon syndrome (Families 1, 2, 4, and 5), whereas the other four were diagnosed with Apert syndrome (Families 3, 6, 7, and 8). At the time of participant recruitment, the clinical diagnosis was based solely on clinical presentations; no clinical genetic testing had been performed, as such tests are lacking in the Ghanaian healthcare system. Craniosynostosis affecting the coronal suture was observed in all probands. However, there was significant phenotype variability even in probands diagnosed with the same syndrome (Table 1). Importantly, the age of probands at the time of recruitment may have influenced the observed phenotypes. For example, ~63% (5/8) of probands were recruited before Age 3, at which time many phenotypes may not be well developed to be clinically obvious. Such phenotypes include (a) malocclusion, which could not be assessed in these 63% of probands because the primary dentition develops at ~0.5–3 years, and (b) neurodevelopmental disorders, which may become more obvious by Ages 3–5. Accordingly, phenotypes listed as absent in Table 1 should be interpreted with caution, as this may reflect their absence at the time of clinical evaluation rather than their absence throughout the proband′s lifespan.

Family 1: The female proband was recruited at Age 12. She presented with craniosynostosis affecting the bilateral coronal and sagittal sutures. Other observed phenotypes included malocclusion, flattened zygomatic arch, retruded forehead, midface deficiency, protruded mandible, and exophthalmos or proptosis.

Family 2: This male proband, recruited at 1 year and 8 months of age, presented with craniosynostosis that impacted all the cranial sutures based on a 3D‐CT scan. Proptosis, bulging anterior fontanelle, retarded midfacial growth, sleep apnea, difficulty breathing, and high‐arched palate were the other clinical phenotypes in this proband.

Family 3: Recruited at ~2 months of age, the male proband presented with craniosynostosis affecting the bilateral coronal and sagittal sutures. Other clinical presentations included syndactyly of fingers and toes, symphalangism, and a high‐arched palate.

Family 4: The male proband was recruited at ~1 month, presenting with bilateral coronal craniosynostosis, as well as proptosis and midface hypoplasia.

Family 5: The proband presented with craniosynostosis affecting the sagittal, bilateral coronal, and metopic sutures, as well as proptosis. She was recruited at the age of 3 years.

Family 6: The female proband was recruited at 1 year and 6 months of age. She presented with craniosynostosis involving the bilateral coronal and metopic sutures. Other observed phenotypes were proptosis, high‐arched palate, syndactyly of fingers and toes, symphalangism, and low‐set ears.

Family 7: Left coronal craniosynostosis, syndactyly of fingers and toes, symphalangism, and a V‐shaped, high‐arched palate were the clinical presentations observed in the female proband recruited at 1 year and 10 months of age.

Family 8: The male proband was recruited at Age 3. The observed craniosynostosis affected all cranial sutures, as seen on a 3D CT head (bone‐only) scan. Other observed phenotypes include complete cleft palate, frontal bossing, flat posterior skull, retarded midfacial growth, wide, low‐set ears, beaked nose, proptosis, downward‐slanting palpebral fissure, ocular hypertelorism, patches of missing hair of eyebrows, mandibular prognathism (maxilla about 1 cm shorter than mandible), crowded teeth (malocclusion), high‐arched palate, syndactyly of toes and fingers, and symphalangism, as well as mild intellectual disability.
