case_text:
A 63‐year‐old woman (62 kg; body mass index, 23.3 kg/m2) underwent robot‐assisted hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo‐oophorectomy for endometrial carcinoma, along with indocyanine green–guided sentinel lymph node biopsy. Her medical history included well‐controlled hypertension treated with amlodipine, with no previous salivary gland disease. General anesthesia was induced with propofol and fentanyl, followed by rocuronium. Mask ventilation with a rigid face mask lasted 3 min, was graded as grade 1 on the Han scale, and required no airway adjuncts. Video laryngoscopy provided a modified Cormack–Lehane grade I view, and the trachea was intubated on the first attempt. The endotracheal tube was secured to the right, followed by placement of a bite block. The patient was positioned in lithotomy with the head neutral, arms secured, and shoulder supports positioned to avoid head and neck pressure. Anesthesia was maintained with sevoflurane in an air/oxygen mixture. She remained in 20° Trendelenburg for 178 min. As part of the institutional protocol, 50 mL of 20% mannitol was administered, beginning 23 min before the end of the 208‐min procedure and completed in the recovery room. Other medications included cefoxitin, ondansetron, dexamethasone, metoclopramide, cimetidine, paracetamol, parecoxib, tramadol, remifentanil, and fentanyl. A total of 1.8 L of lactated Ringer’s solution was administered; urine output was 40 mL, estimated blood loss was 50 mL, and the net perioperative fluid balance was +1.71 L. Neuromuscular blockade was reversed with sugammadex, followed by uneventful emergence and extubation. No facial swelling was noted in the recovery room.

Twenty‐two hours after surgery, the patient noticed painless left preauricular swelling while looking in the mirror; whether onset was sudden or gradual was unknown. She reported no fever or systemic symptoms. Examination revealed soft, diffuse, nonfluctuant left parotid swelling without erythema or crepitus (Figure 1A–C). There was no evidence of upper airway obstruction, stridor, increased work of breathing, or cyanosis, and pulse oximetry remained normal. Bimanual oral examination showed a normal Stensen’s duct without discharge or a palpable hard mass. Cranial nerve (CN) examination was normal, with intact CN V3 and VII and preserved CN IX, X, and XII function, without sensory, motor, or bulbar deficits. No cervical lymphadenopathy was present. Vital signs, complete blood count, and inflammatory markers were normal. Serum amylase and serologic testing were not obtained, and no additional imaging was performed. A presumptive diagnosis of anesthesia mumps was made based on the clinical presentation and absence of findings suggestive of infection, ductal obstruction, or drug reaction. Supportive management included reassurance, hydration, analgesia, oral hygiene, 30° head‐of‐bed elevation, and early ambulation. No additional antibiotics or corticosteroids were administered specifically for the parotid swelling. The swelling resolved within 24 h, with no recurrence or residual symptoms at the 6‐week follow‐up.

case_text:
A 21‐year‐old woman presented with bilateral foot swelling, cough, and shortness of breath (SOB) for 2 weeks. She had delivered vaginally 3 months earlier. She denied any chills or fever. Dyspnea was insidious in onset, initially exertional but later present at rest. She also experienced orthopnea, fatigue, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea.

On examination, she was hypotensive with a blood pressure of 90/70 mmHg, and the rest of her vitals were stable. On general examination, the only finding was bilateral pitting pedal edema. On cardiovascular examination, jugular venous pressure was elevated to 11 cm H2O, with a loud P2 and a pansystolic murmur at the tricuspid area. There were bronchial breath sounds and fine crepitations in the bilateral lower lung fields.

case_text:
A 22‐year‐old Bangladeshi male farmer with no prior medical or surgical history and no documented hereditary risk factors presented with a 1‐year history of recurrent postprandial epigastric pain radiating to the back and intermittent steatorrhea. Three months before admission he developed symmetrical inflammatory polyarthritis of the small joints, a photosensitive malar rash, recurrent oral ulcers (as shown in Figure 1), Raynaud phenomenon of the fingers, and progressive proximal muscle weakness. There was no alcohol use, no gallstone disease, no abdominal trauma, no exposure to cassava or other cyanogenic‐glycoside–rich foods, and no history of pancreatotoxic medication (including azathioprine, valproate, or diuretics).

Examination revealed pallor, a well‐demarcated malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds, hyperpigmented plaques over the lateral neck (Figure 1), hard‐palate ulceration, proximal interphalangeal synovitis, symmetrical proximal muscle weakness (Medical Research Council grade 3/5 in lower limbs), a positive Gower sign, and mild splenomegaly. Vital signs and fundoscopy were unremarkable; neuropsychiatric features were absent.

Laboratory evaluation showed normocytic anemia (Hb 9.2 g/dL), thrombocytopenia (50 × 109/L), elevated ESR (83 mm/h) and CRP (12.5 mg/dL), mildly elevated CPK (312 U/L; normal ≤ 170 U/L), positive direct Coombs test, normal renal and hepatic biochemistry, normal serum amylase and lipase, and normal calcium, triglycerides, and complement. Autoantibody profiling showed ANA 352 AU/mL, anti‐dsDNA 201.26 U/mL, anti‐U1‐RNP, anti‐nucleosome, anti‐Ku, and anti‐ribosomal P positivity; rheumatoid factor and anti‐CCP were negative. Antiphospholipid testing (anti‐cardiolipin, anti‐β2‐glycoprotein I, lupus anticoagulant) was negative. Plain radiograph of the abdomen showed multiple irregular calcified shadows at the L2–L3 level consistent with pancreatic calculi (Figure 2). Non‐contrast abdominal CT demonstrated numerous radio‐dense structures throughout the pancreas and within a dilated main pancreatic duct (11 mm), with the largest calculus measuring ~26 × 13 mm near the pancreatic tail and accompanying parenchymal atrophy; the liver was mildly enlarged (Figure 3). MRCP confirmed beaded main pancreatic duct dilatation (10 mm), diffuse intraductal ductolithiasis, and parenchymal atrophy, without the “sausage‐shaped” pancreas, peripancreatic halo, or delayed‐enhancement pattern of type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis, and without biliary abnormality. Genetic testing for hereditary pancreatitis (PRSS1, SPINK1, CFTR, CTRC) was not performed owing to resource constraints, and serum IgG4 was not available at our facility. No hereditary risk factors were documented, but a hereditary contribution cannot be formally excluded. The patient fulfilled the 2019 EULAR/ACR SLE classification criteria with a weighted score of 22 (entry criterion: ANA ≥ 1:80; clinical domains scored: constitutional, hematologic, mucocutaneous, musculoskeletal; threshold ≥ 10) and Sharp criteria for MCTD overlap. The clinical timeline is summarized in Table 1.

Other common causes of chronic calcific pancreatitis were sought and not found: there was no alcohol use, gallstone disease, or biliary abnormality on MRCP, hypercalcemia, hypertriglyceridemia, abdominal trauma, or pancreatotoxic medication. Differential diagnoses included tropical chronic pancreatitis (considered unlikely given the absence of cassava exposure, the normal nutritional biomarkers, and the evolving multisystem autoimmunity, although it cannot be formally excluded without genetic testing), autoimmune pancreatitis type 1 (not supported by the imaging morphology, although serum IgG4 was unavailable), and seronegative rheumatoid arthritis with extra‐articular involvement (excluded by dominant SLE serology).

Initial management consisted of oral pancreatin, analgesia (avoiding NSAIDs owing to thrombocytopenia), and nutritional support. Hydroxychloroquine 300 mg/day and prednisolone 60 mg/day were started on Days 2–3, once the clinical and serological picture indicated active SLE; prednisolone was tapered to 40 mg/day by Day 7, when mycophenolate mofetil 500 mg/day was added as a steroid‐sparing agent.

Platelet count normalized by Day 9 of admission (50 to 155 × 109/L). Symptomatic improvement across all disease domains was documented: reduced arthralgia, resolution of oral ulcers, and improvement in proximal muscle strength from MRC 3/5 to 4/5. At follow‐up, the improvement in abdominal pain, arthritis, and muscle strength was sustained, with no recurrence of symptoms. Because pancreatic enzyme replacement and supportive care were started together with immunosuppression, the improvement in pancreatic symptoms cannot be attributed to immunosuppression alone, and the calcific ductal changes are structural and not expected to regress. Improvement attributable to immunosuppression was evident in the extra‐pancreatic domains, including platelet normalization, arthritis, oral ulceration, and muscle strength. Multidisciplinary rheumatology–gastroenterology surveillance is continuing with SLE disease‐activity tracking (SLEDAI‐2 K), serial anti‐dsDNA and CPK monitoring, periodic neuropsychiatric symptom screening, baseline and periodic high‐resolution chest CT in view of the documented anti‐Ku‐related interstitial‐lung‐disease risk, and structured pancreatic endocrine (HbA1c, fasting glucose) and exocrine (fecal elastase‐1, nutritional status) surveillance.

case_text:
A 73-year-old man presented with a 12-hour history of continuous generalized abdominal pain accompanied by nausea and abdominal distension. He denied vomiting or fever. His medical history was unremarkable, with no known chronic disease or previous abdominal surgery. On admission, his temperature was 36.3 °C, heart rate 100 beats/min, respiratory rate 24 breaths/min, and blood pressure 143/91 mmHg. The abdomen was distended, with diffuse tenderness and guarding. Rebound tenderness was not marked, and bowel sounds were diminished. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 14.54 × 10^9/L, a neutrophil percentage of 88.1%, and a procalcitonin level of 0.162 ng/mL. Abdominal non-contrast computed tomography (CT) demonstrated pneumoperitoneum, dilatation of the distal ileum, and enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes. However, neither intussusception nor an identifiable intraluminal mass was observed (Figure 1). The non-contrast CT images were retrospectively reviewed; no definite mural thickening or transition point was identified. The 8.5 cm lesion was not detected because non-contrast CT provided limited soft-tissue contrast, the tumor was isodense or hypodense relative to the bowel wall and intraluminal fluid, and there was no intussusception to direct attention to the segment. Non-contrast CT was performed because the patient was admitted acutely with clinical signs of peritonitis and suspected bowel perforation. Contrast-enhanced CT was not performed because the patient required immediate surgical exploration; in this setting, the presence of pneumoperitoneum was sufficient to indicate emergency laparotomy.

After informed consent was obtained, emergency exploratory laparotomy was performed. Intraoperative exploration revealed yellow-green purulent fluid in the abdominal cavity, accompanied by dilatation and edema of the ileum. Approximately 35 cm proximal to the ileocecal valve, a markedly dilated ileal segment contained a firm palpable mass. A full-thickness perforation was present in the bowel wall immediately adjacent to the mass. The exact distance between the perforation and the tumor was not measured intraoperatively, and no separate skip lesion was identified (Figure 2). The affected ileal segment and associated mesentery were resected with approximately 10 cm proximal and distal margins. Intraoperative frozen-section analysis demonstrated a spindle-cell lesion without apparent malignant characteristics, and no lesion involvement was detected at the resection margins. A side-to-side ileoileal anastomosis was subsequently performed. Peritoneal pus was not sent for culture, which is acknowledged as a limitation. Postoperatively, the patient received empirical cefoperazone–sulbactam sodium for 7 days and recovered uneventfully.

Gross pathological examination revealed a polypoid lesion measuring 8.5 × 5.0 × 4.0 cm (Figure 3). Histologically, the lesion was centered in and confined to the submucosa. It was composed of bland spindle cells embedded in a loose fibrovascular stroma containing numerous small vessels, scattered lymphocytes, and occasional eosinophils. No significant cytological atypia, tumor-cell necrosis, or increased mitotic activity was identified. The adjacent bowel wall exhibited acute and chronic inflammation and necrosis, and occasional multinucleated giant cells. The perforation was immediately adjacent to the tumor; mucosal ulceration and vascular thrombosis at the perforation edge were not separately documented in the original pathology report (Figure 4). Immunohistochemically, the lesional cells were positive for CD34 and showed weak membranous β-catenin expression without nuclear accumulation. They were negative for CD117, DOG1, S100, SOX10, SMA, desmin, STAT6, and cytokeratin. The Ki-67 index was approximately 3%. β-catenin staining was performed to assess nuclear accumulation and to exclude desmoid fibromatosis in the differential diagnosis of spindle-cell lesions; the absence of nuclear β-catenin argued against desmoid fibromatosis (6). The morphological and immunohistochemical findings supported IFP and argued against gastrointestinal stromal tumor (CD117-negative, DOG1-negative), schwannoma (S100-negative, SOX10-negative), inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor (SMA-negative, desmin-negative, STAT6-negative), leiomyoma (SMA-negative, desmin-negative), and solitary fibrous tumor (STAT6-negative) (7). Based on the characteristic histological features and immunohistochemical profile, a final diagnosis of IFP was established. No malignancy was identified at either resection margin.

The postoperative course was uneventful, and the patient was discharged in good condition. At the 6-month follow-up, the patient remained clinically well with no evidence of recurrence. Follow-up consisted of outpatient clinical assessment and abdominal CT, without endoscopic surveillance.

A clinical timeline is provided in Table 1.

case_text:
A 48‐year‐old woman with a body mass index (BMI) of 26.08 kg/m2 and past medical history of bipolar disorder and migraines presents for evaluation of a lipoma on the lower left abdomen, which has become more prominent following significant weight loss. The lipoma was initially noticed prior to her weight loss but was less visible at that time. After losing 80 pounds through dietary restrictions and use of semaglutide and trizepitide, the lipoma became more prominent. On physical examination, there is no pain, drainage, or skin changes associated with the lipoma. The patient subsequently underwent an uneventful lipoma excision procedure with the specimen sent to pathology for examination.

On gross examination, the excised tumor was composed of uniform yellow lobulated adipose tissue. On microscopic examination, the lesion is composed of adipose tissue containing a mixture of uniloculated and multivacuolated adipocytes (Figure 1). In some areas, the multivacuolated adipocytes are quite prominent, resembling brown fat. The nuclei are small and round, without atypia. However, given the unusual appearance of the adipocytes, immunohistochemical stains for MDM2 and CDK4 were performed to rule out the possibility of an atypical lipomatous tumor and were negative. On a follow‐up clinic visit, the patient is doing well and is continuing to use GLP‐1 analogs for weight loss.

case_text:
A woman in her 80s (height 135 cm, weight 43.6 kg, body mass index 23.9 kg/m2) presented with urinary frequency. Her history included valvular heart disease, hypertension, diabetes, open gastrectomy, appendectomy, and hysterectomy. Cystoscopy revealed a solitary left‐wall tumor distant from the left ureteral orifice, with irregular posterior‐wall mucosa. Contrast‐enhanced computed tomography (CT) showed a left renal pelvic tumor measuring > 2 cm with additional multifocal lesions in the same collecting system (Figure 1A). The coronal CT distance between the left 12th rib and iliac crest was 41.8 mm. Retrograde pyelography showed an upper‐calyceal filling defect, and selective upper‐tract urine cytology revealed findings indicative of malignancy. The clinical diagnoses were a cTaN0M0 bladder tumor and cT1N0M0 left renal pelvic cancer. Three‐dimensional CT showed a circumaortic left renal vein, with the renal artery coursing between its anterior and posterior limbs (Figure 1B). Transurethral resection of the bladder tumor (TURBT) and left RANU were scheduled during the same anesthetic session. Given her body size and history of prior laparotomies, we selected our previously reported four‐robot‐port free‐access retroperitoneal configuration, as the standard transperitoneal approach could have restricted port spacing and external cart clearance.

Following completion of the 20‐min TURBT, the patient was placed in the right lateral decubitus position with pelvic tilt. Four robotic ports (11‐mm camera, 8‐mm right‐hand, 11‐mm left‐hand, and 8‐mm third‐arm ports) were inserted diagonally at 7‐cm intervals; adjacent port distances after insufflation were 7.5 cm. The camera‐port incision was extended by approximately 4 cm and fitted with a free‐access device. A 12‐mm assistant trocar was introduced through the device, which was rotated between phases to shift the trocar position (Figure 2A). Cart positions and docking angles are illustrated in Figure 2B. The docking process and the majority of the renal phase were performed by a postgraduate‐year seven urology trainee under direct supervision. The supervising surgeon briefly took over the console twice, totaling approximately 3 min, and performed perirenal mobilization after renal vessel division. Using the lower‐pole approach described by Yuan et al., the anterior and posterior venous limbs and the intervening renal artery were sequentially identified (Figure 3A). Lymphadenectomy was performed for mildly enlarged para‐aortic nodes. For the bladder cuff phase, the robotic ports were reassigned as shown in Figure 2A, and all four arm carts were moved caudally and redocked. The bagged kidney and lymph nodes were temporarily exteriorized through the free‐access incision while ureteral continuity was maintained. The ureter was clipped distal to the tumor before entry into the urinary tract. After bladder cuff excision, the kidney, ureter, and bladder cuff were removed en bloc. The supervising surgeon performed distal ureteral dissection, bladder cuff excision, and two‐layer cystotomy closure (Figure 3B). A 150‐mL saline test performed thereafter revealed no leakage. The total elapsed time was 338 min: TURBT, 20 min; repositioning, 31 min; and RANU, 287 min (console, 179 min; inter‐console interval, 18 min); the remainder comprised port placement, fat‐pad excision, docking, drain placement, and closure. Estimated blood loss was 50 mL. No conversion to open surgery or blood transfusion was required, and no perioperative complications occurred. Oral diet resumed on postoperative Day 2; the drain and catheter were removed on Days 4 and 8, and discharge occurred on Day 14. Pathological examination revealed pTa high‐grade urothelial carcinoma of the left‐wall bladder tumor and pT3 high‐grade urothelial carcinoma of the renal pelvis, with no lymphovascular invasion, negative surgical and ureteral margins, and pN0 status (0/5). The posterior‐wall mucosa and seven random biopsies were negative for malignancy. System‐log analysis recorded no arm‐interference errors during the renal phase and one on the camera arm (system arm 3) during the bladder cuff phase, without procedural interruption, unplanned arm repositioning, or clinical consequence. The interfering structure and maneuver were not identifiable retrospectively. Adjuvant therapy was omitted per patient preference; postoperative estimated glomerular filtration rate was approximately 25 mL/min/1.73 m2. At 3 months, cystoscopy and CT showed no recurrence.

case_text:
A 65-year-old man was admitted to the First Affiliated Hospital of Shandong First Medical University in May 2025 with abdominal pain and distension for 5 days and absence of stool and flatus for 3 days. His medical history included hypertension for more than 20 years, coronary artery disease for 15 years with a history of myocardial infarction, and diabetes mellitus for more than 10 years. His height and weight were 170 cm and 70 kg, respectively. Denies any history of smoking or alcohol consumption. Regular medications included valsartan 80 mg once daily for over 20 years, clopidogrel 75 mg once daily for 15 years, and insulin glargine 12 units subcutaneously once daily at bedtime plus insulin aspart 4–6 units subcutaneously three times daily with meals. Recent glycemic control was assessed using fasting blood glucose records (7.8–10.2 mmol/L over the past 2 weeks) and HbA1c (8.5%, May 2025).

On admission, the patient had a temperature of 38.5 °C, heart rate of 135 beats/min, blood pressure of 156/91 mmHg, and respiratory rate of 18 breaths/min. Abdominal examination revealed abdominal distension, muscle guarding, and diffuse tenderness and rebound tenderness throughout the abdomen. Abdominal CT performed after emergency admission predominantly showed dilated small bowel loops with air-fluid levels; clustered and locally encapsulated small bowel loops were also noted (Figure 1A). Initial management included fasting, intravenous fluid resuscitation, enemas, and empirical antibacterial therapy (ceftriaxone 2 g IV once daily; metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 h). During the preoperative evaluation period, symptoms of intestinal obstruction recurred, accompanied by green watery stool. Blood and stool bacterial cultures showed no significant bacterial growth. On hospital day 2, the body temperature rose to 39.5 °C; after 5 days of antibacterial therapy, the fever remained inadequately controlled. Given the patient's history of myocardial infarction and multiple comorbidities including hypertension, coronary heart disease, and diabetes mellitus, which collectively contributed to impaired cardiopulmonary reserve, a comprehensive preoperative assessment of his overall physiological status was performed. Surgery was ultimately scheduled for hospital day 10. Initial laparoscopic exploration revealed adhesions approximately 130 cm proximal to the ileocecal junction. After adhesiolysis, an intestinal perforation was found, with leakage of green intestinal contents. Due to technical difficulties during laparoscopy, the procedure was converted to open surgery. Open exploration revealed a purulent cavity covered by the greater omentum, containing abundant green pus and necrotic small bowel segments with a cotton-wool-like appearance (Figure 2A). The involved segment was located in the ileum. After resection of approximately 70 cm of the diseased bowel segment, side-to-side anastomosis was performed. Pathological examination of the resected specimen was then performed; hematoxylin-eosin staining showed bowel wall congestion, edema, acute and chronic inflammation, abscess formation, proliferative fibrogranulation tissue, full-thickness necrosis with perforation, and focal bacterial colonies (Figures 2B,C). Special PAS staining revealed fungal hyphae, consistent with mucormycosis (Figure 2D). Due to technical limitations, further fungal species identification, PCR, or sequencing was not performed. To exclude secondary infection, the patient also underwent contrast-enhanced MRI of the sinuses and brain and chest CT, which revealed no evidence of active lesions in the sinuses, brain, or lungs.

Systemic antifungal therapy was initiated on the day of surgery. Intravenous amphotericin B lipid complex (ABLC) was administered at 5 mg/kg/day, equivalent to 350 mg/day (based on an estimated body weight of 70 kg), for 14 days. This formulation was selected because the patient had diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and coronary heart disease, requiring minimization of nephrotoxicity; moreover, intraoperative findings of bowel necrosis, perforation, and a cotton-wool-like appearance warranted immediate empirical coverage for Mucorales postoperatively. During treatment, renal function and electrolytes—including serum creatinine, blood urea nitrogen, potassium, and magnesium—were monitored every 2–3 days; the results showed serum creatinine 85–110 μmol/L, potassium 3.6–4.2 mmol/L, and magnesium 0.75–0.95 mmol/L. Mild hypokalemia occurred during treatment and was corrected with potassium supplementation; no nephrotoxicity requiring discontinuation or severe infusion reactions occurred. After the patient's condition stabilized, treatment was switched to oral posaconazole delayed-release tablets starting on postoperative day 14, with a loading dose of 300 mg twice daily on day 1, followed by 300 mg once daily. Therefore, the 14-day ABLC course represented the initial intravenous phase of a sequential antifungal regimen, with systemic treatment subsequently continued using posaconazole. Therapeutic drug monitoring for posaconazole was performed; the predose trough concentration on day 7 after initiation was 1.2 µg/mL (target >1.0 µg/mL), so the dose was not adjusted and the original regimen was maintained. The total duration of targeted antifungal therapy was 6 weeks. Despite the development of an enterocutaneous fistula, the infection was ultimately controlled after completion of the 6-week targeted antifungal therapy (Figures 1B,C). The patient was discharged successfully after receiving a total of 6 weeks of antifungal therapy; regrettably, however, we lost contact with the patient after discharge and were unable to conduct post-discharge follow-up.

case_text:
The patient is a 49‐year‐old male with a history of tobacco use (one to two cigarettes a month, quit 20 years ago), intermittent cocaine use, and inhalant illicit drug use, who initially presented to the ED for left upper extremity and head pain for trauma status post granite falling onto his back while at work. He emigrated from Mexico in the early 2000s and has been employed in the tile and stone installation business for the majority of his adult life. The patient endorsed appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) use. The patient reported associated intermittent cough with wheezing, fatigue, weight loss (20 pounds within the last year), myalgias, and shortness of breath when ambulating longer distances than usual; no fevers, chills, hemoptysis, night sweats, or abdominal pain.

Chest X‐ray was notable for bilateral bronchovascular markings and diffuse nodular opacities (Figure 1). Computed tomography (CT) of the chest revealed findings of moderate left pneumothorax, diffuse miliary pattern, patchy consolidations throughout bilateral lung fields, and mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy (Figure 2). The left pneumothorax was clinically considered traumatic in the setting of the patient′s recent blunt chest trauma and was managed with placement of a left thoravent, which was subsequently removed the following day. Labs pertinent for mild leukocytosis (white blood cell count of 13.7). Fungal and infectious studies were negative for legionella antigen, urine lipoarabinomannan, Streptococcus pneumoniae urine antigen, Coccidioides antibody, mycoplasma pneumonia antibody, mycelial phase antibody (histoplasma), yeast phase antibody (histoplasma), and acid‐fast bacilli (AFB) smear X3 and fungal/anaerobic culture.

Cardiothoracic surgery was consulted and the patient underwent video‐assisted thoracic surgery (VATS). Miliary pattern was found throughout both lungs and large rubber‐textured lymph nodes. Wedge biopsy was positive for hyalinizing granuloma and anthracosis. Pulmonary function testing (PFTs) showed evidence of severe obstruction with no response to bronchodilators, mild restriction, air trapping, and mild diffusion impairment (Figure 3).

In the outpatient setting, the patient was started on albuterol (ventolin HFA) 90 mcg/actuation inhaler as needed for intermittent cough with mild wheezing. Repeat CT chest 3 months later showed worsening nodular changes (Figure 4). The patient was ultimately recommended for lung transplantation evaluation and continues to follow outpatient with pulmonology.

case_text:
A 38‐year‐old woman with obesity (BMI 38), active smoking and sertraline‐treated anxiety was scheduled for her third general anaesthesia for surgical debridement of an infected haematoma of the right buttock.

The first procedure was uneventful except for elevated peak airway pressures (31 cm H₂O). During the second procedure, bronchospasm occurred at induction, followed by desaturation during recovery.

For the third procedure, anaesthesia was induced with remifentanil 100 μg, propofol 200 mg and succinylcholine 100 mg. Shortly after induction, severe bronchospasm developed with rising airway pressures. Suspected endotracheal tube malposition prompted reintubation without improvement. Anaesthesia was converted to sevoflurane, and repeated inhalations of salbutamol and the combination of ipratropium bromide and fenoterol were administered.

Shortly after induction, the patient became briefly hypotensive (80/50 mmHg), refractory to intravenous ephedrine 10 mg, necessitating initiation of a phenylephrine infusion (0.1 mg/mL at 20 mL/h). However, no persistent cardiovascular collapse, cutaneous manifestations or other clinical signs of anaphylaxis were observed.

During attempted emergence from anaesthesia, bronchospasm worsened with high peak airway pressures and low tidal volumes. Treatment was escalated with inhaled adrenaline 1 mg, intravenous magnesium sulphate 10 mmol, ketamine 50 mg, continuous salbutamol infusion, theophylline 240 mg, rocuronium 20 mg, clemastine 2 mg and methylprednisolone 500 mg in divided doses. An adrenaline infusion was subsequently initiated at 0.2 μg/kg/min. Despite maximal therapy, the patient remained critically ill, with tidal volumes decreasing to approximately 200 mL and peak airway pressure increasing from 27 to 40 cm H₂O. The first available arterial blood gas showed respiratory acidosis with pH 7.18 and PaCO₂ 8.7 kPa. Respiratory acidosis subsequently worsened, with a lowest recorded pH of 6.97 and a corresponding PaCO₂ of 14.4 kPa.

As severe hypercapnic respiratory acidosis and critically impaired ventilation persisted despite extensive treatment, VV‐ECMO was initiated at 17:00, approximately 5 h and 20 min after the onset of bronchospasm. By 19:56, pH had normalised to 7.37 and PaCO₂ had decreased to 4.5 kPa. Detailed physiological data and interventions are presented in Table S2.

Serum tryptase measured 2 h after the event was 6.09 μg/L, whereas the baseline level measured 3 days later was 6.87 μg/L; both were within the normal reference range.

Subsequent pulmonary function testing demonstrated FEV₁ 39% of predicted and FEV₁/FVC 46%. Following inhaled salbutamol, FEV₁ increased to 57% and FEV₁/FVC to 58%, corresponding to an absolute improvement of 520 mL (47.7%). A diagnosis of previously unrecognised asthma was established, and appropriate inhalation therapy was initiated.

The patient was referred to the Danish Anaesthesia Allergy Centre, the Danish national reference centre for investigation of perioperative allergic reactions, comprising in vitro testing, skin testing and ultimately drug provocation of all suspected drugs administered prior to the reaction. Allergy investigations for cloxacillin, propofol, remifentanil, ephedrine, lidocaine gel 2%, chlorhexidine, latex, ethylene oxide and excipients were all negative. Skin testing and basophil activation testing for succinylcholine and rocuronium were negative, with a high negative predictive value. However, as asthma control was insufficient at the time of evaluation and given the severity of the perioperative reaction requiring ECMO, drug provocation testing with succinylcholine and rocuronium was deemed unsafe. IgE‐mediated allergy to neuromuscular blocking agents was therefore considered unlikely but could not be definitively excluded in the absence of drug provocation testing. Future use of neuromuscular blocking agents should therefore be undertaken with caution in a controlled setting.

case_text:
A 79‐year‐old male presented to the emergency department with sudden onset right lower quadrant pain that started approximately 45 min after eating fish. There was no associated nausea or vomiting. His bowels had opened that morning. His past medical history included a previous episode of small bowel intussusception, which self‐resolved, and a new diagnosis of Alzheimer’s disease. The patient had no history of previous abdominal surgery. His only regular medication was donepezil.

On examination, he was hemodynamically stable and afebrile (heart rate 58 bpm, systolic blood pressure 144/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 99% on room air and temperature 37.1°). His abdomen was soft, with right‐sided abdominal tenderness maximal in the right lower quadrant, with associated guarding and percussion tenderness. Blood tests showed a lactate of 2.3 mmol/L, WCC 9.5 × 109/L and CRP <0.3 mg/L.

Initial differentials included early acute appendicitis or gastroenteritis given the association with eating fish, and recurrent intussusception was considered due to his past history. Small bowel obstruction was considered less likely due to the absence of obstructive symptoms, such as abdominal distention and vomiting.

Contrast‐enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a loop of small bowel herniating posterior and lateral to the caecum in the retrocaecal recess. The retrocaecal recess is distended by the herniated bowel and therefore expands into the right paracolic gutter, displacing the caecum anteriorly and medially. A transition point was identified at the entrance to the retrocaecal recess, appearing inferior and lateral relative to the displaced caecum. There was proximal small bowel dilation and associated mesenteric venous congestion and trace free fluid surrounding the caecum (Figures 2–4). Specific radiological signs of established ischaemia (bowel wall thickening, pneumatosis or reduced wall enhancement) were absent.

Despite the absence of obstructive symptoms, the presence of a clear transition point at the entrance of the retrocaecal recess with proximal small bowel dilatation, mesenteric congestion and trace free fluid (Figure 3) indicated a closed‐loop small bowel obstruction secondary to pericaecal hernia. These radiological findings raised concern for possible evolving strangulation, even though specific radiological signs of established ischaemia were absent.

Nasogastric decompression was commenced. Urgent emergency laparotomy was performed to facilitate prompt assessment of bowel viability. This occurred 2.5 h after the initial surgical assessment via a routine midline laparotomy.

At laparotomy, the herniated small bowel was spontaneously reduced. A congested but viable small bowel was delivered from the right lower quadrant. The small bowel was run twice from the terminal ileum to the duodenojejunal flexure and was pink with visible peristalsis throughout. Although the small bowel had reduced, a 3 cm peritoneal aperture was identified inferior and medial to the caecum at the entrance to the retrocaecal recess. The location of the recess combined with the preoperative CT findings supports classification as a retrocaecal‐type pericaecal hernia. The inferior and lateral position of the transition point on CT is explained by the anterior and medial displacement of the caecum by the previously herniated small bowel.

There were no masses, visible pathology or adhesions identified in the abdomen. The defect was closed with 3/0 PDS, and then the abdomen was washed with normal saline and closed (0 PDS to fascia and 3/0 Monocryl to skin). There was minimal blood loss.

The post‐operative course was uncomplicated, and the patient was discharged on post‐operative day three. The patient was reviewed 6 weeks post‐operatively and was well, with his abdomen soft and non‐tender and his wound healing without complications. He was advised to return to full activity and exercise as tolerated, with no further follow‐up required. The clinical timeline is summarised in Table 1.

case_text:
A 78-year-old woman presented with a 5-year history of worsening bilateral knee pain, more severe on the left. The pain increasingly affected her daily activities and quality of life. Previous steroid injections provided diminishing benefit. Despite this, she remained active and continued cycling.

On examination, she walked independently with a preserved range of movement. Left knee flexion was ~120°, with mild tenderness along the medial joint line. There was no ligamentous instability, and neurological examination was normal.

Imaging confirmed medial compartment OA. Radiographs showed bilateral medial joint space narrowing, more pronounced on the left (Fig. 1). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated cartilage degeneration, bone marrow oedema within the medial femoral condyle, and medial meniscal degeneration (Fig. 2).

She was then placed on a National Health Service waiting list for TKR. Before surgery, she sought a second opinion and commenced the ARISE OrthoPrehab programme, focusing on joint awareness, balance, movement control, and strengthening (Fig. 3).

At 6 weeks, pain improved from 8/10 to 2–3/10, with reduced analgesia use and no requirement for nocturnal medication. Over 3 months, further improvements in pain, function, and confidence were observed. She subsequently chose to withdraw from the surgical waiting list and continue with nonoperative management. She remains active with ongoing benefit, supported by a patient testimonial (Fig. 4).

case_text:
A gentleman in his mid-30s presented to the emergency department with sudden-onset right-sided flank pain, multiple vomiting episodes, and polyuria. His known background was limited to type 2 diabetes managed with metformin. A week prior to admission, he had visited his general practitioner (GP) with coryzal symptoms and was treated with amoxicillin. On examination, he was extremely tender in the right flank and right iliac fossa. Initial blood results showed a mildly raised white cell count of 11.7 × 10⁹/L and CRP of 8.7 (unit not specified in the original report). CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated an acute right renal infarction affecting up to 70% of the renal parenchyma (Figure 1). From day 2 onwards, he developed persistent episodes of fever despite antipyretics, repeated courses of antibiotics, and microbiology input.

Further investigations into the renal infarction included thrombophilia, anti-phospholipid, and vasculitis screens, all of which were negative. ECG demonstrated normal sinus rhythm. Two transthoracic echocardiograms showed no evidence of infective endocarditis or valvular lesions. Following haematology input, the infarction was considered likely to represent an arterial event, although no clear underlying cause was identified following testing.

From day 2, the patient developed persistent temperatures reaching 39°C despite antipyretics and successive antimicrobial regimens. Initial blood and urine cultures and other infection investigations did not identify a source; chest radiography and echocardiography were unrevealing. Piperacillin-tazobactam was followed by teicoplanin and then meropenem; a maculopapular rash prompted discontinuation of meropenem and use of ciprofloxacin following microbiology advice. Tuberculosis, cytomegalovirus, and Epstein-Barr virus investigations were negative. CT of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis showed mildly enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes and the previously identified infarct; PET-CT did not demonstrate a clear malignant focus.

HLH-specific blood tests were not undertaken until approximately day 12 of admission. Ferritin was initially 6,345 µg/L, rising to a peak of 28,904 µg/L; triglycerides were 8.0 mmol/L. Progressive anaemia and thrombocytopenia developed. For the itemised H-score, the two affected lineages were anaemia (haemoglobin = 91 g/L) and thrombocytopenia (platelets = 54 × 10⁹/L). Temperature would usually rise to around 39°C when a spike was noted, with fibrinogen at 1.7 g/L and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) at 194 U/L. An H-score of 220 was calculated following discussion with the specialist HLH team (Table 1).

The HLH-2004 criteria were also later measured. The patient had fever, two affected blood cell lineages, hypertriglyceridaemia, low fibrinogen, and marked hyperferritinaemia. Bone marrow aspirate did not demonstrate convincing haemophagocytosis, and there was no organomegaly. Flow cytometry reported no NK-cell activity identified and occasional CD25-positive cells. These observations should not be interpreted as a measured elevated soluble CD25 concentration. In view of this, the patient met 5/8 of the HLH-2004 criteria within the limits of the data available.

Whilst further investigations were ongoing, the patient self-discharged following notification that blood cultures taken approximately 24 hours earlier were positive for gram-positive cocci in clusters in both bottles. He was counselled about the risks but chose to leave hospital. He re-presented to the emergency department eight days later with fever and shortness of breath. On re-presentation, he received intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam and a stat dose of gentamicin. Repeat blood cultures obtained on readmission were negative.

Given the renal infarct and positive blood culture, infective endocarditis was considered an important differential diagnosis. Both transthoracic echocardiograms were negative for evidence of infective endocarditis. Transoesophageal echocardiography was discussed with cardiology but not performed. Although subsequent blood cultures were negative, an occult infective source could not be definitively excluded, and the positive result remained a possible clue to the HLH trigger.

The patient initially declined bone marrow aspiration but agreed during his second admission after further discussions supported by an interpretation service. The aspirate showed no evidence of haematological malignancy and no convincing haemophagocytosis, although slide quality was poor. Absence of demonstrable haemophagocytosis in this limited specimen does not rule out HLH.

Following specialist multidisciplinary review, intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for three days and intravenous anakinra 200 mg twice daily were commenced. Fever and cytopenias subsequently improved. He transitioned to a tapering course of oral prednisolone and subcutaneous anakinra, with multidisciplinary outpatient follow-up and resolution of cytopenias reported. The temporal association with treatment is consistent with clinical improvement, yet the cause remains unidentified.

The timeline of the patient's clinical presentation, diagnostic evolution, and treatment is summarised in Table 2.

case_text:
A 53-year-old female patient with a history of chronic hepatitis C, hepatic fibrosis, and substance use disorder presented to a medical facility with a several-month history of epigastric pain, which was exacerbated with food consumption, along with nausea and vomiting. The patient had a past history of appendectomy, hysterectomy, and cesarean delivery. Laboratory workup was significant for mildly elevated lipase, with normal levels of total bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, aspartate transaminase, and alanine transaminase. MRCP demonstrated markedly dilated gallbladder with no evidence of gallstones, as well as dilatation of the CBD with mild intrahepatic biliary dilation and focal distal narrowing, with no evident filling defect. After a multidisciplinary discussion with other specialists, it was decided to perform a combined operation of laparoscopic cholecystectomy and potentially CBD exploration with ERCP during the same anesthetic session.

Access to the abdominal cavity was obtained using a Veress needle at Palmer’s point, after which a four-port laparoscopic cholecystectomy was carried out. Dilation of the extrahepatic biliary tree was noted intraoperatively (Fig. 1). The critical view of safety was achieved, and the cystic artery was clipped and transected. The cystic duct was opened and intraoperative cholangiogram was performed, showing right and left hepatic duct patency, a dilated CBD with a hypertrophied distal papilla with no filling (Fig. 2).

After positioning of a 0.035-inch guidewire through the cystic duct into the CBD, a 4 cm × 8 mm Mustang sphincteroplasty balloon (Boston Scientific, Marlborough, MA) was placed over the wire and deployed around the sphincter papilla until disappearance of its waist. Once that position was reached, it was maintained for an additional 30 s, and then the balloon was removed, leaving the guidewire in place. A duodenoscope was inserted, and the guidewire was identified. The papilla itself was difficult to identify without the guidewire as a landmark; however, cannulation with a sphincterotome was successful in close proximity to the wire, without cannulation of the pancreatic duct. The wire was withdrawn from the cystic duct, and a full sphincterotomy was performed, revealing a hypertrophied sphincter. Minor bleeding was stopped using extraction balloon and tamponade effect. Rectal indomethacin 100 mg was administered for pancreatitis prophylaxis. The laparoscopic cholecystectomy procedure was completed using two 0-polydioxanone Endoloops to ligate cystic duct and dissection of the gallbladder off the hepatic plate. Total combined operative time was 76 min with an estimated blood loss of 5 ml; the patient was discharged on POD0 without complications.

case_text:
A 36-year-old Filipino accountant, previously healthy, presented with 2 weeks of intermittent high-grade fever, chills, fatigue, right upper quadrant and epigastric pain, jaundice, and 4 kg weight loss. She denied respiratory or gastrointestinal symptoms, previous tuberculosis, known exposure, or recent travel. HIV Ag/Ab was negative, HbA1c was 6.0%, and she had no history of diabetes, corticosteroid or other immunosuppressive use, malignancy, transplantation, or known immunodeficiency.

On admission, she was febrile (38.5°C) and tachycardic (heart rate 125 beats/min). Examination revealed scleral icterus, mild jaundice, and right upper quadrant tenderness without guarding or rebound tenderness. There was no hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, ascites, or evidence of chronic liver disease.

Complete blood count and renal function were normal. Liver tests showed a predominantly cholestatic pattern: alkaline phosphatase 349 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase 332 U/L, AST 201 U/L, ALT 168 U/L, and bilirubin 23.3 μmol/L. CRP (73 mg/L) and procalcitonin (2.17 ng/mL) were elevated. Eosinophilia was absent.

Abdominal ultrasound showed focal prominence of the right intrahepatic biliary ducts with adjacent heterogeneous hepatic parenchyma. The common bile duct was not dilated. MRCP demonstrated a 3.6 × 3.1 cm complex multiloculated cystic lesion in hepatic segments V and VI with focal intrahepatic biliary prominence and no extrahepatic biliary obstruction (Fig. 1). There was no abdominal lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, ascites, bowel abnormality, or additional hepatic lesion.

The differential diagnosis included cystic hepatic neoplasm, autoimmune/inflammatory hepatobiliary disease, pyogenic abscess, parasitic disease, and granulomatous infection. Tumor markers revealed mildly elevated CA 125 (63.5 U/mL) and CA 19–9 (43.4 U/mL), while CEA was normal, contributing to concern for a neoplastic mimic. Given the cholestatic liver injury and focal biliary abnormalities, autoimmune hepatobiliary disease was also considered; ANA, AMA, ASMA, anti-LKM antibodies, tissue transglutaminase antibodies, and IgG subclasses including IgG4 were negative. Echinococcus serology and stool ova/parasite examination were also negative.

Empirical antibacterial therapy for suspected cholangitis consisted of ceftriaxone plus metronidazole for 7 days, followed by piperacillin-tazobactam for 4 days and meropenem for 2 days because fever and inflammatory abnormalities persisted. After approximately 2 weeks without meaningful response, ultrasound-guided core biopsy of the heterogeneous right hepatic area yielded two cores (1.5 and 1.8 cm). Histopathological examination showed multiple necrotizing and non-necrotizing granulomas (Figs. 2 and 3). Ziehl-Neelsen staining was focally positive for acid-fast bacilli. Tissue MTB-PCR detected Mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA with no rifampicin resistance detected, and mycobacterial culture confirmed M. tuberculosis complex. Susceptibility was demonstrated to the agents tested: streptomycin, isoniazid, rifampicin, and ethambutol. The exact molecular assay and mycobacterial culture platform were not documented in the available clinical record.

Further evaluation for pulmonary involvement showed negative initial sputum AFB smear and MTB-PCR, with preliminary mycobacterial culture negative at 14 days. QuantiFERON-TB Gold, obtained during subsequent TB evaluation, was positive. Chest radiography was reported as normal on initial interpretation (Fig. 4); however, subsequent CT of the chest demonstrated diffuse bilateral pulmonary micronodules consistent with a miliary pattern (Fig. 5). The final sputum culture became positive for M. tuberculosis at 6 weeks, confirming pulmonary tuberculosis.

At treatment initiation, the patient weighed 51 kg. The patient was started on rifampicin 600 mg, isoniazid 300 mg, pyrazinamide 1600 mg, and ethambutol 1100 mg once daily, with pyridoxine 50 mg daily, planned as 2 months of HRZE followed by 4 months of HR. At the 1-month follow-up, the patient remained adherent to therapy and reported no treatment-related adverse events. Fever had not recurred, and her appetite, abdominal pain, and jaundice had improved. Liver biochemistry also showed improvement, with AST decreasing to 43 U/L, ALT to 18 U/L, ALP to 290 U/L, and total bilirubin to 15.5 μmol/L. Selected laboratory parameters at admission and at the 1-month follow-up are summarized in Table 1. No repeat abdominal or chest imaging had been performed at the time of the follow-up visit.

case_text:
A 44-year-old woman presented with recurrent right-sided chest pain that had persisted for 4 years. Her body mass index (BMI) was 26.2 kg/m2. She reported no gynecological disease, chronic illness, or use of hormone replacement therapy. She had received no previous treatment or intervention for the lesion.

She was admitted to the thoracic surgery department on 23 September 2025. Her general condition was satisfactory, and she was alert with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15. Temperature was 36.6 °C, oxygen saturation was 97%, respiratory rate was 16 breaths/min, heart rate was 65 beats/min, and blood pressure was 120/78 mmHg. Lung auscultation revealed vesicular breath sounds without adventitious sounds. No rash, mucosal lesion, peripheral edema, or meningeal signs were present.

The pain was moderate, did not radiate, and increased with deep inspiration and changes in position. She denied dysphagia, odynophagia, regurgitation, heartburn, or a retrosternal foreign-body sensation. There was no cough, dyspnea, hemoptysis, fever, night sweating, weight loss, or neurological symptoms suggesting spinal cord or nerve root compression.

Preoperative esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed a patent esophageal lumen without external compression, mucosal lesions, or stricture. The gastroesophageal junction, stomach, and duodenum were unremarkable. These findings were consistent with the absence of esophageal symptoms despite the lesion’s proximity to the esophagus.

CT showed a well-defined, thin-walled, unilocular paravertebral lesion measuring 18 × 26 × 32 mm, with homogeneous contents and an attenuation of 8 Hounsfield units (HU), along the anterior surface of the inferior endplate of T5, the T6 vertebral body, and the superior endplate of T7. The lesion displaced the esophagus anteriorly and to the left. MRI confirmed a posterior mediastinal lesion at T5–T7 and showed no spinal pathology. Although the esophagus was displaced, endoscopy showed no luminal compression or involvement. Its proximity to the cyst and thoracic duct informed operative planning.

Imaging established that the lesion was cystic but could not determine its epithelial origin. The differential diagnosis included bronchogenic, esophageal duplication, thoracic duct, and mesothelial cysts, as well as a cystic neurogenic tumor. Hydatid disease was considered unlikely because no epidemiological risk factor was identified and imaging showed no daughter cysts, detached membranes, or calcification. Echinococcus serology was not performed. A simple unilocular appearance cannot by itself exclude a hydatid cyst, so definitive classification depended on examination of the excised specimen.

Table 1 summarizes the clinical course.

On 24 September 2025, the patient underwent right video-assisted thoracoscopic excision. Under endotracheal anesthesia in the left lateral decubitus position, a 3 cm incision was made in the fifth intercostal space at the midaxillary line, and a silicone wound protector was inserted. Exploration showed no pleural effusion and an intact parietal pleura. A lesion measuring approximately 3 cm was identified in the posterior mediastinum at T5–T7. The hemiazygos vein was adherent to its anterior surface, and the cyst was closely adherent anterolaterally to the esophagus and thoracic duct. Operative inspection confirmed that the esophageal wall was intact and was not involved by the cyst (Figure 1).

The lesion was separated from the mediastinal fat using blunt dissection and a Harmonic ultrasonic scalpel. The thoracic duct, intercostal veins, and paraesophageal vessels were identified and clipped sequentially. The lesion was then excised (Figure 2). Aerostasis and hemostasis were confirmed. A single-lumen 0.8 cm silicone drain was placed through the port site, and the wound was closed in layers with an aseptic dressing. No change to the planned thoracoscopic approach was required, and conversion to thoracotomy was unnecessary.

The resected specimen was a thin-walled cyst measuring 3.0 × 2.0 cm, with a wall thickness of no more than 0.3 mm and brown contents. Hematoxylin and eosin staining showed fibrous tissue and smooth muscle fibers beneath cuboidal and columnar ciliated epithelium. Smooth muscle actin (SMA, Leica, clone asm-1) highlighted the muscle fibers in the cyst wall (Figure S1). This finding confirmed a muscular component but did not establish the epithelial lineage.

The cyst-lining epithelial cells expressed paired box protein 8 (PAX8, polyclonal, CellMarque), estrogen receptor (ER), and progesterone receptor (PR). Staining for cytokeratins 5/6 (CK5/6), calretinin, thyroid transcription factor 1 (TTF-1), and D2-40 was negative. Nuclear PAX8 expression is shown in Figure 3. The morphology and immunophenotype supported Hattori’s cyst. No parasitic structures were identified.

The postoperative course was uneventful. During admission, the patient received gastroprotective therapy and analgesia. The pleural drain was removed, and the wound healed by primary intention. Chest radiography showed fully expanded lungs without focal or infiltrative opacities or pleural effusion. She was discharged in satisfactory condition, with no adverse or unanticipated events during the hospital stay. At the 11-month follow-up, she reported complete resolution of chest pain, no other complaints, and a return to her usual activities.

The rare diagnosis initially caused considerable anxiety, and the patient doubted that treatment would succeed. At the 11-month follow-up, she valued the prompt diagnosis and the clinical team’s clear explanation of the treatment plan. She described the care as practical and professional and felt that seeking medical attention had contributed to the outcome. She was pleased that surgery caused little pain and required only one small incision. Having resumed her usual activities, she was satisfied with the result.

title: Posterior Mediastinal Müllerian Cyst (Hattori’s Cyst): A Case Report and Review of Pathogenesis and Diagnostic Features

case_text:
A 48-year-old woman with a giant splenic cyst and no relevant medical history underwent laparoscopic splenectomy in November 2025. Dense adhesions were encountered and a lesion of the posterior left diaphragm was sutured during dissection. She was discharged on the third postoperative day (POD) without complaints.

On POD 94 she attended an emergency department with abdominal pain and dyspnoea. Chest radiography suggested a left pleural effusion and a 32-Fr chest tube was placed, draining food debris. She was kept in nil per os (NPO) and started on broad-spectrum antibiotics and total parenteral nutrition. Output was high, averaging 3200 ml per 24 hours over the following 5 days while she awaited transfer to a tertiary hospital.

After transfer, a computed tomography (CT) scan with iodinated oral contrast (Fig. 1) showed transdiaphragmatic gastric herniation into the left hemithorax with contrast leakage into the pleural cavity and atelectatic lung parenchyma, suggesting a gastropleural fistula.

The following day she underwent a combined video-assisted thoracoscopy and midline laparotomy. Thoracoscopy showed abundant fibrinopurulent tissue and food debris throughout the left hemithorax, and a strangulated hernia through a defect in the left hemidiaphragm containing the necrotic anterior gastric wall, with no other herniated organs, resulting in an extensive gastropleural fistula (Fig. 2). The contents were reduced into the abdominal cavity, the diaphragmatic defect was closed with interrupted 2–0 Polidioxanone (PDS) sutures, extensive thoracic lavage was performed, and anterior and posterior 32-Fr chest drains were placed.

Supra-umbilical midline laparotomy found virtually no peritoneal contamination, as the hernia had prevented downflow of gastric contents. Necrosis of ~12 cm of the anterior gastric wall was identified (Fig. 3A). After extensive debridement of necrotic tissue, the anterior gastric wall was closed with a two-layer continuous 3–0 poliglecaprone suture (Fig. 3B), and a 24-Fr Blake drain was left beneath the left hemidiaphragm.

A liquid diet was started in the immediate postoperative period. On the third POD she developed intense nausea and tachycardia; CT with oral contrast showed no leak (Fig. 4). The liquid diet was maintained for 2 weeks, followed by a pureed diet and a soft diet from the third week, with adequate acceptance.

The Blake drain was removed after 3 days of negligible output; the anterior chest drain was removed on POD 7 and the posterior drain on POD 14. A bloodstream infection with multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter and Candida glabrata was treated with antibiotics and antifungals for 18 days, with adequate clinical and laboratory response. She was discharged after 38 days and referred for follow-up at the original facility. At 3-month review she was asymptomatic, with normal upper endoscopy, chest CT, and laboratory findings, and resumed normal activity.

case_text:
Malignant tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF) causes recurrent aspiration and is commonly palliated with esophageal fully covered self-expanding metal stents (FC-SEMS).1 We present a case of a 71-year-old woman with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma with a 5 mm TEF 25 cm from the incisors. A 23 mm × 10.5 cm FC-SEMS was deployed with over-the-scope clip fixation, and esophagram confirmed fistula exclusion. Weeks later, she developed dyspnea, hypoxia, and recurrent aspiration; computed tomography and bronchoscopy demonstrated tracheal compression with approximately 50% posterior narrowing (Figure 1). During simultaneous bronchoscopy, the stent was removed, immediately improving tracheal caliber. An 18 mm × 10.3 cm FC-SEMS was placed under endoscopic, bronchoscopic, and fluoroscopic guidance, but esophagram revealed proximal leakage into the airway from incomplete wall apposition (Figure 2). After through-the-scope clips failed, a second 18 mm × 10.3 cm FC-SEMS was deployed coaxially within the first (Figure 2), sealing the leak on contrast studies. She was discharged on a modified diet without aspiration.

Although FC-SEMS are frequently employed to treat TEF, failure to seal or airway compression may occur.2,3 This case highlights stent-in-stent placement of submaximal diameter FC-SEMS as a potential salvage strategy to restore an effective seal while preserving airway patency.

case_text:
A 38‐year‐old woman (Gravida 2, Para 1) with B Rh‐positive blood type presented to the emergency department (ED) with painless vaginal bleeding that had persisted for 4 days. She had undergone a CS 2 years earlier. Her last menstrual period had occurred 6 weeks and 2 days prior to presentation. She had no history of other surgeries and no comorbidities.

At an outpatient visit 4 days before admission, her serum β‐hCG level was 1442.6 mIU/mL. TVUS performed at that time did not reveal a GS within the uterine cavity.

The day before presentation to the ED, the serum β‐hCG level was 6213.8 mIU/mL, and on admission it had increased to 10,775 mIU/mL. Complete blood count results were within normal limits. TVUS demonstrated an empty uterine cavity with an endometrial thickness of 10 mm and a GS containing a yolk sac located within the cesarean scar niche (Figures 1, 2, and 3). The mean GS diameter was 8.6 mm, and the crown–rump length (CRL) measured 2.8 mm, corresponding to a gestational age of 5 weeks and 5 days. No adnexal abnormalities were identified.

On the following day, the β‐hCG level increased further to 13,001 mIU/mL. The patient was thoroughly counseled regarding the severe risks associated with CSP, including uterine rupture, catastrophic hemorrhage, and the potential need for an emergency hysterectomy. The available management options, including surgical resection (laparoscopy or HSC), systemic multidose methotrexate, and local ultrasound‐guided treatment were discussed. Given the patient′s stable hemodynamic status, the desire to preserve future fertility, and the thin myometrium at the scar site, a minimally invasive approach was favored. The patient was counseled regarding the risks associated with CSP and the available management options. She consented to local MTX treatment. The intervention was performed under short intravenous anesthesia. A TVUS probe equipped with a sterile needle guide was introduced. Under continuous real‐time ultrasound monitoring, the GS within the cesarean scar niche was clearly visualized, ensuring the bladder wall was safely bypassed. A 16‐gauge, 30‐cm single‐lumen aspiration needle was advanced transvaginally through the anterior vaginal fornix directly into the center of the GS. The total dose of 80 mg of MTX was administered. To ensure even and comprehensive infiltration of the gestational niche and the surrounding trophoblastic tissue, the total dose was divided into four consecutive 20‐mg injections delivered circumferentially into the trophoblast and the sac cavity during this single session. Upon needle withdrawal, color Doppler imaging was utilized to confirm the absence of active bleeding or hematoma formation at the vaginal puncture site and within the scar area. The total procedure time was 55 min, and the estimated blood loss was approximately 15 mL. No perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis was administered.

Three days after the procedure, the patient remained in good clinical condition and reported only mild vaginal bleeding. Ultrasound examination demonstrated resolution of the GS. The serum β‐hCG level decreased to 927.77 mIU/mL, and the patient was discharged in stable condition.

At follow‐up 10 days after treatment, the patient reported moderate vaginal bleeding without additional symptoms. TVUS confirmed an empty uterine cavity with a thin endometrium (Figure 4). No pathological masses or abnormalities were detected in the adnexa. However, within the cesarean scar niche, a well‐demarcated residual lesion measuring 9.4 × 9.5 mm without detectable vascular flow on Doppler imaging was observed. As the β‐hCG level had further declined to 62.04 mIU/mL, no additional therapeutic intervention was required. Given the downward trend of β‐hCG and the absence of active vascularization, expectant management with ongoing outpatient monitoring was continued, and the symptoms resolved spontaneously.

One year later the patient conceived spontaneously. The subsequent pregnancy progressed without any maternal or fetal complications. Because of her obstetric history, she underwent a scheduled, elective CS at term (39 weeks of gestation), resulting in the delivery of a healthy newborn. No signs of abnormal placental invasion (such as PAS) or uterine scar dehiscence were noted intraoperatively.

Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for the publication of this case report and any accompanying images.

To ensure even and comprehensive infiltration of the gestational niche and the surrounding trophoblastic tissue, the total dose was divided into four consecutive 20‐mg injections delivered circumferentially into the trophoblast and the sac cavity during this single session.
Upon needle withdrawal, color Doppler imaging was utilized to confirm the absence of active bleeding or hematoma formation at the vaginal puncture site and within the scar area.
The total procedure time was 55 min, and the estimated blood loss was approximately 15 mL.
No perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis was administered.
Three days after the procedure, the patient remained in good clinical condition and reported only mild vaginal bleeding.
Ultrasound examination demonstrated resolution of the GS.
The serum β‐hCG level decreased to 927.77 mIU/mL, and the patient was discharged in stable condition.
At follow‐up 10 days after treatment, the patient reported moderate vaginal bleeding without additional symptoms.
TVUS confirmed an empty uterine cavity with a thin endometrium (Figure 4).
No pathological masses or abnormalities were detected in the adnexa.
However, within the cesarean scar niche, a well‐demarcated residual lesion measuring 9.4 × 9.5 mm without detectable vascular flow on Doppler imaging was observed.
As the β‐hCG level had further declined to 62.04 mIU/mL, no additional therapeutic intervention was required.
Given the downward trend of β‐hCG and the absence of active vascularization, expectant management with ongoing outpatient monitoring was continued, and the symptoms resolved spontaneously.
One year later the patient conceived spontaneously.
The subsequent pregnancy progressed without any maternal or fetal complications.
Because of her obstetric history, she underwent a scheduled, elective CS at term (39 weeks of gestation), resulting in the delivery of a healthy newborn.
No signs of abnormal placental invasion (such as PAS) or uterine scar dehiscence were noted intraoperatively.
Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for the publication of this case report and any accompanying images.
title: Targeted Methotrexate Treatment in Cesarean Scar Pregnancy: A Case Report and Literature Review

case_text:
The patient was a woman in her 70s with a medical history of an internal carotid artery aneurysm and a hiatal hernia. There was no remarkable family history. She initially presented with a bloody nipple discharge from the left breast 18 years earlier. At that time, imaging findings suggested a benign papillary lesion, and the lesion was managed with clinical observation. Ten years ago, 8 years after the initial consultation, the lesion had increased in size to 1.0 cm in maximum diameter, and a CNB revealed a benign papillary lesion. The patient therefore remained under follow-up, and no findings suggestive of malignancy were observed for the next 8 years.

MG revealed newly developed polymorphic linear calcifications distributed in a segmental pattern in the upper outer quadrant of the contralateral right breast, classified as BI-RADS category 4 (Fig. 1A). US demonstrated extensive ductal dilatation with internal hyperechoic lesions extending from the nipple to the upper outer quadrant. The contrast-enhanced MRI showed a segmental, non-mass enhancement in the right breast, which is categorized as ACR BI-RADS (5th edition) category 5. A CNB confirmed ductal carcinoma of the right breast. Laboratory findings, including tumor markers, were unremarkable. A total mastectomy was performed for the right breast cancer. The disease was predominantly in situ, with a 7 mm solid-type invasive lesion. Hormone receptor analysis by IHC showed that neither the estrogen receptor nor the progesterone receptor was expressed (0%). The HER2 score was 3+, and the Ki-67 labeling index was 15%. These findings are consistent with the HER2-positive surrogate subtype based on IHC. No distant metastases were detected, and the clinical stage was classified as stage I.

Meanwhile, US of the left breast revealed a lobulated, hypoechoic mass with a relatively well-defined margin. The tumor measured 1.2 cm in maximum diameter and showed heterogeneous internal echogenicity with cystic components (Fig. 2A and 2B). MG demonstrated focal asymmetry in the middle portion of the left breast with coarse calcifications, classified as ACR BI-RADS category 3 (Fig. 1B). MRI revealed a dumbbell-shaped tumor with iso-intensity on both T1- and T2-WI, with a partial high-intensity area on T2WI. Contrast-enhanced MRI demonstrated heterogeneous enhancement with internal dark septations. The kinetic analysis showed a fast initial enhancement followed by a plateau pattern, corresponding to ACR BI-RADS category 4 (Fig. 3A). Additionally, a region of non-mass enhancement was noted on the cranial aspect of the tumor (Fig. 3B). Because imaging studies of the left breast lesion showed equivocal findings and could not entirely rule out malignancy, a CNB was re-performed. Although the initial CNB specimen had demonstrated a benign papillomatous lesion (Fig. 4A and 4B), the subsequent CNB specimen exhibited a highly heterogeneous pathological appearance. A dense area containing variable ductal epithelial components and an abundant, hypocellular myxofibrous and myxoid/chondroid stroma was identified; however, a distinct transitional zone between these 2 components was not apparent (Fig. 4D). A medium-magnification view demonstrated a distinct biphasic pattern, characterized by inner epithelial cells forming tubules and outer myoepithelial cells proliferating with pale cytoplasm, without significant cytological atypia (Fig. 4C). Consequently, differentiating between a benign lesion and a low-grade malignancy posed a diagnostic challenge at the biopsy stage. Because the potential for malignant transformation or a low-grade malignancy could not be entirely ruled out, an excisional biopsy (local excision) was performed for both a definitive diagnosis and treatment.

Pathological examination revealed a tumor composed of both epithelial and myoepithelial components within a fibrous capsule, accompanied by myxoid stroma and osseous and cartilaginous differentiation (Fig. 5A and 5B). A gradual transition from the myxoid stroma to the cartilaginous component was observed, supporting the diagnosis of PA of the breast (Fig. 5C and 5D).

An abundant eosinophilic chondroid-to-chondromyxoid matrix was observed, containing scattered round-to-oval chondrocyte-like cells within lacunae. These cells had small, relatively uniform nuclei, inconspicuous nucleoli, and scant cytoplasm. There was no significant cellular atypia or tumor necrosis, and it was determined to be cartilage differentiation (Fig. 6A). In the ductal structures, myoepithelial cells were identified in the basal layer. In the myxoid stroma, these cells exhibited a spindle-shaped morphology (Fig. 6B). Immunohistochemically, the tumor cells were positive for alpha-SMA in both the epithelial and stromal components; however, p63 expression was absent in the myxoid (spindle cell) areas (Fig. 6C and 6D). The absence of significant cytological atypia, together with these findings, supported the exclusion of metaplastic carcinoma. The surgical margins of the excisional biopsy were negative. Postoperative adjuvant therapy for breast cancer was not performed at the patient’s request. The patient has remained free of recurrence during 6 years of follow-up.

case_text:
A 62‐year‐old man with a history of hypertension presented to the emergency department with a 13‐day history of chest pain. Despite the prolonged duration of symptoms, he was hemodynamically stable on admission, with a blood pressure of 110/70 mmHg, heart rate of 65 beats/min, respiratory rate of 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation of 99% on room air.

The initial electrocardiogram (ECG) showed sinus rhythm with ST‐segment elevation in the inferior leads and reciprocal ST‐segment depression in the anterolateral leads (Figure 1). Cardiac troponin I was elevated at 4.78 ng/mL (reference range, 0–0.30 ng/mL). Laboratory investigations showed creatine kinase (CK) of 195 U/L, CK‐MB of 69 U/L, hemoglobin of 15.6 g/dL, creatinine of 1.31 mg/dL, urea of 47 mg/dL, and C‐reactive protein of 321 mg/L.

Although the patient presented 13 days after the onset of symptoms and remained hemodynamically stable, ongoing chest pain, persistent ST‐segment elevation in the inferior leads, and elevated cardiac troponin I (4.78 ng/mL) prompted referral for coronary angiography.

TTE was performed during the initial admission before PCI and repeated before discharge. Neither examination identified a VSR or another mechanical complication. The available records provided for this report do not specify the baseline LVEF or all baseline echocardiographic measurements.

The patient received loading doses of aspirin 300 mg and clopidogrel 600 mg before transfer to the catheterization laboratory. Coronary angiography demonstrated 65%–70% stenosis of the LAD (Figure 2) and 99% stenosis of the RCA (Figure 3).

The RCA lesion was treated with balloon predilatation using a 2.0 × 20 − mm balloon at 14 atm, followed by implantation of a 2.75 × 24 − mm drug‐eluting stent at 18 atm. The final angiographic result was satisfactory, with restoration of TIMI grade III flow and no immediate procedural complications.

The RCA was considered the presumed infarct‐related artery because of the inferior ST‐segment elevation, elevated cardiac biomarkers, and critical 99% RCA stenosis, and PCI was performed by the treating team. The available records do not document persistent or recurrent chest pain, serial dynamic ECG changes, viability testing, or another specific criterion used to justify revascularization at this late stage after symptom onset; therefore, the precise retrospective rationale for the timing of PCI cannot be established beyond identification of the RCA as the presumed culprit vessel. The 65%–70% LAD stenosis was managed medically during the index procedure, and the available records do not document physiological assessment or a separate indication for immediate LAD intervention.

Following PCI, the patient was transferred to the coronary care unit for observation. He remained clinically stable and was discharged the following day on aspirin 100 mg once daily, clopidogrel 75 mg once daily, metoprolol 25 mg once daily, ramipril 2.5 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 80 mg once daily, and lansoprazole 40 mg once daily.

Four days after discharge, the patient returned with worsening exertional dyspnea and orthopnea. Clinical examination revealed bilateral inspiratory crackles consistent with pulmonary edema and a new pansystolic murmur. His other recorded vital signs were within normal limits.

Urgent TTE demonstrated a 21‐mm VSR involving the basal inferior interventricular septum, with left‐to‐right shunting on color Doppler (Figure 4). Left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) was 60%, and right ventricular systolic function was preserved, with a tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE) of 21 mm. Severe mitral regurgitation was also identified, and the estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure (SPAP) was 25 mmHg. The pulmonary‐to‐systemic blood flow ratio (Qp/Qs) was not measured or available in the documented results. The specific echocardiographic acquisition views used to demonstrate the defect and confirm the shunt were not documented in the records available for this report. The mechanism of the severe mitral regurgitation was also not specified in the available echocardiographic or operative records. These findings characterized the septal defect and associated valvular abnormality despite preserved global left ventricular systolic function.

Following confirmation of VSR, the patient was admitted to the coronary care unit for close monitoring, stabilization, and supportive management. After approximately 14 days of stabilization and observation, he underwent surgical repair of the VSR and mechanical mitral valve replacement for severe mitral regurgitation.

Postoperative echocardiography showed no reported residual VSR or other documented residual abnormality. The available records do not provide a more detailed perioperative course or a specific documented rationale for the approximately 14‐day interval to surgery beyond stabilization and observation. At the 2‐month outpatient follow‐up, the patient remained clinically stable and continued under outpatient surveillance.

A chronological summary of the patient′s clinical presentation, diagnostic investigations, revascularization, development of VSR, definitive surgical management, and subsequent follow‐up is provided in Table 1.

case_text:
A 58-year-old Han Chinese female with no history of tobacco or alcohol consumption or other modifiable cardiovascular risk factors.

The patient presented to the emergency department (ED) reporting one hour of acute spontaneous bilateral lower-limb numbness accompanied by progressive weakness. She denied all painful sensations (including chest, back, abdominal and lumbar pain), alongside dizziness, syncope, dyspnea, nausea and vomiting. No other systemic complaints were reported.

She had no clinically documented history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, coronary artery disease, or connective-tissue disorders. There was no family history of aortic dissection, aortic aneurysm, or hereditary vasculopathy. Although traditional cardiovascular risk factors were absent from her clinical record, preoperative CT imaging demonstrated mild aortic and coronary calcification, indicative of underlying subclinical atherosclerotic change.

No prior medical or surgical interventions relevant to vascular or neurological disease had been performed before admission.
