case_text:
A 52‐year‐old healthy woman presented to the gastroenterology clinic for routine colorectal cancer screening and investigation of unexplained iron deficiency without anemia. She reported no abdominal pain, gastrointestinal bleeding, changes in bowel habits, weight loss, or other GI‐related symptoms. Her family history was notable for Crohn’s disease in a second‐degree relative, but there was no known family history of intestinal malignancy. Physical examination was unremarkable. Her iron deficiency had been documented for approximately 1 year prior to referral, with a ferritin nadir of 11 ng/mL and an incomplete response to oral supplementation. Hemoglobin remained normal throughout, ranging from 12.6 to 13.7 g/dL, with a mean corpuscular volume of 95.3 fL.

The EGD was performed without complication. The esophagus, stomach, and duodenal mucosa appeared normal, and biopsies were taken from the stomach and duodenum for histologic evaluation as part of the workup for iron deficiency. Gastric biopsies were negative for Helicobacter pylori, and duodenal biopsies were normal, without histologic evidence of celiac disease. Screening colonoscopy performed during the same session was also unremarkable. However, during the retroflexed examination of the stomach, a nonpulsatile extrinsic compression was observed along the lesser curvature of the gastric body (Figure 1).

Given the potential differential diagnoses, including pancreatic mass, lymphadenopathy, or perigastric pathology, a contrast‐enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis was ordered. The CT demonstrated normal liver, biliary system, adrenal glands, spleen, and kidneys. The pancreas showed a lobulated extension arising from the body and extending superiorly toward the posterior aspect of the stomach (Figure 2). This morphology represented an exaggerated tuber omentale, which lay in direct apposition to the posterior aspect of the lesser curvature without an intervening fat plane and accounted for the impression seen on EGD. No ductal dilatation, mass, or inflammatory changes were observed.

The CT also revealed a small benign hepatic cyst and a suspected uterine fibroid, the latter initially considered a possible contributor to the patient’s iron deficiency. The patient was reassured regarding the benign nature of the pancreatic anatomical variant, and no further imaging or intervention was deemed necessary. She was subsequently evaluated for abnormal uterine bleeding in the setting of perimenopause and underwent hysteroscopy with dilation and curettage, which demonstrated no intracavitary myoma or polyp. The fibroid suspected on cross‐sectional imaging was therefore not confirmed. Her iron deficiency was attributed to abnormal uterine bleeding, with no gastrointestinal source identified. She received intravenous iron after an inadequate response to oral supplementation, with subsequent normalization and maintenance of ferritin.

case_text:
A 36-year-old male patient was admitted to our hospital with a left retroperitoneal mass, which had been identified by computed tomography (CT) scan at an outside hospital after the patient experienced a one-month history of distending pain in the left flank and abdomen. The patient had no significant past medical history. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed a 5 × 6 cm hypervascular paravertebral mass at the upper level of the left psoas major muscle. A neurogenic tumor was suspected (Fig. 1).

After multidisciplinary team discussion, the patient underwent complete extraperitoneal resection of the left retroperitoneal tumor via a midline incision through the pre-transversalis fascia space (Fig. 2). The principal operative steps were as follows. First, with the patient in the supine position, a midline incision was made from the xiphoid process to 3 cm below the umbilicus (Fig. 3A). Second, the layers of the abdominal wall were incised sequentially down to the superficial surface of the transversalis fascia, thereby entering the pre-transversalis fascia space. Dissection was carried leftward along the superficial surface of the transversalis fascia (i.e. the deep surface of the fascia of the rectus abdominis and transversus abdominis), and then continued along the anterior surface of the quadratus lumborum and psoas major (i.e. the posterior surface of the posterior renal fascia) to the left margin of the abdominal aorta (Fig. 3B and C). Third, the anterior aspect of the tumor was dissected, followed by its medial aspect, and the left lumbar arteries and veins entering the tumor were ligated and divided. The main tumor mass, together with the enlarged caudal lymph nodes was completely resected (Fig. 3D). Fourth, abdominal wall retraction was released, and the dissected retroperitoneal space spontaneously return to its anatomical position (Fig. 3E). Finally, the surgical specimen was opened for pathological examination. Its capsule was intact.

No peritoneal injury occurred during dissection, and the peritoneal cavity remained intact. Operative time was 220 min, and estimated blood loss was 20 ml. The patient was discharged on postoperative Day 3. Histopathological examination showed an encapsulated lesion with prominent lymphoid hyperplasia and follicular architecture. In some areas, the mantle-zone lymphocytes formed a hyaline, concentric onion-skin pattern, accompanied by marked vascular proliferation. Numerous plasma cells and proliferating vessels were present in the interfollicular regions. Immunohistochemistry showed ‘positive expression of CD20, CD3, and CD23’. The diagnosis was hyaline vascular-type Castleman disease (Fig. 4).

At outpatient follow-up 3 months postoperatively, contrast-enhanced CT showed no tumor recurrence, and the local anatomy appeared normal (Fig. 5).

case_text:
A 75-year-old man with abdominal distension developed severe abdominal pain following bowel preparation for colonoscopy and was transferred to our hospital. His medical history was unremarkable.

On admission, his body temperature was 36.4°C, blood pressure 115/79 mmHg, heart rate 91 beats/min, respiratory rate 26 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Physical examination revealed generalized peritonitis. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 7500/μl and C-reactive protein level of 0.06 mg/dl. Arterial blood gas analysis showed a pH of 7.37 and lactate level of 3.1 mmol/l. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained before intravenous meropenem administration. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) demonstrated rectal cancer and sigmoid colon perforation (Fig. 1), and emergency surgery was performed.

Laparotomy revealed generalized fecal peritonitis, a rectal tumor, and sigmoid colon perforation. The perforation was located close to the rectal tumor, and the intervening bowel wall was markedly thinned and fragile. Therefore, we decided to resect the rectal tumor together with the perforated sigmoid colon. Hartmann’s procedure with abdominal lavage and drainage was performed. Peritoneal fluid was collected after initiation of meropenem. Histopathological examination revealed rectal adenocarcinoma (pT3N0M0, pStage IIA).

The patient developed postoperative septic shock requiring noradrenaline and vasopressin, which were discontinued on postoperative day (POD) 2. He was extubated on POD 4.

Peritoneal fluid culture yielded AmpC-producing Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron, anaerobic Gram-negative rods, and Candida spp. The three identified bacterial species were susceptible to meropenem and cefmetazole.

The anaerobic bottles from both sets of blood cultures became positive after 77 h. MALDI-TOF MS (MALDI Biotyper, Bruker Daltonics, Bremen, Germany) identified G. massiliensis (score 2.39) and B. faecihominis (score 2.13). The identification log score reflects the similarity between the measured mass spectrum and reference spectra in the database. Scores of ≥2.0 generally support species-level identification, whereas scores of 1.7–1.99 support genus-level identification. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing was not performed for either organism. Follow-up blood cultures on POD 7 were negative. Meropenem was continued until POD 13 and then de-escalated to cefmetazole based on the culture and susceptibility results of the major pathogens isolated from the peritoneal fluid. Cefmetazole was administered for an additional 5 days.

The patient recovered without recurrence of infection and was transferred for rehabilitation on POD 36.

case_text:
A 56‐year‐old woman presented with gait disturbance and pain radiating from the right back to the lateral thoracic region. Her symptoms had gradually worsened over 3 months, and she was referred to our department by a neurosurgeon at our institution. Ten years ago, she had undergone resection and radiation therapy for an ependymoma of the medulla oblongata at our hospital. At the time of the initial diagnosis, brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed; however, MRI of the cervical, thoracic, and lumbosacral spine was not performed. Therefore, the presence or absence of spinal dissemination at the initial diagnosis could not be assessed. During the subsequent follow‐up period, brain MRI was performed regularly, approximately two to six times per year; however, spinal MRI surveillance was not performed.

Neurological examination revealed normal strength in both upper and lower limbs. The biceps, brachioradialis, and triceps reflexes were normal, whereas mild hyperreflexia was observed in the patellar and Achilles tendon reflexes. Sensory examination revealed mild hypoesthesia below the T11 dermatome. She exhibited spastic gait with instability. Routine laboratory tests showed no remarkable abnormalities. Spinal MRI was then performed and demonstrated multiple intradural extramedullary tumors distributed along the thoracic and lumbar spinal canal (Figure 1a,b). Based on these findings and her history of intracranial ependymoma, dissemination of ependymoma to the spinal intradural extramedullary space was suspected. Because the lesions were widespread, a two‐stage surgery was planned to avoid the anticipated surgical burden of attempting complete resection in a single procedure. The first stage consisted of resection and fixation from T4 to T10, followed by tumor removal from T11 to L1 in the second stage.

During the first surgery, laminectomies and posterior fusion were performed from T4 to T10, followed by tumor resection at the same levels. Histopathological examination revealed an ependymoma. The tumor showed papillary and tubular proliferation around fibrovascular stromal cores with characteristic perivascular pseudorosettes (moose track pattern). Although cellularity was relatively high, mitotic figures were inconspicuous and no regional necrosis was identified. The MIB‐1 labeling index was approximately 7%. The findings were consistent with a WHO Grade II ependymoma based on the fourth Edition of the WHO Classification of Tumors of the Central Nervous System. The dura mater was closed with sutures and further reinforced using Beriplast P Combi‐Set (fibrin sealant containing fibrinogen and factor XIII; CSL Behring K.K., Tokyo, Japan) and Neoveil Sheet (absorbable polyglycolic acid [PGA] sheet for tissue reinforcement; Gunze Medical Limited, Osaka, Japan). Finally, posterior fixation from T4 to T10 was performed. Motor evoked potential (MEP) monitoring remained stable throughout the surgery. The total blood loss was 720 mL, and the surgical time was 7 h and 14 min. No immediate postoperative weakness was observed. However, on postoperative day 1, mild right lower limb weakness was observed, with the iliopsoas muscle strength graded as MMT 3 on the right and MMT 4 on the left. Initially, spinal cord compression due to a postoperative hematoma was suspected, and an MRI scan was performed. However, MRI showed spinal cord edema, and no hematoma was detected. There was no radiological evidence of tumor migration at that time. On postoperative day 11, the patient suddenly developed severe weakness of the right lower limb, with the right tibialis anterior muscle strength graded as MMT 1. MRI was performed again and revealed cranial migration of the residual tumor. The lesion, which had been located at the superior aspect of the T12 vertebral body before surgery (Figure 2a), had migrated cranially beyond the inferior endplate of T11 (Figure 2b).

The second planned operation was performed 2 weeks after the first surgery, involving tumor resection following laminectomies from T11 to L1. The dura mater was carefully sutured and reinforced using the same method as in the first surgery. The total blood loss was 320 mL, and the surgical time was 3 h and 44 min. Histopathological examination of the second‐stage specimen showed findings similar to those of the first‐stage specimen, including papillary proliferation around fibrovascular stromal cores and a characteristic perivascular pseudorosette (moose track pattern). No obvious necrosis, marked nuclear atypia, or mitotic figures were identified. The MIB‐1 labeling index was approximately 7%–8%. During the procedure, the MEP waveform of the tibialis anterior muscle reappeared (Figure 3a,b).

After the second surgery, the patient was followed clinically and with MRI for 9 months. At the 9‐month follow‐up, she had regained full muscle strength. She subsequently did not attend scheduled follow‐up visits. Approximately 4 years after surgery, MRI of the thoracolumbar spine was performed for another clinical indication and showed no evidence of tumor recurrence. The clinical course and treatment timeline are summarized in Figure 4.

title: Cranial Migration of a Disseminated Thoracic Ependymoma Causing Transient Paraparesis: A Case Report

case_text:
A 52‐year‐old man, a former smoker (16 pack‐years), was referred after microscopic hematuria was detected on screening urinalysis. Preoperative voided urine cytology was suspicious, and right renal pelvic urothelial carcinoma, clinical stage cT3N0M0, was diagnosed. During retroperitoneoscopy‐assisted right radical nephroureterectomy, transurethral resection of the intramural ureter and bladder cuff using the ureteral stripping technique proved technically difficult and required repeated insertion and manipulation of a rigid cystoscope via the urethra. A 24‐Fr or 21‐Fr rigid cystoscope was inserted approximately 10 times, and the transurethral procedure lasted approximately 30–40 min. Difficult urethral passage, urethral bleeding, or visible mucosal injury was not documented. An 18‐Fr urethral catheter was removed on postoperative Day 7, with no subsequent dysuria, urethral pain, or voiding difficulty. Pathological examination confirmed high‐grade invasive urothelial carcinoma of the renal pelvis (pT3 pN0, 0/1 regional lymph node; distant metastasis was not detected on preoperative imaging). Cystoscopy and urine cytology were performed every 3 months postoperatively.

At the 3‐month cystoscopy, two polyps absent on preoperative cystoscopy were found in the anterior urethra: a filiform polyp in the bulbar urethra at the 10‐o'clock position, within 2 cm of the membranous urethra (Figure 1A), and a rod‐shaped polyp at the junction of the bulbar and pendulous urethra, approximately 3 cm distal to the first (Figure 1B). The patient had no lower urinary tract symptoms, and urine cytology was negative. Because neoplasia was considered unlikely, the polyps were observed. At the 6‐month cystoscopy, the polyps were unchanged, and no new lesions were found. At the 9‐month cystoscopy, the polyps were again unchanged; however, a papillary lesion suspicious for recurrent urothelial carcinoma was detected at the bladder neck, and urine cytology was negative. During transurethral resection of the bladder tumor, the urethral polyps were also resected (the filiform polyp en bloc and the rod‐shaped polyp in fragments). The bladder‐neck lesion was noninvasive papillary urothelial carcinoma, low grade (pTa). At follow‐up cystoscopy 3 months after resection, the urethral polyps had not recurred; urinalysis showed no occult blood, urine cytology showed no atypical cells, and the patient had no urethral stricture, dysuria, weak urinary stream, urethral bleeding, or other lower urinary tract symptoms.

Histologically, both polyps had a fibrovascular stromal core covered by urothelium, without cytologic atypia, neoplasia, overt inflammation, prominent stromal edema, or granulation tissue (Figure 2A,B). Masson trichrome staining showed no evident increase in stromal collagen, whereas Elastica van Gieson staining showed abundant elastic fibers throughout the polyp stroma (Figure 2C,D). The lesions were diagnosed as elongated fibroepithelial polyps with prominent elastic fibers.

case_text:
A 72-year-old female presented with acute chest pain and palpitations on waking. An ECG demonstrated 1–2 mm precordial ST elevation. Past medical history included hypertension, dyslipidaemia, intermittent palpitations, and a recent episode of transient global amnesia. Her regular medications included amlodipine 5 mg daily, aspirin 100 mg daily, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, and rosuvastatin 5 mg daily. There was no prior history of exertional symptoms, syncope, cardiac murmurs, or any family history of sudden cardiac death. No previous echocardiography was available for comparison.

ECG changes (Figure 1A) prompted urgent coronary angiography and monitoring of high-sensitivity Troponin I to rule out an acute coronary occlusion myocardial infarction. No obstructive coronary disease was identified on coronary angiography; however, left ventriculography demonstrated moderately impaired LV systolic function with apical ballooning. (see Supplementary material online, Video S1). The initial troponin was 8107 ng/L, which peaked at 11492 ng/l later that day. Initial C-reactive protein (CRP) was also elevated at 88 mg/l. In subsequent days, the patient became increasingly haemodynamically unstable, with the development of LVOTO on echocardiography. The jugular venous pulse was not easily appreciable, and pulsus paradoxus was not observed.

Pericarditis was considered as a cause of chest pain, ECG changes, and elevated CRP; however, the patient’s chest pain was not positional or pleuritic and did not explain apical ballooning or LVOTO. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) as a cause of LVOTO and apical ballooning was considered but excluded given that measurements of septal and inferolateral walls did not meet HCM criteria. Periprocedural complications related to angiography were considered as a cause of haemodynamic instability, although no complications were noted during the angiogram and no echocardiographic evidence of ventricular perforation was identified.

Ultimately, the patient’s presentation and progression of disease were considered to represent Takotsubo cardiomyopathy due to the patient’s age, apical ballooning, and akinesis on left ventriculography with new dynamic ST segment changes on ECG (Figure 1A and B).

Four serial TTEs were performed over the course of the admission—TTE performed the morning after presentation (Morning of Day 2) identified a severely reduced ejection fraction (∼30%–35%) with apical and mid LV hypokinesis and brisk basal LV contraction. MR and mitral SAM were present, with a peak LVOT gradient of 58 mmHg. A trivial pericardial effusion was noted.

TTE performed mid-afternoon the following day (Afternoon of Day 3) showed similar systolic dysfunction with a peak LVOT gradient of ∼50 mmHg. A small circumferential pericardial effusion was now evident measuring 0.5 cm anteriorly and 0.9–1.0 cm elsewhere, with minor right ventricular (RV) inversion, but no evidence of tamponade physiology. Despite cautious IV fluid resuscitation and treatment with beta-blockers following this TTE, the patient developed haemodynamic compromise with hypotension, tachycardia, rising lactate and oliguria. She was admitted to the intensive care unit for invasive monitoring and use of vasopressors, however her hypotension remained refractory despite metaraminol and phenylephrine infusions.

After a failure to respond to vasopressors, a repeat TTE was performed 4 h later (Evening of Day 3) demonstrating persistent LV dysfunction with an increased peak LVOT gradient of 77 mmHg. The pericardial effusion had enlarged (1.0 cm anteriorly, 0.9 cm posteriorly, and maximal 1.4 cm adjacent to the inferior RV free wall) with a compressed RV. The IVC was dilated with reduced response to forced inspiration, consistent with echocardiographic tamponade. Moderate to severe mitral regurgitation was noted. (see Supplementary material online, Videos S2 and S3; Figures 2 and 3).

Following this TTE, emergent pericardiocentesis was performed under ultrasound and fluoroscopic guidance. 370 ml of dark, non-clotting haemoserous fluid was aspirated. There was immediate haemodynamic improvement after pericardiocentesis, and echocardiography during the procedure demonstrated immediate resolution of LVOT obstruction and SAM, with significant improvement in MR.

The patient saw rapid clinical and biochemical improvement post-pericardiocentesis and was able to be weaned off phenylephrine within 10 h. A repeat TTE at 12 h after pericardiocentesis (Morning of Day 4) demonstrated persistent apical ballooning and hypokinesis but almost total resolution of the pericardial effusion, with no significant mitral SAM or resting LVOT gradient. (see Supplementary material online, Videos S4 and S5; Figures 4 and 5).

Given the patient’s clinical improvement, she was restarted on metoprolol. The patient suffered no further cardiovascular issues and was discharged to inpatient rehabilitation 2 weeks after presentation.

case_text:
A 55-year-old male presented following a motorcycle collision, struck by a car to his left side at an intersection while travelling at 60 km/hr. On arrival to the emergency department, he had a patent airway, oxygen saturations above 90% on 4 L of oxygen, and had reduced left sided air entry with thoraco-abdominal tenderness. His systolic blood pressure (SBP) was 90-95 mmHg without tachycardia, and blood product resuscitation was commenced. A chest X-Ray (CXR) was performed (Fig. 1) in the resuscitation bay, demonstrating left-sided rib fractures with upper to mid-zone pulmonary contusions, and left lower zone atelectasis. An extended Focussed Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (eFAST) scan was positive for a left sided haemothorax, and free fluid in the splenorenal fossa. A pelvic X-ray showed a left proximal diaphysis fracture, with an intact pelvic ring. Given his transient responsiveness to resuscitation, a trauma pan-CT scan was performed.

His trauma pan-CT (Fig. 2) revealed multiple left sided rib fractures (left 4-11th), and an associated left hemidiaphragmatic defect, splenic herniation into the left hemithorax, and an associated haemothorax. Approximately 25% of the spleen appeared devascularised, with an intra-parenchymal hyperenhancing focus concerning for active haemorrhage (American Association for the Surgery of Trauma Grade IV splenic laceration). His other injuries included left humeral head, glenoid fossa, and scapular fractures, left proximal femur and fibular fractures, and right-sided L1-L4 transverse process fractures. Given his labile SBP despite resuscitation, a decision was made to perform a trauma laparotomy for surgical exploration of his intra-abdominal injuries and management of the TDH.

A trauma laparotomy was then performed. Moderate volume haemoperitoneum was demonstrated and following four-quadrant packing, the spleen was found to have almost completely herniated into the left haemothorax, via a posterior left diaphragmatic defect. The spleen was reduced into the abdominal cavity, and appeared almost completely devascularised, with minor lacerations. Following 2/0 vicryl suture ligation of splenic vessels, a splenectomy was performed. The remaining abdominal viscera (including lesser sac) were inspected, and no injuries were identified. The diaphragmatic defect was primarily repaired with multiple figure-of-8 0/0 Ethibond sutures. A left 28Fr intercostal catheter (ICC) was inserted, and positioned basally adjacent to the diaphragmatic repair site, with no air leak identified from the diaphragm repair site on Valsalva manoeuvre. A 15Fr Blake drain was inserted into the left upper quadrant, and following copious irrigation and haemostasis, routine closure was performed. His abdominal drain tube was removed once drain tube output was minimal, and he was discharged 2 weeks post-operatively with no complications on follow-up.

An extended Focussed Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (eFAST) scan was positive for a left sided haemothorax, and free fluid in the splenorenal fossa.
A pelvic X-ray showed a left proximal diaphysis fracture, with an intact pelvic ring.
Given his transient responsiveness to resuscitation, a trauma pan-CT scan was performed.
His trauma pan-CT (Fig.
2) revealed multiple left sided rib fractures (left 4-11th), and an associated left hemidiaphragmatic defect, splenic herniation into the left hemithorax, and an associated haemothorax.

Approximately 25% of the spleen appeared devascularised, with an intra-parenchymal hyperenhancing focus concerning for active haemorrhage (American Association for the Surgery of Trauma Grade IV splenic laceration).
His other injuries included left humeral head, glenoid fossa, and scapular fractures, left proximal femur and fibular fractures, and right-sided L1-L4 transverse process fractures.
Given his labile SBP despite resuscitation, a decision was made to perform a trauma laparotomy for surgical exploration of his intra-abdominal injuries and management of the TDH.
A trauma laparotomy was then performed.

Moderate volume haemoperitoneum was demonstrated and following four-quadrant packing, the spleen was found to have almost completely herniated into the left haemothorax, via a posterior left diaphragmatic defect.
The spleen was reduced into the abdominal cavity, and appeared almost completely devascularised, with minor lacerations.
Following 2/0 vicryl suture ligation of splenic vessels, a splenectomy was performed.
The remaining abdominal viscera (including lesser sac) were inspected, and no injuries were identified.
The diaphragmatic defect was primarily repaired with multiple figure-of-8 0/0 Ethibond sutures.

A left 28Fr intercostal catheter (ICC) was inserted, and positioned basally adjacent to the diaphragmatic repair site, with no air leak identified from the diaphragm repair site on Valsalva manoeuvre.
A 15Fr Blake drain was inserted into the left upper quadrant, and following copious irrigation and haemostasis, routine closure was performed.
His abdominal drain tube was removed once drain tube output was minimal, and he was discharged 2 weeks post-operatively with no complications on follow-up.
title: Traumatic diaphragmatic herniation of spleen: a case report

case_text:
We report the case of a 28-year-old male with biopsy-proven IgA nephropathy (2018) that demonstrated accelerated progression to stage 5 chronic kidney disease by 2022 despite optimized angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor and corticosteroid therapy. He underwent pre-emptive living-donor kidney transplantation from his mother (4/6 human leukocyte antigen match with negative donor-specific antibody and negative lymphocyte cross-match tests). Baseline pre-transplant laboratory values were as follows: hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL, platelet count 162 × 103/L, creatinine 6.15 mg/dL, and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 223 U/L. Induction immunosuppression consisted of basiliximab and methylprednisolone, followed by standard triple maintenance therapy with tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), and prednisone.

His post-transplant course became clinically significant for an early-onset subcapsular hematoma occurring immediately after transplant surgery, which was preceded by decreasing urine output. This was followed by rapidly evolving thrombocytopenia (nadir 57 × 103/L), hemolytic anemia (nadir 5.3 g/dL), elevated LDH (364 U/L), undetectable haptoglobin (< 0.1 g/L), and low C3 (0.65 g/L). Serum C4 level was in normal range. Peripheral smear revealed schistocytes, and disseminated intravascular coagulation was excluded by normal fibrinogen levels. Tacrolimus was discontinued and given the early graft dysfunction and inability to perform biopsy due to bleeding risk, he underwent plasma exchange (PLEX) (5 sessions) and received empiric low-dose anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG) (total 3 mg/kg) to cover a possible early rejection component. ADAMTS13 activity was measured before initiation of PLEX (90%), which excluded thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. Dialysis treatment was started concurrently. Cyclosporin was introduced with target trough levels of 100 ng/mL. MMF was continued with a dose of 1,000 mg/day. With no hematologic or renal recovery, therapy with eculizumab, a complement 5 inhibitor, was initiated for probable aHUS at a dose of 900 mg weekly for 4 weeks, resulting in platelet normalization, hemoglobin stabilization, and partial graft recovery. Dialysis was discontinued prior to discharge at week 4, with a creatinine of 4.9 mg/dL (Figure 1). Thereafter, graft function gradually improved under 1,200 mg maintenance eculizumab therapy every 2 weeks, as the creatinine level stabilized at 1.8 mg/dL under cyclosporin, MMF, and low-dose prednisolone treatment. A 6-month biopsy later confirmed chronic TMA without immune-complex deposition (Figure 2). Complement genetic testing revealed a rare pathogenic complement factor I (CFI) mutation (p.R474X, c.1420C>T). Cyclosporin was later replaced with tacrolimus to provide optimal immunosuppression.

At 3 years post-transplant, kidney function remains stable (creatinine 1.6 – 1.8 mg/dL) without active TMA findings under eculizumab therapy along with tacrolimus (target trough level 6 – 8 ng/mL), MMF 2,000 mg/day, and prednisolone 5 mg. Blood pressure remained well controlled throughout follow-up, and C3 improved over time. Follow-up data for estimated glomerular filtration rate and proteinuria are shown in Figure 3.

title: Post-transplant diagnosis of atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome due to a pathogenic mutation in complement factor I in a patient with IgA nephropathy

case_text:
A 54-year-old woman presented to the primary care physician with complaints of right upper quadrant abdominal pain, pale-colored stool, and dark yellow urine. An inflammatory process of the gallbladder was suspected, and laparoscopic cholecystectomy was performed in March 2019. Histology revealed gallbladder adenocarcinoma pT2N0. The patient underwent computed tomography (CT) in April 2019. Two lesions in S4b-5 and 4a of the liver were found and were resected. In October 2019, she was diagnosed with recurrent disease. Metastatic lesions on the abdominal wall were the main signs of recurrence. The patient then started first-line chemotherapy with gemcitabine and cisplatin in December 2019, and after four cycles, a partial response (PR) was achieved in April 2020. In June 2020, the patient underwent resection of metastatic lesions on the abdominal wall, and adjuvant therapy with capecitabine was started. The patient received five courses of capecitabine chemotherapy, which was stopped in January 2021. In January 2021, disease recurrence in the soft tissue of the abdominal wall was registered.

In April 2021, the patient underwent comprehensive molecular profiling (CMP) using a primary tumor specimen obtained in 2020. CMP was performed via Solo Complex (TM), including Solo ABC panel with a total of 411 genes analyzed (1.3 coding megabases). Additionally, immunohistochemical (IHC) screening for NTRK1–3 fusions and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) analysis for RET translocations were performed. Testing revealed a low tumor mutational burden (TMB, 4.2 mutations/Mb), microsatellite stability (MSS) determined by polymerase chain reaction (PCR), and proficient mismatch repair (pMMR) confirmed by immunohistochemistry, with no signs of a homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) phenotype based on copy number variation (CNV) and allelic imbalance analysis. The following potentially targetable genomic alterations were also identified: potentially somatic ARID1A p.Ala1466CysfsTer25 and PIK3CA p.Glu542Lys variants, and a potentially germline ATM p.Glu1978Ter variant. The ATM p.Glu1978Ter variant was detected in tumor DNA and was considered potentially germline based on its variant allele frequency; however, confirmatory germline testing of non-tumor DNA and genetic counseling were not performed. Both ARID1A and ATM variants were hypothesized to be deleterious, while the PIK3CA variant was a known hotspot oncogenic mutation. Therefore, several off-label therapeutic options were suggested, including a PARP inhibitor (olaparib) due to the ATM variant, a PI3K inhibitor (alpelisib) due to the PIK3CA mutation, and ICIs due to the presence of a deleterious ARID1A variant (Fig. 1). The rationale for considering ICIs was based on exploratory evidence suggesting an association between ARID1A alterations and response to immune checkpoint inhibition; however, ARID1A is not an established predictive biomarker for immunotherapy in GBC.

In May 2021, recurrence in the anterior abdominal wall and metastatic axillary and supraclavicular lymph nodes was detected. The patient then started pembrolizumab monotherapy from June 2021 until November 2021. No adverse events were detected during treatment. Disease progression was registered in January 2022. Due to the presence of a PIK3CA oncogenic variant, monotherapy with alpelisib was initiated in January 2022. Therapy was well tolerated with grade 1 diarrhea and hyperglycemia that did not require dose adjustment or interruption, and the patient remained stable during 14 months of molecularly matched therapy. The best response was SD. In March 2023, progressive disease (PD) was detected due to enlargement of target lesions (+58% Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) 1.1) and appearance of new lesions in the left ovary and sternum. Given platinum sensitivity, defined as no disease progression for 6 months after completion of cisplatin-based therapy (from May 2020 to January 2021), and the presence of an ATM alteration detected in tumor DNA, PARP inhibition was considered a potential therapeutic option. Considering limited standard treatment options, the patient then started olaparib in March 2023.

In order to identify other potentially effective treatment options, subsequent CMP was performed in May 2023 using a specimen from a skin metastasis obtained in February 2023. A total of 484 genes (1.5 coding megabases) were analyzed via Solo Complex (TM). Testing again identified the activating somatic PIK3CA p.Glu542Lys variant with high variant allele frequency. Despite no signs of an HRD phenotype based on CNV and allelic imbalance analysis, a secondary somatic deleterious ATM p.Arg1204Ter variant was detected, suggesting a potential loss of heterozygosity at the ATM locus. Two additional variants were identified that are not currently therapeutically actionable, either due to variant of uncertain significance (VUS) status (BRCA2) or the absence of an associated targeted therapy (SPINK1) (Table 1). In June 2023, signs of pleural carcinomatosis, pleural effusion, enlargement of the left ovary, and bile duct dilatation were revealed. The patient then discontinued olaparib and underwent biliary decompression and bilateral adnexectomy. The patient passed away shortly after in June 2023.

case_text:
A 74‐year‐old male presented to the emergency department for evaluation of altered mental status and abdominal pain. Past medical history for this patient included diabetes mellitus Type II, blindness, bilateral below‐knee amputations, L4 and L5 kyphoplasty, and chronic back pain in the setting of multiple bridging osteophytes in the thoracolumbar spine. He was admitted, found to be septic secondary to urinary tract infection, and diagnosed with an NSTEMI, a CHF exacerbation, and an AKI. The patient also noted worsening of chronic back pain, though denied any trauma or acute injury. At the time of admission, a CT scan of the chest, abdomen, pelvis, and cervical spine was performed in the ED. Though initially not recognized by Radiology, this scan revealed a unilateral, nondisplaced facet fracture at T12 (Figure 1). As this fracture was not identified, orthopedics was not involved in the patient′s care at that time. The patient was on bed rest throughout this period due to his baseline status, history of bilateral BKAs, and active medical problems.

The patient continued to complain of back pain, and the Orthopedic Spine Service was consulted. The patient denied any traumatic event and reported no bladder or bowel incontinence, though he was not at baseline mental status. Exam findings at that time revealed no motor or sensory deficit in his proximal lower extremity. Upon further review of prior whole‐spine imaging, the T12 fracture was identified. An MRI of the lumbar spine was obtained at this point to further characterize the fracture. This demonstrated the same fracture at T12, though now with moderate displacement (Figure 2). The fracture at this stage was considered an AO Spine classification Type C, due to the displacement seen. Though surgical stabilization was desired at this point, his ongoing myocardial infarction and urosepsis prevented surgical intervention. The patient was placed on strict bed rest and spinal precautions at this point. External bracing was felt to be futile due to the patient′s obese body habitus.

A subsequent CT of his thoracic spine, 2 days from the prior MRI, was performed to evaluate for possible further displacement. This scan showed progressive displacement of the T12 fracture, now up to 30 mm (Figures 3 and 4). Again, surgical intervention was postponed due to ongoing myocardial infarction and sepsis.

The patient, at this point, was stable enough for surgical intervention. The patient was brought to the OR where a T12 corpectomy with application of a corpectomy cage and T9‐L3 posterolateral fusion with pedicle screws was performed. The corpectomy cage was placed via posterior approach with the sacrifice of the unilateral T12 nerve root for access. A transthoracic approach was considered, though single lung ventilation was felt to be too unsafe in the setting of poor baseline pulmonary function. It was felt that anterior support with the use of an expandable cage was necessary to provide appropriate stability to the construct and ultimately achieve fusion across levels. Due to the size of the anterior defect, a posterior‐only construct would likely have fallen into kyphosis and failed. Intraoperative films were obtained, which demonstrated appropriately placed corpectomy cage and pedicle screws (Figure 5). The patient remained intubated and was transferred directly to the ICU from the OR.

He was extubated on postoperative Day 1.

Additional postoperative x‐rays and a CT scan were obtained on postoperative Day 6, which demonstrated intact and stable hardware (Figures 6 and 7). The patient has had no motor or sensory deficit postoperatively. The patient was fit for a TSLO with sternal pad and instructed to wear this when out of bed for 3 months postoperatively. The patient would remain admitted for 3 months in the setting of multiple medical and social issues.

The patient was seen in follow‐up at 1 year from surgery. His surgical wound had completely healed, and his reported VAS pain score was 0/10. He had returned to his preoperative functional status, which was nonambulatory in the setting of bilateral BKAs.

title: Progressive Displacement of a T12 Vertebral Fracture in the Setting of an Ankylosed Spine: A Case Report

case_text:
A 47‐year‐old woman with CF and related comorbidities including pancreatic insufficiency, diabetes and chronic sinus disease was admitted with non‐specific malaise in November 2025.

Initial assessment suggested a pulmonary exacerbation due to progressive respiratory symptoms and fatigue on a background of prolonged decline in lung function (FEV1 91% to 67% predicted). As the patient's sputum was chronically infected with Pseudomonas aeruginosa, IV piperacillin–tazobactam with oral ciprofloxacin was commenced (she was intolerant to aminoglycosides), with access via her TIVAD (which had been in situ for 10 years).

Within hours of the TIVAD access, she developed acute systemic symptoms including fever, nausea, dizziness and a rise in inflammatory markers (C‐reactive protein 2 to 70 mg/L). On detailed history, she reported a similar reaction following TIVAD flushing 3 months earlier and subsequently described low‐level constitutional symptoms for the 5 months preceding admission.

Whilst the TIVAD and overlying skin appeared externally unremarkable, infection was suspected and access via the device was ceased. Paired blood cultures were obtained from both the TIVAD and peripheral sites on two separate days. Oral co‐trimoxazole was started pending alternative IV access.

Initial blood cultures were positive for a ‘difficult to identify’ pathogen, described as gram‐variable rods and coccobacilli. Positive cultures from the line were flagged at 36, 43, 70 and 85 h. Beaded rods were seen on microscopy in one set. Our hospital does not routinely perform Ziehl‐Neelsen or auramine staining on blood cultures. Vancomycin was added to the antibiotic regimen until further microbiological elucidation was available.

The organism could not be identified using the standard clinical Matrix‐Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionisation Time‐of‐Flight (MALDI‐TOF) database. Subsequent analysis using a research‐use MALDI‐TOF database suggested Mycobacterium senegalense , an RGM within the M. fortuitum complex. Given the use of a non‐validated identification platform, further testing was undertaken. Hain line‐probe assay identified the isolate as M. fortuitum , whilst whole‐genome sequencing performed at the National Mycobacterial Reference Laboratory identified a presumptive Mycobacterium conceptionense . Although species‐level identification varied between methodologies, all analyses consistently identified the isolate as belonging to the M. fortuitum group.

Vancomycin was discontinued after 48 h, whilst a 14‐day piperacillin–tazobactam and oral co‐trimoxazole course was completed to treat the presumed pulmonary exacerbation. No NTM‐directed antimicrobial therapy was initiated.

Nine days after admission, the TIVAD was removed in its entirety under general anaesthesia. The catheter tip cultured the same M. fortuitum group organism. Subsequent peripheral blood cultures obtained over the subsequent 4 days and further sets taken 2 months following device removal showed no growth.

Respiratory samples during admission continued to show heavy growths of P. aeruginosa with no isolation of mycobacteria.

At clinic review 6 weeks after discharge, lung function had recovered (FEV1 2.67 L; 93% predicted). The patient reported no ongoing constitutional symptoms or night sweats. She developed minor superficial wound dehiscence which resolved with conservative management.

At further follow‐up 5 months following device removal, the patient remained well with no recurrence of constitutional symptoms. The wound site had healed completely. C‐reactive protein had normalised, and sputum cultures continued to grow P. aeruginosa without isolation of mycobacteria.

case_text:
A man in his late 50s with no documented prior medical history and no laboratory testing on electronic records for several years presented to the Emergency Department in December 2024 with inferior ST‐elevation myocardial infarction. He underwent urgent PCI with drug‐eluting stent implantation to the left posterior descending artery and posterolateral branch. Initial laboratory testing during this admission therefore provided the first available hematological reference point in several years.

He had no personal or family history of gastrointestinal or autoimmune disease and denied diarrhea, steatorrhoea, haematochezia, weight loss, or other alarm gastrointestinal symptoms throughout follow‐up. After discharge, he was treated with dual antiplatelet therapy and guideline‐directed secondary prevention, including ticagrelor, aspirin, beta‐blocker therapy, angiotensin‐converting enzyme inhibitor therapy, high‐intensity statin therapy, and ezetimibe. He was not prescribed a proton pump inhibitor or metformin at any point in the disease course. He had no history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidaemia, or tobacco use, and no family history of premature coronary artery disease.
